title: Second Cursor: Moving Day
pitch: AI has entered the web. Second Cursor gives it a visible hand—and keeps the human in control.
about_excerpt: AI has entered the web. Second Cursor gives it a visible hand—and keeps the human in control. Like Comment Story Updates The Second Cursor interaction stays legible on mobile, including Agent status and human decisions. Human and Agent share one live room: visible intent, protected choices, and an explicit handoff. One workspace. Two cursors. A first step toward giving AI a visible hand on the web. The web was built for one cursor AI agents change that assumption. They introduce a second actor that can inspect, decide, and operate—but most interfaces still hide that work behind a chat box. We see the request and, later, the result. We do not see what the agent is targeting, what it is allowed to change, why it is waiting, or when control has returned to us. Second Cursor is a first step toward giving AI a visible hand on the web. One workspace. Two cursors. The white cursor belongs to the human. The blue cursor belongs to the agent. Both work on the same live surface, and the interface makes collaboration legible: target, intent, progress, constraints, changes, and handoff. Why a moving room? Moving Day turns an abstract interaction model into something everyone understands. A person and an agent arrange a room together. The agent can: inspect the live room and its constraints; point out a problem without changing anything; move or rotate unlocked furniture; ask the human to choose between equally valid options; finish with a visible summary of what changed. Every operation happens through a structured WebMCP tool and appears directly in the interface. The blue cursor travels to the object it is about to affect and explains why. Actionable transparency, not chain-of-thought Second Cursor does not expose or imitate private model reasoning. It reveals the information a person needs to supervise real work: the agent's target, intended action, resulting change, active constraints, waiting state, and control handoff. This is transparency at the interaction layer—the place where trust becomes a product behavior instead of a promise. Human authority is built into the surface The agent is capable, but it is not the owner. Lock an object and the agent must preserve it. Grab an item during an operation and the agent yields. When two placements are both valid but depend on taste, the agent asks instead of guessing. The human owns preference and final authority. The agent contributes attention, structured action, and speed. Why WebMCP? WebMCP lets a web page describe meaningful capabilities to compatible agents. That changes more than automation; it changes the basic grammar of the web. A page is no longer only a place where a person clicks. It can become a shared world where humans and agents act together. Second Cursor uses six real tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : inspect_room , point_out_issue , move_item , rotate_item , request_choice , and finish_layout . The tools use bounded JSON schemas, stable furniture IDs, live page state, human locks, room constraints, explicit handoffs, and abort signals. No proprietary server-side model is required: the intelligence comes from the visiting WebMCP-compatible agent, while the page supplies capabilities, constraints, and visible feedback. What becomes possible Traditional software gives one person one cursor. Second Cursor imagines software where an agent can guide you, work for you, or work beside you—without becoming an invisible operator. The Moving Day prototype is intentionally simple, but the model can extend to design tools, spreadsheets, dashboards, editors, planning canvases, and any shared workspace where people need to understand and govern agent actions in real time. Built and verified The product is built with React, TypeScript, Vinext, Vite, and WebMCP, and hosted on ChatGPT Sites. It includes a scripted fallback so judges can experience the collaboration even when their current browser does not expose WebMCP. OpenAI Codex supported product research, concept refinement, implementation, schema design, automated testing, browser QA, deployment, demo production, and submission packaging. The public deployment was tested in ChatGPT's in-app browser: all six tools were discovered, and a live inspect_room call returned the current furniture, human locks, room bounds, and constraints. The automated suite passes 3/3 tests and the production build succeeds. AI has entered the web. Second Cursor makes its hand visible—and keeps the human in control. title: INTENT//FOR SALE
pitch: A fictional WebMCP marketplace that exposes paid influence in agent recommendations, then lets the person remove it and compare the clean-room result.
about_excerpt: A fictional WebMCP marketplace that exposes paid influence in agent recommendations, then lets the person remove it and compare the clean-room result. Like Comment Story Updates Market versus clean room: KinoForge rises from commercial #4 to sponsor-free #1 after sponsorship is blocked. Influence Receipt: OmniMotion's 84.6 score is exposed as 54.6 fit plus 30.0 paid contribution. Complete seven-call ledger, staged KinoForge result, and explicit no-purchase boundary. Original commercial market with OmniMotion ranked #1 before the policy intervention. Inspiration As people delegate research and purchasing decisions to agents, advertising may stop competing for human attention and start competing for the structured results an agent trusts. A commercially influenced recommendation can still sound objective while the money, scoring changes, and conflicts behind it remain difficult to inspect. A sponsored label names the commercial relationship, but it does not show what changed or what the result would have been without the paid factor. INTENT//FOR SALE turns that uncomfortable possibility into a transparent, fictional product demo. What it does A person asks an agent to recommend an AI video-generation platform at or under an $80 monthly budget with five concrete requirements. Seven page-defined WebMCP tools let the agent: create a structured intent; run a synthetic advertiser auction; retrieve the commercially ranked offers; inspect an Influence Receipt; apply the person's recommendation policy; compare the historical market result with a sponsor-free clean room; and stage a fictional selection. The fixed scenario makes the manipulation measurable. OmniMotion Ultra reaches commercial rank #1 at 84.6 : 54.6 user-fit points plus 30.0 sponsor-derived score points tied to a simulated $24 CPA. KinoForge Studio has the strongest sponsor-free fit at 92.0 , but commercial weighting pushes it to rank #4. When the person blocks sponsorship and keeps inferred signals off, KinoForge becomes the clean-room winner and OmniMotion falls to #5. The original market result stays visible. The person can inspect the bidstream, receipt, score arithmetic, policy, ranking reversal, and seven-call ledger instead of being asked to trust a confident answer. Nothing is purchased. Every brand, offer, bid, claim, score, and payout is synthetic. Why WebMCP fits WebMCP drives the product experience. The page registers seven bounded tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Strict inputs and structured outputs carry rankings, commercial disclosures, policy settings, evidence, state versions, and recoverable errors. The tools replace brittle clicks and rendered-text parsing with explicit operations and machine-readable evidence. The agent and person operate on the same live browser state while the intent, bidstream, receipt, policy, ranking reversal, and activity ledger change in view. How it creates a better user experience Instead of asking the person to trust a confident recommendation, the interface separates user-fit points, sponsor-derived score points, simulated money, advertiser claims, policy state, and rank impact. The Influence Receipt explains the commercial winner; the clean-room comparison preserves the historical result while showing exactly what changes when sponsorship is removed. The agent handles the seven-step workflow while the person gets an understandable audit surface. In a browser without WebMCP, the complete manual fallback invokes the same local state actions and preserves the same disclosures. Try it with an agent Open the live demo in a WebMCP-capable browser and expand Try it with an agent . The panel has four copy-ready prompts: an ordinary recommendation, an influence audit, a native-tool check, and a confirmation-boundary check. The first request does not mention advertising. The follow-up asks the agent to show the paid contribution, block sponsorship, and compare the ranking again. If the browser substitutes clicks or manual fallback handlers, it has not shown native WebMCP invocation. The page reports when native WebMCP is unavailable instead of treating the fallback as proof. What people and agents can do together The agent performs repeatable structured operations and returns evidence. The person defines the goal and constraints, questions the commercial result, chooses the acceptable influence policy, and reviews the staged outcome. In one session, they can preserve the historical answer, expose its commercial inputs, remove the paid factor, and compare both outcomes. An ordinary recommendation flow does not expose those operations or their evidence. How we built it The project is a static Vite, React, and TypeScript client. Zustand holds ephemeral browser state. A deterministic local engine computes the auction, commercial ranking, Influence Receipt, policy result, and clean-room comparison. Zod-backed handlers enforce strict bounded schemas at the WebMCP boundary, and advertiser-authored claims are marked as untrusted content. WebMCP caller or manual control | strict Zod schemas | shared Zustand actions | deterministic ranking engine | React audit UI Manual controls and WebMCP handlers use the same state actions, so the visible fallback and native tool path cannot quietly tell different stories. Invalid or out-of-order calls return structured recovery guidance instead of skipping required stages. There is no backend, account system, payment path, analytics integration, application data fetch, external model call, advertiser connection, or browser persistence. All seven operations change only the local demo state. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making an intentionally provocative concept precise enough to audit. Fit points, sponsor-derived points, and simulated dollars had to remain visibly separate; otherwise the demo would reproduce the ambiguity it is criticizing. The historical commercial ranking also had to remain intact after the policy changed so the clean-room view compared both outcomes without rewriting the original. We also had to keep native WebMCP and the manual fallback behaviorally identical, enforce state ordering across seven calls, treat advertiser claims as untrusted, and avoid overstating what a userConfirmed boolean proves. Here it is only a caller declaration, not proof of a human click, identity, consent, or authorization. That boundary is safe only because the staged result is fictional, local, reversible, and incapable of an external side effect. Accomplishments we are proud of A complete seven-tool WebMCP workflow with strict schemas and recoverable errors. An Influence Receipt that exposes commercial score arithmetic and simulated money. A policy-controlled market-versus-clean-room comparison with a visible rank reversal. One shared implementation for native WebMCP operation and the complete manual fallback. A live activity ledger and explicit NO PURCHASE boundary. A deterministic, account-free demo that judges can inspect without setup. What we learned Transparency works better as a structured operation than as a disclaimer. When ranking components, reason codes, policy state, and the historical result are machine-readable, the agent can help the person interrogate a recommendation instead of merely presenting it. WebMCP can support both sides of the premise: a future market may try to sell influence to agents, while page-defined tools can also expose and remove that influence. We also learned that a consequential agent action needs a stronger approval primitive than a boolean in tool input. A production system would need trusted, single-use approval bound to the exact person, session, and action, plus real security and data review. Testing The current repository passes 30 Vitest tests, 11 Playwright tests, TypeScript checking, the production build, and a high-severity npm audit with zero findings. Coverage includes the deterministic engine, schemas, tool registration and cleanup, invalid and out-of-order calls, the full manual flow, confirmation boundary, responsive layouts, reduced motion, keyboard/reflow behavior, prompt copy feedback, and console cleanliness. Native discovery and all seven calls were verified in fresh documents in a WebMCP-capable in-app browser host. Google Chrome did not expose WebMCP in that run, so it verified only the explicit unsupported-browser manual fallback. What's next This challenge build deliberately stays one deterministic fictional scenario. Next steps could explore the same transparency pattern across shopping, flights, hotels, subscriptions, and local services; model competing influence policies; and test trusted approval capabilities. Any production version would require real advertiser and catalog data, privacy controls, abuse prevention, independent scoring review, and a much stronger authorization boundary. title: VisaFlow: The Adaptive WebMCP Agent
pitch: VisaFlow turns a 55-field visa form into a guided voice conversation. It uses WebMCP to select the right path, derive answers, fill the live application, and flag only what needs review.
about_excerpt: VisaFlow turns a 55-field visa form into a guided voice conversation. It uses WebMCP to select the right path, derive answers, fill the live application, and flag only what needs review. Like Comment Story Updates Application completed Meet VisaFlow WebMCP in action One answer, many fields Inspiration Long forms force people to translate their life story into an unfamiliar sequence of fields. Conditional applications make this worse: users answer questions that may not apply, repeat information across sections, and often discover missing evidence only near the end. We wanted to explore a different future for the web—one where a person explains their situation naturally, an agent connects the details, and the website remains responsible for its own rules and safety constraints. What it does VisaFlow turns a deliberately long 55-field visitor-visa application into a guided voice or text conversation. A user can describe their trip naturally, speak their answers, type them, or attach supporting documents. The agent then: identifies whether the application is for tourism, business, or a family visit; selects the correct funding and prior-travel branches; removes questions that do not apply; extracts multiple supported facts from each answer; calculates transparent derived values such as trip duration; fills reasonable interpretations while clearly flagging them for review; asks one story-shaped follow-up covering several related gaps; shows every WebMCP action and live application progress; and consolidates uncertain and sensitive values into one editable final-review queue. After every applicable field and review item is resolved, the user can finish the fictional application and see a completion receipt. Why WebMCP An LLM alone could generate a possible JSON object, but it would need a hardcoded copy of the form schema, routing rules, and validation logic. Alternatively, it would have to manipulate fragile DOM selectors and click through every conditional page. WebMCP gives the agent a live semantic contract owned by the website. VisaFlow publishes 22 typed tools that let an agent inspect possible routes, select the applicable flow, discover missing requirements, apply structured answers, attach evidence references, calculate derived insights, resolve conflicts, and request human review. WebMCP is not decorative in this project: application changes go through website-owned tool handlers. Every write is validated for route applicability, field type, allowed choices, date ranges, confidence, provenance, and review requirements before it reaches shared application state. This enables something that was previously difficult: a person can tell one coherent story, an agent can connect that story across many conditional fields, and the website can safely accept only the values allowed by its current rules—without page-by-page navigation. Human-agent collaboration The human provides meaning and judgment. The agent extracts, connects, derives, and decides what to ask next. The website validates every action and keeps uncertainty visible. Explicit user statements, document facts, deterministic derivations, and AI proposals remain visibly separate. Sensitive or uncertain values are never silently treated as verified. The user reviews and corrects them once before completing the application. How we built it The application uses React, TypeScript, and Vite with a government-service-inspired interface. On page load, VisaFlow registers 22 tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . A WebMCP-capable agent can discover these tools at runtime and execute them without knowing the DOM structure. A same-origin Worker endpoint uses the OpenAI Responses API with GPT-5.6 Terra and a strict structured-output schema. Each turn includes the current route, resolved answers, remaining applicable questions, recent conversation history, remembered partial facts, and pending review fields. The LLM returns a plan containing explicit facts, document facts, safe derivations, reviewable proposals, route decisions, and the next question. It never writes application state directly. The client converts the plan into WebMCP calls, and the website validates and applies them. Voice recognition, spoken questions, multilingual interfaces, document extraction, visible WebMCP activity, browser-local drafts, and the completion flow are integrated into one coherent experience. Challenges The hardest problems were preventing the conversation from forgetting previously stated facts, resolving phrases such as “this year,” extracting many useful facts from one answer, and avoiding repeated address questions. We also had to ensure route changes happened before field validation, preserve incomplete facts between turns, batch WebMCP writes safely, distinguish derived values from invented values, and keep document extraction useful without allowing documents to act as instructions. Accomplishments A working 55-field adaptive application rather than a single autofill demo 22 non-trivial WebMCP tools with typed schemas and validation Dynamic application routing with irrelevant-question removal Voice, text, document, and multilingual interaction Visible provenance, derived values, progress, and semantic actions A consolidated final-review experience A gated fictional completion receipt 32 automated tests across domain, WebMCP, and integrated UI behavior What we learned The most important lesson was that an agent should not own a website’s rules. The website should publish capabilities and remain authoritative, while the model focuses on understanding natural language and planning. WebMCP makes that separation possible. It allows an agent to be flexible without making application writes opaque or unsafe. We also learned that conversational form completion works best when the agent asks for coherent parts of a person’s story, rather than disguising several traditional form labels as a chatbot question. What's next Next, we would test VisaFlow with more external WebMCP agents, expand accessibility testing, support additional document formats and application domains, and add encrypted cross-device draft storage. The same architecture could support healthcare enrollment, insurance claims, benefits applications, university admissions, and other conditional workflows. pitch: MatchRV uses WebMCP to turn messy RV shopping requests into exact matches, explain why each RV fits, flag unknowns, show data freshness, and prepare dealer contact with human approval.

 Inspiration 

 What it does 

 MatchRV is an AI-native RV marketplace built to make complex RV shopping simple, trustworthy, and actionable. 

 Most RV shoppers do not search in clean filters. They ask things like: “I need a bunkhouse under 30 feet, less than 7,000 lbs, with two entry doors, a private bedroom, under my budget, and close to Tacoma.” Traditional marketplaces struggle with requests like that because the information is scattered across inconsistent dealer listings. 

 MatchRV uses WebMCP to turn those messy real-world shopping requests into structured requirements and match them against normalized RV inventory. 

 Our challenge entry focuses on three things: 

 Search: MatchRV converts multi-condition natural-language requests into precise structured matching across RV inventory. 

 Trust: Every result explains why it matched, which requirements were verified, what information is still unknown, and how fresh the inventory data appears. 

 Action: Once the shopper finds the right RV, the agent can prepare dealer contact and show the user exactly what will happen before requiring explicit human approval. 

 This demonstrates how WebMCP can transform an ordinary dealer inventory website into something an AI agent can understand and act on safely. 

 Our larger vision is to make RV inventory AI-readable across the industry, allowing shoppers to find the right RV through ChatGPT and other AI agents instead of manually searching hundreds of listings.

title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: FitCheck
pitch: A shoe fit profile you own, that any AI agent can read — on any store, with no merchant integration.
about_excerpt: A shoe fit profile you own, that any AI agent can read — on any store, with no merchant integration. Like Comment Story Updates The seven-brand terminal output The passing WebMCP Evals output The profile panel showing the conflict message find sneakers results across both stores with differing sizes Seven real shoes, all labelled men's US 9: Nike 263 mm Salomon 264 mm Converse 265 mm ASICS 268 mm Adidas 270 mm Birkenstock 270 mm New Balance 270 mm Seven millimetres of spread on an identical label. It gets worse. I read Kith's live catalog the way a shopping agent would. Every US-family product uses the same 3–18 size axis regardless of whether it's tagged mens, wmns, or both — and most are tagged both. So a label that just says "7" is ambiguous by roughly 15 mm inside a single brand, wider than the spread across all seven brands. The catalog structurally cannot tell you which. Neither can the agent shopping on your behalf. That fact only exists on the buyer's side of the transaction. Every agentic commerce protocol shipped in the last eighteen months standardises the merchant — UCP and ACP for the shopping journey, AP2 for payment authorization, x402 for settlement. None of them model the buyer past a payment instrument and a shipping address. Fit Check is the smallest useful version of the buyer's half. Apparel returns run around 25% (31% on shoes), size and fit cause roughly half to two-thirds of them, and each costs a merchant about $30. The person's half of the transaction is missing, and it's expensive. What it does You enter shoes you already own that fit — never millimetres. Brands and sizes, which sneaker shoppers know from memory. Those statements resolve to a foot length range in millimetres, which is the canonical stored value. Brand labels resolve against that length. Labels never convert directly to other labels. Any shopping agent can read the profile, write to it, and check products against it through WebMCP tools registered on the page. The server reads any store's public UCP catalog. Merchants install nothing and don't know it exists. When a verdict is wrong, you say so, and the profile updates. It sharpens across stores instead of being rebuilt at each one. Verdicts are deliberately not binary: fits · size_up · size_down · between_sizes · no_size out_of_stock · unmapped_brand · unknown Three design decisions that matter more than they sound: Rounding is always up. A shoe shorter than your foot doesn't fit; slightly long is wearable. A property test sweeps 240–300 mm across all seven brands asserting no recommendation is ever shorter than the foot. Conflicting statements produce a question, not an average. If your Nike 9 and your Converse 9.5 disagree by more than a half size, the tool says so and asks which fits better. Only the person can answer that, and answering it improves the profile permanently. That's the collaboration: the agent finds the contradiction, the human resolves it. unmapped_brand is a real answer. Veja appears on Stomping Ground and there's no mapping for it. Saying so beats guessing — especially for the people this serves best, who have been burned by confident sizing widgets before. Nine tools registered on document.modelContext, with navigator.modelContext as a fallback. readOnlyHint on the read-shaped tools, untrustedContentHint on anything returning merchant catalog text. The architecture is inverted on purpose. WebMCP tools are scoped to a document — an agent on a merchant's page cannot see tools registered by another origin, and cross-tab visibility is unspecified. So Fit Check is the page the agent works on, and the server reaches out to stores. The merchant is never in the loop, which is also what makes the portability claim true rather than aspirational. There's no integration to sell, no widget to install, and no store that has to say yes. UCP. The server fetches a store's /.well-known/ucp, negotiates capabilities, and reads the catalog over MCP. Everything below came from live stores, not fixtures: Store Protocol Size data Brand coverage kith.com 2026-08-25 100% clean variant.options, option Size 95% stompingground.myshopify.com 2026-08-25 100% clean, option Shoe Size 80% knifewear-inc.myshopify.com 2026-08-25 no size axis at all n/a — degrades to unknown The knife shop is included deliberately: a store sharing none of the assumptions, which the layer negotiates with, reads, and correctly reports it has nothing to say about. Three tiers of data access, degrading gracefully: find_shoe — one query across multiple UCP stores in parallel, verdicts attached, ~0.9s warm check_fit — authoritative single-product read with the full option matrix check_labels — no store, no catalog, no protocol. The agent reads the size dropdown off any page and hands over the labels. Works on stores with no UCP manifest at all. Sizing data. Brand-to-foot-length mappings for Nike, Adidas, New Balance, Converse, ASICS, Birkenstock and Salomon come from a read-only sample shared by Sizely / Size AI for this submission. Their guidance shaped the design: resolve on foot length rather than labels, read Birkenstock via EU because its own US labels are internally inconsistent, alias Jordan to Nike, and leave out the women's rows they didn't trust rather than invent them. Challenges Version mismatch is silent. UCP negotiation intersects capabilities by name and version, and a capability with no mutual version is dropped rather than erroring. The symptom is "this store has no catalog search," not "you advertised the wrong date." Two stores on the same platform were four months apart, and Kith upgraded mid-week. The platform profile advertises every version it can parse. There is no size filter. Standard UCP search filters are categories and price only. Fit has to be filtered client-side after retrieval — which is exactly why this layer needs to exist. A bug that looked right. I added a 10 mm toe allowance to recommendations. Plausible, and wrong: the dataset's foot_length_mm already means "the foot this size fits," so the manufacturer's toe room was being counted twice and every recommendation moved up a size. It surfaced because recommend_size and check_fit disagreed on the same profile. Now there's a round-trip test for all seven brands: a profile built solely from " 9 fits" must return US 9 from both paths. A bug only an agent could find. I ran the project through Google's WebMCP Evals CLI against the live deployment. add_fit_statement passed; check_labels immediately after returned "no foot-length estimate yet." The mutation was resolving before the estimate it implied had landed. A human typing never hits that gap — an agent calling two tools back to back hits it every time. The mutations now await the recompute, and the error message names what's actually missing instead of sending an agent in a loop. What I learned Consistent parameter naming across a tool surface is a discovery requirement, not a style preference. check_fit took store_domain while search_catalog took domain. An agent priming on one tool called the other with the wrong key and read it as broken. Nothing was internally inconsistent — the vocabulary just drifted between siblings. Catalogs cannot supply gender, and no parsing recovers it. This is different from a fact that's badly labelled but present. It's the clearest example I found of something that only exists on the buyer's side, and it's the whole argument for the profile. Honest verdicts beat confident ones. The audience this serves best — wide feet, half sizes, one foot larger than the other — has been failed by confident sizing tools before. unmapped_brand and "these two don't agree, which fits better?" read as trustworthy in a way a guess never would. What's next Width grades are the obvious next field: they're in the data, three of seven brands offer them, and they matter most to the people this serves. Longer term, the right home for a buyer profile is probably the browser — held like autofill, queryable by any page's agent, with no app in between. The spec isn't there yet; tools are document-scoped and cross-tab isolation is still maturing. But the schema outlives whoever holds it. Someone has to decide that the canonical value is foot length rather than a label, that both feet are recorded separately, that statements carry provenance, and that an unresolvable brand says so. That's the part this is really proposing. The mechanism generalises past shoes. Any category where the reference data is public and the person's half is missing — bike geometry against inseam, knives against hand and board — has the same shape. title: Mapbox AI Trip Planner
pitch: Ask an AI to plan your trip and watch it find real places, draw a real route, and pin your itinerary live on a Mapbox map. No backend, no extension. Just WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Ask an AI to plan your trip and watch it find real places, draw a real route, and pin your itinerary live on a Mapbox map. No backend, no extension. Just WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Walking trip planned in Paris New Window to plan a trip Inspiration The WebMCP Challenge asks what the open web looks like when it's built for humans and agents at once. We'd already been building @mapbox/web-mcp-server , a library that registers Mapbox GL JS map interactions as WebMCP tools, and had written up a design thesis for it before ever building a demo: a geospatial AI agent needs two things to be genuinely useful, a data layer (geocoding, search, directions) and a live rendering surface it can actually act on. Most "AI + maps" demos fake the second half: a chat response describing a trip, maybe a static image. WebMCP is the first browser API that lets a page hand an agent direct control over a live map instead, the same way an MCP server hands it a data source. We wanted to prove that idea end-to-end, not just describe it. What it does Open the demo, paste an Anthropic API key, and ask for a trip: "Plan a half-day trip in Paris: the Eiffel Tower, a nearby cafe, and the Louvre, with walking directions between each stop." An agent geocodes the real places, drops pins, pulls a real walking route, draws it on the map, and frames the whole trip, live, while you watch. An itinerary panel and an activity log rebuild themselves from the actual tool calls as they happen, so the WebMCP mechanism is visible, not just its output. How we built it The core is a small TypeScript library ( src/ , strict mode, pure ESM) where every map capability is a factory function, createFlyToTool(map) , createAddMarkerTool(map, markers, stops) , returning a ToolDescriptor that closes over the live mapboxgl.Map instance. registerMapboxTools(map) wires all of them up against navigator.modelContext.registerTool() , plus an onToolCall hook so a host page can observe every call live. On top of that, the demo does two things most WebMCP demos skip. First, it closes the "two data layers" loop from our own design doc for real: alongside the map-control tools, the page registers a small second set, geocode_place , search_category , get_directions , that call Mapbox's public Search Box and Directions REST APIs directly via fetch() . These are demo-only and never exported from the published library, but they mean the whole trip-planning loop works from one deployed page with no server standing in as an MCP host. Second, the deployed demo is usable with zero setup: an embedded BYOK (bring-your-own-key) chat widget ( demo/chat.ts ) using the official @anthropic-ai/sdk with dangerouslyAllowBrowser: true , running a manual agentic loop against claude-opus-5 . List the registered tools, send them as the model's tools , execute whatever it calls via navigator.modelContextTesting.executeTool() , feed results back, repeat. The key never leaves the visitor's browser except to Anthropic directly. For anyone who'd rather not paste a key, the page also exposes a copyable system prompt for driving it via Claude Desktop or any other WebMCP-compatible extension instead: same tools, different agent. It's deployed as a static Vite build on Vercel, with the Mapbox token set as a public build-time config variable (Mapbox tokens are meant to be client-embedded, unlike the Anthropic key). Challenges we ran into Geocoding is pickier than it looks. Early on, a query like "Louvre Museum, Paris" returned an unrelated Airbnb listing ranked above the actual landmark; the city qualifier confused relevance ranking more than it helped. The fix was querying just the bare place name and using proximity bias to disambiguate instead, which we had to encode directly into the tool description and system prompt so the agent wouldn't do it wrong on its own. Some organizations block this pattern entirely. Mid-testing, a live call to Anthropic's API came back with authentication_error: CORS requests are not allowed for this Organization . Some orgs disable direct-from-browser API access as a security policy, which is exactly the risk dangerouslyAllowBrowser warns about, just enforced server-side. No client code can work around an org policy, so instead we made the failure mode honest: detect it and point the visitor at the Claude Desktop fallback with an accurate explanation, instead of a misleading "invalid API key." LLM tool-calling isn't perfectly deterministic. During a real end-to-end run, the agent issued an identical add_marker call twice in one turn, producing a visible duplicate row in the itinerary. We added a small guard against adjacent duplicate stops and nudged the system prompt to clear stale markers before replanning, a good reminder that a UI built on top of agent tool calls has to defend against the agent occasionally repeating itself. Accomplishments that we're proud of We shipped and verified a genuine end-to-end run, not just isolated pieces in a demo script: a real Anthropic API call driving real Mapbox geocoding and directions calls, ending in a route drawn on real streets and an itinerary that matches exactly what the agent did. The zero-backend architecture holds up under that test too: no server anywhere in the loop, yet the demo still closes the "data layer plus rendering layer" idea we set out to prove. We're also proud of how we found problems: not by guessing, but by watching the itinerary and activity log disagree with what we expected, then chasing the real cause. That's how we caught the geocoding query issue, the org CORS policy, and the duplicate tool call, each a real bug against a real API, not a hypothetical. What we learned That the "two MCPs, one agent loop" idea holds up in practice, not just on paper, and that most of the real engineering in an agent-facing feature isn't the tool-calling plumbing (which is refreshingly thin once you commit to the tool-factory pattern). It's the edge cases: query phrasing that reads fine to a human but confuses a search API, org-level policies that only surface as a runtime error, and an agent's own occasional non-determinism. Building the itinerary and activity log to render straight off live tool calls, rather than trusting the model's narration, turned out to be the single best debugging tool we had. It's also what makes the demo convincing: you're not watching a chat bot describe a trip, you're watching WebMCP actually happen. What's next for Mapbox AI Trip Planner The bigger opportunity is first-party integration. The same tool-factory pattern that controls this demo map could register Studio-specific tools, select_layer , publish_style , undo and redo , directly against Mapbox Studio's live style editor, turning "how do I write this expression" into a conversation instead of a documentation search. Closer to home, we'd like to stream the chat widget's responses instead of waiting for a full reply, and give the agent a way to search points of interest by category, price, and rating rather than just name, so trip planning can go beyond landmarks into real day-to-day recommendations. title: Finite
pitch: Change your plans without rebuilding them.
about_excerpt: Change your plans without rebuilding them. Like Comment Story Updates Change your plans without rebuilding them. Finite keeps you and Codex working from the same live plan. A trip, renovation and event get different structures from the same connected planning model. WebMCP connects Codex to the same live plan on screen, so the conversation and the product become one workflow. Finite checks the connected plan, rules out what no longer fits and returns every meaningfully different workable direction. The chosen direction becomes revision 2 with the complete before and after result saved for the next planning conversation. Inspiration Planning software is usually good at storing the first version of a plan. It is much less useful after something changes. A delayed supplier, a new date, a smaller budget or one fixed booking can affect everything around it. At that point, people often end up rebuilding the plan in chat, patching a spreadsheet and checking every dependency by hand. Finite started with a simple comparison. Most software gives you the kitchen and still expects you to cook. With Finite, you are the diner, Codex is the chef, and Finite is the kitchen and service system. You describe the outcome and judge the result. Codex does the work. WebMCP gives Codex a real way to operate the kitchen. The goal was to build a planning system that stays useful when the original plan stops being correct. What it does Finite is a planning partner for plans that need to survive change. You can start with an outcome in ordinary language. Finite turns it into a working plan with the right structure for the job. A trip needs dates, routes, bookings and a budget. A renovation needs phases, dependencies, suppliers and contingency. An event needs capacity, commitments and a run of show. Interview preparation and recurring practice need different records again. These are different product surfaces built from the same planning model. The same system can support all of them because it understands the connected facts, constraints, choices and revisions underneath each plan. Codex can enter the live plan through WebMCP and read its current facts, limits, evidence and open work. When something changes, Codex can explore what is movable, test the available combinations and bring back the distinct directions that fit the plan. The public Spotlight shows this with a request to add three nights in Paris. The international flights are fixed, the total budget still matters and at least AUD 500 must remain free. Finite checks 26 possible combinations. Eighteen satisfy the encoded constraints, eight do not, and five meaningfully different directions exist for this plan. If only one direction worked, Finite would return one. The person chooses Protect breathing room and reviews the exact effect before confirming it. Codex can then apply that approved route. The plan moves from revision 1 to revision 2 once, retains AUD 910 of freedom and saves a before and after receipt that survives reload. Finite keeps research, comparison, verification, booking and payment as separate states. It does not claim that finding an option means the option is available or that a saved plan means anything has been purchased. How we used WebMCP WebMCP is the connection between Codex and the live plan. The page that the person sees also exposes typed, page-scoped tools to Codex. That means Codex works with the same accepted plan, current revision and visible decision state instead of guessing its way through buttons or using a hidden copy of the data. Finite registers seven stable document tools. Codex uses them to enter the current work, discover the available capability group, invoke the relevant planning action and read exact parts of a larger result when needed. The available actions are checked again against the active plan and revision before they run. Codex handles language, research and orchestration. Finite handles the calculations, constraints, saved state and receipts. You decide which direction becomes part of the plan. The person makes the final choice on the visible planning surface. WebMCP lets Codex prepare the alternatives and carry the selected direction into the same live plan. Codex does not just send advice back to chat. With your permission, it can guide you through the real Finite interface: move to the relevant section, highlight the actual controls, explain them in an on-page popup, and pause for questions or Next. These are built-in, page-scoped WebMCP capabilities, not a prerecorded tour. You can work manually, let Codex develop the plan, or switch between both in the same workspace. Guidance never grants permission to choose or approve a plan change for you. How it improves the human and agent experience Without this connection, the person has to carry information between the app and the agent. They explain the plan in chat, receive a recommendation, then update every affected field themselves. With Finite, Codex can enter the current plan in one call and see what is already known. It can work across the whole plan, then stop when a real decision is required. The person sees the trade-offs and the exact proposed change instead of operating the planning machinery. This makes the relationship straightforward. Codex does the planning work. Finite keeps that work consistent. The person stays responsible for the outcome. How it was built Finite uses TypeScript, Vite, Cloudflare Workers, D1, R2 and ChatGPT Sites. The planning kernel uses integer money, revision-bound candidates, constraint checks, short-lived approval challenges, optimistic concurrency, atomic receipts and idempotent replay. Accepted plan state is stored in D1 and can be restored after reload. An adaptive surface compiler builds each type of plan from a limited set of validated components. The same plan definition also limits what Codex can discover and do through WebMCP. Large results are stored temporarily by content hash. Codex receives a compact summary and can request the exact section it needs. This keeps the tool responses small without cutting important values in half. Codex provides the reasoning. Finite provides the connected state, calculations and persistence that make that reasoning useful inside a real product. Challenges The difficult part was keeping the plan correct while the person and Codex were both involved. A reported change is not an accepted change. A proposed option is not a decision. A click on an approval control is not the same as a completed plan update. Those states have to remain separate through retries, reloads and stale browser sessions. The first implementation also exposed too many route-specific tools and returned too much data. It was replaced with seven stable tools, smaller capability groups and exact retrieval for larger results. Testing also found small wording problems that could cause large mistakes. For example, value: 3 could be read as either an absolute duration or an instruction to add three days. The final contract separates value from delta and rejects contradictory inputs. Accomplishments A complete public WebMCP plan change from revision 1 to revision 2 A situation-dependent set of distinct suggestions derived from 26 checked combinations Seven stable WebMCP tools for the lifetime of the page Human choice kept inside the visible planning conversation Persistent receipts with the exact before and after state Distinct travel, renovation, event, interview, practice and general planning surfaces 373 passing tests, including 20 repeated Spotlight transaction runs Three calls to the first useful action in the measured production route What we learned More tools do not automatically make an agent more capable. A small toolset with current state and clear boundaries is easier for Codex to use well. We also learned that honest status matters. Research is not verification. A valid route is not approval. An updated plan is not a booking. Showing those differences makes the product easier to trust and easier to understand. The best division of work is built into the workflow. Codex can do the repetitive planning work while the person decides what becomes part of the plan. What's next The next step is to watch new users bring their own outcomes into Finite and see where the planning model is unclear without explanation. After that, the adaptive grammar and evidence connections can expand to cover more kinds of plans while keeping the same rules for accepted state and human approval. title: Acoustom
pitch: Great sound is personal. Acoustom takes the guesswork and uncertainty out of buying decisions.
about_excerpt: Great sound is personal. Acoustom takes the guesswork and uncertainty out of buying decisions. Like Comment 1 Story Updates Room Audio Simulation Custom Speaker Builder Acoustom — Great sound is personal. Acoustom takes the guesswork out of buying decisions. Acoustom is an AI-assisted speaker builder and listening-room simulator that helps people find the setup that best fits their room, music, budget, equipment, and preferences . With WebMCP, an agent can bring relevant user context into Acoustom, guide the user through the experience, build and customize products with them, explore technically compatible alternatives, test them through simulation, compare the trade-offs, and recommend the strongest option — all in the same shared interface. At a glance Personalized to the listener Acoustom works around the user's room, music, budget, aesthetics, existing equipment, and priorities rather than offering a generic “best speaker” ranking. Bring your context with you The agent can bring in relevant context from services the user has already connected to their AI environment such as room information from Google Drive, or listening preferences from Spotify history without Acoustom needing a native integration with every platform. Privacy stays with the user The user's own agent works with data that user decides to share rather than asking user for personal data or source files. The user stays in control of what is shared with Acoustom, Navigate and guide through the shared experience The agent can navigate visibly through Acoustom's catalog, product details, builder, room setup, simulation, and comparison views while explaining what it is doing and why. The user follows the same journey, sees the progress, collaborate and can redirect the agent at any point. Build and customize together in 3D The agent can actively build and customize a speaker inside Acoustom's shared 3D builder — selecting components and configuration, and iterating on the design while the user watches, evaluates, and makes changes alongside it. Generate and test alternatives quickly Instead of building one option at a time, the agent can rapidly configure several viable builds in one workflow, test them, eliminate weaker options, and refine the strongest candidates. Simulation-backed recommendations and trade-offs Acoustom uses technical data and simulation to test candidate builds before recommending them. The agent weighs sound, size, price, aesthetics, power requirements, room suitability, and compatibility with existing equipment against the user's priorities, then recommends the strongest overall option and explains the trade-offs. Users can inspect the evidence visually, technically, and through simulated audio using a standard reference track or their own audio. Technical complexity, simplified The agent turns specifications, compatibility constraints, and simulation results into practical explanations such as better bass but a larger enclosure , or a smoother response from your listening position . Explore before you commit Users and their agents can browse the catalog, enter the builder, configure speakers, run simulations, and compare options without creating an account until the purchase step. The workflow Bring context → explore → build together → generate alternatives → check compatibility → simulate & compare → explain trade-offs → optimize → recommend → refine → decide The problem Buying or building the right speaker is difficult because the listening experience is shaped by far more than the speaker itself. A speaker that sounds great in a showroom, in a reviewer's room, or on a specification sheet may sound very different once it is placed in the user's own space. Room size, wall distance, furniture, listening position, amplifier, enclosure, and component choices all affect the result. That often turns the buying process into expensive trial and error: research → compare → buy → set up → listen → discover it sounds different → adjust or return → try again For custom speakers, the problem is even harder. Drivers, crossovers, amplification, enclosure design, placement, and room conditions interact with one another, so changing one choice can affect several others. Finding a good combination can require repeated configuration, compatibility checks, and testing. Most users do not have the time or technical knowledge to explore all of those combinations confidently. The context needed to make that decision personal may already exist elsewhere such as room plans and measurements in Google Drive, existing equipment details in Shopify shopping history, or listening preferences reflected in Spotify history. Traditional shopping experiences usually leave the user to connect all of these pieces themselves, and go through the process repeatedly while the real answer only becomes clear after the product arrives. Acoustom is designed to reduce that uncertainty before the user buys or builds. What I built Acoustom is a WebMCP-powered custom speaker builder, product catalog, and virtual listening-room simulator. Users can browse products and components, build and customize a speaker in 3D, configure their room and listening position, compare alternatives, and hear simulated differences through the normal visual interface. With WebMCP, an agent can work directly with those same structured capabilities. It can understand the user's requirements, move through the product experience, build and modify configurations in the shared builder, propose compatible alternatives, test them through Acoustom's simulation, compare the trade-offs, and recommend the option that best matches the user's priorities. The key difference is that the agent does not stop at a plausible recommendation. It tests the proposal using Acoustom's technical data and simulation before recommending it. That turns the process from product search into: understand → build → test → validate → compare → optimize The core Acoustom experience is also intentionally open. Users do not need to create an account before browsing the catalog, entering the builder, configuring a speaker, exploring the room simulator, or comparing alternatives. That matters even more in an agent-assisted experience. The agent can start helping immediately — bringing in relevant context, guiding the user through the experience, configuring options, running tests, and explaining the results — without interrupting the journey with registration before the user has received any value. The experience starts with exploration and product immersion, not account creation . A realistic demo scenario Imagine someone wants compact speakers for a home office. They open Acoustom without creating an account and ask: I have a floor plan and photos of my office in Google Drive. Use them to understand my room and desk space. Consider the kind of music I listen to, and build three compact options under $1,000 that work with my existing amplifier. Test the strongest options and recommend the best trade-off. With the user's permission, the agent uses context from their connected services. It does not need to pass Acoustom the user's entire Google Drive files, music history, or broader personal profile. Instead, it translates that context into the design constraints Acoustom needs: available room and desk space approximate listening position existing equipment budget listening preferences size or aesthetic priorities The agent then guides the user visibly through Acoustom. It navigates to the relevant products, enters the builder, and begins creating candidate designs. Inside the shared 3D builder, the user sees the builds take shape and can intervene as the agent works. The complete flow is: understand the user's context and constraints navigate to the relevant products and builder create several viable speaker configurations in the 3D builder check cross-component and system compatibility configure the room and listening position simulate the strongest candidates compare sound, size, price, aesthetics, power requirements, room suitability, and compatibility with existing equipment eliminate weaker alternatives explain the important trade-offs recommend the strongest overall fit based on the user's priorities and simulation results The user can compare the finalists using the same standard reference audio, then upload a familiar track and repeat the comparison using their own music. After listening, they might say: I prefer the second one, but it is still too large. Keep what works about that design, make it smaller, and stay under $800. The agent does not start over. It returns to the existing build, preserves the relevant choices, modifies the design in the shared builder, reruns the required tests, and shows the updated comparison. The interaction becomes an iterative optimization loop: build → test → compare → refine → rebuild → retest Key Features Personalized speaker design based on room, listening preferences, budget, aesthetics, and existing equ

title: Builder.run
pitch: A local-first application runtime where humans and agents can build, shape, and use custom information systems together.
about_excerpt: A local-first application runtime where humans and agents can build, shape, and use custom information systems together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Builder.run is inspired by configurable systems like Drupal, where a small set of primitives can be combined into custom information systems. I wanted to explore what that model looks like in an agentic world, with the application spec as the canonical artefact rather than generated code. What it does Builder.run is a local-first application runtime that humans and agents can build, shape, and use together . Apps are composed from types, fields, views, summaries, forms, pages, widgets, and rules, and the browser runtime turns that spec into working software backed by local SQLite storage. How I built it The current runtime uses Svelte 5, SvelteKit 3, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn-svelte, and wa-sqlite in a Web Worker, with browser-local persistence through OPFS where available. The project was built in roughly three days using an agent-heavy development workflow with Codex and Grok, which made it possible to iterate quickly on the runtime, WebMCP integration, and UI. WebMCP is exposed in two layers: fixed builder tools let an agent shape the application itself, while application tools are generated dynamically from the live app spec so the agent can immediately use the app it just created. Challenges I ran into I started late, so a major constraint was deciding what to prioritise. I focused on proving the complete loop: build the app, generate its capabilities, use them, then evolve the app again , rather than expanding the feature surface. The biggest challenge was keeping the system based on a small set of reusable primitives rather than adding special-purpose features for every use case. WebMCP also introduced lifecycle challenges because the tool surface itself can change as the application changes, without disrupting ordinary data operations or in-flight tool calls. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I've been thinking about configurable information systems since I first started using Drupal more than 15 years ago. This hackathon gave me the excuse to finally turn that long-running idea into a working runtime. The part I am most pleased with is the full loop: Agent shapes app → spec changes → UI, storage, and tools update → agent uses the new capabilities. The generated WebMCP tools are not a fixed API bolted onto the application; they are derived from the application the user and agent create together. What I learned The main thing I learned is that WebMCP can be more than an integration layer for an existing website. In a malleable runtime, it can become part of the application model itself, allowing agents both to shape the software and immediately use the capabilities they create . What's next for Builder.run Builder.run is still an early runtime, with plenty of rough edges to refine — particularly around the UI and the current Rules experience. Next I want to explore richer primitives, expand Rules into more capable workflows and automations, support more flexible presentation, make app data more portable, strengthen permissions and actor support, and build hosted or multiplayer runtimes that can consume the same application spec. title: RAI
pitch: RAI is a Robot, Agent Interface that allows agents to control and make robots using WebMCP tools, limited to actions like moving joints by angle and seeing through the robot’s camera.\n
about_excerpt:
RAI is a Robot, Agent Interface that allows agents to control and make robots using WebMCP tools, limited to actions like moving joints by angle and seeing through the robot’s camera.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 I had wanted to build a robotic arm project for a long time, and one day while I was using Codex I thought: what is actually stopping me from giving an AI tools to control a robot arm? 

 It can have tools to move the joints, and it can also have a tool to look through a camera. So I decided to build the physical arm and experiment with letting an LLM see, move, and interact with real objects. 

 I think AI controlling physical things through vision and tools is still really underexplored, and I wanted to make it easier for other people to experiment with this idea too. 

 For this challenge, I made a lighter web version of the project where an agent can control a simulated robot using WebMCP tools. 

 What RAI does 

 RAI lets users watch AI trials and experiment with models controlling a robot. 

 The agent can look through the robot camera, read information about the arm, move its joints, and try to complete tasks. 

 It does not get hidden object positions or shortcuts. It has to look at what happened, make a move, see the result, and adjust if it fails. 

 Users can also try different prompts and compare how the agent behaves. 

 How I built it 

 I mainly used Codex to build the project. 

 I already had a lot of the control logic and ideas from my physical robot arm and my experiments with Isaac Sim, so I adapted those ideas into a lightweight web simulation that could run in the browser and be controlled through WebMCP. 

 Codex helped me build most of the interface, simulation, and WebMCP integration. 

 Challenges 

 At first I wanted RAI to be much bigger. I wanted agents to control multiple robots and experiment in more complicated environments. 

 That became too much for the time I had, and I also had some personal things happening during the submission period, so I came pretty close to missing the deadline. 

 Because of that, I focused on making one smaller environment that clearly shows the main idea instead of trying to build everything. 

 What I learned 

 One of the most interesting things I noticed is that sometimes the agent is too careful. 

 It can hesitate to move the arm far enough or avoid moves that seem risky, even when those moves are needed to complete the task. 

 My favorite experiment is tipping over a can. With the right prompt, Sol can usually figure it out in around 2 minutes using only the camera and the arm controls. 

 It is really interesting to watch the model try something, see that it did not work, and then change its next move. 

 I think models could become much better at this if training and evaluation included more examples of vision + tool use for controlling physical systems. 

 What's next 

 I want to turn RAI into a better environment for testing how different AI models control robots. 

 One thing I am especially interested in is letting an AI look at its own failed experiments and then change its prompt or strategy to improve the next attempt. 

 Longer term, I want to do more research on this and look into collecting large amounts of robot interaction data in simulation. 

 Because the same experiments can be repeated many times in a simulator, I think this could be useful for evaluating or training future models that are better at interacting with the physical world.

about_excerpt: Merge Queue gives AI agents a branch instead of giving them the last word. Humans and agents can edit the same live application simultaneously, then safely merge their work without silent overwrites. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most agent demos quietly assume the human stops touching the application while the agent works. That assumption will not survive the real world. A person might reassign an urgent task while an agent reorganizes the project board. A store manager might correct inventory while an agent prepares a merchandising update. Both actions can be reasonable, yet the application normally accepts whichever write arrives last and silently erases the other participant’s intent. Software teams solved a similar problem for source code with branches and three-way merges. We wanted to explore what that collaboration model could look like for everyday web applications. That became Merge Queue: humans keep working, agents get a branch. What it does Merge Queue is a local-first project board where a person and an AI agent can edit the same workspace concurrently without overwriting each other. When the agent begins a task, Merge Queue snapshots the current workspace and creates an isolated agent branch. The agent can stage multiple structured changes—moving tasks, assigning owners, changing priorities, updating deadlines, or archiving stale work—without mutating the live board. Meanwhile, the human continues working normally. When the agent finishes, Merge Queue performs a semantic three-way merge between: Base: the workspace when the agent started Human: the current live workspace Agent: the agent’s proposed workspace For every changed field, the merge engine determines whether: Only the human changed it, so the human value is preserved. Only the agent changed it, so the proposal can merge safely. Both selected the same value, so the duplicate change is collapsed. Both selected different values, so the decision returns to the human. Compatible work is merged automatically. Genuine disagreements appear as focused conflict cards showing the original value, the human’s choice, the agent’s proposal, and the consequence of each decision. The agent can request a merge review, but it cannot approve its own work. There is intentionally no agent-accessible commit tool. The final merge is committed through the visible human interface as one atomic revision. How we built it Merge Queue is a dependency-free web application built with JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. It runs entirely in the browser, persists versioned state locally, and requires no API key or backend service. The application is organized around a shared deterministic command layer. Human interface actions and WebMCP tool calls invoke the same underlying operations, which prevents the agent from using a hidden automation path with different behavior from the visible application. We implemented WebMCP using imperative tools registered on the top-level page with document.modelContext.registerTool . The tool surface allows an agent to: Read the live workspace and its revision Open an isolated agent branch Stage bounded task updates Stage new tasks Inspect the branch diff Generate a semantic merge preview Read unresolved conflicts Request visible human review Check the branch status Abort an uncommitted branch Revert the latest completed merge Each tool uses a narrow JSON Schema, validates its inputs again inside the domain layer, clearly describes its side effects, and returns enough structured information for the agent to verify the result and select the correct next action. Agent proposals are visually distinguished from live state. A moved task can appear as a proposed destination while its original live card remains intact. An activity timeline interleaves human actions, agent proposals, and system merge events so the collaboration remains understandable throughout the workflow. Merge previews are bound to a specific workspace revision. If the human changes the board after a preview is generated, that preview becomes stale and cannot be committed. The merge must be recalculated against the latest human state. Commits are atomic and idempotent. Repeated commit attempts cannot apply the same branch twice. The previous workspace snapshot is retained so an approved merge can be reverted as a new revision without deleting history. We also built a deterministic walkthrough that consistently produces safe changes, duplicate choices, and three meaningful conflicts. This makes the concurrency problem—and the value of the merge—visible in under ninety seconds. Challenges we faced Defining what a “conflict” means outside source code Text files have lines. Application state has meaning. Moving a task and changing its owner are independent operations that should usually merge. Moving the same task into two different workflow stages is a real conflict. Archiving a task while the other participant edits it also requires special handling. We had to model these cases semantically instead of treating every modified object as one large conflict. Preserving live human work The most important invariant was that an agent proposal must never mutate the human workspace before approval. We maintained separate base, human, and agent snapshots and forced every staged operation through the isolated branch. We added tests for independent edits, overlapping edits, creation, archival, stale previews, repeated commits, aborts, and reverts. Designing human control without approval fatigue Confirming every agent action would technically keep the human in control, but it would make the product painful to use. We moved approval from the individual-action level to the merge level. The agent can prepare a substantial body of work, while the human reviews only the places where their intentions actually differ. Making the agent understand what happened A correct interface is not enough if the agent receives an ambiguous result. Every tool response includes the current revision, branch status, affected records, and valid next step. The agent can distinguish between “staged,” “waiting for human resolution,” “ready for approval,” “merged,” and “aborted” without guessing from the page. Remaining useful without WebMCP The complete human interface and deterministic walkthrough work in ordinary browsers. When WebMCP is available, the agent discovers the structured tools and participates directly. When it is unavailable, the project remains a functional demonstration of the merge model rather than displaying a broken screen. What we learned The most important lesson was that safe agent collaboration is not only about restricting what an agent can do. It is also about defining how agent intent coexists with human intent. Audit logs explain what happened after the fact. Approval dialogs interrupt actions before they happen. Merge Queue explores a third primitive: allow both participants to work, calculate where their intentions are compatible, and return only the irreducible decisions to the person. We also learned that tool results are part of the user experience. A useful WebMCP tool needs more than a successful return value—it should explain what changed, what remained untouched, what state the workflow is now in, and what the agent should do next. Most importantly, WebMCP feels strongest when it enables a collaboration model that ordinary browser automation cannot reproduce reliably. Merge Queue is not simply a faster way for an agent to click task-board buttons. It gives the agent a typed, versioned role inside the application. What we are proud of Agent proposals never mutate live state before approval. Human work can continue while the agent stages a multi-step plan. Compatible changes merge automatically. Genuine conflicts remain human decisions. Stale previews cannot commit. Commits are atomic and idempotent. Completed merges remain recoverable. Human actions and WebMCP calls share the same application logic. The complete experience runs locally without an API key or backend. What’s next Merge Queue’s engine is intentionally domain-independent. The same protocol could power a wedding seating planner where a couple moves family members while an agent balances tables, or a merchant catalog where a store manager protects prices while an agent prepares a collection update. Future versions could add multiple agent branches, collaborative network persistence, configurable application schemas, dependency-aware conflict explanations, and a reusable withMergeQueue() library for adding branch-and-merge semantics to existing WebMCP applications. Our broader goal is to make concurrent human-agent editing a standard capability of the agentic web. Humans keep working. Agents get a branch. Intent gets merged.  Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming increasingly capable, but collaboration across sessions, tools, and people is still fragile. When a conversation ends, the next person or agent often has to reconstruct what happened, what decisions were made, and what work should happen next. 

 Handoff explores a different model: a shared web workspace where humans and AI agents operate on the same project state. 

 What it does 

 Handoff gives a project a persistent shared state built around: 

 
 goals 
 open work 
 evidence 
 decisions 
 activity 
 the next handoff 
 

 Humans interact with that state through the web interface. AI agents interact with the same underlying capabilities through WebMCP tools. 

 An agent can inspect the current project, understand unfinished work, search existing evidence, contribute findings, propose results, record agreed decisions, complete work, and determine the next handoff. 

 The key idea is simple: 

 The conversation can end. The work doesn't. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Without WebMCP, an agent would need to infer how to use the interface by reading the page and manipulating UI elements. 

 With WebMCP, Handoff exposes the application's meaningful actions directly as structured tools. 

 The human UI and the agent tools operate on the same domain actions and shared state. WebMCP is therefore not an add-on to Handoff; it is what allows the application to become a genuine human-agent workspace. 

 Human + agent collaboration 

 A human can define a goal, add context, review evidence, and make important decisions. 

 An agent can then pick up the project, determine what remains unfinished, inspect existing evidence, contribute work, and leave the project in a clean state for whoever comes next. 

 The next worker can be the same person, another person, or another AI agent. 

 Built for the WebMCP Challenge 

 Handoff was created for the 2026 WebMCP Challenge as an experiment in agent-native web applications. 

 The goal is to demonstrate that websites do not only need to be readable by agents — they can explicitly expose the actions and state that agents need to collaborate safely and effectively with humans.

Real-time web trainer for Poland's iconic wedding dance (Szuraniec / 2-on-1). Powered by WebMCP, Web Audio & Web Vibration API to teach footwork with AI agents.
