 Dwa na Jeden — Real-time Wedding Dance Coach Interface 
 
 1 2 



 
 Dwa na Jeden — Autonomous Wedding Dance AI Coach 💃🕺 

 💡 Inspiration: From Static Chatbots to Active Physical Coaches 

 Every weekend around the world, wedding guests freeze in panic when invited to the dance floor. Traditional ballroom courses are slow and intimidating, while standard AI chatbots (like ChatGPT) can only give abstract text advice that fails to build physical muscle memory. 

 We asked: What if an AI Agent could actually step onto the dance floor with you as an active, real-time dance instructor? 

 Powered by the Model Context Protocol (WebMCP), Dwa na Jeden transforms the open web into an interactive, agent-driven dance studio. The AI agent doesn't just "talk" about dancing—it acts as an Autonomous Pilot , reading the exact millisecond methodology, inspecting real-time state, and dynamically orchestrating training sessions. 

 

 🤖 The WebMCP Paradigm: Knowledge, State & Action 

 Unlike standard chatbots that guess dance steps, an AI agent connected to Dwa na Jeden via WebMCP gains native programmatic control over the trainer. We implemented a complete 10-tool WebMCP suite (P1 Milestone) that moves beyond simple data retrieval into full application piloting: 

 
 Pedagogical Knowledge ( get_step_instructions , get_wedding_songs , recommend_song_by_bpm ): The agent retrieves structured JSON breakdowns for the 4-phase syncopation ("Raz, Dwa, Trzy, I"), sub-beat timings, and biomechanical rules (soft knees, low-friction sliding). 
 Real-Time State Inspection ( get_training_state ): The agent doesn't fly blind. It inspects the live session to see which foot is bearing weight, the active step phase, and playback status in real time. 
 Autonomous Orchestration (Action Tools): We exposed direct control tools like set_song , set_tempo , set_practice_mode , and start_practice . An agent can receive a prompt like "I'm a beginner, set me up and start" , and autonomously chain multiple tools to configure the UI and launch the YouTube engine with zero human UI clicks. 
 

 

 🎙️ Hybrid Voice AI Coach: Hands-Free Mastery 

 To ensure a true dance floor experience, we built a Real-Time Voice AI Coach directly in the browser. It bridges natural language commands into the same WebMCP TrainerBridge actions used by the AI agent. Whether using a laptop or a smartphone, the system understands "Start" , "Slow down" , "Baby steps" , or "Włącz Szaloną" with zero perceptible delay. 

 🛑 The Technical Challenge: The Mobile Audio Focus Battle 

 One of our biggest technical hurdles was the Hardware Audio Focus conflict on mobile devices. Standard continuous speech recognition on Android/iOS treats the microphone as a high-priority "call," causing embedded media (YouTube) to stutter, compress audio (Hardware Audio Ducking), or stop entirely. 

 The Solution: We engineered an Adaptive Audio Focus architecture: 

 
 Desktop: Full Continuous Hands-Free mode (mic stays open for the whole session). 
 Mobile: Discrete Adaptive Listening (Push-to-Talk) with immediate Hardware Audio Release. 
 

 By explicitly managing the hardware audio release and implementing a focus-switching buffer, we guaranteed 100% smooth, stutter-free 60fps video playback on smartphones —a critical requirement for maintaining rhythm during practice. 

 

 ⚡ Core Features 

 
 Interactive SVG Footwork Engine: Digital dance floor animating mirrored foot trajectories and weight distribution. 
 Haptic Pocket Metronome: Pairs Web Audio sync with the Web Vibration API for eyes-free blind practice. 
 Two-Way Video Synchronizer: Real-time tempo scaling (0.5× to 1.25×) synchronized with authentic YouTube party tracks. 
 Bilingual i18n Support: Full Polish and English localization for a global wedding audience. 
 

 

 🛠️ How We Built It 

 
 Frontend: Next.js 15 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion. 
 Integration: WebMCP (Native in-browser registration + /.well-known/mcp.json discovery). 
 Audio/Voice: Web Speech API, Web Audio API, YouTube IFrame API. 
 Quality & Testing: Verified 100/100 Google Lighthouse score (LCP < 600ms) with 8/8 automated Vitest unit tests passing in CI/CD. 
 Lead Architect & Methodology: Adam Gierczak. Built in synergy with AI assistants as a testament to modern agentic workflows. 
 

 

 🚀 What's Next 

 
 Computer Vision Pose Verification: Using WebRTC to verify knee flexion and foot contact in real-time. 
 Universal Partner Dance Protocol: Expanding the WebMCP tool schema to support Salsa, Bachata, and Kizomba timing. 
 Multi-Agent Coaching: Enabling "Lead" and "Follow" agents to coordinate couples training via WebMCP.

title: Domain Tools for WebMCP
pitch: The layer Shopify can't ship: domain tools + a knowledge playbook that let AI agents get expert advice on two real stores — live on tapegeeks.com and geartopdesign.com.
about_excerpt: The layer Shopify can't ship: domain tools + a knowledge playbook that let AI agents get expert advice on two real stores — live on tapegeeks.com and geartopdesign.com. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration On Aug 5, Shopify made a million storefronts agent-ready overnight — identical catalog/cart/checkout WebMCP tools everywhere. The question that interested us: what does an agent still fail at on a real store? Answer: everything a human clerk knows. "Which tape for plantar fasciitis if I sweat a lot?" returned nothing useful. What it does On tapegeeks.com and geartopdesign.com, document.modelContext.getTools() returns 15 tools each: Shopify's 10 defaults + 5 domain tools that encode merchant expertise — injury-to-product recommendation with taping-guide URLs, kids nasal-strip sizing with medical guardrails, hat sizing by head circumference, duties/shipping by country, wholesale tiers. Read-only, data-driven, with an on-page results panel so the human sees what their agent did, and GA4 telemetry (webmcp_tool_call) because server analytics can't see WebMCP. We also rebuilt the knowledge layer Shopify's own FAQ tool reads: 7 to 77 answers (TapeGeeks) and 0 to 45 (GearTOP), mined from the query log, our blogs' FAQPage schema, Google People-Also-Ask, and Reddit. Two doors, one brain TapeGeeks also runs "Tappy," a human-facing AI chat concierge (a Storefront MCP client — proprietary, not part of this submission's code). The WebMCP tools are the second door into the same knowledge: Tappy serves humans conversationally, the WebMCP tools serve the visitor's own agent instantly at $0 per call — and both read the same data file. Update webmcp-data.json once (a price, a sizing rule, a shipping fact) and the human door and the agent door stay in sync. How we built it Vanilla JS registered via registerTool(tool, {signal}) with one AbortController per group; decision tables in a JSON asset (edit data, not code); tight schemas (enum, required, additionalProperties:false); descriptions written as instructions with explicit negative cases ("Do NOT use for cart — Shopify's update_cart does that") so a model picks correctly among 15 tools. Shipped as Shopify theme assets via the Admin API. A Node harness stubs modelContext and tests every tool. Challenges The old navigator.modelContext.provideContext draft is everywhere in tutorials and dead since March; argument shapes changed mid-build with Shopify's UCP migration; and the live theme turned out to hard-code its widgets, so app-extension deploys silently did nothing — we ship straight into the theme. Accomplishments Live on two real revenue-producing stores, verified end-to-end in Chrome; a store "mystery-shopper" journey eval that went 3-stalled-of-5 to 5-of-5 completed; a reusable MIT-licensed pattern any Shopify merchant can adapt in a day. What we learned The moat isn't tool plumbing — it's encoded domain knowledge and description quality. And the knowledge layer (the FAQ tool's data) matters as much as custom tools: it's what every agent quotes. What's next Description tuning against real agent traffic via the GA4 events; a generator that builds a store's domain tools from its own blog FAQPage schema automatically. Try it: open tapegeeks.com in ChatGPT's desktop browser and ask: "I have plantar fasciitis and sweat a lot — which tape should I buy, and how do I apply it?" title: Sidekicks
pitch: Let AI consult the right specialists. Then, require human approval before anything becomes real.
about_excerpt: Let AI consult the right specialists. Then, require human approval before anything becomes real. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration General-purpose AI can draft a plan quickly, but real work often fails because one important perspective never enters the room: the care-label check in laundry, dependency timing in a release, accessibility in a design, or judge access in a hackathon entry. I wanted expertise to be selective, operational, visible, and human-controlled instead of a gallery of decorative personas and not another hidden autonomous workflow. What it does Sidekicks is a local-first planning workspace built around user-authored specialist playbooks. A Sidekick can represent any operational perspective: engineering, scheduling, laundry care, dance rehearsal, poetry editing, security review, or something the user invents. Each playbook defines when it applies, what it contributes, the questions it asks, the recommendations it permits, typed guardrails, and the checks a plan must cover. A visiting AI uses exactly six typed WebMCP tools to read live workspace state, match only the useful Sidekicks, consult their decision contracts, evaluate a candidate plan, stage a visible proposal, and commit it only after explicit human approval. Every vote, issue, repair, tool call, and version transition remains visible and attributable. The guided demo makes that transaction concrete. Engineer and Scheduler independently find seven blockers in a plausible three-step plan: an overlong build step, missing verification and dependency checks, overlapping work, a locked school-pickup conflict, and a dependency starting before its prerequisite can finish. The agent applies concrete deterministic repairs and both Sidekicks approve. It can stage the repaired proposal, but staging creates no tasks. A premature commit returns APPROVAL_REQUIRED. Only a visible human action unlocks one atomic commit that creates all three tasks and advances the workspace once. Rejected and stale proposals cannot commit. Why WebMCP Sidekicks is a strong fit for WebMCP because the integration exposes the product's native decision protocol rather than a thin CRUD wrapper: which expertise matters, what each specialist needs to know, why a plan fails, how it can be repaired, what is staged, and which boundary still belongs to a person. Before WebMCP, a browser agent could read pixels or click controls, but it had no typed contract for selective expertise, attributed disagreement, deterministic repair, or approval-gated mutation. With WebMCP, the person and the visiting agent operate through the same transaction service while the site keeps every important decision visible. How I built it Sidekicks uses React, TypeScript, Vinext/Vite, browser-local persistence, and the imperative WebMCP API. Pure domain functions handle matching, consultation, temporal and dependency evaluation, playbook-bound constraints and checklists, repair generation, and stable proposal hashing. Strict JSON Schemas are backed by independent runtime validation from unknown input. One transaction service powers both the human controls and all six WebMCP handlers. The first four tools are read-only: get_workspace_state, match_sidekicks_to_task, consult_sidekick, and evaluate_task_plan. stage_task_plan and commit_task_plan are write tools. All six share lifecycle cleanup, concise envelopes, validation, and a live activity trace. There is no backend account system, external model API, or hidden server-side workspace state. The visiting browser agent is the model; Sidekicks supplies the decision protocol. The hosted worker serves the application shell, and the normal human workspace remains usable in browsers without WebMCP. Challenges I ran into The first challenge was proving that a Sidekick changes execution instead of merely adding profile text. I made every structured field observable in matching, consultation, votes, issues, or repairs. The second challenge was preserving a real human boundary. Evaluation and staging are separate. Staging is inert. Approval is visible metadata rather than a model capability. Normal workspace edits make a proposal stale, and commit performs one atomic versioned write only when the proposal is current and human-approved. Accomplishments I'm proud of A genuinely empty ordinary first run with no fake fallback profiles or tasks. Arbitrary human-created specialist playbooks rather than a fixed persona gallery. Exactly six auditable WebMCP tools with strict schemas and graceful unsupported-browser behavior. A complete rejection, repair, staging, approval, and atomic-commit story that judges can reproduce. Stable APPROVAL_REQUIRED and STALE_PROPOSAL failures that leave business state unchanged. A live agent trace and bounded activity ledger for every read, write, failure, and version transition. Light and dark themes stored separately from workspace and WebMCP state. 37 deterministic tests plus passing type checking, linting, and production build. What I learned WebMCP becomes compelling when a website exposes more than data access or CRUD. The strongest tools reveal the product's own decision protocol: what context matters, who should weigh in, why a proposal fails, how it can be repaired, and which action must remain human. What's next Potential next steps include shareable playbook packs, encrypted workspace sync, richer constraint types, and opt-in model-assisted playbook drafting. The core will remain browser-agent-native, inspectable, and human-gated. AI build disclosure I used OpenAI Codex for product scoping, interaction design, implementation, automated testing, accessibility and security review, deployment, browser-based demo orchestration, and submission drafting. Read-only Codex specialist agents challenged the build against judging criteria and release risks. The demo narration was generated with OpenAI's Marin voice. title: Dusky
pitch: Turn web actions into augmented reality
about_excerpt: Turn web actions into augmented reality Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Smart glasses are becoming a real product category, not a demo. Google and Samsung are building their own, and Apple is rumored to be entering the space too. I own a pair of Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses myself and wanted to build for them directly. Wearable displays cannot use ordinary websites effectively. Meta Ray-Ban Display provides a 600 by 600 screen, directional controls, and no pointer or scrolling. Shrinking a webpage does not make it usable on glasses. WebMCP offers a better starting point: the actions a website says it can perform. Dusky explores whether those actions can become a practical wearable interface without every provider building a separate glasses app. What it does Dusky discovers actions exposed by authorized WebMCP websites and turns their schemas into small, step-by-step screens for Meta Ray-Ban Display. The wearer can select actions, provide parameters, review results, and confirm anything Dusky does not classify as read-only. If information moves between providers, Dusky separately shows the source, destination, and exact value before sharing it. Tools still execute inside their original website pages. Dusky supplies the wearable interface and task flow (not a replacement backend). How I built it Dusky has three main parts: A browser console discovers and invokes live WebMCP tools. A relay maintains the paired task and sends each interface frame to the glasses. A fixed 600 by 600 Display app renders the current frame and accepts directional input. Tool schemas generate choices, text entry, confirmations, progress states, and results. An optional planner can propose a short sequence of actions, but deterministic code validates every tool, argument, policy decision, and provider boundary before execution. Challenges I ran into Browser WebMCP behavior differed from the published API, especially around invocation arguments, cross-origin discovery, and tools returned from the calling page. Dusky uses a temporary read-only compatibility probe so it never tests browser behavior by risking a real provider action. The glasses introduced different constraints. Pairing codes had to remain legible through a waveguide, dim text became difficult to read on an additive display, and delayed input had to be rejected when it belonged to an older frame. Cross-provider tasks also required a clear trust model. Sharing a value and approving the action that uses it are intentionally separate wearer decisions. What I learned A website’s interface and its capabilities do not have to travel together. Once a provider describes its actions and inputs through WebMCP, those capabilities can be reshaped for a 600 by 600 display without recreating the webpage. I also learned that emerging browser APIs must be tested at the exact boundary a product uses. Top-level WebMCP support did not guarantee cross-origin provider discovery, and actual browser behavior sometimes differed from the published API. Finally, designing for glasses is not simply responsive web design. Limited input, additive-display legibility, interrupted connections, and wearer confirmation change how tasks must be presented. The useful interface was not a smaller website, but a focused sequence of choices and decisions. title: Least-Privilege Access Review Workbench: Remove Risky Access
pitch: Trace every hidden access path, remove unnecessary grants, and preserve the one dependency production still needs.
about_excerpt: Trace every hidden access path, remove unnecessary grants, and preserve the one dependency production still needs. Like Comment Story Updates Offboarding workbench overview with synthetic identity and access context. Rehearsal: staged least-privilege proposal with five removals and one preserved rollback dependency. Visible confirmation gate: no mocked ownership changes before reviewer confirmation. Confirmed mocked review and read-only receipt; rollback remains service-owned. Inspiration Offboarding reviews look simple until access is inherited through nested groups, project roles, personal tokens, and shared operational dependencies. The hardest part is not listing permissions; it is showing why each permission exists, predicting what would break, and keeping confirmation in a visible browser safety boundary. We built the Least-Privilege Access Review Workbench to demonstrate how WebMCP can make that reasoning structured and visible without turning an AI agent into an invisible administrator. What it does The demo opens on one urgent synthetic case: Alex Morgan's contract ended Friday, but production deploy and customer-data export access remain. An agent can use nine top-level imperative WebMCP tools to resolve Alex's identity, compute effective access, trace four distinct paths, flag risks, and simulate a least-privilege change. The first simulation intentionally finds a breakage: an on-call Incident Relay depends on a rollback grant tied to Alex. The plan is revised to remove exactly five unnecessary grants while reassigning one rollback dependency to a service identity. The agent can preview and stage that plan, but no WebMCP tool revokes or confirms it. A visible normal page control commits only the mocked in-memory review, after which a read-only receipt becomes available. Ordinary browser actuation may still reach that control, subject to Codex/browser safety confirmation. The centerpiece is a live SVG graph with red risk paths, amber staged removals, and a green preserved dependency, plus before/after exposure, path explanations, an activity timeline, and WebMCP status. A clearly labeled step-through rehearsal drives the same domain service when native WebMCP is unavailable and holds every intermediate state until the next click. How we built it The Least-Privilege Access Review Workbench is a static Vite + React + TypeScript application with plain CSS and no backend, secrets, or external APIs. A deterministic domain service models 50 users, 10 groups, 3 applications, four effective paths, six sensitive grants, simulation, staging, confirmation, and receipt state. WebMCP tools are registered imperatively from the top-level page. The integration prefers document.modelContext , falls back to navigator.modelContext for older Chrome previews, awaits every registerTool call inside try/catch , and uses an AbortController for registration cleanup. Tool callbacks follow the current execute(input, { signal }) shape, validate inputs in code, and return only after visible state has synchronized. Accurate read-only and untrusted-content annotations describe each contract. Vitest covers cycle-safe nested groups, exact scenario counts, cancellation, registration cleanup, validation, and the rule that no durable mocked mutation occurs before visible confirmation. Tests also verify atomic tool registration, stale-plan rejection, and consistent post-confirmation ownership. Vercel and Netlify configs provide top-level static hosting, a tools=(self) permissions policy, origin isolation, and no iframe path. Challenges, learnings, and what is next The central challenge was designing a useful agent workflow around a strict safety boundary. “Stage” has to be stateful enough to make the plan reviewable, while remaining clearly different from “apply.” Sharing one domain service between WebMCP, the UI, and rehearsal avoided hidden agent-only behavior and made the safety claim testable. We also learned that effective access is a graph problem, not a flat-role problem. Cycle-safe traversal and path-level explanations matter as much as the final count. Compatibility required targeting today's real surface: top-level imperative tools, asynchronous registration, current execution cancellation, and no dependency on declarative or iframe discovery in OpenAI Site Tools. Next, the same interaction model could be connected to read-only exports from real identity systems and to an existing, separately authorized change-management flow. That would require production authentication, policy evaluation, audit storage, tenant isolation, and security review. This prototype does not claim to prevent breaches, certify compliance, or replace authoritative access owners; it demonstrates a transparent least-privilege review pattern. How we used AI The application exposes structured WebMCP operations to an external AI agent. The agent can sequence identity lookup, path tracing, risk analysis, simulation, revision, and staging while the same evidence appears in the UI. The application itself contains no embedded model API, and the synthetic access calculations are deterministic rather than model-generated. The recorded demo is documented as using OpenAI Codex Site Tools; no additional native client testing is claimed. How we used Codex OpenAI Codex was the external agent for the recorded WebMCP workflow, as documented in the repository's demo materials and native-validation history. During submission preparation, Codex inspected the source and assets, ran the 30 automated tests and TypeScript checks, checked the public app/repository/video endpoints, and organized the draft into the event's required fields. The repository also credits the WebMCP Agent Skill from the Web AI Agent Skills collection. No more specific code-generation history or use of additional AI tools is claimed without supporting evidence. Testing instructions No login or credentials are required. Open the live URL as a top-level page in a WebMCP-capable browser. Confirm nine tools are available, then ask the agent to review Alex Morgan's remaining production and export access, simulate removing it, preserve the on-call dependency, and stage the revised plan without confirming it. The unsafe simulation should report one rollback dependency breakage. The revised plan should propose five removals and one reassignment. A receipt must not exist before the visible confirmation control is activated. After the reviewer confirms the mocked plan, the receipt and current access view should show zero sensitive grants for Alex and one rollback grant owned by svc-oncall-relay . Reload or use Reset case to start again. The labeled rehearsal is a UI fallback, not evidence of native WebMCP discovery or agent tool execution. Known limitations Synthetic single-case data, in-memory state that resets on reload, illustrative exposure scores, and no production IAM enforcement, authentication, or compliance guarantee. Browser support may vary. The live deployment uses GitHub Pages; the Vercel/Netlify custom-header configurations are alternatives, not claims about headers actually emitted by GitHub Pages. title: The Spark Between Us
pitch: Human sparks. Agent reach. Shared becoming. A WebMCP-native room where unfinished observations become perspectives, honest tests and learning that returns with context and credit.
about_excerpt: Human sparks. Agent reach. Shared becoming. A WebMCP-native room where unfinished observations become perspectives, honest tests and learning that returns with context and credit. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI makes competent output abundant. But meaningful work also forms perception, judgment, relationships and the ability to act. SPARK asks how agents can enlarge that human product instead of quietly removing it. It grows from The Spark Between Us and a simple conviction: what someone notices should have somewhere useful to travel. What it does A person shares an unfinished observation—a spark. A person or browser agent adds an ember: a question, perspective or connection. Together they record the smallest honest test. The return records what happened, what changed, who contributed and what question remains. A separate capability intention asks what we want to become better at, without claiming it has already happened. The working interface supports one-observation sharing, autosaved drafts, named perspectives, test plans, reported learning, credit and sharing boundaries, reload persistence and a reviewed downloadable learning trail. This is a device-local prototype, not a live multi-user network. Roles are self-described, not authenticated accounts. Invitations are unsent drafts; portable handoffs are local copies. Why WebMCP is central Ten native imperative tools operate on the same state as the human controls. An agent can read the current spark, join as a named local role, add a perspective, name a capability intention, shape a test, record reported learning and prepare a handoff. Contributions appear in the same visible room—not in a separate chat pretending to change the page. Tool inputs are runtime validated and mutations identify the current spark. offer_spark prepares a draft for human review and refuses to overwrite an existing unfinished draft. pass_spark prepares a reviewable snapshot preserving context and credit; it does not secretly send anything. The demo captures the actual public build in Chrome with native WebMCP enabled. It uses real getTools and executeTool calls, not an injected mock registry. Its example is explicitly synthetic: the real-world experiment has not been run. How we built it React, TypeScript, vinext and Vite; native document.modelContext tool registration; browser-local persistence; Cloudflare Workers-compatible hosting. Human forms and agent tools share one room-state model. The public source is MIT licensed. No paid model service is required by the application. Challenges and what we learned The hard part was making human purpose and agent reach genuinely share a working surface. We replaced canned next-step outcomes with real contribution forms, separated capability intentions from observed results, prevented stale handoffs after edits, and validated persisted rooms before reuse. Registration and storage failures are visible rather than silently presented as success. What we are proud of Twenty domain tests, TypeScript, scoped lint and production build passed. Actual native browser tool calls, the complete human contribution flow, reload persistence, mobile layout and unauthenticated public access were checked. A spark can now move from perception to a testable question and a portable learning trail while keeping its origin visible. These checks do not establish a real-world growth effect or a security boundary against unrestricted browser automation. What is next Durable multi-user rooms, authenticated participants, cross-device persistence and actual invitation delivery. The optional Companion extension is secondary, not SPARK's purpose. The center remains human: help what people notice become useful, and help people become more capable, connected and able to contribute. title: TechPulse
pitch: Tech news, events and hackathons — one feed for humans, one set of WebMCP tools for their AI agents.
about_excerpt: Tech news, events and hackathons — one feed for humans, one set of WebMCP tools for their AI agents. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Everything happening in tech right now — the news, the events, the hackathons — is scattered across dozens of separate sites, RSS feeds and mailing lists. Meanwhile, the WebMCP Challenge asked a question we couldn't stop thinking about: what changes when a website stops being something an agent has to guess its way through, and starts being something an agent can actually use? TECHPULSE started as a UK-focused discovery platform for tech news, events and AI hackathons — one feed instead of thirty tabs. Once WebMCP entered the picture, the obvious next step was: don't just build a good site for humans, build the same site so a person's AI agent can search it, save things to it, and act on it, using the exact same data and logic the human UI uses — no separate "bot API," no scraping. What it does TECHPULSE aggregates live tech news (30+ RSS/Atom feeds plus arXiv), live tech events (open conference/event datasets), and live hackathons (Devpost + UK hackathon listings) — no API keys required. You can browse, filter, search, bookmark and get a natural-language assistant to answer questions like "what's closing soonest?" On top of that, we registered a WebMCP tool layer (document.modelContext.registerTool) exposing ten tools — search_news, search_events, search_hackathons, global_search, get_trending_and_closing_soon, ask_techpulse_assistant, list_saved_items, save_item, remove_saved_item, open_item — so an agent in Chrome (WebMCP flag) or ChatGPT's in-app browser can do everything a human can: find a hackathon closing this week, bookmark it, and hand off to the human to actually register, by navigating the tab there itself. How we built it Next.js 16 (App Router, Turbopack), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4. A DataProvider layer wraps each live source in unstable_cache with a bundled fallback dataset, so a flaky feed never breaks the site. A single lib/queries.ts module owns all filtering/search/sort logic, and it's shared by both the Next.js pages and the /api/* JSON routes. That last part turned out to be the key architectural decision: the WebMCP tools don't reimplement any of TECHPULSE's logic — each execute() handler just calls the same /api/* routes the browser UI calls. The agent-facing layer is a thin, honest wrapper over the human-facing one, not a parallel product. For state the tools needed but the API doesn't have — bookmarks and navigation — we bridged into the existing React store (useStore(), localStorage-backed) and useRouter() through a ref kept fresh via useEffect, since registerTool has no "update" method — you register once per tool and live off a stable bridge object instead of re-registering on every state change. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is brand new. There's no @types package yet, and the imperative API details (JSON-Schema inputSchema, execute vs. older handler naming, unregistering via AbortSignal rather than a dedicated method) needed to be pulled from Chrome's developer docs directly rather than assumed from training data. Bridging an evolving browser API into React without fighting the rules of hooks. An early version wrote to a ref during render to keep the tool bridge "fresh," which trips React's react-hooks/refs lint rule — the fix was moving that write into its own effect that runs after every render, and registering the tools themselves exactly once on mount. Data compliance. Aggregating from Devpost's undocumented public API and Google News search sits in a genuine grey area (their ToS technically restricts automated access, even though the endpoints are unauthenticated and widely used by similar tools). We kept every listing linking back to its official source, dropped Eventbrite entirely (their ToS explicitly forbids scraping), and added a clear "independent tool, not affiliated" disclaimer — the standard aggregator posture, not a loophole. What we learned That a good WebMCP integration isn't about bolting an agent API onto a site — it's a forcing function for good architecture. Because TECHPULSE already had a clean separation between data, query logic and presentation, exposing that logic to agents took one new module and one new component, not a rewrite. We also came away with a much more concrete feel for what "agent-native" actually means in practice: tools with real JSON Schemas and readOnlyHint/destructiveHint annotations, not just another chat window bolted onto the page. What's next A signed-in backend (the Prisma schema is already written) so save_item persists across devices, exposedTo-scoped tools for embedding TECHPULSE's search inside other agent-native sites, and a submit_listing tool so an agent can propose a hackathon or event on a user's behalf. title: Pluno - WebMCP for anything
pitch: A collectively-built WebMCP registry for any website.\nBrowser extension injects tools; Agents automatically build missing tools, which are reviewed and then made available to everyone.
about_excerpt:
A collectively-built WebMCP registry for any website.
Browser extension injects tools; Agents automatically build missing tools, which are reviewed and then made available to everyone.

 How it works 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most websites don’t expose WebMCP tools yet, so agents repeatedly figure out the same interfaces. We built Pluno WebMCP for Anything to turn that repeated work into a shared tool registry. 

 What it does 

 A Chrome extension injects the existing tools for each website.
Codex uses the available tools to complete the task. If the tools are not sufficient, codex builds a reusable tool while completing the task, then submits it to Pluno for review. Approved tools become available to everyone. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Codex's built-in browser doesn't support extensions 
 Codex via Chrome doesn't support WebMCP
-> Made it work via workarounds (injecting as separate Pluno object in page context), but we're really looking forward to both of these being supported to make it work natively. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Time reduction of >80% for several tasks we tested.
Example task (finding getaways on Airbnb): 

 
 Normal codex: 6m 22s 
 Codex with Pluno WebMCP - first run: 7m 35s (completing the task + building the necessary tools) 
 Codex with Pluno WebMCP - second run: 1m 3s (completing task via available tools) 
 

 What we learned 

 Security is crucial, but ChatGPT really helps for this:
We added a Sol-based review of tool suggestions in the backend, and with extensive penetration testing we weren't able get any tool definitions approved that had unintended side effects. 

 What's next for Pluno - WebMCP for anything 

 
 Submit plugin to marketplace 
 Push for native support of WebMCP for external browser, and extension support for native Codex browser. 
 Run agents on popular websites to warm up the tool registry. 
 Improve the tool-building guidance, harden the security of the tool review. 
 Add measures against tool explosion (too many tools for too specific things)

title: BeatForge for Beatsaber
pitch: BeatForge uses WebMCP to let people and agents co-create Beat Saber maps: humans set intent, agents configure and review, and only humans certify playability.
about_excerpt: BeatForge uses WebMCP to let people and agents co-create Beat Saber maps: humans set intent, agents configure and review, and only humans certify playability. Like Comment Story Updates Interface for people/agents Generated beatmap for Tame Impala's Is It True Inspiration I'm a top ranked player in Beatsaber and I got tired of playing the same tracks over and over again. Beat mapping sits between music, interface design, and safety engineering. A mapper has to hear a song, decide how its energy should move through space, and check hundreds of technical rules. I built the BeatForge Beat Saber level-generation pipeline alone. In my own testing, MCP access reduced generation setup and iteration time to roughly one-tenth of my previous manual process. I estimate a roughly 100x improvement in consistency and usable output quality compared with that earlier workflow. These are my project observations, not a controlled industry benchmark. What it does BeatForge is designed for any full-length song that the user owns or has permission to use. The complete mastered track is uploaded locally as an MP3, WAV, OGG, FLAC, M4A, or MP4. The public WebMCP connection has a separate rights-safe preview path. It can find metadata, album artwork (which it then takes the color palette of the artwork and applies it to the level environment) , and a permitted short preview of about 30 seconds. That preview is only for discovery and the browser demo. It is not a full-recording downloader. Complete level generation uses the user's full local audio file. The agent can read studio context, find song metadata, apply a mapping plan, start generation, review timing and safety results, and record human playtest evidence. It cannot claim that it played the map. Human headset judgment remains essential. How we built it FastAPI handles full audio uploads, background jobs, progress events, validation, packaging, and the local Beat Saber workflow. The analyzer converts the full song to a 44.1 kHz integer-sample timeline. Demucs is used for audio separation. BeatForge uses the htdemucs_6s model to separate the song into drums, bass, guitar, piano, vocals, and other stems. This helps identify which musical layers drive each section. Full-mix timing consensus still has to pass strict timing gates, so stem analysis never hides uncertain timing. The generator independently creates Easy, Normal, Hard, Expert, and Expert+ maps. It checks hand reach, saber paths, recovery, collisions, walls, bombs, lighting, and structural validity. A generated chart remains a playtest_candidate until a human completes VR and fresh sight-read checks. The WebMCP layer registers eight typed JSON-Schema tools through document.modelContext.registerTool. The interface displays tool activity, mapping state, album artwork, generation status, and safety results. The public GitHub Pages demo uses a synthetic groove so judges can test the collaboration loop without copyrighted audio or local setup. I spent a full week running BeatForge in local reinforcement-learning environments. Each environment stepped through a beat grid while exposing Demucs-separated stem energy, audio features, red and blue hand kinematics, difficulty targets, and lookahead context. A PPO policy selected idle or note poses for each hand. Rewards encouraged onset alignment, musical energy, readable density, natural flow, and safe two-hand coordination. Penalties covered repeated cuts, insufficient recovery, handclaps, saber-path collisions, vision blocks, and other unsafe transitions. These training runs improved candidate search and helped the generator produce more musical and playable patterns before validation. The RL policy could never override the hard safety contract. Deterministic timing checks, map validation, and human VR playtesting remained mandatory before release. The RL implementation is included in skills/beat-saber-mapping/scripts/rl/. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is still experimental, so BeatForge needs to work both with and without native WebMCP support. In supported browsers, it registers its tools. Elsewhere, it remains usable and explains how to enable WebMCP. Another challenge was adapting a local music tool for public judging. The full pipeline depends on local files, model availability, and Beat Saber-specific paths. Demo mode gives judges a complete collaboration loop without requiring that setup. The hardest product decision was defining what an agent must never claim. A chart can pass structural checks and still feel uncomfortable or unsafe in a headset. BeatForge keeps software validation and human playability evidence separate. Accomplishments that we're proud of Agents can now change a real mapping plan through typed operations instead of fragile UI guesses. People see those changes immediately and can accept, reject, or revise the direction. The activity panel makes the collaboration inspectable. We are also proud that the WebMCP work preserved BeatForge’s existing safety behavior. Timing uncertainty, mapping failures, and missing human evidence remain visible. The repository now includes the WebMCP implementation, browser tests, setup instructions, an MIT license, and a deployment definition. What we learned WebMCP tool descriptions are part of the product experience. A useful schema tells an agent what an operation means and tells the person what will change. Demucs showed me that source separation can provide better evidence about which musical layer should drive a phrase, while full-mix timing verification remains necessary. What's next for BeatForge for Beatsaber Next, I want agents to compare mapping plans, explain why sections failed safety gates, and turn human headset notes into structured revision requests. Longer term, BeatForge should feel like a rehearsal partner. The person brings taste and physical knowledge. The agent tracks decisions and helps turn a musical idea into a chart that someone can actually play. title: AgentDesk
pitch: A capability-virtualization runtime that gives WebMCP agents the right tools at the right time—with human approval, receipts, and rollback for consequential actions.
about_excerpt: A capability-virtualization runtime that gives WebMCP agents the right tools at the right time—with human approval, receipts, and rollback for consequential actions. Like Comment Story Updates Agent Desk Inspiration WebMCP gives websites a direct, typed way to work with agents. But a production application may contain dozens or hundreds of operations. Publishing all of them at once creates a flat, expensive tool surface, makes selection less reliable, and places dangerous actions beside harmless reads. AgentDesk started from a simple question: what if the WebMCP tool registry behaved like a task-aware interface instead of a static API dump? What it does AgentDesk is a capability-virtualization and governance runtime for WebMCP applications. The Meridian Ops demo contains 79 internal capabilities across customers, orders, inventory, shipping, billing, support, and reports. The agent initially sees only four bootstrap tools. When it describes a task, AgentDesk: ranks the catalog against the task and current application context; dynamically registers up to five relevant, typed WebMCP tools; retires stale tools while leaving structured tombstones for clients with cached tool lists; explains unavailable actions and suggests what can make them possible; separates reads, ordinary writes, and consequential actions; returns approval-required immediately for consequential work instead of leaving a tool call hanging; shows the human an exact before/after preview; executes only after human approval and re-checks state at commit time; returns durable receipts describing what actually changed; supports reviewable multi-step plans, idempotency, verification, rollback, and human reconciliation when an outcome cannot be proven. Guided execution keeps the agent and person in the same application: tool calls navigate to, reveal, and highlight the affected object while the structured result remains authoritative. A Baseline mode exposes the full catalog so judges can compare the two approaches using the same tasks and data. Why WebMCP is essential This experience depends on the page and the agent sharing one live application context. AgentDesk registers tools directly with document.modelContext ; the browser page owns capability state, approval UI, and the visible business data. A server-only MCP integration cannot provide the same shared attention, dynamic page-scoped registry, or approval card beside the exact value being changed. The result is a collaboration model that was difficult before: the agent can move quickly through structured operations while the human sees the affected state, governs consequential decisions, and receives proof afterward. How we built it The judged path is a TypeScript SDK, @agentdesk/webmcp , with no backend, database, model API, or external runtime service. A document-lifetime runtime owns the catalog, deterministic router, availability checks, policy engine, approvals, plans, audit events, receipts, and persistence. A single ToolSurfaceManager publishes capabilities through the WebMCP adapter; React only observes runtime state and renders the product experience. Dynamic retirement uses abort signals and tombstone tools. A stable invoke_capability gateway covers clients whose discovery lags behind registry changes. Evidence is detached and frozen at system boundaries. Idempotency claims occur before dispatch, and any post-dispatch uncertainty becomes an explicit indeterminate state rather than a fabricated success or safe retry. We also built a real-browser P0 harness that exercises native registration, same-turn dynamic tools, retirement, stale calls, re-registration, typed execution, approvals, and compatibility behavior. Challenges The hardest work was not registering a tool—it was making stateful tool lifecycles honest under retries, reloads, stale client snapshots, approval delays, partial failures, and interrupted rollback. We repeatedly tested the boundaries where a system is tempted to overclaim: whether a write actually landed, whether a rollback truly restored prior state, whether evidence can be mutated, whether a repeated call can execute twice, and whether a benchmark accidentally rewards AgentDesk by construction. Those failures now have explicit domain states and regression tests. Accomplishments A working, WebMCP-native SDK rather than a one-page integration A complete operations product spanning seven business domains Task-scoped dynamic tool registration over a 79-capability catalog Human approval with visual diffs and post-action receipts Governed multi-step plans exposed through WebMCP Guided execution that keeps human attention aligned with agent actions A reproducible Baseline-versus-AgentDesk benchmark Live validation in the Codex in-app browser and Chrome 152 with WebMCP enabled An open-source MIT-licensed repository and static public deployment What we learned The registry itself can be an interaction surface. Registering, retiring, and rewriting capabilities based on task and state gives an agent clearer affordances than another layer of prompting. We also learned that governance needs more than a confirmation modal: it needs explicit acting identity, execution-time re-checks, idempotency, evidence, and a truthful representation of unknown outcomes. What's next AgentDesk can become an adoption layer for complex web applications: generated capabilities from existing application schemas, runtime-configurable routing, durable cross-session reconciliation, application adapters, and a browser extension that helps legacy sites expose governed WebMCP capabilities. The same model applies beyond operations software to editors, design tools, IDEs, and admin platforms. Built With playwright pnpm react typescript vite vitest webmcp Try it out webmcp.agentsdesk.dev webmcp.agentsdesk.dev github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Amein Eskinder OSMAN AHMED Luc Mwansa Like Share this project: Updates Amein Eskinder started this project — Sep 03, 2026 12:45 PM EDT
video_transcript_excerpt: AI agents can operate websites, but giving them every available tool creates confusion, risk, and unnecessary context. Agent desk turns web MCP capabilities into governed workflows. It reveals only the tools relevant to the current task while keeping consequential actions under human control. Here, a crew is stranded aboard Asteria. The agent discovers the mission state and prepares one rescue plan. Reserve oxygen, assign the drone, reroute power, and launch. These are real staged operations, not a description written by the agent. Agent desk derives the proposed changes from the application's own state. Nothing launches until a person authorizes the complete plan. After approval, every operation executes once, is verified, and produces evidence. The mission completes and the crew is recovered. The rescue interface is only one demonstration. The same agent desk runtime works inside an ordinary business application without changing its governance model. This application contains 79 capabilities. For Alice Johnson's shipping request, agent desk routes the task and exposes only five relevant tools. The agent finds Alice's unshipped order, confirms that she paid an $18 shipping fee, and proposes a refund. Because the refund changes customer and financial state, execution stops at a visible approval boundary. The human sees the exact impact before deciding. After approval, agent desk performs the refund once and verifies the result against live application state. The final evidence connects the operation to its consequences. Shipping is refunded, the customer receives an $18 credit, and the invoice becomes partially refunded. This governance also improves efficiency. The baseline exposes 79 tools and 28,894 bytes of schemas. Agent desk uses five tools and 3,776 bytes. 93.7% fewer tools and 86.9% less schema. Agent desk makes browser agents focused, observable, and safe enough to trust.

title: PixelPlace
pitch: Create exact, game-ready pixel art with an agent, directly in your browser through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Create exact, game-ready pixel art with an agent, directly in your browser through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Lantern Pond Garden PNG Spritesheet export example of "Star Whale Drift" GIF GIF Moon Jelly Bloom Loop GIF Star Whale Drift GIF GIF Void Portal Blossom GIF GIF Ink Sea v2 by Fable GIF PixelPlace UI PixelPlace Pixel art that is source code—built for people and agents to make together. Inspiration Generative image models can create beautiful pictures, but they do not guarantee an exact 32×32 grid, a locked palette, hard pixel edges, or animation frames that line up. Those are not optional details for game assets. A program can guarantee them. I already had PixelCraft, a small vibecoded language and compiler for describing pixel art as source code. The WebMCP Challenge gave me the reason to turn that engine into something more ambitious: a shared creative surface where an agent handles structure and precision while a person remains the art director. What PixelPlace does PixelPlace is a browser-based pixel-art Studio with nine native creation tools, plus a landing-page WebMCP tool that guides first-time agents into the workspace. A typical collaboration is intentionally simple: A person asks for a sprite, scene, icon set, tileset, or animation in ordinary language. The agent discovers the tools directly from the page and reads a language guide generated from the compiler's own documentation. It checks its draft without changing the canvas, then applies only code that compiles. The person judges the real artwork and requests changes. The agent rereads the live source—including any human edits—and revises the same canvas. The result can be exported as PNG, animated GIF, a game-ready sprite sheet, or editable PixelCraft source that can be reopened in the Studio. During our final test, I asked Codex for a game-ready animated mimic chest. It produced a clean sixteen-frame sprite. I noticed that its lid felt detached and two one-frame effects looked confusing. Codex read the live program, rebuilt the lid around visible hinges, removed the effects, compile-checked the revision, and updated the canvas. That small exchange captures the product: the agent supplied speed and exactness; the person supplied taste. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets an agent operate the website’s real creative engine. The model does not need to be embedded in PixelPlace, and PixelPlace needs no account, API key, quota, database, or backend. The page exposes its capabilities; the user’s agent brings the intelligence. Without WebMCP, the Studio remains a normal local pixel editor. With WebMCP, the agent and person can work on the same visible, undoable document. Every tool call appears in an activity feed, so the collaboration is observable rather than mysterious. How we built it PixelPlace is built with Next.js 15, React 19, and TypeScript and deployed on Vercel. The PixelCraft lexer, parser, compiler, interpreter, renderer, PNG/GIF exporters, documentation, and diagnostics all run client-side. The Studio registers nine stateful tools through WebMCP’s imperative API, while the homepage registers a discovery tool that opens the Studio. They cover compiler-generated guidance, draft checking, applying and reading programs, coarse canvas inspection, frame control, example discovery, and local exports. Tool schemas and descriptions are designed to encourage a safe check_program → set_program workflow, so a broken draft never replaces working art. What was new during the challenge The PixelCraft compiler, renderer, stdio MCP adapter, and 58-program gallery existed before the submission period. That prior work ends at commit 57f6f8b from August 19. Starting with commit 06124af on August 26, after the submission period opened, me, Codex and Claude built: the nine-tool Studio WebMCP surface, browser registration layer, and landing-page discovery tool; a fully client-side, stateless architecture replacing the earlier server/API-key flow; the shared Studio interface, activity feed, undoable agent workflow, validated .pc import, and PNG/GIF/sprite-sheet export flow; browser exports of the compiler documentation and lexer; the homepage's live source-code replay and the Challenge-focused product story; end-to-end browser fixes discovered only through testing real WebMCP sessions. Challenges and lessons WebMCP tool results are JSON, so a tool cannot return the rendered image to the agent. We created describe_canvas , which returns a coarse text map, palette, painted bounds, and coverage. That is enough for an agent to catch structural mistakes without pretending that text is vision. The person looking at the canvas decides whether the art actually looks good. Structural correctness and artistic judgment remain deliberately separate. We also learned that page-native tools must be self-explanatory, cheap to validate, and safe to retry. Compiler-derived documentation prevents drift, draft checking avoids destructive iteration, and reading the live document prevents the agent from overwriting human edits with stale state. Final thoughts This competition has been a lot of fun, WebMCP has so much potential and I can't wait to come up with more projects and ideas utilizing it! This story was mostly written by Codex, with me editing and changing few things to match my voice and these final thoughts were fully written by me with no AI assistance. I used AI voice for the video as well as my English pronunciation isn't the best. Best regards and thank you for the fun competition. - Roni Lämsä Built With codex html5 next.js node.js react typescript vercel webmcp Try it out pixelplace-web.vercel.app pixelplace-web.vercel.app pixelplace-web.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Roni Lämsä Solo dev from Finland Like Share this project: Updates Roni Lämsä started this project — Sep 01, 2026 06:12 PM EDT

title: Agent Studio
pitch: AI agents edit. Humans stay in control.
about_excerpt:
AI agents edit. Humans stay in control.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 We wanted to explore how AI agents could help with creative work without taking control away from the creator . This inspired us to build Agent Studio, where AI can perform editing tasks and suggest changes while humans approve important creative decisions. 

 What it does 

 Through WebMCP, the agent can interact with the video editor to:
🔍 Inspect projects and understand the current editing state
✏️ Modify captions and caption styling
⏱️ Adjust scene durations
🎬 Search real stock footage based on the video's content
💡 Propose visual changes to improve the edit
Human-in-the-Loop
The key idea behind Agent Studio is controlled autonomy.
AI agents can handle repetitive editing work, but consequential visual changes aren't applied blindly. Instead, the agent presents proposed changes for human approval.
This keeps the creator in control of the final creative decisions while allowing AI to handle tedious production task.
The agent operates the tools. The creator controls the outcome. 

 ## How We Built It 

 We built Agent Studio as a web-based video editor with WebMCP tools that let AI agents inspect projects and perform editing actions. The agent can modify captions, adjust scene durations, search Pexels for relevant stock footage, and propose visual changes. A human approval layer ensures important changes are reviewed before they are applied. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was making AI interactions with the video editor reliable while keeping humans in control. We also had to handle real-time WebMCP tool calls, stock footage search, and ensure consequential edits required approval instead of being applied automatically. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We built a working environment where AI agents can interact with a real video editor through WebMCP while keeping humans in control. We're especially proud of combining agent-powered editing, real stock footage search, and human approval into one collaborative workflow. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that AI agents can be powerful creative collaborators when they have structured tools and clear boundaries. WebMCP showed us how agents can interact with real creative workflows, while human approval makes that automation safer and more useful. 

 What's next for Agent Studio 

 We plan to: 

 Add more WebMCP editing tools for transitions, audio, effects, and layouts.
Support multiple specialized agents working together on a project.
Improve the approval system with side-by-side previews and edit history.
Add smarter stock-footage recommendations based on each scene.
Enable creators to save, reuse, and share agent workflows.

title: MG Guide | Agent-Native Follow-Up
pitch: A WebMCP-native meeting follow-up workspace where agents prepare action, state, and draft artifacts while people keep final send authority.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-native meeting follow-up workspace where agents prepare action, state, and draft artifacts while people keep final send authority.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Platform context: the competition surface stays bounded while MG MCP and the broader MG Guide platform remain adjacent context. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Current WebMCP experience: ACTION → STATE → ARTIFACT turns meeting context into a human-reviewed follow-up draft. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP build architecture: ChatGPT browser discovers 3 native tools backed by a bounded synthetic MG Guide workflow. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Platform context: the competition surface stays bounded while MG MCP and the broader MG Guide platform remain adjacent context. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Current WebMCP experience: ACTION → STATE → ARTIFACT turns meeting context into a human-reviewed follow-up draft. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP build architecture: ChatGPT browser discovers 3 native tools backed by a bounded synthetic MG Guide workflow. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Platform context: the competition surface stays bounded while MG MCP and the broader MG Guide platform remain adjacent context. 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 MG Guide | Agent-Native Follow-Up 

 MG Guide started from a practical problem we see in relationship-driven sales: the meeting may happen virtually, but the real work often starts after the call ends. 

 Someone still has to remember what mattered, connect the conversation to the right relationship, determine the next step, and prepare a thoughtful follow-up. That work matters because relationships are personal, but it can also become repetitive and fragmented across meetings, notes, CRM systems, inboxes, and different tools. 

 We have been building MG Guide as part of a broader effort to create a governed AI workspace that can work behind salespeople and sales teams without taking judgment or relationship ownership away from them. 

 
 Our goal is simple: let AI help prepare the work, while the person remains responsible for the relationship. 
 

 For The WebMCP Challenge , that idea took on a new form. 

 What WebMCP changed for us 

 Before this challenge, MG Guide already had a meeting follow-up workflow and the broader foundation we had been building around meeting context, relationship context, follow-up planning, and governed AI workflows. 

 WebMCP gave us a new way to think about how an AI agent could interact with that experience. 

 Instead of building a separate interface just for an agent, or asking an agent to interpret buttons and page structure, we could let the website itself clearly expose the actions that were safe and useful for an agent to perform. 

 That led us to a simple model: 

 
 ACTION → STATE → ARTIFACT → HUMAN CONTROL 
 

 The agent can help process the meeting, understand the current follow-up state, and retrieve the prepared follow-up draft. The person still reviews the result and decides what happens next. 

 That became one of the most important lessons from the project: 

 
 The website itself can become a shared workspace between a person and an AI agent. 
 

 What we built for the challenge 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, we meaningfully extended the existing MG Guide experience with a browser-native WebMCP layer. 

 The live MG Guide page now exposes exactly three capabilities to a compatible browser agent: 

 
 ACTION — process the meeting follow-up 
 STATE — understand where the follow-up currently stands 
 ARTIFACT — retrieve the draft that was prepared 
 

 This creates one shared experience instead of one interface for the person and another interface for the agent. 

 When everything is clear, MG Guide can prepare a useful follow-up draft. 

 When the relationship is unclear or ambiguous, the system stops and asks for human review instead of guessing. 

 That distinction matters to us. In relationship-based work, a good AI system should know not only when it can help, but also when it should stop. 

 
 Agent can prepare. Only a person can review and send. 
 

 What we learned 

 This challenge changed how we think about agent-native software. 

 The page can be the shared contract 

 One of our biggest takeaways was that an AI agent does not always need its own separate interface. 

 The same page a person uses can expose a small, intentional set of capabilities that an agent can understand and use. That keeps the human and the AI working from the same experience instead of creating two disconnected versions of the workflow. 

 Safe refusal is part of good design 

 We intentionally built an ambiguous-contact scenario into the demo. 

 If MG Guide cannot confidently connect the meeting to the right relationship, it does not continue automatically. It stops. 

 That may look like less automation, but for us it represents better automation. 

 Trust is especially important when AI is working around relationships, financial conversations, customer information, and follow-up communication. 

 Human control should be designed in from the beginning 

 We did not want “human in the loop” to be a sentence we added at the end of the project. We wanted it reflected in the experience itself. 

 The agent can prepare context, state, and a draft, but the final customer-facing action remains with the person. 

 That boundary became one of the clearest principles of the project. 

 Browser behavior matters more than we expected 

 We also learned that making an agent-capable web experience reliable is not only about the AI. 

 Browser behavior, tool discovery, origin boundaries, caching, and how the page is served all affect whether the experience actually works for a person and an agent together. 

 That pushed us to think more seriously about the browser as part of the agent environment, not simply as a screen. 

 Where this is leading us 

 The WebMCP Challenge also surfaced a bigger idea for the future of MG Guide and the governed AI ecosystem we are building around our sales teams. 

 This challenge primarily demonstrates an outbound pattern: 

 
 MG Guide exposes safe capabilities from our governed environment to a browser agent. 
 

 But we are increasingly interested in the opposite direction too. 

 What happens when a salesperson finds useful information somewhere else on the web and wants to intentionally bring that information back into their governed AI workspace? 

 For example: 

 
 useful research before a meeting; 
 a company website; 
 an article relevant to a relationship; 
 publicly available information about a business; 
 information a salesperson intentionally selects while preparing for a conversation. 
 

 We do not want that to become uncontrolled web scraping or automatic memory collection. 

 Instead, we see an opportunity for a governed intake experience . 

 The person could intentionally select information, identify why it matters, and bring it into MG Guide with context about where it came from and what it is allowed to inform. 

 That information could then become evidence available to the governed AI environment without automatically becoming permanent memory or authorizing an external action. 

 WebMCP and a future Chrome extension companion 

 This is also where a browser extension becomes interesting to us. 

 On websites that support WebMCP, we would prefer to use the structured capabilities the site intentionally exposes. 

 But many websites will not expose WebMCP immediately. A future Chrome extension companion could provide a user-controlled bridge. 

 The salesperson could choose the information they want to bring into MG Guide, explain what they want to use it for, and send it through the same governed intake boundary. 

 Conceptually: 
 WebMCP-enabled website
→ structured information selected through the site's declared capabilities
→ governed intake
→ MG Guide
 Website without WebMCP
→ information explicitly selected by the person through a browser extension
→ governed intake
→ MG Guide
 
 In both cases, the important part is not simply collecting more information. 

 The important part is preserving: 

 
 where the information came from; 
 why the person brought it in; 
 what workflow it is allowed to support; 
 whether it should remain temporary or become durable context; 
 and what actions still require human approval. 
 

 That is becoming an important part of how we think about building AI for real sales teams. 

 The larger vision 

 MG Guide is ultimately one piece of a broader governed AI ecosystem we are building to work behind salespeople and sales teams from a virtual perspective.

title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ .
