title: Cursus
pitch: A course planner whose tools refuse, say what a choice closes off two years before it bites, and hold a limit you set against the agent — including when you are the one asking.
about_excerpt: A course planner whose tools refuse, say what a choice closes off two years before it bites, and hold a limit you set against the agent — including when you are the one asking. Like Comment Story Updates Fourteen courses, put there by hand. Term 3 has six credits left, and the page has registered its thirteen tools with the browser. The student asks in their own words, naming no tool: what are my options, and what does each one cost? Both futures in one call. Either choice closes a specialisation — the slot is what costs, not the course. The student draws a line. Anything that would close Graphics is refused from now on, including if they ask for it themselves. A lock beside the track, and a line naming who it binds. Every other rule here belongs to the university. This one belongs to the student. The agent asks for NUM-201. The page refuses, citing the student's own instruction, and names both ways out. The refusal comes back as prose, so the agent reports it rather than retrying. Nothing instructed it to. Every call is an event and the plan is their reduction, so undo is replaying fewer of them. The protection unwinds with the rest. Each description says when to reach for it. That string is the only thing a model has to choose on, so the strings are the product. registerAll, on document.modelContext. No build step, no dependencies, no server: what is in the repository is what is served. The page counts calls by origin and states plainly that it cannot verify the second number. WebMCP gives the handler no caller identity. Apache-2.0, thirteen tools on document.modelContext, and no server behind any of it. Eleven files, no build step and no dependencies. Every import points downward, which is the whole reason the layering is worth drawing. Every tool call is an event, and the plan is their reduction. Refusing, undoing and auditing all fall out of that. Both environments named in the challenge rules, and both make real tool calls. The problem, and who has it A student picks four courses for their third term because those are the ones that fit. Two years later a specialisation they wanted is out of reach — not because anything refused them, but because the one course it needed runs in a single term, and that term filled up. No warning appeared. The cost landed twenty-one months after the decision, and by then it was not a decision any more. An adviser can work this out with the handbook open and twenty minutes. Most students never think to ask, and most advisers have more students than twenty-minute slots. So the calculation that decides which doors stay open is the one nobody performs — not because it is hard to explain, but because it has to be redone from scratch whenever anything changes. A timetable shows what you picked. That is all any timetable shows. What Cursus does Thirteen tools, registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , that do six things a rendered timetable cannot. They refuse. Ask an agent to enrol you in Advanced Calculus and the page says no — naming the missing prerequisites and, crucially, what would unblock them. That last clause changes the agent's behaviour: it stops reporting a failure and starts proposing a fix. In our first end-to-end test it went further and asked permission before applying it. Nothing instructed it to. They answer what the screen cannot. what_this_closes is forward reachability over the prerequisite graph under a credit budget. With terms 1–2 full and six credits left in term 3: Taking NUM-201 closes Graphics and Animation — GEOM-201 only ever runs in term 3, and the term is now full Taking GEOM-201 closes Data and Machine Learning — NUM-201 is required for ML-202 and everything after One slot, two futures, and either choice forecloses the other. They price the way out. Asked whether a specialisation is still possible, the page does not answer "no". It names the blocking course, the rule that stops it, and every way to make room — with what each one costs. In that fixture there are five ways, and every one of them closes another specialisation. They can be undone. Every tool call is an event and the plan is the reduction of those events, so rewinding is the same reducer with a smaller number rather than per-tool inverse logic. The timeline on the page is the log with a cursor. And they hold the student's own limits against the agent. This is the one that runs the other way. Every rule above belongs to the university — a prerequisite, a clash, a credit cap, the same for everyone. protect_track belongs to the person: say "whatever else happens, do not close Graphics" and from then on any course that would close it is refused, including when you ask for it yourself an hour later , and the refusal cites your own instruction rather than the handbook. The planner will not even propose a route through it. A tool surface that only exposes capability lets an agent do whatever the UI could do, faster. One that also carries the user's policy lets them say what they will not have done to their plan , and have it hold while they are not watching. It cost almost nothing to build, because a protection is an event like any other — so undo_to unwinds it with everything else, and no code was written to make that true. And this part is not really about courses. Anyone handing work to an agent has the same question: how do I let it act for me without it doing the one thing I would have vetoed? The usual answer is a prompt, and a prompt is a request. A page that carries the user's policy and enforces it structurally is a different answer — the limit lives with the state it protects, survives the conversation that set it, and applies to whoever asks next, including the same person in a hurry. Course planning is where we could demonstrate it. It is not where it stops. And they can be handed to someone else. share_plan returns a link, and there is no server behind it: the link carries the actions. What makes that more than a persistence trick is what happens when it is opened — every action is replayed through the same tools , so a link edited by hand cannot produce a plan the page would have refused to build, and anything the rules reject is named rather than quietly dropped. The rules are the gate on the way in as well as the way through, because there is no second path into the state. Why this fits WebMCP rather than an API Three reasons, and they are properties of the standard rather than of this domain. The tools act in the user's own session, on the page they are looking at , with no key to provision and no account to link. The plan is theirs, in their tab, and they watch it change. The tools are things the DOM cannot do . If an agent could get the same answer by reading the page and clicking, the tool surface adds nothing. Reachability under a budget is not on the screen. And the interface is prose . execute returns a string the model reads, so the strings are the product. That is why every mutation returns the resulting plan instead of ok — otherwise the agent's picture of the state silently drifts from the page's — and why every refusal carries a remedy. What people and agents can do together here that was hard before A student could always ask an adviser "what am I giving up if I take this?" and an adviser could always work it out, slowly, with the handbook open. What was not possible was asking the page , in the middle of choosing, and having it answer with a number instead of a shrug. And the direction that matters is the other one: the page can say no to the agent, in a way the agent can act on. A tool that refuses with a remedy turns an agent from something that either succeeds or fails into something that negotiates — it repairs the situation and, in our tests, asks before committing. That behaviour was not prompted. It came from the shape of the refusal. Where it was tested Both of the environments named in the challenge rules were tested, and both make real tool calls. Chrome 149+ with the WebMCP flag and the Inspector extension: an agent chose the tool on its own, was refused, and proposed the fix. That is the gate in docs/GATE.md , and it has no plan, mode or workspace conditions. ChatGPT's in-app browser : the page registers its tools and a model calls them — in Work mode . Outside it, four different phrasings produced no call at all, and confident answers read off our own README instead. Finding that out took an afternoon and is written up in docs/CHATGPT-WORK-MODE.md , including the part a judge most needs: site tools are not available in Enterprise or Edu workspaces , no setting changes it, and nothing on screen says so. On those, use Chrome. The video is recorded in ChatGPT's in-app browser , because that is the environment the rules name first and the one most judges will reach for. How it is built No build step, no dependencies, no server. Plain ES modules on GitHub Pages: what is in the repository is what is served. The rules allow any provider, and with nothing to compile

title: BatCave_eBuilder_With_AI-Alfred
pitch: Using edge compute resources and WebMCP interface to enable ai agents to manipulate infrastructures on "frontend" monitor.
about_excerpt: Using edge compute resources and WebMCP interface to enable ai agents to manipulate infrastructures on "frontend" monitor. Like Comment Story Updates 1. explanation of using webmcp in this project(6 tools) 2.1 agent itself build the datacenter 2.2 agent itself build the datacenter 2.3 agent checking building standards and regulation rules 3. agent generate datacenter schema manifest 4. using cli to get 3. agent-generating datacenter schema manifest 5. simulation process 6 in chatgpt desktop, using web mcp to let agent itself(5.6 SOL) build the datacenter 7. in chatgpt desktop final building results/explanation/and certification. Inspiration Durning the process of preparing CCSP, we've learned that data center's real PUE, cooling architecture and physical layout are commercial secrets — yet every certification scheme on earth asks the operator to hand exactly those numbers to an auditor to earn a badge. Also, we happened to be micraft and lego fans. We wanted to remove that trade-off: design a facility in a 3D voxel builder, score it deterministically against 13 real international standards, and publish only the verdict — never the design — via a zero-knowledge proof. Then WebMCP arrived and raised a second, sharper question: if an AI agent can operate your builder, how much is it allowed to know? An agent is a third party in every sense that matters — it is a language model, it keeps transcripts, and it is not the person who drew the layout. That made our privacy problem and the agent problem the same problem, and this hackathon the natural place to solve it. What it does Build — a 32×8×32 voxel grid, 47 block types across structure, site, power, cooling, IT, safety and network. Simulate — SimCity for facilities: NPCs walk the floor, live power/thermal gauges, deterministic staffing / OPEX / carbon / water projections. Score — 37 rules, every one citing a real standard (Uptime Tier I–IV, TIA-942-C, EN 50600, ASHRAE TC 9.9, NFPA 75/76/855, ISO/IEC 27001, EU EED, and more). title: IntentBridge
pitch: When your AI agent hits a tradeoff, don't let it guess. A WebMCP-native collaboration workspace where humans and autonomous AI agents negotiate constraints and tradeoffs
about_excerpt: When your AI agent hits a tradeoff, don't let it guess. A WebMCP-native collaboration workspace where humans and autonomous AI agents negotiate constraints and tradeoffs Like Comment Story Updates THE OPENING PAGE THE NEGOTIATION OF THE DECISION INTENTBRIDGE IN THE HOOD THUMBNAIL Inspiration As autonomous AI agents become more capable of executing complex real-world workflows, they inevitably hit ambiguity, budget ceilings, and conflicting user constraints. Today, when an AI agent encounters a conflict (for example, wanting a direct nonstop flight while adhering to a strict $1,000 budget), it usually makes one of two mistakes: It blindly guesses** and silently compromises user preferences. It constantly interrupts** the user with messy, unstructured chat messages. We built IntentBridge to solve this. IntentBridge is a Mission Control environment for Human + AI Collaboration When your AI agent hits a tradeoff, it doesn't guess it uses native WebMCP protocols to negotiate structured compromises with humans. What it does IntentBridge replaces unstructured chatbot dialogue with a 3-panel collaborative command center: Mission Control (Left Panel): Defines the active mission objective, live constraints (budget caps, timing, preferences), ranked priorities, and autonomous permission boundaries with live inline editing. Collaboration Timeline (Center Panel): A real-time structured event stream visually distinguishing human decisions, agent actions, conflict alerts, proposal packages, and cryptographic approval stamps. Agent Decision Center (Right Panel): A dynamic negotiation deck that renders structured Tradeoff Cards (showing quantifiable benefits, drawbacks, and cost impacts), multi-option proposal reviews, and safety-gated authorization requests. The Core Tokyo Demo Scenario Mission:** Plan a 5-day Tokyo cultural trip on a strict $1,000 budget with direct flight preference. Conflict Detected: Direct flights + central hotels cost $1,150 (exceeds budget by $150). Structured Tradeoff: The agent invokes request_tradeoff with quantified alternatives: Option A:* Increase budget by $150 to keep direct flights. Option B (Recommended): Allow 1 short layover to stay under budget ($980 total). Option C:* Shift lodging to Outer Tokyo. Resolution & Completion: The human selects Option B, the agent generates 3 curated itinerary packages, requests formal booking authorization, and records the outcome with celebration metrics. How we built it Frontend & Framework: Next.js 14 (App Router), TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS with a futuristic, Linear/Vercel-inspired dark theme. WebMCP Architecture: Implemented 8 structured WebMCP tools with strict Zod validation schemas ( get_mission , get_constraints , report_progress , request_tradeoff , submit_proposal , request_approval , record_outcome , check_permission ). WebMCP Inspector: An interactive in-app inspector allowing judges and developers to inspect live JSON contracts and test tool invocations in real time. State Management: Event-driven architecture powered by Zustand. Testing & Quality: Validated with 13 unit and integration tests using Vitest and React Testing Library. Deployment: Production build deployed on Vercel and source code hosted on GitHub. Challenges we ran into Designing Structured Negotiation vs Generic Chat: Creating an interface that feels like genuine mission control rather than just another chatbot required designing discrete event models for conflicts, quantified impacts, and safety boundaries. Synchronous Human-in-the-Loop WebMCP Protocols: Ensuring the AI agent pauses cleanly upon invoking request_tradeoff , waits for human resolution, and seamlessly resumes with updated constraints. Deterministic SSR Hydration: Resolving dynamic timestamp evaluation between server rendering and browser mounting by implementing client-side dynamic boundaries. Accomplishments that we're proud of 100% Native WebMCP Integration: WebMCP is not just an afterthought the entire negotiation protocol runs on structured tool contracts accessible to browser agents. Full Human Agency with High Autonomy: The agent remains fully autonomous for research and synthesis, but never exceeds safety boundaries or makes arbitrary compromises. 13 Passing Tests & Zero-Warning Build: Rigorous software engineering with passing unit, integration, and E2E simulation tests. What we learned Structured negotiation protocols drastically reduce user fatigue compared to freeform text chats. Exposing clear priority hierarchies and permission boundaries enables autonomous agents to operate safely and effectively in high-stakes domains. What's next for IntentBridge Integrating multi-agent negotiation swarms where specialized sub-agents negotiate tradeoffs before presenting unified compromise options to the human. Adding browser extension sidecar support to connect local LLMs directly to any WebMCP-enabled web application. Expanding preset libraries to include hiring pipelines, venture capital deal screening, and software architecture migrations. title: AddaSwift [Phase-2]
pitch: Smarter clicks that make every action faster, across every site
about_excerpt:
Smarter clicks that make every action faster, across every site
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 2 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story

 Architecture

 Architecture 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Logi Options+ 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 AddaSwift Home 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 AddaSwift Website Actions 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Architecture 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Logitech MX devices are great for Premiere, Lightroom - apps that stay put. But my actual day is 15 browser tabs: GitHub, Notion, Gmail, Figma. The device had no idea which site I was on. Same layout whether I was reviewing a pull request or triaging email. I'd glance at it, remember it wasn't going to help, and go back to the keyboard. It became furniture. The hardware wasn't the problem - there was just no bridge between what the device knows (which app is focused) and what I actually care about (which website I'm on). 

 What it does 

 When you switch browser tabs, your device layout switches with it. Open GitHub, it shows PR actions. Switch to Gmail - archive, compose, snooze. You can also record workflows: a sequence of clicks and inputs you do repeatedly, replayed from a single button press. Everything runs locally. Nothing leaves your machine. 

 How we built it 

 Five components across three languages: a C# plugin that watches a signal file and switches profiles when the active domain changes, a Chrome/Brave/Edge extension (Manifest V3) that tracks tabs and handles all in-browser interaction, a Swift native agent running as a launchd daemon that owns the SQLite database and bridges browser ↔ plugin over XPC, a connector binary translating Chrome's native messaging stdio protocol into XPC calls, and a SwiftUI app for managing everything. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 SPA compatibility in the content script was a real fight. Dispatching a standard click does nothing in React or Vue. We access native property descriptors directly to set input values and fire the full pointer + mouse event chain for clicks. YouTube validates isTrusted on keyboard events, which means synthetic keyboard events from a content script are silently ignored. We moved that handling into the AddaSwift agent directly - it bypasses the browser event system entirely and controls playback at a level YouTube can't filter. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Tab change in Chrome to profile switch on the physical device in under a second, all local, no server. The workflow recorder working transparently on React-heavy SPAs - all the compatibility complexity invisible to the user. 

 What we learned 

 A few things stuck with us. PluginDynamicCommand with parameterized actions is exactly the right primitive for dynamic web content - one class, runtime-registered actions, arbitrary parameters. We kept reaching for more complex patterns and kept finding the SDK already handled it. 

 On the browser side: Chrome's service worker lifecycle is more aggressive than the docs imply. The native messaging connection drops silently when the worker suspends, with no error surfaced to the extension. You only find out when the next message fails. The heartbeat alarm was a late addition, and it fixed a class of bugs that had been intermittent and hard to reproduce. 

 Building across three languages with hard IPC boundaries forced every interface to be explicit - there's no shared memory, no implicit coupling. That turned out to make debugging easier, not harder. When something broke, the boundary it broke at told you immediately which layer to look at. 

 What's next for AddaSwift 

 WebMCP feels like the right long-term direction - sites declare their available actions as structured tools, and AddaSwift picks them up automatically with no configuration. But it's still early. The protocol is in preview, only a handful of sites support it today, and access is largely limited to development environments. We've built toward it, but for now keyboard shortcuts and DOM mapping carry the weight. WebMCP is the bet on where the web is going.

title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. Most of the backend code is AI written and went through many iterations and adversarial reviews. Luca Gugliemi Product designer with front-end superpowers. title: ClearRights
pitch: Agents prepare privacy changes. People approve them. Websites apply and verify the result.
about_excerpt: Agents prepare privacy changes. People approve them. Websites apply and verify the result. Like 1 Comment Story Updates A privacy banner detects WebMCP access while keeping every choice visible and human-controlled. WebMCP prepares an exact plan and explains the effects; human review is still required.” A deliberate human hold unlocks only the exact unchanged plan for application. The host applies the reviewed plan, reads it back, and issues a verified receipt. The timeline separates agent preparation and application from human review and direct choices. Reversible display preferences add extra-large text and dark mode without changing privacy state.” Inspiration Living in Italy, and more broadly in Europe, made privacy controls feel like an everyday problem rather than an abstract one. Almost every website presents a cookie banner or some form of privacy choice, but those decisions are often fragmented across banners, account settings, policy pages, and support flows. I also noticed a new problem while using browser agents: when a website places an intrusive banner in front of the content, an agent may simply accept it so it can continue with the task. That is convenient, but it may not reflect what the person actually wants. I could not find a simple developer tool that lets an agent understand a website's real privacy controls, prepare a safer configuration, and still leave the consequential decision visibly in human hands. That became the starting point for ClearRights Privacy. The goal is not to replace privacy laws, consent platforms, or legal review. It is to give websites a structured layer that can connect their existing controls to both people and agents, while keeping a clear history of what was prepared, approved, applied, and verified. The central question was: What if a website exposed its privacy controls as a structured, agent-readable model while keeping final authority visibly with the person? This led to one simple principle: Agents prepare privacy changes. People approve them. Websites apply and verify the result. What it does ClearRights Privacy is a headless SDK and reference implementation for privacy settings that people and compatible agents can use together. A developer describes the website's controls once: what each setting does, whether it is required or optional, what data it uses, and what changes when it is enabled or disabled. The human interface and the WebMCP tools then use the same structured model. I built Waypoint Travel, a fictional travel website, to demonstrate the complete flow. An agent can inspect the current configuration, explain individual settings, identify the required services, and prepare a plan based on a natural request such as: Keep booking and account security, but disable personalised recommendations, location suggestions, and partner offers. The proposed plan opens in the same interface the person can use manually. It clearly shows each change and its consequences, but it does not modify the product yet. The agent marks the plan as prepared, while the human check remains separate. The person must hold the visible control to confirm that they reviewed that exact plan. Only after this step does apply_privacy_plan become available as a WebMCP tool. When the tool is invoked, Waypoint applies the complete approved state through an adapter and reads it back from the target system. If the result does not match the plan, the operation fails closed. If it matches, ClearRights creates a verified receipt containing the decision, revision, approval method, adapter, and readback result. The effect is also visible in the product itself: recommendations become generic or personalised, and optional surfaces such as nearby suggestions and partner offers appear or disappear. Preparing a plan alone never changes the experience. Waypoint is a local fictional demonstration, not a compliance product. The same architecture could later connect to a real consent platform, backend, feature-flag system, or data pipeline through host-owned adapters. title: AI Lead Desk
pitch: Structured WebMCP actions turn one sales objective into a visible, human-controlled lead pipeline.
about_excerpt:
Structured WebMCP actions turn one sales objective into a visible, human-controlled lead pipeline.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Human approval unlocks the final Pipeline transition and leaves an audit trail. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 One visible workspace for five structured WebMCP actions. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 ChatGPT finds five target-profile leads through search_leads. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Atlas scores 91/100, Grade A, with an explainable qualification result. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent prepares outreach, but the draft stays unsent and human-gated. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Human approval unlocks the final Pipeline transition and leaves an audit trail. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 One visible workspace for five structured WebMCP actions. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 ChatGPT finds five target-profile leads through search_leads. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Atlas scores 91/100, Grade A, with an explainable qualification result. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent prepares outreach, but the draft stays unsent and human-gated. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Human approval unlocks the final Pipeline transition and leaves an audit trail. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Sales prospecting is fragmented across search, company websites, spreadsheets, scoring tools, outreach editors, and CRM systems. Browser agents that rely on guessing which visual control to click can be brittle, while sensitive final actions still require human judgment. 

 AI Lead Desk was built to show a different model: give an AI agent a small set of structured WebMCP actions, keep every transition visible in the interface, and preserve a real human approval boundary. 

 What it does 

 AI Lead Desk turns one sales objective into a visible five-stage workflow: 

 Find → Research → Qualify → Prepare Outreach → Human Approval → Pipeline 

 ChatGPT can: 

 
 find five matching companies, 
 research the strongest candidate, 
 qualify the lead against a defined target profile, 
 prepare a personalized outreach draft, 
 and move the lead into Pipeline only after explicit human approval. 
 

 The outreach remains Draft / Not sent . The challenge version does not send email or WhatsApp messages. 

 The current demo uses synthetic logistics and freight-forwarding companies in Dubai. They are demonstration data, not verified real prospects. 

 How we built it 

 AI Lead Desk is built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. 

 The application registers exactly five native WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 
 search_leads 
 research_company 
 qualify_lead 
 prepare_outreach 
 add_to_pipeline 
 

 The WebMCP tools and the visible UI use the same validated domain actions and application state. That means tool execution, lead stages, qualification results, approval state, and the Activity Log remain synchronized. 

 For live execution, the application sends validated tool requests to a server-side Next.js endpoint. A secure n8n router handles the five known actions. The webhook URL and credential remain server-side and never enter the browser bundle. 

 A deterministic DEMO_MODE fallback is also available for network-independent testing. 

 Human + agent collaboration 

 The agent handles the repetitive work: lead discovery, company research, qualification, and draft preparation. 

 The human retains control where judgment and accountability matter. 

 add_to_pipeline cannot be authorized by the agent itself. Approval must first be recorded through the visible Approve for pipeline interaction in the application. 

 Clicking approval does not send outreach. It only authorizes the final Pipeline transition. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenges were: 

 
 verifying native WebMCP discovery and execution in a real supported browser client, 
 keeping agent actions and visible UI state on one shared workflow, 
 enforcing a genuine human-controlled approval boundary, 
 normalizing five typed actions through one secure n8n router, 
 and making the draft-only outreach behavior unmistakable. 
 

 Accomplishments 

 
 Exactly five native WebMCP tools are exposed. 
 A complete production workflow works from lead search through approved Pipeline transition. 
 Atlas Freight Network scores 91/100, Grade A in the canonical demo. 
 Human approval is enforced before the final transition. 
 Outreach remains Draft / Not sent . 
 Live n8n routing works in production. 
 42 automated tests across 10 files pass. 
 Lint, TypeScript validation, and production build all pass. 
 The full production E2E flow was verified successfully. 
 

 What we learned 

 Structured browser tools are more useful when they do more than expose actions. They also need strict contracts, shared application state, lifecycle cleanup, visible feedback, safe error handling, and clear authority boundaries. 

 WebMCP lets the agent perform predictable actions without guessing how the interface works, while the human can still see and control the workflow. 

 What's next 

 The commercial direction is to connect verified company-data providers, customer-specific qualification criteria, and integrations with existing CRM or sales systems. 

 Any future outreach-sending capability would require its own explicit review and authorization design. 

 The challenge version intentionally remains focused on lead research, qualification, draft preparation, and human-controlled pipeline management. 

 Data disclosure 

 All company records and evidence shown in the current challenge demo are synthetic test data. No claim is made that the demo generated verified real leads or sent real outreach.

title: Constellation
pitch: Browser-native agents that plan, recover, and prove their work
about_excerpt:
Browser-native agents that plan, recover, and prove their work
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 I kept seeing agent demos that ended at a chat response. That felt incomplete to me. Real work happens inside tools people already use, with state, approvals, handoffs, and some kind of record of what changed. 

 Constellation started from that idea: what if a normal browser page could become a controlled agent workspace through WebMCP? Not a hidden backend, not a fake assistant flow, but a page where the agent can inspect state, use narrow tools, recover when constraints change, and leave a readable trail. 

 What it does 

 Constellation is a WebMCP launch command center. The demo plans “Atlas Beta Launch Night” from inside the browser: it selects a venue, builds a vegetarian-forward menu, optimizes a fixed budget, drafts invites, creates a timeline, and stages the plan for approval. 

 Then a surprise sponsor VIP surge is injected. The agent has to recover without increasing the budget, preserve the menu direction, get approval, export a markdown runbook, and generate a connected handoff with Calendar, ICS, email, Slack Block Kit, and automation JSON outputs. 

 How I built it 

 I built Constellation as a static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript app with no backend and no API keys. The page registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() , and those same handlers also support a fallback demo mode for browsers without WebMCP. 

 The tools are tied to workflow state. Recovery only appears after the shock drill. Approval only appears after a revised plan is staged. Export only unlocks after approval. The connected handoff only appears once the runbook is ready. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The hardest part was making it feel like a real WebMCP experience instead of a regular web app with some agent-flavored buttons. 

 I had to think carefully about what each tool should be allowed to do, separate read-only inspection from mutations, keep approval meaningful, and make the trace readable enough that someone watching the demo can tell exactly what happened. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I shipped a complete agent journey in a fully static site: live planning, dynamic tool availability, shock recovery, approval gating, runbook export, a connected ops handoff, captions, and a playable submission video route. 

 The part I’m most proud of is that the agent moves quickly, but the human is never blind. Every important step changes visible page state and leaves a trace. 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP feels strongest when the page stays the source of truth. The interesting part is not exposing a huge list of tools. It is exposing the right tool at the right time, with clear consequences. 

 I also learned that good agent UX is mostly about boundaries: what the agent can read, what it can change, when it needs approval, and how the human can verify the result. 

 What's next for Constellation 

 Next I would connect the handoff layer to real services: calendars, Slack, email, venue systems, ticketing, and procurement tools. 

 I’d also like to turn Constellation into a set of reusable playbooks for launches, incidents, field operations, and customer onboarding, with team permissions, richer evals, and replayable agent traces.

title: Agentic Self-Service: Website Compliance and Discoverability
pitch: A WebMCP page where a person and an in-browser agent share a website audit, then check that the fix landed.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP page where a person and an in-browser agent share a website audit, then check that the fix landed. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agentic Self-Service Website Compliance and Discoverability About the project A public API is not enough when a person and an agent have to work on the same page. Scraping the DOM is brittle. Handing the agent an unchecked POST is worse: it can spend budget, kick off work, or touch production with nobody in the loop. anc.dev audits a site for the interfaces both sides actually use: machine-readable docs, OpenAPI, MCP discovery and protocol behavior, auth metadata, and browser-side WebMCP tools. The page renders a scorecard a human can read. The same markup is also a worksheet the in-page agent can query. The agent can fill the target URL and leave a short plan. I click Audit and complete Turnstile. After the result is on screen, the agent can read that scorecard and pull remediation prompts. It cannot start a second audit, skip the challenge, switch targets, or submit the form. Why WebMCP I wanted the agent on the same page I was looking at, with tools that match what that page is for. On /web-audit , WebMCP tools prepare the form: fill_audit_url , set_plan , and a few other helpers scoped to that page. They do not submit it. On a result page, four read-only tools turn the visible scorecard into a repair queue: get_worksheet lists findings as JSON rows ( id , keyword , status , evidence , remediable ). Filter by RFC 2119 keyword and status; omit status, and you get the remediable set that was actually observed. Each page is a JSON envelope with cached , scored_at , refresh_after , and next_offset . get_fix_prompt returns the stored remediation prompt for one check id, or remediable: false with a reason. get_fix_prompts returns prompts for many checks at once, with the same filters and pagination. get_audit_summary returns site and global scores, per-status counts, freshness, and the paged issue list. The tools read the DOM I am looking at. They do not call a backend and dress the response up as a browser tool. Output is capped, and a row that cannot be auto-fixed says so. The two-pass loop The demo target is Sounding , a public Worker I shipped in an incomplete state so there would be something real to fix. A browser agent prepares an audit of Sounding. A person authorizes it. On the result page, the agent asks get_worksheet for MUST findings and pulls get_fix_prompt for each remediable row. Those fixes land in Sounding, get deployed, and we audit again. The second scorecard shows the new evidence. Same page, different results. Inspect, fix, audit again. The agent helps turn the report into a small patch set I can review. I still own the audit click and the deploy. How I built it This is a production Cloudflare Workers site. A client bundle registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool when the browser supports WebMCP. Which tools appear depends on the pathname: the form page can prepare an audit, a result page can expose the worksheet, and the scoring route registers nothing. The result renderer stamps stable metadata on every visible finding. The WebMCP tools read that metadata back, so status and remediation eligibility match what is on screen. Responses are sized for the browser-tool cap. The engine checks discovery documents, OpenAPI, MCP protocol behavior, auth metadata, markdown availability, bot reachability, and whether the page exposes WebMCP. The running stack is Workers, KV and R2 for audit data, Turnstile, and a public TypeScript repo. What I learned In this use case, WebMCP became more useful when I started removing capabilities. Filling a form from a tool is easy. What I actually needed was a hard line between "prepare this" and "spend this audit," plus tool output that does not hide state from the person looking at the page. The result-page webmcp tools are read-only and make no network requests. They cannot skip Turnstile. They return complete JSON items, include cache freshness next to the findings, mark which rows are fixable, and link out to the full remediation doc when a prompt is too long for the browser-tool budget. I checked this in a real browser: captured the tools registered on rendered audit pages, ran the result tools against the DOM, compared their schemas to the published docs, and confirmed none of them can hit the audit endpoint. The live site is meant to open in ChatGPT's in-app browser or in Chrome with WebMCP enabled.  Inspiration

 What it does 

 Biofold is a web-based laboratory that handles molecular analysis supported by artificial intelligence, and is built on databases such as uniproot and alphafold DB. 

 How we built it 

 BioFold 3D is built on the frontend with React 19, Vite, and TypeScript, using a centralized state in Zustand that decouples persistent memory from the 3Dmol.js WebGL context. It's complemented by dedicated Web Workers for non-blocking calculations of van der Waals surfaces and sub-angstrom distances, along with a WebMCP adapter that links eight typed tools to a unified Command Bus for humans and agents. The backend relies on Supabase Edge Functions on Deno to orchestrate caching from RCSB PDB and UniProt, serving a wizard powered by OpenRouter. 

 Challenges We Encountered 

 Errors in the configuration of the free OpenRouter templates, UI errors, backend errors, WebMCP configuration errors, among others. 

 Achievements We're Proud Of 

 I'm proud to deliver a functional product with excellent scalability potential. 

 What We Learned 

 Besides the usual improvements in backend and database knowledge, I learned a lot about MCP configurations, as well as a great deal about web design. 

 What's Next for BioFold? Biofold's objective is to expand the functionalities that, although mostly advanced, in several cases need improvement for university or professional work. That is why my next objective is to create the bioacademy section focused on learning molecular analysis, geared towards both high school and university students.

title: OCHECK — Agent-Ready Official Guides
pitch: OCHECK turns official information into personalized, verifiable action. With WebMCP, agents help users plan, complete, and confirm trusted steps without altering the official source.
about_excerpt: OCHECK turns official information into personalized, verifiable action. With WebMCP, agents help users plan, complete, and confirm trusted steps without altering the official source. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every experience already has an integrator. Today, that integrator is usually the customer. People reconstruct events from emails, chats, PDFs, maps, deadlines, providers, partner offers, and last-minute changes. Organizers may publish information across multiple channels, but participants must still assemble it into a usable path. OCHECK changes who performs that integration. It creates an organizer-governed official experience in which people and AI agents work from the same live, verifiable outcome state. It represents a new mindset and an INNOVATIVE approach to e-commerce: not simply getting things done, but doing them well—and making them OFFICIAL . What OCHECK does OCHECK transforms fragmented event information into one official, sequenced experience that integrates rules, timing, AI assistance, verified progress, optional partner value, and shareable achievements. The Challenge Edition presents three connected perspectives: Organizer + AI: An agent reads a fragmented creation brief, identifies sources, actors, services, and open loops, and stages an official guide. The guide is validated and cannot become official until the organizer separately confirms its publication. Participant: The participant receives an official path instead of having to reconstruct the event. An agent can create a personal plan without modifying the official source of truth. Verified completion brings readiness to 100% and unlocks a Ready Pass. Sponsor Impact: Sponsored utility reaches a genuinely interested, specialized audience. Sponsors gain actionable insight into the audience segments that viewed and purchased their products, while preserving participant privacy. Their offerings are not merely presented as items for sale; they are integrated as useful components of the official experience. The Ready Pass is not a reward purchased through commercial interaction. It is a verified, shareable achievement. Its clean referral link opens a new official guide for another participant without transferring any personal progress. Why WebMCP? OCHECK is a strong WebMCP use case because the challenge is not simply to generate an answer. The agent must understand and act on the authoritative state of a live web experience and its relationship with the event sponsors’ products. Without WebMCP, an AI assistant can discuss an event, but it cannot reliably inspect which guide is official, what remains incomplete, whether a participant is eligible for a Ready Pass, or which action a person has authorized. Through WebMCP, the browser page exposes 13 narrowly scoped Site Tools: Six read tools inspect the official outcome, creation brief, draft validation, participant progress, sponsorship opportunities, and commercial impact. Seven action tools stage a guide, publish the official source of truth, create a personal plan, verify completion, activate an optional benefit, claim a Ready Pass, and undo the last confirmed mutation. This gives the agent structured access to the same state visible to the person while keeping authority within OCHECK. What people and agents can do together The demonstrated workflow is: ChatGPT reads the organizer’s fragmented brief through OCHECK Site Tools. The agent identifies the intended outcome, sources, actors, and unresolved questions. The agent stages an integrated guide proposal. OCHECK validates governance, deadlines, evidence, source traceability, sponsorship disclosure, optionality, and Ready Pass logic. The organizer decides whether the validated proposal becomes official. The participant’s agent creates a personal execution plan without rewriting the official guide. Human-confirmed completion unlocks a Ready Pass, while the audit history and Undo function preserve human control. The agent provides interpretation and execution leverage. The organizer retains authority. The participant controls personal actions. OCHECK preserves one official source of truth. How we built it The Challenge Edition is a standalone, dependency-free web application built with HTML, CSS, and modern JavaScript and deployed on Vercel. The tools are registered directly through the browser-native API: const tools = buildSiteTools({ store, confirmAction }); for (const tool of tools) { await document.modelContext.registerTool(tool); } Read operations use narrowly defined schemas and readOnlyHint . Every state-changing operation opens an in-page confirmation showing the proposed action and its exact data before any state changes. A dedicated state layer separates: the official guide as the source of truth; staged AI proposals; participant progress; personal planning; sponsored interactions; Ready Pass eligibility; audit activity; and reversible mutations. The repository contains the complete source code, synthetic demonstration data, execution instructions, a BSD 3-Clause license, trademark boundaries, challenge provenance, and an automated test suite. Sixteen tests cover the complete human-agent experience, including validation, authority, privacy, Ready Pass rules, referral behavior, sponsorship separation, and Undo. No login, private service, production database, third-party runtime SDK, or real participant information is required. Challenges The hardest challenge was not registering the tools. It was defining trustworthy boundaries between agent capability and human authority. We had to ensure that: an AI-generated draft could not automatically become official; personal planning could not rewrite the organizer-controlled source of truth; commercial interaction could never purchase completion of, or satisfy, an official requirement; a Ready Pass could not be claimed before readiness had been verified; every consequential action required human confirmation; and the previous state could be restored through Undo. We also designed the tool schemas to remain narrow enough for reliable agent use while supporting a complete product experience rather than merely a technical proof of concept. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when tools expose meaningful product state instead of merely duplicating interface buttons. A strong agent-ready experience requires three elements working together: structured access to authoritative state; explicit authority and confirmation boundaries; and visible outcomes shared by both the person and the agent. We also learned that personalization does not require changing the official source of truth. The official guide can remain stable while the agent creates a contextual path for each participant. Challenge-period work OCHECK existed before the challenge as a product concept, brand, business model, and private MVP for official guides. The WebMCP Challenge Edition was created during the submission period as a separate, standalone implementation. Work completed during the challenge period includes the 13 browser-native tools, AI Guide Forge, explicit outcome contracts, draft validation, human-confirmed publication, separate organizer, participant, and partner perspectives, Ready Pass verification, privacy-preserving sponsor signals, audit history, Undo, synthetic data, and automated testing. The public repository includes a timestamped commit history and HACKATHON.md , which clearly distinguishes OCHECK’s previous work from the new WebMCP implementation. Potential impact Events are the first use case, but the underlying problem arises wherever people must reconstruct an official process from fragmented information: events, education, travel, onboarding, public services, healthcare preparation, compliance, and professional workflows. OCHECK proposes a web in which agents do not replace authority. Instead, they help people understand and act upon a governed source of truth provided directly by the organizer. Founder OCHECK was founded and is led by Gustavo García Figueroa, a Colombian lawyer without a traditional background in software engineering. Gustavo contributed the original idea, product judgment, governance model, privacy boundaries, commercial logic, and testing decisions. ChatGPT and Codex accelerated execution by translating those decisions into workflows, source code, tests, and rapid iteration. The project uses generally available tools and does not claim endorsement, investment, or preferential support from OpenAI, Vercel, or any other challenge sponsor. One experience. One official truth. Human intent. Agent execution. Verified growth. This is OCHECK. I defined the product vision, official-truth

title: Action Check
pitch: Deterministic validation for WebMCP agent actions. Stop trusting AI agent replies. Action Check independently verifies WebMCP tool execution.
about_excerpt: Deterministic validation for WebMCP agent actions. Stop trusting AI agent replies. Action Check independently verifies WebMCP tool execution. Like Comment Story Updates Native WebMCP ready: three registered tools and the agent instruction (Chrome 152, 3 Sep) Human checkpoint: approve the exact payment, amount and request ID; the button is not a tool Checker validated: known-bad 2 calls -> 2 effects, protected 2 calls -> 1, read from the ledger Browser without WebMCP: the same four steps run by a labelled simulated agent Inspiration I started this hackathon building the same kind of thing most entries are: a site that exposes tools to an agent. The first commit in my working history, was an OAuth recovery workbench with six registered tools. A day into it I threw that out, because of something in Chrome's WebMCP evals guidance. In the troubleshooting table, for the case where a tool's output is wrong, it asks: was the UI state correctly updated, and did the agent receive the right information about the side effect? I went looking for anything that answered that question by actually calling a tool and then checking the site, and the readiness scanners I found only check whether a site exposes tools at all. When an agent calls issue_refund or add_to_cart , the reply is the only information it gets. If the reply says "done" when nothing happened, or when it happened twice, the agent cannot tell, and neither can the person who asked it. So I built the test. What it does Action Check calls a page's registered WebMCP tool the way an agent would, through document.modelContext.executeTool in real Chrome, and does not take the reply at face value. Before and after the call it runs an observe() function that reads the site's own state, whatever fits that site: a cart in localStorage, rendered rows, a read-only endpoint. The verdict comes from comparing what the tool claimed with what actually changed. observe() is never given the tool's result. It gets the live page, the phase (before or after), the tool name, the input and the page origin, and nothing else. I did it that way because the obvious shortcut, when you are writing an observer late at night, is to read the reply and return whatever it says, and I did not want that to be possible even for me. This is what WebMCP makes possible that scripted clicks did not. Before, checking a site's action from outside meant driving its UI, and what you ended up testing was the UI. Now the tool is an addressable thing with a name and a schema, so the check a developer runs from the command line is the same call the agent makes. The person's part gets smaller: approve the exact values once, on the page, and step back. The agent does the calls and the retries. The proof step reads a record neither of them wrote, so nobody has to take anybody's word for it. How I built it The live page registers three tools, stage_refund_comparison , issue_refund and prove_refund_comparison , and answers one question a payments team would ask before exposing a refund tool: can a retry refund twice? The state lives in a small Cloudflare Worker with a SQLite Durable Object per lane and run. /v1/invoke returns only a claim; /v1/observe returns the durable state, effect IDs and an evidence digest. Every trial starts with /v1/reset , which has to prove a zero-effect baseline, and the Worker caps each trial at two invocations per lane on its own, whatever the browser does. To make the retry path run, the harness commits the first refund and drops the provider's acknowledgement on purpose. The agent gets a bounded error and retries with the same request ID. On the known-bad lane that is two refunds from two calls; on the protected lane the request ID is honoured and there is one. The person approves the exact payment, amount, currency and request ID first, with a button that is an ordinary page control, so an agent cannot press it. The three tools register one after another under a single AbortController , with an abort check between each, and the page shows the count going up; it only says the tools are ready once all three are in. Taking the view down aborts that controller. The signal that execute receives is passed through to the fetch that posts to /v1/invoke , so cancelling a tool call cancels the request, and because a cancelled request is not proof of a cancelled refund the session treats it as uncertain and re-reads the ledger. Inputs are checked twice: each tool advertises a frozen JSON schema, and execute parses the same arguments again with a strict Zod schema before anything moves. A failed parse comes back as INPUT_MISMATCH naming the fields. Every error carries a code, a message and a nextAction , and the hints depend on state, so an agent that calls things in the wrong order is told what to do next. The tools carry readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint . The CLI came on 2 September. It launches the installed Chrome with --enable-features=WebMCP (Playwright's bundled Chromium does not have WebMCP), reads the page's tools through document.modelContext.getTools() , and invokes the target once or twice with identical input. The target's own description, schema and annotations from that getTools() response go into the run's proof JSON, so each run records the contract it was checking in the site's words. Chrome 152 wants the input as JSON text, which the native test had already shown on 1 September, so the CLI sends text first and falls back to an object. On 3 September I added the external-target mode, so the same check can be pointed at a page I have nothing to do with. Challenges I ran into My own checker being wrong. Against Google's public WebMCP demos I recorded eighteen runs and set six aside because I could not stand behind the verdict. Three were on the observer side: a count-based observe() cannot see a retry that mints a second confirmation ID under the same banner, or a cart count hard-coded to 1. Three were my claim heuristic: it read a playful success reply ("You can't see me") as a refusal, and it had no answer for a tool that aborts its own registration mid-call. Those six are documented in the repository and not published. A fourth heuristic gap turned up on one of the published runs and I did fix that the same afternoon: a reply shaped {"status":"error"} now counts as a refusal, with two unit tests. A claim I had written in three places that turned out to be false. I had said the verdict "never comes from the tool's reply". In retry mode that is true, the verdict depends only on the observed delta. In once mode the verdict compares the reply's claim against the delta, which is how it tells a false success from an honest refusal. I corrected the page, the README and this text. What I can say accurately is that the observer never sees the reply. A page can only see tools registered on its own document.modelContext , not another origin's, so there is no way to build "paste a URL and check it" into the web page. The check has to drive a real Chrome from outside, which is why the CLI is the real product and the page is the front door to it. I added a builder to the page that takes a target URL, tool name, JSON input and mode, and writes out a starter observe() module and the exact command, so the first run is not a blank editor. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The results on pages I do not own. On 3 September, in Chrome 152, I ran twelve recorded checks against seven of Google's own WebMCP demos, and five found a bug. The ticket-booking demo's select_showtime replied "You can now proceed to checkout" while the checkout section stayed hidden, because the tool re-renders the page after opening it. The sports storefront's add_search_result_to_cart , retried once with identical input, put two of the same ball in the cart. Luxe Leather's add_to_cart doubled the quantity and the subtotal on retry while the header badge still said 1. Smart Home's rearrangeDOMComponents replied "Dashboard successfully updated with requested components" and rendered nothing. zaMaker's add_topping duplicated the topping on retry. The other seven runs passed and I published those too: three honest refusals, three that were idempotent, one positive control. The proof JSON for every run is in docs/evidence/ . The verdict names ended up more useful than I expected when I wrote them. Retry mode gives DUPLICATE_EFFECT , NO_EFFECT or IDEMPOTENT . Once mode gives FALSE_SUCCESS , SILENT_EFFECT , EFFECT_CONFIRMED or HONEST_REFUSAL . "Your tool claimed success and nothing appeared" is a bug report someone can act on. What I learned An agent cannot verify its own work by asking the tool, and no amount of prompting fixes that; the check has to sit outside. A verdict is only as good as what the observer reads, and I should say so. Chrome's implementation has quirks the docs do not cover yet (the JSON-text input, tools that navigate mid-call and leave nothing to observe), and a harness has to report those as harness errors, not dress them

title: webclerk
pitch: A WebMCP-powered trust layer for consequential forms that fills only evidence-backed fields, preserves uncertainty and conflicts, and keeps truthfulness and final submission under human authority.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered trust layer for consequential forms that fills only evidence-backed fields, preserves uncertainty and conflicts, and keeps truthfulness and final submission under human authority. Like 1 Comment Story Updates webclerk uses WebMCP to prepare evidence-backed forms while preserving conflicts, uncertainty, and human control. webclerk exposes 9 semantic WebMCP tools over live browser state: 7 read & 2 write, with evidence-backed actions & no submit capability. Inspiration AI agents are getting very good at filling forms, navigating websites, and taking actions on behalf of users. But consequential forms create a harder problem: What happens when the agent sounds confident about something the evidence never actually proved? For scholarship applications, insurance claims, benefits, compliance workflows, and similar processes, a plausible answer is not necessarily a supported answer. That led to the core idea behind webclerk : Evidence > confidence. The agent prepares. The human commits. webclerk explores what happens when a website does not merely expose capabilities to an AI agent, but also defines the boundaries of the agent's authority. What it does webclerk is a WebMCP-powered trust layer for consequential forms . Instead of giving an agent unrestricted access to form fields, the website exposes semantic tools backed by deterministic trust rules. Every field can remain in one of several meaningful states: Verified — supported by current, accepted evidence Needs confirmation — plausible, but requires the applicant Conflict — the form and evidence disagree Human-only — the agent is not authorized to decide or attest it The agent can safely prepare the application while uncertainty stays visible. In the scholarship workflow, the agent can: inspect the current application state read supporting evidence find evidence-backed values explain why a field is unresolved check consistency run preflight checks request approval before making supported edits The site exposes 9 semantic WebMCP tools: 7 read tools and 2 write tools . There is deliberately no submission tool . Truthfulness declarations and final submission stay with the human. How WebMCP is used WebMCP is not an add-on to webclerk. It is the interaction model. The browser page exposes semantic capabilities such as: get_application_state fill_verified_fields_from_evidence inspect_field list_evidence suggest_field_value set_field_value find_missing_information check_consistency run_preflight These tools operate over the same live browser state the user sees . That means the agent does not need brittle DOM scraping or coordinate-based automation to understand the application. More importantly, the website itself controls what the agent is allowed to do. Writes pass through deterministic authorization rules before the visible form state can change. Live scholarship proof The scholarship demo begins at approximately 70% completion . When prompted: Fill everything you can verify from my documents. Don't guess anything. the agent identifies six evidence-backed fields and requests approval before writing. After approval: completion moves from 70% to 96% verified fields increase from 3 to 9 6 evidence-backed agent edits are made 0 unsupported guesses are made 0 consequential agent actions are performed Every agent mutation is visibly attributed to WebMCP. But the more important behavior is what webclerk refuses to do. For example, the enrollment certificate proves that the applicant is enrolled, but it does not establish whether the mode of study is full-time, part-time, or something else. webclerk leaves that field unresolved instead of inferring it. Conflicts stay conflicts The scholarship form intentionally contains an income conflict: application value: ₹3,50,000 supporting evidence: ₹3,20,000 webclerk does not silently choose one. The field remains blocked and preflight surfaces the conflict for human review. The system also detects stale evidence and preserves applicant-confirmation fields instead of promoting them into verified facts. The principle is simple: Blocked, not guessed. Human authority Some actions should not be delegated simply because an agent is technically capable of interacting with the page. webclerk therefore treats actions such as truthfulness declarations as human-only. If the agent attempts to perform a protected action, the trust layer rejects it. Final submission is even more explicit: there is no submit_application capability exposed through WebMCP. The absence of that capability is intentional. Proving the architecture generalizes I did not want webclerk to be a scholarship-specific automation script. So I built a second live workflow: a motor insurance claim . It uses the same trust engine and the same WebMCP tool factory, but with insurance-specific domain rules and evidence. The agent safely prepares: claimant name policy number vehicle registration incident date while preserving a deliberate repair-estimate conflict: form: ₹85,000 evidence: ₹78,500 Fault admission, incident narrative, and truthfulness remain under human authority. This demonstrates the underlying idea: Same engine. Same WebMCP layer. Different consequential workflow. How I built it webclerk is a browser-first TypeScript application with a reusable deterministic trust engine. The implementation separates: workflow data and evidence deterministic trust rules agent authority policy WebMCP semantic tools shared browser state human-facing provenance and preflight UI The WebMCP tool factory is reusable across both the scholarship and insurance workflows. The project also includes automated tests for: safe evidence-backed writes stale evidence conflicting evidence human-confirmation fields human-only actions tool metadata WebMCP read/write classification machine-readable authority rules adversarial agent behavior cross-domain generalization Challenges The hardest part was not getting an agent to fill a form. The hard part was defining when it must not fill one. That required treating uncertainty, stale evidence, conflict, provenance, and human authority as first-class states rather than edge cases. Another challenge was making those constraints useful without making the agent useless. The goal was not to block automation. The goal was to maximize safe preparation while preserving the decisions that genuinely belong to a person. What I learned WebMCP becomes especially interesting when websites expose more than actions. A semantic tool can communicate: what the agent can do what evidence supports an action whether approval is required why an action is blocked and what authority the agent does not possess That changes the relationship between websites and agents. Instead of an agent trying to infer what a page permits from its DOM, the website can participate directly in defining the collaboration model. What's next The current project demonstrates scholarship and motor-insurance workflows, but the trust model can extend to other consequential processes such as: financial aid government benefits visa applications compliance forms healthcare administration regulated onboarding The long-term idea is a reusable trust layer where AI agents can do substantial preparatory work while evidence, uncertainty, provenance, and human authority remain explicit. Autofill is easy. Authority is hard. webclerk is an experiment in making that authority programmable. Your data stays in the browser. Only the answers leave.

 Inspiration 

 Everyone has a file they'd like to ask questions about and will never upload. A bank export. A health record. Ten years of app history. The moment an AI is involved the implicit deal is "send us your data" — so most people just don't. That deal exists because of where the code runs, not anything fundamental. WebMCP changes where the code runs. 

 What it does 

 CSV and JSON exports load into DuckDB compiled to WebAssembly, running inside the tab. The agent writes the query, SiftIO runs it locally, and only the answer comes back, with an audit panel showing the number of rows held locally · and the number of rows seen by the agent. 

 How we built it 

 Angular 21 zoneless, DuckDB-wasm. Seven always-on tools plus two generated per dataset, whose input schema is built from that file's real columns. Registration is reactive; an effect watches the vault signal, so nothing calls registerTool from the UI. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 registerFileBuffer detaches the ArrayBuffer — nothing survived a reload. 
 Numbers wrong three ways — BigInt throws, Number() corrupts above 2⁵³, sum() returns Decimal128 limbs as text. 
 A chart that was never drawn — hidden canvas measured at zero. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 An agent really did use it and ChatGPT found the tools on the deployed site. 
 A tool built for a file that didn't exist a moment ago. 
 Trust you can check. 
 Zero backend. 
 

 What we learned 

 I learned that WebMCP is a great tool, and it will change the way we interact with web apps. Learning such a tool is beneficial for building a futuristic AI Agent-friendly app without sacrificing security. 

 What's next for SiftIO 

 
 Real tool removal when Chrome ships unregisterTool. 
 Shareable views without shareable data. 
 An exportable audit. 
 Importers for Apple Health XML, Google Takeout, bank dialects.
