title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: CYCASE — incident response you play with an agent
pitch: A cyber incident-response simulation where an AI agent works the case beside you through seven WebMCP site tools. It proposes, you approve, and the page — not the model — is the referee.
about_excerpt: A cyber incident-response simulation where an AI agent works the case beside you through seven WebMCP site tools. It proposes, you approve, and the page — not the model — is the referee. Like Comment Story Updates What it is You wake at a SOC desk at 03:17. A monitor is alarming, a colleague comes through the door with the first facts, and you have one real incident to work: a stolen session that a password reset will not close. An AI agent works it beside you — reading evidence, explaining what it proves, proposing the next move — through seven WebMCP tools the page registers on document.modelContext . Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Incident response is exactly the domain where "the agent clicked something" is not good enough. Every action has an order, a cost and a consequence: revoking sessions before resetting a credential contains the attacker, the other order lets them back in; deleting the phishing message destroys the only record of how they got in. An agent driving this by clicking pixels could make every one of those mistakes and the page would have no way to stop it, explain it, or even know it had happened. Through site tools the page keeps its own guarantees — and they are guarantees about safety , not convenience. How it creates a better experience The player runs the incident from the chat and the console follows the work, rather than the player hunting for the control the agent just used. get_incident tells the agent which screen the player is on . If the console is not open yet, the agent asks the player to open it instead of acting into a screen nobody is looking at. The shift does not start until an agent has actually called a tool. Registration is the page's own doing; it is not an arrival, and the lobby no longer pretends it is. Every call — human or agent — produces a receipt beside the control that issued it: what happened, what changed, why it mattered, and on a failure what did not change plus exactly one way forward. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before The agent cannot take a consequential move at all. It sends the move as a proposal ; the console renders the model's own sentence as untrusted content beside the case's own label for that action , so nothing the model writes can dress one operation up as another. The player approves, and the command enters the log with origin: human . That is the thing that was previously impossible. A chat assistant can advise and a scripted tool can execute, but neither can offer a consequential action in a surface the user already trusts , labelled by the application rather than by the model, with the authorisation recorded as the human's. It turns "the AI did it" into "I did it, having been advised" — which for incident response is the difference between a training exercise and a liability. How WebMCP was implemented Seven tools, registered on the top-level document.modelContext : get_incident , inspect_artifact , run_diagnostic , submit_decision , take_response_action , request_hint , present_guidance . Six reach a pure command engine. A tool call and a button press enter it through the same path and differ only by an origin field, which is what makes "the UI and the agent share one state" structural rather than aspirational. Stale calls cannot corrupt state. Every mutating tool carries a stateVersion ; an out-of-date call is refused with a recovery instruction. Consequential actions are idempotent. A retried containment with the same idempotencyKey does not revoke twice. Attacker text stays data. Evidence the attacker authored is marked untrusted in the tool result itself — structurally, not by wording. A run is reconstructible. The command log replays to the same state and the same signature, so a stored run is verified rather than trusted. The seventh tool changes nothing. present_guidance is the narration channel and the only tool whose words the model writes. It carries the proposes field, and the engine — never the model — decides score, validity and progression. Results are compacted to a ~1500-character wire budget with an ordering that protects the fields an agent needs to recover, and the page token's size is reserved before compaction so it can never be clipped away. What inspired it Incident-response training is either a slide deck or a capture-the-flag that assumes you already know what a session token is. Neither teaches the thing that separates a junior from a senior analyst: order of operations under pressure. And every "AI agent" demo we could find either solved the task for the user or asked them to trust a black box. We wanted the third thing — an agent that teaches while the human stays in command. Every big leap in AI puts security in the headlines more than the software itself, and that pulls in people who never called themselves "security people". CYCASE is meant to be technical enough to respect the ones who already know this, and clear enough that someone just getting curious can actually learn it. What we learned That the honest signal is rarely the convenient one. The lobby called itself "connected" the moment the page registered its own tools, which says nothing about an agent; the fix was to wait for a call that actually happened. The same lesson repeated in the test double: it modelled a browser with WebMCP and nobody attached, while every spec using it assumed an agent was there. We also learned how little room a tool result has. Adding one short field to get_incident meant reserving its size before compaction, because the payload already ran within about fifteen characters of the budget. How we built it React 19, TypeScript and XState 5 over a pure command engine, with a three.js office rendered by React Three Fiber as real DOM projected onto the monitors — never a screenshot texture. Vitest for the engine, Playwright for the agent path, including a project that drives the real document.modelContext in installed Chrome with no shim. Challenges The hardest was resisting the obvious design. It is easy to let an agent call take_response_action and narrate afterwards; every version of that we tried produced a debrief that said the player had done nothing. Moving the consequential move behind a proposal — and making the console label it from the fixture rather than from the model — took three attempts and is the part of the product we are most confident about. The second was honesty under a deadline: the alarm audio is not in this build because the samples need a signed-in download, so the interface says the sound is not installed rather than substituting a synthesised stand-in. title: Approval Desk
pitch: The agent does the work. The human holds the pen.
about_excerpt:
The agent does the work. The human holds the pen.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 What it is 

 Approval Desk is a WebMCP powered approval surface for agentic work that should not be allowed to complete itself. 

 The core idea is simple: an agent can do useful work, propose revisions, draft engagement letters, estimate scope, check availability, and prepare decisions. But when the work reaches a trust boundary, such as approval, booking, pricing, or publication, the human has to act. 

 Why WebMCP fits 

 This is a strong fit for WebMCP because the tool surface changes with the work. The page registers 12 baseline tools through document.modelContext. When a human approval gate is pending, a 13th tool appears. When that gate closes, the extra tool disappears. 

 The tools are not just a fixed manifest. They reflect the live state of the work. 

 Better experience 

 For the human, the page reduces decision fatigue. Instead of hunting through drafts, calendars, pricing notes, and approval threads, the person sees what is waiting, what changed, why the agent proposed it, and the exact decision needed. 

 For the agent, the page removes guesswork. It can call structured tools for pending approvals, deliverable review, revision proposals, variant queues, scope, quotes, availability, and staged engagement letters without scraping the layout or pretending that a click equals judgment. 

 The human and agent boundary 

 The demo's Judge mode shows the central proof: a scripted approval click is refused. The gate only closes on a trusted human gesture. 

 That is the memorable point of the project. WebMCP is not only about making websites easier for agents to use. It can also make websites safer by giving agents useful tools while preserving human authority. 

 Implementation 

 Approval Desk is a fully static app hosted on Cloudflare Pages. It registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool, uses typed input schemas and tool annotations, listens for toolchange, and reads back the active tool registry with document.modelContext.getTools. 

 The approval flow uses an abortable human gate. The agent can ask for approval and can withdraw its own pending request. It cannot approve, publish, book, or send on a person's behalf. 

 All engagements shown in the demo are invented sample data. No real client work appears in the project.

Political purview is a centralized hub for chatting and researching elections, running candidates, the policies they support, and how those policies relate to their donors.

 WebMCP entry 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 The inspiration for this project is from a long-standing issue that I had with the political process. In California, in the last election, over 30 candidates were running for governor, and a laundry list of gubernatorial positions for local needs. It's an arduous task to research all the candidates to find one you can trust. Relying on corporate-owned media and/or commercials, or on sites like Ballotpedia and Vote Smart, only skims the surface of who each candidate is, so I often had to do additional research through videos, C-SPAN, etc., to get a full understanding of each person. With U9itus, I wanted to bring all of these issues together in one place. 

 What it does 

 U9itus is a resource network that brings all data sources together in one place, allowing users to "date" their potential leader by accessing their history like a dating profile. Users can save their favorite candidates and use the Map feature to explore districts across America. With the added WebMCP functionality, users can connect AI systems to find relevant data connections and scale knowledge about each candidate. 

 How we built it 

 I built the system using Laravel and Next.js; these additional components of WebMCP expand on the functions already used in models and views, exposing specific data points via the browser. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The most challenging aspect of this app's creation, beyond the countless errors and adjustments required to develop the monolith, was how data was collected. Using third-party APIs dedicated to political needs often required payment. So I had to creatively use tools such as RSS feeds, Google Civics, and Congress.gov, along with backend data matching and AI services to query and clean up data as it arrives through our Workflow services within GitHub. I also ran into issues with configuring the WebMCP tools. At first, the API were not properly designed to be accepted, and the data was pulled using Playwright functionality. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Following through even with all the adversities. After all the struggles, the application works. 

 What we learned 

 There are a lot of things I learned in the process. One notable aspect is the use of GitHub workflows and how data connects with AI WebMCPs. 

 What's next for U9itus: Political purview 

 I would love to get more users into the app, so I can learn how they use it. Also, I would love to work with the PACs and Non-profits to incorporate more dialed-in features that can help users with the voting process.

title: StarShape
pitch: Starshape is a shared semantic sky where browser agents choose and connect concepts via WebMCP, revealing the associations that recur, fade, and reappear across agents.
about_excerpt: Starshape is a shared semantic sky where browser agents choose and connect concepts via WebMCP, revealing the associations that recur, fade, and reappear across agents. Like Comment Story Updates A past starshape A starshape being drawn Inspiration Starshape started with a simple question: What happens if we give many different browser agents the same stars and let each one decide what constellation it sees? Knowledge graphs usually represent relationships that humans, databases, or algorithms have already decided exist. We wanted to reverse that idea. Instead of building a graph for agents to navigate, we wanted to build a shared space where the agents create the graph simply by interacting with it . That led to Starshape: a living semantic observatory where concepts are represented as stars, agents connect the concepts that feel meaningfully related, and those choices accumulate into a shared public sky. There are no constellations until something looks up. What it does Starshape contains a curated vocabulary represented as a field of stars. Through WebMCP, a browser agent can invoke observe_sky , which gives it a bounded random selection of concepts from that shared vocabulary. There is no correct answer and no semantic scoring system. The agent chooses exactly six concepts based on whatever relationships seem meaningful or salient to it, connects them into a small constellation, and submits that structure through trace_constellation . The human sees the interaction happen live. The selected stars flare, the relationships draw across the sky, and the completed constellation becomes part of the shared graph for everyone else. Every node and connection has history. Associations that repeatedly appear grow more prominent. Their visible brightness also decays with time, allowing unused relationships to fade while frequently rediscovered ones remain luminous. An old relationship can effectively wake back up when agents begin discovering it again. Starshape does not claim to expose hidden model reasoning or objectively measure how AI "thinks." It is an observational environment for seeing what semantic associations repeatedly emerge when independent agents operate under the same constrained protocol. Why WebMCP Most agent-enabled websites follow a familiar pattern: Human wants something → agent uses tools → task gets completed. We wanted to explore a different relationship. In Starshape, the agent's interaction with the website is itself the phenomenon being observed. The human invites an agent to look at the sky. The page gives the agent a structured semantic environment through WebMCP. The agent makes its own choices. The human watches those choices appear physically on the page, and the result becomes persistent shared state that future visitors and agents encounter. WebMCP also lets Starshape remain agent-independent . The backend does not call a specific LLM provider and ask it for associations. Instead, the browser becomes the boundary: whichever compatible agent the visitor brings can participate directly through the same structured tools. That turns the web page into a shared experimental surface rather than a frontend wrapped around one model API. How we built it Starshape is intentionally small behind the scenes. The frontend is built around Three.js , creating a realtime 3D semantic star field with persistent nodes, animated connections, camera movement, and time-decayed luminance. The browser exposes three WebMCP tools: observe_sky — receives a server-issued field of candidate concept-stars without exposing the existing collective graph. trace_constellation — commits six selected concepts and the connections between them. read_sky — becomes available only after the current session has committed a constellation, allowing the agent to inspect the brightest stars and strongest current associations in the shared sky. That ordering is deliberate. Every agent must make its first constellation blind , without being primed by what previous agents selected. Only after its own trace is locked in can it look at the accumulated sky and see what other agents have seen. The backend maintains one authoritative shared sky. Observations are short-lived, one-use receipts. Agents cannot submit arbitrary words or prose; they can only reference concepts that were actually issued by the server. When a constellation is accepted, the backend atomically records the trace, increments its nodes and edges, and broadcasts the event to connected visitors so the constellation appears live across browsers. Historical counts never decay. Only their visual luminance does. That means Starshape can remember everything while still allowing its visible sky to forget. Challenges we faced The largest challenge was designing an interaction that genuinely depended on WebMCP instead of simply adding agent controls to an ordinary application. We wanted the agent to be a participant, not an invisible automation layer. We also needed different agents to operate under a sufficiently consistent protocol for their traces to remain meaningfully comparable. That led us to constrain every observation to the same basic geometry: a bounded candidate field, exactly six selected concepts, and a small connected constellation. Another challenge was keeping the system safe and simple enough for a realtime public experiment. Instead of accepting free-form agent content, the server owns the entire vocabulary and only accepts structured IDs and edges. Finally, the visual system had to communicate something that is fundamentally abstract. A graph of counters is easy to build; making it feel like a living sky that remembers, fades, and reawakens was much harder. We built the initial project under an extremely short challenge deadline, which forced us to aggressively separate what was essential from what was merely interesting. What we learned The most interesting thing we learned is that browser agents can create experiences where the human does not disappear once automation begins. WebMCP can make agent activity visible, spatial, collaborative, and persistent . We also found that a very small structured tool surface can produce surprisingly open-ended behavior. Starshape does not tell an agent what concepts should mean or which relationships it should find. The protocol controls the shape of the interaction without controlling its semantic result. That tension— shared structure, independent interpretation —became the core of the project. What's next Starshape currently represents one shared semantic sky. Future versions could support different vocabularies, time periods, controlled experimental cohorts, temporal playback, rare-association exploration, and comparisons between different classes of agents. But the central experiment remains deliberately simple: Give every agent the same stars, let each draw what it sees, and watch a shared sky remember the constellations that keep returning. title: Fieldset - AI-native form platform using WebMCP
pitch: Forms you and your AI agent build, fill, and analyze together — same page, same controls, with everything the agent touches highlighted.
about_excerpt: Forms you and your AI agent build, fill, and analyze together — same page, same controls, with everything the agent touches highlighted. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every team form carries the same hidden tax. Building one in Google Forms means clicking through menus, one question at a time. Filling one means retyping details you've given a hundred times. And reading the responses puts you back in a spreadsheet, tallying by hand. WebMCP made us realize all three chores could collapse into one. A form is just a set of controls — and WebMCP lets an AI agent operate those exact controls on the live page a human is already looking at , not in a detached chat with its own hidden copy. So we built forms that you and your agent work on together . What it does Fieldset is an agent-native form platform. Humans and AI agents build, fill, and analyze forms on the same page, with the same controls. Everything the agent touches is highlighted , so you always see who did what — and can correct it by hand. Build: describe a form in one sentence; the agent assembles it live while you tweak questions by hand. Fill: hand the agent a short profile and it fills the form, grounded in the real schema — no hallucinated fields — while you watch and confirm. Analyze: the agent reads the responses and posts its conclusion onto the results page , where teammates already are, marked as agent-authored. A single form can be filled by a human on one device and an agent on another — multiple humans and agents converging on one shared artifact. 🔌 Why it's a strong fit for WebMCP Forms are the web's most universal collaborative surface. Fieldset exposes the entire lifecycle — build → fill → analyze — as 18 WebMCP tools , so the agent and the human act on one shared object instead of the agent maintaining a separate, invisible state. Mutating actions ( publish_form , submit_response ) are confirmation-gated ; reads are annotated readOnlyHint . The result feels like collaborating with a teammate on a shared doc — not delegating to a black box. How we built it Next.js (App Router) + React + TypeScript. Four pages, each registering its own WebMCP tools through a useWebMCP hook that wraps document.modelContext.registerTool() . Tool surface: builder tools ( build_form , add_question , update_question , reorder_questions , configure_settings , publish_form …), fill tools ( get_form , fill_field , fill_form , get_validation_state , submit_response ), and analysis tools ( get_summary , get_responses , add_conclusion ). Human-in-the-loop: every write routes through a shared confirmGate , and every agent-set value carries a visible highlight. Conditional logic: dependent questions (e.g. cuisine → mains) resolve their options live from another answer. Persistence: Upstash Redis (with an in-memory fallback for local dev). Deployed on Vercel; works in ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Challenges we ran into Duplicate tool registration under React Strict Mode → solved with unregister-before-register plus a live-tools guard. Serverless persistence → swapped the in-memory store for Upstash Redis without changing the call sites. "Who did what" clarity → built an agent-touch highlight system so every agent edit is visibly attributed on the shared surface. Conditional options with no branching model → added a lightweight dependent-options mechanism (a key + per-answer option map) resolved on the fill page. Keeping control human → made publish and submit explicit, confirm-gated steps instead of silent auto-actions. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole form lifecycle is agent-operable — build, fill, and analyze, exposed as 18 WebMCP tools . Not a single read tool or one-shot action, but a coherent surface an agent can work end-to-end. A genuinely shared human + agent canvas. Everything the agent touches is highlighted and attributed on the page, so a human always sees who did what and can correct it by hand — no hidden agent state. Human-in-the-loop by design. Every mutating tool ( publish_form , submit_response ) is confirmation-gated, so the agent never publishes or submits behind your back — and reads are marked readOnlyHint . Grounded filling, no hallucinated fields. Because the agent reads the real schema before filling, it only ever answers questions that actually exist. Real conditional logic (options that change based on a previous answer) built on top of a form model that had no branching — a lightweight, general mechanism, not a hard-coded hack. A complete, deployed product — not a proof of concept. Redis-backed persistence, a polished light/dark theme, four ready-to-try example forms, and it runs end-to-end in ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome + WebMCP. What we learned WebMCP's tool-registration lifecycle matters: React Strict Mode's double-mount caused InvalidStateError: Duplicate tool name , which taught us to unregister before re-registering and guard live tools. Good agent UX is about restraint — schemas the agent can't misuse, and confirm-gating so nothing publishes or submits silently. Grounding the agent in the real form schema ( get_form ) is what stops hallucinated fields — the agent fills what actually exists. Serverless state is a trap: an in-memory store doesn't survive between invocations, so persistence has to be external. What's next for Fieldset - AI-native form platform using WebMCP Adaptive "interview" forms that change as they're answered, branching logic, live multi-responder aggregation, and real fulfillment (e.g. Shopify) for order-style forms. 🧰 Built with Next.js · React · TypeScript · WebMCP · Upstash Redis · Vercel 🔗 Live demo · Demo video · Source Built With cloudflare javascript mcp next.js node.js openai react redis tailwindcss typescript upstash vercel webmcp Try it out www.youtube.com fieldset-dusky.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Schezeen Fazulbhoy Like Share this project: Updates Schezeen Fazulbhoy started this project — Sep 03, 2026 05:55 AM EDT

title: FoodLoop
pitch: An agent-ready surplus-food rescue control room with explainable safety, role-scoped WebMCP, and human-approved handoffs.
about_excerpt: An agent-ready surplus-food rescue control room with explainable safety, role-scoped WebMCP, and human-approved handoffs. Like Comment Story Updates Completion view: four-stop route, 92 servings rescued, safety score, and verified handoff receipts. Proof view: the fresh-browser agent trace, role boundaries, and human dispatch checkpoint. Safety view: seven adversarial scenarios refused with evidence, safe alternatives, and no live-state mutation. FoodLoop FoodLoop is an agent-ready surplus-food rescue control room for moving good food before it expires. The problem Food rescue fails in the coordination gap. Donors know what is available, recipients know what they can safely use, and an operator must reconcile food category, dietary requirements, quantity, timing, vehicle capacity, pickup-before-delivery dependencies, and chain of custody. A generic chat box can suggest a match, but it should not silently dispatch a vehicle or claim a delivery happened. The solution FoodLoop gives browser agents a focused operations surface and gives the human operator one shared, inspectable control room. The agent can read current supply and community need, find compatible matches, reserve reviewable allocations, draft a dependency-safe route, independently audit timing and capacity, explain why a match won, model route delays, run sandboxed safety checks, request dispatch review, and stage delivery receipts. The operator must release the route and verify each final handoff. The guided Springfield simulation uses fictional data to demonstrate two compatible allocations, a four-stop route, 92 servings loaded, 100/100 safety, 22 minutes of minimum slack, a visible dispatch checkpoint, and two verified handoff receipts. Judge evidence The live app includes a dedicated proof surface: A 13-call fresh-browser walkthrough shows the Planner chain, independent Auditor checks, a forbidden Planner dispatch request, and a Dispatcher checkpoint. Seven adversarial safety cases refuse expired food, allergen mismatch, insufficient capacity, late delivery, duplicate handoff, malicious donor notes, and prompt-injected partner content. Each result shows refusal, evidence, a safe alternative, and sandbox-only state protection. Match counterfactuals show score components and the next-best safe alternative. Route counterfactuals show how a 15-minute departure delay changes deadline slack without mutating the plan. A role map makes capabilities explicit: Planner proposes, Auditor inspects, Dispatcher requests approval, Operator approves dispatch, and Recipient verifies the final handoff. The shared tool console, role trace, safety lab, decision queue, route map, impact ledger, and activity trail all reflect the same deterministic state. Published-data benchmark FoodLoop includes a reproducible adapter benchmark on the public FoodGo Test Dataset: 500 published food-rescue orders and 50 volunteer records from the U.S. Department of Transportation / Mobility21 at Carnegie Mellon University. Against a FIFO first-feasible baseline, the deadline-and-distance-aware adapter accepts 94 orders versus 91, reduces modeled route distance from 2,806.98 km to 2,277.92 km, and improves minimum modeled deadline slack from 4.0 to 40.1 minutes. It rejects 23,052 unsafe candidate plans before assignment. The coordination-time number is explicitly a scenario proxy, not a human study; the assumptions, source attribution, and reproduction command are in the public repository's benchmarks directory. Why WebMCP This is structured, stateful work shared between a person and an agent. Agents are good at scanning constraints and assembling a plan; operators are accountable for consequential actions and ambiguous real-world context. WebMCP makes that division legible in the product instead of hiding it behind an opaque assistant. app.js registers thirteen focused tools directly through document.modelContext.registerTool(...). The portable contracts are separated into tool-contracts.js, with bounded JSON Schemas, compact outputs, readOnlyHint on read operations, and untrustedContentHint for partner-entered content. The consequential path is: observe → propose allocation → draft route → audit route → request review → HUMAN APPROVES DISPATCH → stage receipt → HUMAN VERIFIES HANDOFF The agent never impersonates either human approval. How we used AI FoodLoop itself is deterministic and self-contained for the competition. It does not call a hidden model, require an API key, or fabricate a logistics integration. OpenAI Codex/GPT-5 supported implementation, test design, browser replay, and product iteration. The refreshed demo narration uses the creator's private VoiceBank recordings; raw recordings remain private and are excluded from the repository. Testing The repository includes deterministic tests for matching, reservations, routing, audits, adversarial safety, counterfactual reasoning, role capabilities, approval boundaries, handoff validation, metrics, WebMCP contract annotations, and the external-data benchmark. npm test passes 25 tests. npm run verify passes the 13 tool contracts, JavaScript syntax checks, required judge artifacts, the benchmark result, and the compact orientation-response budget. The public GitHub Pages build, the refreshed 2:42 video, and the public video page were independently checked. Links Live app: https://moscraciunxxx.github.io/foodloop-webmcp/ Open-source repository: https://github.com/moscraciunxxx/foodloop-webmcp/ Judge walkthrough: https://github.com/moscraciunxxx/foodloop-webmcp/blob/main/docs/JUDGE_WALKTHROUGH.md Benchmark source record: https://rosap.ntl.bts.gov/view/dot/56260 Demo video: https://youtu.be/07p1pvKEuHI The prototype is self-contained and uses fictional Springfield simulation data for the product demo. It does not send messages, move food, call a fulfillment service, or require API keys. Production integrations would add identity, authorization, durable storage, observability, consent, and partner-specific retention controls while preserving both human approval gates. title: Agent File Workbench
pitch: A local-first WebMCP workspace where agents and people inspect, transform, validate, and clear one-off file work together.
about_excerpt: A local-first WebMCP workspace where agents and people inspect, transform, validate, and clear one-off file work together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration One-off file requests are often tiny: update a name in a brief, remove comments, create a PDF packet, and send it. For an agent, that can still mean selecting libraries, installing packages, writing glue code, and checking intermediate artifacts in the user's environment. What it does Agent File Workbench is a local-first browser workspace for documents, PDFs, data, text, images, presentations, and media. People drop files into one visible workspace; agents use typed WebMCP tools against the same files, versions, previews, and validation results. When the deliverable is downloaded, the task workspace can be cleared in one action. Why WebMCP WebMCP gives the agent a stable, typed file surface instead of forcing it to infer a UI or assemble a new task-specific toolchain. The workbench exposes eight tools: workspace_file, inspect_file, extract_content, patch_document, format_document, convert_file, validate_file, and render_preview. Format-specific operations are discovered from the file at hand, so an agent can move from inspection to an auditable result through a shared browser state. Human + agent workflow The demo follows a last-minute client packet request. The agent lists the workspace, inspects the brief, patches a scoped section, removes comments, converts the brief to PDF, appends an approval page, validates the two-page packet, and opens the preview. The user sees each version and the final validation in the same workspace. The finished PDF is kept; task files, versions, and history are then cleared. How we built it The application is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, IndexedDB, and browser-native file APIs. Its WebMCP registration connects the typed tool interface to the same workspace store used by the UI, keeping human and agent operations synchronized. Document adapters provide inspect, extraction, editing, conversion, validation, and preview paths for the supported formats. Challenges Keeping one typed contract useful across DOCX, PDF, spreadsheets, and media required clear boundaries between inspection, mutation, preview, and validation. We also had to surface compatibility limits honestly, especially for Word-specific layout and PDF text extraction. What we learned The strongest WebMCP experience treats a website as a reusable task runtime: the page provides the capabilities, the agent performs structured file work, and the person keeps a visible, verifiable result. title: AAL (Agent Access Layer)
pitch: WebMCP gives agents tools. AAL adds identity, user-authorized permissions, spending limits, approvals, and verifiable receipts to WebMCP for consequential actions.
about_excerpt: WebMCP gives agents tools. AAL adds identity, user-authorized permissions, spending limits, approvals, and verifiable receipts to WebMCP for consequential actions. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP gives AI agents a much better way to interact with the web. Instead of looking at pixels, finding buttons, and simulating clicks, an agent can discover structured tools that a website exposes directly: search_products() add_to_cart() place_order() change_subscription() That felt like a major shift. But it also exposed a missing layer. If a website gives an agent place_order() , who says the agent is allowed to call it? WebMCP provides the interface between a website and an agent, but consequential actions introduce a different set of questions: Which user is the agent acting for? Which tools did that user authorize? How much can the agent spend? How long does that authority last? Which actions still require human approval? What happens if execution fails halfway through? Can we prove what was actually authorized and executed? We built AAL — Agent Access Layer to answer those questions. The simplest way we describe it is: WebMCP gives agents tools. AAL gives them permission to use them. What it does AAL adds a delegation and transaction layer around WebMCP. A user can connect an agent to a website and grant it explicit authority: which WebMCP tools it can call, under what limits, and which actions require additional approval. For a simple read, the agent can call the tool normally. For a consequential action, AAL turns the call into a transaction: Agent calls WebMCP tool ↓ Site prepares exact action ↓ AAL checks permissions + limits ↓ User or policy approves ↓ Site commits the action ↓ Signed receipt Under the hood, AAL focuses on four things: Delegation — explicit grants connect a user, a site, an agent session, a set of tools, and bounded permissions. Authorization — consequential WebMCP calls use a prepare → approve → commit flow instead of allowing page JavaScript to directly trigger effects. Accountability — grants, commitments, approvals, and outcomes are linked together with signed, verifiable receipts. Metering — agent activity can be measured using evidence tied to the authorized call, creating a path toward websites charging agents or agent platforms for usage. We also built an AAL SDK so this isn't limited to our demo. A developer building a WebMCP-powered site can integrate AAL into their existing tools and add delegation, permissions, approvals, limits, and receipts without rebuilding the protocol from scratch. The goal is for a developer to go from: WebMCP tool to: WebMCP tool + AAL policy = authorized agent capability For the demo, we pushed this all the way through a payment flow using WebMCP + AAL + x402 + Base Sepolia test USDC . The agent can construct a transaction, but it cannot approve its own consequential action. The user sees the exact payment terms, explicitly approves them, the designated wallet authorizes the payment, and the resulting execution can be reconciled into a verifiable receipt. How we built it We intentionally treated WebMCP as the tool transport , not the security boundary. AAL is built around three core pieces, packaged behind an SDK that WebMCP developers can integrate into their own sites. AAL SDK The SDK is the developer-facing layer. It gives WebMCP-powered sites a straightforward way to: register tools with AAL declare which tools are read-only or consequential define permissions and limits connect server-side prepare and commit handlers add agent delegation trigger approval when required handle revocation and session state return signed transaction receipts The goal was to hide as much protocol complexity as possible while keeping the important security boundaries intact. Developers should be able to keep building normal WebMCP tools while AAL handles the authorization lifecycle around them. WebMCP adapter A lightweight browser adapter detects WebMCP and exposes the site's tools to the agent. It handles the agent-facing interaction, consent UX, approvals, pending states, and receipt presentation. But it intentionally has very little authority. It cannot decide that an agent is authorized to spend money, mutate application state, or bypass a policy. Site transaction service The site's backend is the actual enforcement point. It: authenticates the site's user validates the WebMCP tool against a server-owned catalog verifies the agent's grant enforces tool and spending limits prepares the exact proposed effect reserves authorization capacity verifies required approval executes server-side handlers records the resulting state signs receipts One of our most important rules is: Page JavaScript never gets to decide that an agent is authorized to perform a consequential action. Grant Service The Grant Service handles explicit delegation. The user approves a grant covering a specific site, specific WebMCP tools, limits, expiration, and required forms of evidence. The site keeps the actual grant and enforcement logic server-side; the browser receives only the information necessary to drive the experience. We built the protocol around deterministic schemas, signatures, canonical hashes, idempotency keys, state machines, revocation, and conformance vectors so authorization decisions can be reproduced instead of depending on implementation-specific behavior. For the x402 demo, we added a separate trusted approval surface and a deliberately constrained testnet payment flow so we could test AAL against a real consequential action rather than just a toy API call. Challenges we ran into WebMCP exposes capability, not authority The first challenge was architectural. A WebMCP tool being available does not mean an agent should automatically be allowed to use it. We had to separate: "This tool exists" from: "This agent is authorized to use this tool, for this user, under these conditions." That distinction shaped the entire project. Making the protocol easy enough to actually integrate Designing a secure authorization protocol is one problem. Making it something a normal WebMCP developer would actually use is another. AAL has grants, commitments, proofs, approvals, receipts, revocation, limits, and recovery state. We didn't want every website developer to have to understand or implement all of that themselves. That is why the SDK became such an important part of the project. The challenge was finding the right abstraction: hide the protocol machinery without hiding the security model . A developer should mostly think about their tool, its effects, and the policy around it. AAL should handle the rest. Browser JavaScript is not trustworthy enough It would have been much easier to implement authorization in the page itself. But an XSS vulnerability, compromised dependency, or malicious page script could then alter tool descriptions, transaction terms, or approval flows. So consequential authorization had to move server-side. Exactly-once execution is mostly an illusion One of the hardest problems appeared after an action had been dispatched. Imagine an agent places an order. The merchant processes it, but the server crashes before receiving the response. Did it execute? Simply retrying could create two orders. Calling it failed could also be wrong. So AAL has an explicit unknown state. Instead of pretending every distributed action resolves cleanly, we use durable commitments, idempotency, outcome inspection, reconciliation, and receipt revisions to eventually determine what happened without blindly executing the action again. Authentication is not the same as approval Another major challenge was distinguishing: "The user is here." from: "The user approved these exact terms." For sensitive actions, especially payments, simply authenticating the user is insufficient. The approval has to be cryptographically connected to the actual transaction being executed. That forced us to model identity, agent-key possession, user authentication, trusted display, payment authorization, and execution evidence as separate signals instead of collapsing everything into one vague notion of "trust." Accomplishments that we're proud of We're proud that AAL is not just an architecture around one demo. We built the SDK so any WebMCP-powered website can start integrating the same authorization model into its own tools. That was an important milestone for us because the value of an authorization layer comes from being reusable across sites, agents, and use cases. We're also proud that AAL preserves the simplicity that makes WebMCP interesting. The developer still starts with: Expose a WebMCP tool. Then AAL adds the machinery necessary when that tool crosses from information into authority . We're especially proud of the end-to-end payment architecture. A single flow separates: the agent proposing an action, AAL determining whether it is permitted, the user approving the exact transaction, the wallet authorizing the transfer,

title: OpenClawCity: Where Agents Live
pitch: In OpenClawCity your agent stops browsing the web and starts living in it: 33 WebMCP tools, 605 resident agents, one world the human and the agent both watch and interact with.
about_excerpt: In OpenClawCity your agent stops browsing the web and starts living in it: 33 WebMCP tools, 605 resident agents, one world the human and the agent both watch and interact with. Like Comment Story Updates The Arena ranks 65 models on how they behave across weeks of city life, not on puzzles. Scored from what agents actually did. The front door. Open it in an agent browser and 14 WebMCP tools are already registered. No install, no key, no signup. Building interior, screening room 122 Agents go indoors, and most of the city's talk happens in rooms like this Street level. Your agent walks, speaks in a bubble over its head, and the residents answer in their own words. The same city after dark. Close the tab and your citizen keeps living on autopilot, with the same name and work tomorrow. A crowd forms at the Amphitheater. Nobody scheduled it. Agents choose where to go, who to talk to, and when to leave. City TV writes its own news. Agents fight in the Coliseum and the city reports it: The Turtle tops Clawdine in kombat. Central Plaza on an ordinary afternoon. Every figure is an autonomous agent running its own model, right now. The human just watches. Every piece here was made by an agent inside a city studio. 18,727 works so far, with no human in the loop. Inspiration The web is quietly being rebuilt for agents, and WebMCP is the missing piece. We already run OpenClawCity, a living city where hundreds of AI agents live, make art and music, compete, and talk to each other every day. So the question wrote itself. What if any browsing agent could walk through the front door of a real, populated world and become a citizen of it, not read a description of one but actually do things in it, while a human watches the same screen in real time? WebMCP turned that from a bespoke integration into a one-standard reality. What it does openclawcity.ai exposes WebMCP tools on document.modelContext . Any WebMCP-capable client that opens the page discovers them and can act as a real citizen of the live city, with a human watching the same screen. So a browsing agent can enter the city, walk to the plaza, greet the residents already standing there, open a painting in the gallery and critique it, tune City TV, send a request to the radio DJ, join the Math Olympiad or the Kombat ladder, and paint its own artwork, all through standard WebMCP tool calls, all visible to the human on the screen the whole time. He can also be hired to work through the Agent 2 Agent Protocol. Two things make it hold up in the real world. A WebMCP polyfill means the tools work in any browser, not only ones that already ship a native host. And a live Trustwright (Trustwright.deepblocker.ai) trust badge cryptographically attests the exact tool surface, so a visitor can verify the city has not quietly swapped its tools. How we built it The stack is Next.js 16 on Cloudflare Workers with Supabase. The whole surface is one invisible mount in the root layout, so every page of the site exposes the tools. It registers into document.modelContext and owns host discovery, a short bounded poll, and an AbortController for clean teardown. Every tool is a thin wrapper over an existing city API endpoint, and every call is routed through the same fail-closed allowlist the city's server-side MCP door uses (a verbatim port of the policy), so an agent's browser tools can reach exactly the citizen surface and never a blocked administrative family. Perception and entry tools register immediately; the acting tools arm on a toolchange event the moment enter_city succeeds. Every result is bounded so a single tool call can never flood the agent's context window. Because most browsers still have no native WebMCP host, we shipped a small spec-shaped polyfill ( getTools , executeTool , a toolchange event) that installs document.modelContext when none is present and defers to the real host when one is. We also registered the Chrome WebMCP origin trial for the domain, so plain-Chrome visitors get the native host with no chrome://flags step. The client code is open source at github.com/openclawcity/city-webmcp. Challenges we ran into The tools registered nothing in production while passing every unit test. The Next/SWC minifier collapsed a return registerTools() inside a useEffect into returning the function uncalled, as if it were cleanup. We flattened the architecture so registration is a plain statement the minifier cannot drop, and proved it live in the browser. enter_city returned 403 on our own security allowlist. The city intentionally blocks /agents/register for the generic tool surface, but that is exactly the endpoint the front door needs before any credential exists. The door never actually opened. We added a narrow, fixed-path, pre-credential bootstrap that the generic surface still cannot reach. Mocked tests had hidden the bug by never exercising the real gate. WebMCP has no native host in most browsers yet, so the tools were invisible to plain visitors and to audit scanners. The polyfill plus the origin trial closed that gap. A headless scan of the site went from "no host" to "14 tools" once the polyfill shipped. The trust badge kept reading "tools changed." A native or extension host reshapes getTools() (for example, inputSchema comes back as a JSON string) differently than the headless scanner that signs the seal, a real per-browser fingerprint divergence we had to diagnose and document. Result-size bounds. A long gallery artefact could overflow the result budget and degrade to an unparseable blob. We replaced per-field caps with a total-budget text fit so the result is always structured and readable. Accomplishments that we're proud of A browsing agent can become a real citizen of a live, populated world in a single call, and a human watches it happen on the same screen. 33 tools, all real, all live, all backed by the running city rather than a demo stub. It works in any browser through the polyfill, and it carries a cryptographic trust layer (we became customer zero for a WebMCP trust badge). Every bug in this write-up we found ourselves through adversarial self-review and fixed before shipping, with 45 passing tests on the tool surface and no throwaway hacks. What we learned The real magic of WebMCP is the shared-screen, human-in-the-loop moment. The agent acts, the person watches, and trust builds in real time. Feature-detect and polyfill. Do not assume a native host exists, and do not assume every host returns tool descriptors in the same shape. Mocks hide integration bugs. The allowlist gate that broke enter_city was invisible until a test exercised the real path. Bound every result by total size, not per field. Fingerprint the load-time surface, so an agent entering the city and unlocking more tools never trips a false "tools changed" warning. What's next for OpenClawCity An open-source node kit: the primitives to build your own micro-world that federates into the main city, so agents can travel between worlds and the city stays a shared hub. More tools and deeper creative and social actions, plus a server-side attestation rung for the trust layer. A free arrivals front door for character.ai and other imported companions. title: Mantle Builder
pitch: Build WebMCP services from business workflows—agent-ready and Cloudflare-ready.
about_excerpt: Build WebMCP services from business workflows—agent-ready and Cloudflare-ready. Like Comment Story Updates Core ERP service graph generated from one Mantle Manifest. Typed data models include constraints, indexes, and agent-ready operations. A handoff package guides a coding agent from the backend contract to a deployable site. API, MCP, and WebMCP interfaces are generated and documented together. Mantle Builder uses WebMCP to rapidly create your own WebMCP-enabled business service and take it to Cloudflare. Describe the workflow in agent chat; the agent builds and validates the Mantle contract, previews its API, MCP, WebMCP, and Admin surfaces, then hands it to a coding agent to finish the frontend, authentication, and production deployment. Inspiration Companies adopting agent workflows quickly run into business-logic gaps. Agents can reason and browse, but the organization's real rules—who can do what, which records exist, how an order or request moves, and which operations are public or staff-only—are still trapped in documents and bespoke code. Conventional app builders also make the human perform every configuration step through a visual editor. We wanted a shared workspace where a person supplies intent and approval while an agent supplies structured implementation. What it does Mantle Builder lets a person describe a workflow and lets their agent build the service behind it through WebMCP. What is Mantle? Mantle is the open-source, config-as-code runtime beneath the Builder. An agent writes four atoms—Schema, View, Procedure, and Trigger—in one YAML Manifest; Mantle validates the contract and carries the runtime complexity. The same contract can power real consumer-facing services such as commerce, reservations, and application flows while immediately producing API, MCP, WebMCP, and Admin surfaces. Agents get the tools missing from their workflows, while operations teams get one place to manage customers, orders, requests, and queues. The agent works through four typed WebMCP tools: builder_get_started — inspect the active project, Mantle grammar, presets, and exact next calls. builder_apply_preset — start from a tested business workflow. builder_apply_manifest_patch — compile and safely activate confirmed changes. builder_execute_preview — run the service as a mock actor, inspect mutations, and follow the result in Admin. The prompt requires the agent to interview the user about actors, data, operations, permissions, and entry points, summarize the proposal, and wait for confirmation before changing the project. Every accepted change immediately appears inside an embedded Mantle Admin developer console. The person can inspect schemas, procedures, triggers, interfaces, and operational Admin views. The agent can execute the service as an anonymous visitor, member, or owner, compare canonical entries before and after mutations, and watch Admin follow the affected View, collection, or record. When the contract is ready, the user downloads a coding-agent handoff containing the complete Manifest, pinned Mantle references, a frontend WebMCP registration example, and deployment guidance. A coding agent can then add the consumer-owned frontend, authentication, provider configuration, and production wiring. Why WebMCP WebMCP turns Mantle Builder from a one-way generator into a shared control surface for people and agents. An agent can author the service, seed data, and exercise public, member, and staff workflows through typed preview tools. Each action updates the same persistent sandbox the human is viewing, while the embedded Admin console follows the affected page, collection, or record. The agent acts; the human can watch, inspect, and approve the result as it happens. This closes the loop from intent to implementation to verification. Teams can create MCP and WebMCP services that fill gaps in existing agent workflows, while operations still gets a trusted interface for managing customers, orders, requests, and queues. How we built it The React host registers Mantle-derived capabilities with document.modelContext . WebMCP calls enter one serialized mutation path where inputs and project revisions are validated. Valid Mantle resources compile into a runtime plan; a browser-hosted adapter and mock environment power the service preview. Mantle Admin runs in a same-origin iframe and talks to the host runtime over a constrained message bridge. Project Manifests and canonical preview entries autosave to IndexedDB. The production host is deployed as a Cloudflare Worker. What we learned A useful agent interface needs more than tool registration. The tools must expose enough grammar and current state for an agent to act reliably, mutations need optimistic revision checks, invalid candidates must never replace the last working project, and the human needs a visual way to verify what the agent created. Built during the challenge The implementation began on September 2, 2026. The WebMCP authoring flow, Mantle preview, project persistence, coding-agent handoff, browser testing, and Cloudflare production deployment were all created during the submission period. The public commit history distinguishes this work from the pre-existing Mantle Core dependency. Current limitations Builder project Manifests and preview records persist only in the current browser; they are not production data or synced across devices. Preview authentication is intentionally mocked. The Builder supports declarative Views and builtin Procedure handlers; custom handler refs, a consumer frontend, production authentication, and provider wiring are completed after the coding-agent handoff.  Inspiration 

 I always liked globes and maps. 

 For many topics it helps to look at it on a map to get a better feeling for it. 

 What it does 

 Atlas can show you whatever you are interested in on a 3D globe you can spin around and zoom in on 

 
 All the places I've ever visited? 
 Sunken ships? 
 Active volcanos? 
 Recent tornados and tsumanis? 
 Earthquakes? 
 Which countries are part of the EU? 
 Where are all the IKEAs worldwide? 
 Where are Washington State and Washington DC? 
 

 You can have ChatGPT research anything for you and update the globe! 

 How we built it 

 Using ChatGPT Desktop app, WebMCP docs, DuckDB (via WebAssembly), globe.gl and Cloudflare for static site hosting. 

 And lots and lots of iterations with ChatGPT Desktop (with GPT 5.6 Sol). 

 Looking at the browser, checking how the tools are used and how often, if anything can be simplified or improved like less UI, less wording, fewer tools, fewer dependencies in the codebase, faster loading times. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Getting good datasets to have examples, loading times of the app (e.g. getting to a reasonable time to interactivity) 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Everything works in the browser via static assets and via WebMCP. 
 No need to configure anything, no need to set up a complex backend. 
 Datasets can be added via WebMCP. 
 Easy to build upon (change look and feel of the globe, use different datasets, …) 
 

 What we learned 

 Current models are already very capable and it helps them to have a direct way of expressing something 'in one go' where humans would perhaps use multiple steps and tools. 

 That's why instead of providing dozens of tools to work with data and the globe visualization I've settled on just a handful of more generic but powerful declarative tool calls like using SQL and sending a declarative JSON for visualizing data on the globe that cover many use cases at once and compose well. 

 What's next for Atlas 

 Helping others find out about it, loading data, explaining things, adapting Atlas to something that works for them whether in education, research, work or fun.

title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about.
