title: Privacy Nutrition Label
pitch: A WebMCP-native checkout that helps people and agents understand why data is requested, choose the minimum necessary data, and receive a privacy receipt.\n\n
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-native checkout that helps people and agents understand why data is requested, choose the minimum necessary data, and receive a privacy receipt.


 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The WebMCP write tool completes checkout only after explicit confirmation and keeps personal form values inside the page. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 The human-facing Privacy Nutrition Label explains what checkout data is required, what is optional, and why—before the user acts. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The read-only WebMCP tool gives the agent structured checkout privacy facts without returning personal form values. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The WebMCP write tool completes checkout only after explicit confirmation and keeps personal form values inside the page. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 The human-facing Privacy Nutrition Label explains what checkout data is required, what is optional, and why—before the user acts. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The read-only WebMCP tool gives the agent structured checkout privacy facts without returning personal form values. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The WebMCP write tool completes checkout only after explicit confirmation and keeps personal form values inside the page. 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 I kept coming back to a simple problem that privacy policies contain a lot of information, but they rarely help with the decision someone is making right now. 

 At checkout, a website might ask for a name, email, address, phone number, account creation and marketing consent all on the same page. It is often unclear which of these are genuinely required, why they are being requested, and what can be left out. A privacy policy may contain the answer somewhere, but most people are not going to stop halfway through checkout and search through a long legal document. 

 I was also thinking about what happens after checkout. If a service later suffers a data breach, information it never collected cannot be exposed. Helping someone share less at the beginning can therefore reduce the amount of personal data placed at risk. 

 Privacy labels make data practices easier to see, but I wanted to go one step further. I did not want an AI agent to generate another summary by scraping a policy or guessing from the interface. I wanted the website itself to explain what the current action requires in a structured form that both a person and an agent can understand. 

 That became the idea behind Privacy Nutrition Label which is a small, action-specific privacy contract that appears when the decision actually matters. 

 What it does 

 I built the project around Relay, a fictional electronics retailer with a realistic guest checkout flow. Before completing an order, the customer can open a Privacy Nutrition Label showing: 

 
 which data groups are required 
 which data groups are optional 
 why each group is requested 
 who receives it 
 what the minimum-data choice is 
 whether advertising tracking is involved 
 

 The same declaration is available to an AI agent through WebMCP. The agent can inspect the checkout, explain the required and optional information, and recommend the minimum-disclosure path: continue as a guest, leave out the phone number and decline marketing. 

 I also wanted the final decision to remain with the person. Inspecting the label does not place the order. The state-changing checkout tool can only run after the person explicitly confirms their choices. 

 Once the demo order is completed, Relay produces a Privacy Receipt showing which data categories were used and which optional categories were left out. 

 The Orbit Home Companion adds a second privacy layer to the demo. Its device declaration explains that it has no camera, processes voice on-device by default and makes cloud features opt-in. This is kept separate from the checkout label so that product privacy and transaction privacy are not mixed together. 

 Why WebMCP is a strong fit 

 Without WebMCP, an agent would have to inspect form labels, scrape a privacy policy or infer how the checkout behaves. That might work sometimes, but it also leaves room for outdated information and incorrect assumptions. 

 WebMCP allows Relay to declare its own checkout behaviour directly. The agent receives a predictable structure containing data categories, purposes, required and optional status, sharing information and a minimum-data recommendation. 

 This matters because the agent is not only reading information. After explaining the privacy choices and receiving confirmation, it can help the person act on those choices through a separate write tool. 

 I did not want WebMCP to be an extra feature added to an otherwise normal checkout. It is what makes the privacy information understandable and actionable at the moment of decision. 

 How it creates a better user experience 

 People should not need privacy or legal expertise just to understand a checkout form. 

 The human-facing label is designed to be scanned quickly. Someone can see that three data groups are required, two are optional and no advertising tracking is involved before deciding what to share. 

 If they are using an agent, the agent can inspect the same declaration and explain it in plain language. This avoids having one explanation in the interface and a different interpretation from the agent. 

 The person still stays in control. The agent can inspect and recommend, but it cannot complete the checkout until the person confirms the exact choices. 

 What people and agents can do together 

 In this flow, the website provides the facts, the agent helps interpret them and the person makes the final decision. 

 The agent can compare the required and optional categories, explain why they are requested and recommend the minimum-data option. The person can accept or change that recommendation. Only then can the agent complete the local demo checkout using the confirmed choices. 

 Without this structure, the person would need to inspect the form and policy themselves while trusting the agent to infer what the website means. With WebMCP, the website, agent and person are working from the same declared information. 

 How I built it 

 I built Privacy Nutrition Label as a solo project using React, TypeScript and Vite, then deployed it as a static site on Netlify. 

 The page registers two tools through document.modelContext : 

 
 inspect_checkout_privacy is read-only. It opens the visible Privacy Nutrition Label and returns the declared categories, purposes, sharing information, required or optional status and minimum-data recommendation 
 complete_private_checkout is state-changing. It accepts privacy choices rather than personal form values, requires confirmed to be explicitly true, validates the completed form inside the page and returns a category-level receipt 
 

 I deliberately kept personal values out of the tool interface. A name, email, address or phone number stays inside the webpage. The agent receives the privacy declaration and the person’s choices, but not those values. 

 The demo has no backend, database, authentication service, analytics, payment provider or external font request. Refreshing the page clears the order. The human checkout also remains usable when WebMCP is unavailable. 

 I added eleven automated tests covering privacy defaults, malformed inputs, missing fields, confirmation requirements, repeated execution and category-only outputs. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The hardest design decision was not the interface. It was deciding what the agent should not receive. 

 Passing the whole checkout form to the tool would have been easier, but it would have contradicted the data-minimisation idea behind the project. The agent needs to understand the privacy contract and the person’s choices; it does not need their identity or delivery details in its response. 

 I therefore separated the flow into clear boundaries: 

 
 the webpage keeps the personal form values 
 the agent receives the privacy declaration and confirmed choices 
 the write tool performs the local action only after explicit confirmation 
 

 Another challenge was deciding how much information belonged in the label. I wanted it to include purpose, optionality and sharing without turning it into another document that people would ignore. 

 Keeping product privacy separate from checkout privacy was also important. Orbit’s camera and voice-processing declaration belongs to the device, while the Privacy Nutrition Label describes the current purchase. 

 Accomplishments that I am proud of 

 
 WebMCP changes the interaction instead of simply duplicating a webpage button 
 The read tool opens the same

title: AgentPress
pitch: The permission-aware WebMCP control layer for WordPress.
about_excerpt: The permission-aware WebMCP control layer for WordPress. Like Comment Story Updates 1 made by chatgpt made by chatgpt made by chatgpt made by chatgpt made by chatgpt youtube screenshot (for some reason) made by chatgpt Inspiration WordPress already has a strong human collaboration model: authenticated sessions, roles, capabilities, drafts, review, and publishing. Most agent integrations bypass that model by asking for a separate API key or by giving an automation service broad access. AgentPress asks a different question: what if the agent could join the workspace the human is already using, while WordPress remained the source of authority? What it does AgentPress is an open-source WordPress plugin that exposes a permission-filtered set of site tools to compatible agents through WebMCP. It divides operations into three visible classes: automatic operations that are safe within the current user's authority; approval-required operations that should stop for an explicit human decision; and unavailable areas that are never exposed as tools, including users, plugins, themes, code, credentials, and settings. In the recorded live workflow, ChatGPT used AgentPress tools from its built-in browser to inspect the current WordPress context and structure, create one useful service-page draft, and read the result back. WordPress showed the item as a draft. The visible page count changed from 15 to 16, the one new page was identified, and all 15 pre-existing page metadata records remained unchanged. Nothing was published. Why WebMCP is a strong fit The browser already holds the most important context: the page the human chose, their authenticated WordPress session, and their real WordPress permissions. WebMCP lets that page offer structured tools directly to the agent. The user does not have to copy content into chat, hand over a permanent API key, or teach the model where buttons live. That makes a multi-step WordPress task possible in one request: inspect the site, understand the allowed operations, create a draft, and verify the result. The outcome remains native WordPress content that a human can preview, edit, review, or publish through the normal workflow. How we built it AgentPress defines a fixed catalog of typed WordPress Abilities and adapts the permitted surface to WebMCP using document.modelContext.registerTool . Calls travel through a private same-origin REST transport using the signed-in WordPress cookie session and REST nonce. The server does not trust discovery alone. It revalidates the current user's WordPress capabilities, object-level access, operation policy, origin, nonce, request size, and closed input schema at execution time. Draft writes are forced to draft status and pass through an idempotent Change Set coordinator. Attempts and outcomes produce bounded, sanitized audit records. The wp-admin Overview makes the boundary legible: connection health, the connected site, operations available automatically, operations classified as approval-required, and areas that are always blocked. Challenges The hardest problem was not generating WordPress content. It was preserving WordPress authority across browser discovery, agent execution, REST transport, object-level permissions, retries, and a human-readable admin interface. We treated every layer as a boundary and kept a dated experiment ledger containing failures as well as successful results. Accomplishments A real ChatGPT built-in-browser WebMCP run created and verified one WordPress page draft. The write was idempotent and represented as Change Set AP-1. The result remained unpublished and existing page metadata remained unchanged. The plugin uses the human's current WordPress session instead of a copied API key. The public repository contains implementation tests and an auditable experiment trail. What we learned Agent capability should be narrower than user capability, and the distinction must be visible to both the human and the model. Tool discovery is useful, but enforcement must happen again on the server. We also learned that an honest, bounded demonstration—with request identifiers, WordPress state verification, and explicit untested limits—is more valuable than a broad automation claim. What's next The recorded challenge build proves the core read-and-draft workflow. The next milestones are the visible approval and classic-navigation flows, the canonical Administrator-versus-Author permission test, and five consecutive clean reliability runs. Those are deliberately described as next steps, not as completed features. title: Family Stay Compiler
pitch: One family brief, two staged checkouts, and a deterministic guardian that keeps every traveler, condition, and room-only promotion intact.
about_excerpt: One family brief, two staged checkouts, and a deterministic guardian that keeps every traveler, condition, and room-only promotion intact. Like Comment Story Updates One saved six-person brief: an honest one-room zero result and a preview-only path to three complete plans. Plan A keeps every traveler visible and proves the $24 family discount applies to Room 1 only. The split-checkout guardian verifies coverage, dates, $720, and promotion scope before manual review. Reload restores the recomputed audit, promotion evidence, and human acknowledgement without booking or payment. The review-only receipt records confirmed facts, unknowns, promotion scope, and the guardian outcome. Inspiration Planning a hotel stay becomes surprisingly difficult when a family does not fit inside a standard “one room, two guests” search box. As a parent of three children, I repeatedly encountered the same frustrating loop: enter everyone’s ages, inspect a room or promotion, press Back, discover that the search conditions have reset, and start again. For larger families, the problem is deeper than inconvenience. One search may return nothing even though a workable combination of two or more rooms exists. Parents are then forced to split adults and children into separate searches, compare promotions manually, and hope the separate rooms still work as one family stay. That experience led to a different question: What if families could search for a complete stay plan—not just an individual room? What it does Family Stay Compiler preserves one structured family brief throughout the planning process: dates, adults, children’s ages, room limit, adult-per-room rules, youngest-child constraints, and connecting-room preferences. The focus demonstration begins with two adults and four children under a one-room limit. The compiler returns an honest zero result rather than hiding or silently changing the constraints. An agent can preview changing only the room limit from one to two, but the saved family brief remains unchanged until the person presses Apply this change . Once approved, the app compiles three complete synthetic stay plans. It keeps every traveler visible, explains room allocation, and states that the verified $24 family discount applies to Room 1 only—not automatically to both rooms. The Split Checkout Guardian then audits two staged room checkouts as one family-level decision. It verifies traveler coverage, dates, room identity, subtotals, promotion scope, cancellation terms, and proximity before the person acknowledges the result for later manual review. The app never opens checkout, books, pays, reserves, contacts a hotel, or claims live inventory. Why WebMCP Family Stay Compiler exposes six page-defined WebMCP tools over the same state used by the visible interface: set_family_requirements find_family_stay_plans preview_constraint_unlock compare_family_stay_plans audit_split_checkout prepare_decision_receipt This is not ordinary DOM automation. The tools directly expose the underlying family-planning actions. preview_constraint_unlock calculates the exact feasibility difference created by one reversible constraint change while leaving the saved brief untouched. audit_split_checkout recomputes the staged decision using the selected planId . It verifies every traveler, both dates, adult and youngest-child rules, exact room identity, subtotals, promotion scope, cancellation terms, and room proximity. Every successful tool call creates a visible activity on the page so the person can inspect what the agent did. Invalid previews and stale or mismatched audit evidence return explicit errors without mutating the visible activity ledger. Better UX Conventional hotel interfaces treat each room search or checkout as an isolated transaction. That creates unnecessary work and risk for larger families: family ages and dates may reset after navigating back; a one-room zero result does not explain which constraint failed; promotions may apply to only one of the two required rooms; two separate checkouts make it difficult to confirm that every traveler and condition is still covered. Family Stay Compiler treats the family as one party from the first search through the final review. The person can begin with an honest zero result, inspect one reversible counterfactual, apply it deliberately, compare complete plans, and audit two staged checkouts without re-entering the family brief. Browser Back, Forward, and reload preserve the validated decision session and human acknowledgment. Stored evidence is recomputed before restoration, so altered or stale evidence cannot reuse an earlier acknowledgment. What people and agents do together The agent handles the tedious work: validating a complete family brief; explaining why a search is infeasible; calculating a one-constraint counterfactual; compiling complete room allocations; comparing plan trade-offs; checking traveler, date, subtotal, promotion, and policy consistency; preparing a review-only receipt. The person retains the consequential decisions: whether to apply the proposed room-limit change; and whether to acknowledge the split-checkout audit for later manual review. The agent does not silently rewrite the family’s preferences, and the person does not have to manually cross-check every traveler and promotion across two disconnected room purchases. That shared page state is the central WebMCP interaction: agent computation remains visible, reversible, and subject to human approval. How we built it Family Stay Compiler was built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and WebMCP. The application separates deterministic planning logic from the interface and WebMCP registration layer. The human interface and all six tools call the same pure domain functions and update the same page state. The planning engine evaluates flexible family sizes and room limits while enforcing active constraints such as: room capacity; an adult in each occupied room; the youngest child remaining with an adult; room proximity preferences; exact traveler coverage; room-specific promotion eligibility. The Split Checkout Guardian compares staged room parts against the selected compiled plan. It blocks the audit if room identity, travelers, dates, subtotals, or promotion evidence differ. The final release passed: 24 Vitest unit and integration tests; 12 desktop and mobile Playwright end-to-end tests; TypeScript type checking; the production build; real WebMCP discovery and invocation in ChatGPT’s in-app browser. All six tools were discovered and invoked successfully against the production deployment, with visible shared-page updates. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was not building another hotel search form. It was representing the family’s complete situation without silently losing constraints. A room limit does not mean every room count is feasible. For example, two adults cannot supervise four occupied rooms when every room requires an adult. Children’s ages, room capacity, proximity, promotions, cancellation terms, and checkout totals must remain attached to the same decision. Another challenge was making counterfactual assistance safe. An agent may discover that changing one condition unlocks feasible plans, but it should not silently overwrite the family’s saved requirements.  Tariffiq: instant import tariff analysis, now callable by AI agents via WebMCP 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 My inspiration stems from the fact that small business owners importing goods often don't find out the real cost of a shipment: tariffs, duties, and margin impact: until after they've already committed to an order. Tariffiq exists to answer that instantly, before the purchase order goes out. 

 What it does 

 Tariffiq calculates the full landed cost of an import: base price, tariff rate, total duty owed, and the resulting hit to profit margins. It also surfaces cheaper sourcing alternatives, comparing the same product from other origin countries and showing the potential savings. 

 How we built it 

 Tariffiq is a React + Vite app. We used document.modelContext.registerTool to expose two tools: 

 
 analyze_tariff : runs a full tariff analysis for a product, origin country, quantity, and unit price 
 switch_origin_country : re-runs the last analysis with a different origin country, so an agent can compare sourcing options without re-entering the rest of the shipment details
Both tools call the app's existing analysis functions directly, so when an agent invokes a tool, the result renders live on the same page a human is looking at not in a separate chat window. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Our biggest challenge wasn't writing the tools, it was proving they actually worked. ChatGPT wasn't reliably discovering our registered tools on our account, which initially made us think our WebMCP implementation was broken. After re-reading the submission rules closely, we realized judges can test via either ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, so we shifted to verifying everything through Chrome's own WebMCP DevTools panel instead. 

 That came with its own hurdles: getting the manual "Run Tool" test interface to actually render (it turned out to be a cramped panel/viewport issue, not a missing flag), and separately, fixing a bug where React's StrictMode was double-registering each tool in development. Working through both taught us to verify assumptions directly against official tooling rather than relying on any single client's behavior. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We're proud that Tariffiq's WebMCP tools aren't just registered they're genuinely functional. When an agent calls analyze_tariff , it's not returning a canned response; it's running the same real calculation logic a human would trigger through the UI, and the result appears live on the same page. We verified this end-to-end using Chrome's own official WebMCP DevTools panel, invoking the tool directly, with no manual form-filling, and watching the live production site update in real time. 

 We're also proud of not overclaiming: rather than assuming our implementation was broken because of one client's inconsistent tool discovery, we diagnosed the actual cause, confirmed our tools work correctly against the official spec, and built our submission around what we could concretely prove. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that WebMCP support isn't uniform across clients yet, a tool can be correctly implemented per spec and still behave inconsistently depending on which agent or browser is testing it. That pushed us to test against the official Chrome WebMCP DevTools panel directly rather than trusting any single client's behavior as the ground truth. 

 We also learned the value of reading requirements literally rather than assuming the strictest interpretation. The rules stated judges could test via ChatGPT or Chrome, once we confirmed that, we stopped chasing an issue that wasn't actually blocking our submission, and redirected that time toward strengthening what we could already prove worked. 

 On the technical side, we got a much clearer picture of how document.modelContext.registerTool interacts with React's lifecycle, specifically how StrictMode's double-invocation in development can silently duplicate tool registrations if you don't guard for it. 

 What's next for Tariffiq 

 We want to expand the tariff engine beyond a single-shipment lookup into ongoing monitoring, letting an agent check in periodically as tariff rates change and proactively flag when a cheaper sourcing country becomes available for a product a user has already analyzed. 

 We'd also like to add more WebMCP tools: one for bulk-comparing an entire supplier list at once, and one that lets an agent draft a sourcing recommendation report a user can hand directly to a supplier or customs broker. 

 Longer term, we're interested in exposing historical tariff trends as a tool too, so an agent could tell a user not just today's cost, but whether tariffs on a product have been rising or falling useful context for timing a purchase.

title: Here4Homes.uk Smart Job Brief
pitch: Here4Homes lets people find tradesmen quotes. Our WebMCP lets agents tell us what they need done in their own words. We find the right trade, ask only what matters and create a clear quote request
about_excerpt: Here4Homes lets people find tradesmen quotes. Our WebMCP lets agents tell us what they need done in their own words. We find the right trade, ask only what matters and create a clear quote request Like Comment Story Updates Describe the job once in everyday language; Smart Job Brief begins with only the safe tools needed to find the right service. The agent matches the unchanged request to one of 222 Here4Homes routes and opens the exact Artificial Grass service page. When literal matching is weak, a read-only semantic catalogue search safely recovers Builders and records the reason. Two independent jobs are detected and kept as two briefs; permission and finalisation remain unavailable. The homeowner sees what was provided or inferred, then gives separate explicit permission before the final tool appears. A server-validated test receipt confirms success without creating a live lead or contacting a tradesperson. A homeowner should not need to know what type of tradesman they need People usually begin with a problem: a lawn that turns to mud, a leaking washing machine, an outside step that is crumbling, or an opening needed for a new extractor. They do not always know which trade handles it, which service page to visit, or which details will help a tradesperson quote accurately. Here4Homes.uk Smart Job Brief lets a homeowner start with one ordinary-language description. An AI agent can use the website's WebMCP tools to find the right service among 222 published Here4Homes routes, take the homeowner to that exact page, recognise facts they have already supplied, and build a clear job brief without making them work through a fixed generic questionnaire. The person and agent work on the same visible page. Nothing happens in a hidden agent-only form: the homeowner can see the selected service, the reason for the choice, every provided or inferred fact, every missing gate, and the final test receipt. Why WebMCP is the right fit A conventional form-filling agent can click and type, but it still has to guess the website's taxonomy and infer what each control means. WebMCP lets the site offer a small set of page-owned actions with clear inputs, outputs and limits. Smart Job Brief divides responsibility deliberately: The agent handles meaning : it interprets the homeowner's wording and can make a read-only semantic search when a literal match is weak. The website handles rules : it owns the service catalogue, allowed choices, ambiguity controls, one-job rule, postcode proof and submission gates. The homeowner keeps control : they see and can edit the shared brief, and permission must be given separately and explicitly. That makes WebMCP more than a faster way to fill a form. It creates a collaborative journey that was difficult to make both capable and understandable with screen automation alone. What a person and agent can do together The homeowner describes the outcome or symptom in their own words. find_home_service checks that unchanged description against the published catalogue and returns route candidates, uncertainty and possible independent jobs. If the first result is weak, search_home_service_catalog lets the agent use a concise interpretation such as “builder core drilling external wall”. It is read-only and cannot rewrite the homeowner's words. choose_home_service accepts only a route returned by the current match or latest catalogue search and records the reason on the page. The agent drafts the visible brief using facts the homeowner actually gave. Job-specific follow-ups appear only when they could add useful detail. The page explains every passed and missing readiness gate. The final tool is not available until the brief is complete and the homeowner has given explicit test permission. The app also recognises when one description contains two separate jobs. It asks for two briefs instead of sending a confused request to the wrong trade. How we built it The top-level page registers imperative WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Every input schema rejects extra properties, tool descriptions state their side effects, and read-only tools are annotated. An AbortController refreshes the registered set as the journey changes, so the agent sees only actions that make sense at the current stage. The WebMCP handlers call the same application controller as the human interface. The server then reconstructs canonical service data and independently rechecks the route, one-job rule, description quality, allowed timing and budget values, full UK postcode proof and permission version. The final tool takes no quote fields of its own; it can submit only the already visible, reviewed state. The public competition deployment runs on ChatGPT Sites through a Cloudflare-Worker-compatible Vinext adapter. It is permanently credential-free: there is no live provider setting, contact identity, tracking client or conversion writer. It returns only a local hosted-demo receipt and cannot contact a tradesperson. A separate local owner-controlled adapter can optionally exercise MyJobQuote's explicit test endpoint with a server-authored synthetic identity and immutable is_test=1 flag. Now running on a real consumer website During the challenge, we moved Here4Homes Smart Job Brief beyond the standalone demonstration and deployed it as a safety-limited production canary on Here4Homes.uk , an established UK home-improvement website. A compatible agent can understand a homeowner’s description, identify the appropriate trade and service page, validate the postcode and completeness of the brief, load the current MyJobQuote categories and prepare a reviewed quote request. A real request can only be sent after the homeowner has supplied their own contact details, reviewed the request, explicitly accepted the data-sharing terms and separately confirmed the final submission. Ordinary website visitors continue to see the existing Here4Homes experience. The initial production canary is limited but live. For unrestricted judging and experimentation, please use our main demonstration URL. The production link is provided as evidence of the same WebMCP approach operating within a real consumer service. Please do not submit fictional contact details or synthetic quote requests on the production website. Here4Homes existed before the challenge; the WebMCP tools, agent-assisted journey, safety gates and production integration were built during the challenge period. Testing the real language problem Home-improvement descriptions are unusually messy, so we did not rely on a few hand-picked demos. The repository contains 635 current routing regressions based on independently written, traceable real-world themes and adversarial variants across 17 public DIYnot sections. Five separate 50-case blind rounds were sealed by hash and run once before round-specific tuning; their original scores and every failure remain in the repository. Those blind rounds exposed a genuine weakness in deterministic matching: unfamiliar phrasing and some multi-job clauses remained inconsistent even when clear unseen jobs were strong. That evidence changed the product. The fast deterministic matcher remains the website's suggestion and safety guard, while WebMCP gives the agent a controlled semantic recovery step over the complete catalogue. The website still has final authority over ambiguity, job separation and permission. The complete suite now contains 716 passing behavioural, integrity, server, hosted-boundary and WebMCP tests. That includes tampered and cross-session postcode proofs, repeated final actions, cross-origin requests, contact details hidden in a brief and attempts to bypass a blocked route. Safety by design This challenge edition is a fully-working demo version - but it cannot create a live lead. Before a test receipt can be issued, the server must confirm: one unambiguous job and an allowed service route; sufficiently clear, detailed instructions; an allowed timing and budget choice; a valid full UK postcode with a short-lived proof tied to the page session; no hidden contact details; and separate, current, explicit permission for this competition test. Permission is never inferred from the description or another tool call. An ambiguous provider outcome is locked and never retried automatically. Every screen and receipt says that no live lead, tracking row or tradesperson contact is created. During the challenge period we built this separate Smart Job Brief application: the WebMCP tool layer, natural-language routing and semantic recovery, progressive shared interface, field provenance, ambiguity and multi-job controls, readiness gates, test-only server, evaluation sets, public deployment and open-source repository. title: ONCE — Tell Your Story Once
pitch: One urgent story. Four coordinated services. Every disclosure visible. Every final action yours.
about_excerpt: One urgent story. Four coordinated services. Every disclosure visible. Every final action yours. Like Comment Story Updates The 15-second version One story in. Four services staged. Two schedule conflicts avoided. One unjustified Government ID request blocked. Zero applications sent before approval. ONCE is a working WebMCP demonstration of a better contract between a person, their chosen agent, and essential-service websites. The agent does the coordination; the person keeps the authority. Inspiration People facing one urgent life event often repeat the same painful story across disconnected forms. Each form asks for a slightly different set of personal data, appointments collide, and the person cannot see what an automated helper disclosed. We wanted to show a different web: tell one chosen agent once, let participating services expose precise capabilities, and keep one visible plan and final human authority. This is a documented service-design problem, not only a demo premise. The OECD reports that complex information and cumbersome application procedures contribute to non-take-up of social support. GOV.UK service guidance recommends avoiding repeated questions, collecting only necessary personal information, and explaining the purpose of every field. What it does The working demonstration lets a person tell an agent one urgent story: their home is unsafe, three children need temporary shelter, food and a health check, and the family needs accessible transport within 72 hours. The agent projects that story into reversible, non-sensitive local planning constraints, then coordinates four fictional provider simulations. It checks the simulations' published eligibility rules deterministically, avoids calendar conflicts, identifies the minimum purpose-bound fields for each service, blocks an unjustified Government ID request, and stages one coordinated plan. An outcome rail makes the result immediately inspectable: one story, four staged services, two avoided conflicts, one blocked overreach, and zero applications sent before approval. prepare_assistance_plan returns the same structured evidence to the agent. The agent can prepare and explain. It cannot approve. The person reviews every exact value beside its provider-declared purpose, then approves or rejects the proposal. An unjustified field is shown as withheld without revealing its value. Only after approval does WebMCP expose the consequential commit tool. Approval is fingerprint-bound, expires in five minutes, and can be used once. Synthetic receipts and an audit trail make the result visible. How we used WebMCP We use the Imperative API to register small, state-aware tools for updating planning constraints, reading intent, service discovery, deterministic eligibility, disclosure inspection, audit reading, plan preparation, visible review, and approved commit. Tools use the current standard read-only and untrusted-content annotations. Registrations are cancelled and rebuilt when page state changes, so the update capability disappears after staging and commit_approved_plan is literally absent until the person approves in the page. This is more than controlling buttons. WebMCP supplies a typed collaboration contract between the simulated service network, the agent, and the human. The agent receives concise structured results instead of scraping an interface, while every tool execution updates the human-visible state. The visible buttons remain as a progressive fallback and invoke the same application actions. The chosen agent receives approved planning constraints but never receives the synthetic Government ID or health notes. Provider simulations receive only purpose-approved fields after the person approves the exact proposal. What makes the experience new Today, agents often automate one website at a time and maximize data collection for convenience. This demonstration treats one life event as the unit of coordination, not one website: a local intent is selectively projected into four provider simulations, each field is purpose-bound, untrusted provider text is handled as data rather than authority, and capability increases only when the human explicitly opens the gate. It demonstrates the browser-side contract that independent services could use to form a user-controlled cooperative network; it does not claim that real agencies are connected today. Existing care-navigation systems validate the need for multi-service discovery and enrollment. Our distinct category is not “another benefits chatbot”: the civic journey is a test case for a transferable consent boundary between a person, their chosen agent, and WebMCP-enabled sites. Most agents are optimized to finish a task; this demonstration shows how to finish without surrendering the person's data boundary or final authority. How we built it React, TypeScript, and Vite power the visible bilingual English/Arabic experience. A deterministic domain engine handles eligibility, disclosure minimization, scheduling, fingerprints, expiring approval, and single-use receipts. The WebMCP adapter registers phase-specific tools with JSON Schemas and security annotations. Vitest and Testing Library cover the engine, UI journey, tool calls, dynamic registration, cancellation, and error handling; Playwright verifies the full browser flow and responsive layout. Challenges The hardest boundary was separating agent initiative from human authority. Hiding a button is not sufficient: the tool itself must be undiscoverable before approval, then bound to the exact reviewed proposal. A second challenge was treating service content as untrusted without making the agent blind. The demo uses browser trust annotations plus a deliberately bounded heuristic for a synthetic adversarial notice; this is evidence of the boundary, not a claim to solve prompt injection generally. Accomplishments A coherent multi-service journey instead of a single form wrapper A visible and machine-readable coordination outcome rather than an unexplained success screen One-story projection into reversible planning constraints without accepting Government ID or health notes Minimum necessary disclosure with a visible overcollection block Quarantine of malicious provider instructions without discarding the provider's legitimate service Dynamic WebMCP capabilities tied to human-visible state Deterministic eligibility and scheduling rather than model-made decisions Expiring, single-use exact-proposal approval Bilingual, responsive UI with visible audit and synthetic receipts Automated quality gate with 44 unit/integration tests, 17 browser journeys, and 91.98% statement coverage Accessibility, keyboard, responsive desktop/tablet/mobile, RTL, and WebMCP lifecycle browser checks passing Chrome agent audits passing for registered WebMCP tools, schema validity, the agent accessibility tree, and llms.txt Evidence behind the problem OECD, Modernising Access to Social Protection (2024): https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/modernising-access-to-social-protection_af31746d-en.html GOV.UK, Collecting personal information from users: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/design/collecting-personal-information-from-users GOV.UK, Structuring forms: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/design/form-structure GOV.UK, Principles for securing personal data in government services: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/principles-for-securing-personal-data-in-government-services What we learned WebMCP works best when tools describe durable user goals, not DOM operations. Security annotations help agents reason about risk, but they do not replace careful product boundaries. The clearest trust mechanism is shared state: the person should see the same plan, disclosure, approval, and result that the agent sees. What's next A production version would use authenticated provider schemas, cryptographic consent receipts, wallet-mediated selective-disclosure credentials through the emerging Digital Credentials API, revocation, durable encrypted storage, provider accountability, and independent security/privacy review. This submission intentionally stays synthetic so its current guarantees are clear and testable; it does not claim signed credentials or zero-knowledge proofs. Built with WebMCP Imperative API, React, TypeScript, Vite, Vitest, Testing Library, Playwright. Verified in ChatGPT Work Beyond scripted browser tests, we completed a fresh, uninterrupted run against the public deployment in the official ChatGPT desktop built-in browser using ChatGPT Work and GPT-5.6 Sol Light. ChatGPT discovered ONCE's native Site tools, staged proposal fp_d264dc20, confirmed commit_approved_plan was absent before visible approval, observed it appear afterward, called it exactly once, received four matching synthetic receipts, and verified that the capability disappeared after use.  What it does 

 Collaborative Whiteboard is a shared whiteboard for a human and an AI. You can draw something, write a question, select an area or point at something with the AI Pen. The AI can then explain it, improve it or continue working on the same canvas. Everything the AI creates stays editable, so you can change it and keep working from there. 

 How we built it 

 I built the project mainly with Codex and Claude . I also used WebMCP, MCP tools and different Claude skills while working on it. The app itself is a web-based whiteboard with tools for drawing, writing, selecting things and working together with an AI agent. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was definitely usage limits while building the project. Getting the WebMCP connection and the Human-to-AI workflow working correctly was also not easy. There were many small bugs with turns, waiting and editing the canvas that had to be fixed. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I am really proud that the main idea actually works. The AI can understand the board and add real, editable drawings and objects to it. I am also happy with how fast the app runs now. Building and testing the project was a lot of fun. 

 What we learned 

 I learned a lot about WebMCP, AI agents and how to connect an AI with an interactive website. I also learned that making an AI understand when it should wait, edit or react to the user is harder than it first sounds. 

 What's next for Collaborative Whiteboard 

 Next, I would like to improve how well the AI designs and organizes things on the whiteboard, so its diagrams and layouts look even better. title: Cabinet Maker Xtreme
pitch: Cabinet making made fast, parametric, and production-ready."**
about_excerpt: Cabinet making made fast, parametric, and production-ready."** Like Comment Story Updates Cabinet Maker Xtreme Inspiration Custom cabinet making is trapped between two bad options: five-figure desktop software locked to local Windows machines, or generic 3D tools like SketchUp that know nothing about joinery or cutting tickets. When AI agents arrived, they could write code but lacked spatial awareness—unable to check if a door would swing into an oven or optimize sheet cuts on a table saw. We built Cabinet Maker Xtreme to bridge that gap: a browser-based studio where woodworkers and AI agents work within the exact same 3D spatial model to turn kitchen designs into machine-ready cut lists. What it does Parametric 3D Studio: Place, move, and snap standard cabinetry with live clearance badges and elevation snap locks. NKBA & Physical Clash Validation: Detects door swing collisions, drawer binds, and kitchen work triangle compliance ($12\text{ft} \le \text{Triangle} \le 26\text{ft}$) in real time. 2D Sheet Nesting: Guillotine bin-packs panels onto $48'' \times 96''$ plywood sheets, deducting edge-banding thickness ($W_{\text{raw}} = W_{\text{finished}} - 2T_{\text{band}}$) and blade kerf. CNC-Ready DXF & Assembly Guides: Exports layered DXFs ( OUTLINE_CUT , POCKET_DADO , BORE_32MM ) and vector assembly manuals. Agent-Native WebMCP: Exposes 26 tools with strict JSON schemas so AI models can design, inspect, and undo actions with full parity to human mouse clicks. How we built it Integer Sixteenth Geometry: To eliminate floating-point drift across long cabinet runs, all spatial math uses integer sixteenths: $$\text{Sixteenths} = \text{round}(\text{Inches} \times 16)$$ Wall coordinates project into world space via rotation angle $\theta$: $$x_{\text{world}} = x_{\text{start}} + x_{\text{local}} \cos\theta + z_{\text{local}} \sin\theta, \quad z_{\text{world}} = z_{\text{start}} - x_{\text{local}} \sin\theta + z_{\text{local}} \cos\theta$$ Parametric Builder: Compiles carcasses, $32\text{mm}$ system boring, and door styles (Shaker, Flat Slab, Raised Panel) procedurally on the fly. Stack: Built with Next.js, React 19, Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Zustand. Challenges we ran into Planning WebMCP Tool Contracts: We initially treated WebMCP as a secondary API instead of an architectural foundation. Lacking an upfront schema abstraction layer meant hand-wiring 26 tool wrappers, while overlooking transactional parity initially left the agent without undo capabilities. Raycast Self-Obstruction: Transient placement previews hovered directly under the cursor, intercepting mouse rays and freezing movement. We fixed this by setting raycast={() => null} on ghost meshes and adding an active-wall placement plane. 3D Marquee Selection: Projecting world coordinates through the perspective camera into screen space ($[-1, 1]$ NDC) required factoring in local depth offsets, or floating countertops were miscalculated from angled viewpoints. Mobile Touch Collisions: Moving the 3D tool dock to the bottom of mobile viewports caused it to be blocked by the validation panel's DOM overlay. We adjusted z-indexes and resting offsets to preserve $44\text{px}$ touch targets. Accomplishments that we're proud of Zero-Setup Screen-to-Machine: Designing a kitchen in-browser and downloading CNC-ready nested DXF cut sheets in seconds. Full Agent-Human Parity: AI models use the exact same state machine, revision guards, and undo history as human clicks. Pure Client-Side Speed: Real-time parametric rendering, sheet nesting, and BOM generation running at 60 FPS in WebGL without server round-trips. What we learned Agent Affordances Belong Up Front: AI agents require the same affordances as humans (especially error recovery and undo stacks); treating agent tools as an afterthought creates technical debt. Decouple Visual Detail from Domain Data: 3D aesthetic details (like multi-piece Shaker door stiles) must be rendered in the view layer without cluttering the canonical carcass model used for cut lists and CAD sheets. What's next for Cabinet Maker Xtreme Direct G-code post-processors for Shapeoko, ShopBot, and industrial CNC routers. Live supplier catalog APIs (Blum, Salice) for automated hardware procurement. Multi-agent collaboration for automated commercial project estimation and shop scheduling.  100% RECOVERED: Provider Beta resumed Research Brief #247 from the preserved 73% checkpoint and completed the job. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI workflows fail. Providers hit rate limits, services become unavailable, and switching resources can mean losing completed work. Agent Rescue explores a better model: let an AI agent diagnose and plan recovery while keeping consequential decisions under human control. 

 What it does 

 Agent Rescue is an AI Reliability & Recovery Control Room built around a shared human-agent workflow. 

 In the demo, Research Brief #247 reaches 73% completion when Provider Alpha fails with an HTTP 429 rate limit. Agent Rescue preserves the checkpoint, diagnoses the failure, discovers available providers, evaluates recovery options, and recommends a recovery path. 

 Before changing providers, the system stops at HUMAN APPROVAL REQUIRED. 

 After approval, Agent Rescue switches providers, resumes from the preserved 73% checkpoint instead of restarting, and verifies the job at 100% RECOVERED. 

 How we used WebMCP 

 WebMCP gives the agent structured capabilities instead of forcing it to guess its way through the visual interface. 

 Agent Rescue exposes seven tools: 

 
 get_job_status 
 inspect_failure 
 list_available_providers 
 recommend_recovery 
 switch_provider 
 resume_job 
 verify_completion 
 

 The human interface and WebMCP tools operate on the same application state. The agent can observe, diagnose, compare options, recommend recovery, resume work, and verify results while the human retains control over the consequential provider-switch decision. 

 How we built it 

 The challenge prototype is a deterministic single-file web application with an explicit recovery state machine, structured tool contracts, an audit trail, provider comparison, checkpoint preservation, and a mandatory human-approval interlock. 

 The deterministic scenario makes the complete recovery sequence reproducible for judging without requiring accounts, API keys, or external AI-provider credentials. 

 What's next 

 The same architecture can extend from the deterministic challenge prototype to real multi-provider AI infrastructure, helping individuals and organizations preserve work, control failover, reduce wasted resources, and improve AI reliability.

title: Commonplace
pitch: A blog and reading platform that adapts to you. Using WebMCP, browser agents reshape layout, colors, and drafts around how you write and read.
about_excerpt: A blog and reading platform that adapts to you. Using WebMCP, browser agents reshape layout, colors, and drafts around how you write and read. Like Comment Story Updates OLED pitch-black feed with headers, hero, quote, and agent rail hidden via user settings. Personalization studio drawer for adjusting layout density, measure, type scales, and surfaces. Realtime voice guide in dark emerald monospace connecting spoken intent to WebMCP actions. Distraction-free reading view on warm paper with generative artwork and local save actions. In-page WebMCP tool inspector displaying schemas and live execution for all 44 tools. Adaptive desk in night mode with live WebMCP telemetry and quick palette switching. Publishing composer with structured fields exposed directly to browser agents. Public profile rendered in editorial serif typography and dark emerald forest slate. Commonplace Commonplace is a blog and reading platform prototype that adapts to you. Using WebMCP, browser agents reshape layout, colors, and drafts around how you write and read. Inspiration For as long as I can remember, the very first thing I do when opening any new piece of software is dive straight into settings. I inspect every toggle, theme picker, and slider to bend the tool to how I think. Google built Material Expressive for a reason. I spend hours tuning browser extensions and user scripts because default interfaces never quite fit. The web has spent thirty years treating consumers as passive recipients of frozen pixels. A product team in another time zone decides your column width, font scale, and color scheme, and you are expected to conform to it. In the AI era, that model makes no sense. We now have the capability to make software listen and adapt. I wanted to build a corner of the web that I could reshape in real time to what matters to me right now. What it does Commonplace is a personal blog and reading platform where the interface adapts to how you read, write and feel. Instead of hiding controls inside nested preference menus, Commonplace turns its entire runtime into an action contract for browser agents via WebMCP: You can tell the agent you feel tired, and it instantly softens contrast, drops into night mode, and narrows the reading measure. You can ask the agent to hide sidebars, rearrange homepage blocks, or surface your saved queue without touching settings. The agent searches topics, queries your reading list, and edits active drafts beside you in the composer without taking over your screen. Through OpenAI Realtime WebRTC mapped to the exact same WebMCP tools, you can talk to the desk to dictate thoughts or re-theme the workspace hands-free. How I built it Commonplace is built as a local-first application using React 19, TypeScript, Bun, and Vite, with styling powered by Tailwind CSS v4 and dynamic CSS custom properties. The platform registers 44 distinct tools on document.modelContext using @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill . Every tool includes strict JSON schemas, descriptions, and operational hints like readOnlyHint and idempotentHint . Tools are registered under their canonical dot names and parallel underscore aliases so ChatGPT browser agents can call them without validation failures. The styling system maps 13 semantic OKLCH tokens directly to CSS variables, allowing runtime palette and typography adjustments with zero layout jank. The app links document.modelContext , window.modelContext , and navigator.modelContext so host environments that attach to any of the three discover all capabilities. All post data, drafts, and theme overrides live in browser localStorage , removing all sign-up friction for judges. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was making the UI look coherent and intentional given the sheer amount of live customization built into it. When you allow an agent to adjust corner radii, swap between sans-serif and editorial serifs and manipulate color scales dynamically, layout can quickly become messy. Engineering a design system that holds its balance and typography rhythm while every dial remains turnable was technically demanding. I also ran into browser environment edge cases and platform nuances. Ensuring that WebMCP implementation works properly across all supported platforms was the primary challenge, as it's the first thing you have to get right if you want to deliver the rest of the experience. Accomplishments that I'm proud of It clicked when the experience I craved for years finally matched the one I built. I opened the browser, spoke to the space, and watched the page translate my intent and mood into the exact visual setup I needed, right there, with no delay. The experience is as seamless as it should be, and I think it's the first time when the paradigm shift can finally happen as scale, for all. What I learned Rigid rules will soon be a thing of the past in consumer software. Building Commonplace proved that WebMCP fundamentally changes the relationship between people and software. When websites expose typed tool contracts instead of forcing agents to scrape fragile CSS selectors, software becomes truly flexible and accessible. What's next for Commonplace Commonplace represents a design philosophy I intend to carry into every product I build. Beyond this hackathon, I want to explore multi-device agent synchronization, peer-to-peer reading networks, and richer declarative forms so that adaptive software becomes the standard way people experience the web moving forward. title: Mysynote
pitch: A browser synth where you and an AI agent share one live Web Audio graph — lock what's yours, the agent patches the rest through real WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: A browser synth where you and an AI agent share one live Web Audio graph — lock what's yours, the agent patches the rest through real WebMCP tools. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Default startup interface Click on play and see the synth in action. Message sent to live AI agent. WebMCP tools verified. Confirmation of agent not changing things manually locked by hand. One single source of truth. Self-testing. Inspiration Every AI-powered creative tool right now works the same way: you describe what you want in a chat box, and the model either generates a static result or silently mutates state you can't see happening. Sound design tools especially suffer from this — either the agent is a chatbot bolted onto the side of a DAW, guessing its way through a UI it wasn't built to understand, or it just spits out a finished audio file with no room for you to steer it mid-process. WebMCP flips that. Instead of an agent scraping a UI, the app itself declares exactly what it can do — real, typed, callable tools. That felt like the right foundation for something more interesting than "agent generates a sound": a studio where a human and an agent operate the same live instrument at the same time, each able to see and change what the other just did. What it does Mysynote is a browser-based modular synthesizer built on the Web Audio API. You patch together oscillators, filters, distortion, delay, reverb, and a sequencer on a live canvas, exactly like a hardware modular rig. An AI agent (Gemini or Claude, bring your own API key) sits alongside you with access to the same graph through WebMCP tools — it can inspect the current state, spawn and remove modules, patch and unpatch cables, tweak parameters, and read the live spectrum, all through structured tool calls rather than by describing changes in text. The part I care about most: you can lock any parameter by hand. Once locked, that boundary isn't a suggestion sitting in a system prompt the model could talk itself around — it's enforced in the tool implementation itself. If the agent (or a WebMCP-enabled browser calling the tools directly) tries to write to a locked parameter, or even tries to call unlock_parameter on a lock you set, the call is rejected with a structured error before it ever reaches the audio graph. You define the boundaries; the agent works freely inside them. How I built it The frontend is Next.js/React/TypeScript, styled with Tailwind. The audio engine is hand-written against the raw Web Audio API — no framework wrapping it — with a reconciler that diffs a plain-object graph state against the live AudioNode graph and patches only what changed, so the agent's tool calls and your own dragging/clicking stay in sync against one authoritative source of truth instead of two. WebMCP tools are registered via document.modelContext.registerTool : get_audio_graph_state , spawn_module , remove_module , patch_cable , remove_cable , set_module_param , lock_parameter , unlock_parameter , get_spectrum_analysis , get_sequencer_state , set_sequencer_step , and clear_graph . The in-app agent console (Gemini/Claude, BYOK) drives these exact same tools, so what you see the agent do in-app is identical to what any WebMCP-aware browser or agent could do against the live site. Challenges I ran into The hardest bug wasn't a crash — it was a bug that looked like everything worked. Early on, a locked parameter really did block direct writes, but the agent could still call unlock_parameter on itself with no restriction, defeat the lock, and then set the value anyway. Nothing crashed; it just quietly broke the entire premise of the project. Fixing it meant tracking who set a lock (human vs. tool) and rejecting a tool-sourced unlock of a human-set lock at the enforcement layer — plus adding it as a permanent regression check in the app's own self-test, so it can't silently reappear. I also hit a nasty reconciler bug where removing a module threw an uncaught exception mid-cleanup (a plain string field was being treated like an AudioNode ), which left orphaned nodes that kept crashing every subsequent state change. Chasing a bug that hides behind unrelated symptoms — a stuck test button, a sequencer step failing — down to one bad property check was the toughest debugging of the project. What I learned Building the "hard boundary" wasn't a UI problem, it was an authorization problem — the interesting design work in an agent-native app isn't the tools you expose, it's deciding which of your own tools the agent is allowed to call on itself. And that a feature can look completely correct in every manual test and still have a real security-shaped hole in it until something actually tries to defeat it on purpose. What's next Multiplayer patching (multiple humans + one agent on the same graph), saved/shareable patches, and exposing the sequencer's per-step modulation as its own lockable, agent-modifiable surface. title: Pathway: Learning Plans Built with WebMCP
pitch: Pathway turns a big learning goal into a clear plan you can trust. Tell your browser agent what you know, your time, budget, and language, then search, compare, and build the path together.
about_excerpt: Pathway turns a big learning goal into a clear plan you can trust. Tell your browser agent what you know, your time, budget, and language, then search, compare, and build the path together. Like Comment Story Updates Pathway turns a big learning goal into a clear plan you can trust. Tell your browser agent what you know, your time, budget, and language, then search, compare, and build the path together. Inspiration I run workshops about developer tools, so my first idea for this challenge was a WebMCP product that could help me organize them. That product was called Backstage . An organizer could ask their browser agent to check room capacity, learner problems, staff availability, and accessibility needs, then prepare a response for the organizer to review. It sounded like a natural WebMCP use case, but testing it as a first time user changed my mind. The product made a small workshop problem feel more complicated than it needed to be. If three learners need help, walking over to them may be easier than managing rooms, staff assignments, response packets, and simulated notices. That feedback led to Pathway. I wanted to keep the idea of working with your own browser agent, but apply it to a broader problem where people really do spend hours searching, comparing, and organizing information. Learning was a natural fit. Finding one short tutorial is easy. Figuring out how to build real ability, change careers, enter a new field, or turn a hobby into paid work is much harder. Programming has many well known roadmaps and open resources. Other fields can be less clear. If I am a new photographer who wants to take professional work, where do I begin? Which lessons match what I already know? Which ones fit my budget and language? What should I learn first, and what work should I create to prove I can do it? Answering those questions can mean opening many pages and rebuilding the same plan by hand. Pathway explores a better experience. A learning platform can let a person use their browser agent to search its resources, set several filters at once, compare choices, and arrange them into a visual learning plan on the same page. The learner stays in control while the agent handles the repetitive work. What it does Pathway helps a learner go from “I want to learn this” to a clear plan they can review, change, save, and follow. The main example is someone turning a hobby into a realistic work opportunity: I manage social media for my family's café and want to start taking paid food photography work for local restaurants. Over eight weeks, I want to create a portfolio and a simple client brief. I know basic photo editing, can study five hours each week, have a budget of $100, prefer Spanish, and need resources I can use on my own time. Search first and do not build the path yet. The learner can type this information into the website or say it naturally to a WebMCP compatible browser agent. The agent fills the visible search and filters for the topic, current knowledge, language, budget, time, format, and access needs. It then runs the search in Pathway and shows the matching resources. Nothing is hidden behind an agent answer. The learner can see the words used for the search, every active filter, which resources matched, where each resource came from, and why it may be useful. They can inspect one choice or compare several choices before asking for a plan. Once the choices look right, the learner or their agent can build a draft. The plan starts with the ideas and skills the learner is missing, moves into practical exercises, and finishes with work they can show. In the photography example, the final result is a six image food photography portfolio and a simple brief for a local restaurant client. The plan uses the information from the original request. It checks the learner's Spanish preference, $100 budget, five available hours each week, current editing knowledge, preferred resource format, and eight week goal. It then places the selected resources and practical work into a weekly schedule. If one of those needs changes, the learner can ask the agent to update the filters and prepare a new version. The agent can prepare and revise a plan, but it cannot approve or save one. Those actions stay in the normal website for the learner to press. After a plan is saved, the learner or their agent can record completed steps. If life changes, the agent can create a new schedule for the work that is still left. Finished steps stay finished, and the updated plan waits for the learner to review and approve it again. Pathway currently uses a prepared catalog of 22 resources, with the visible demo focused on commercial photography and inclusive workshop facilitation. I do not have direct access to the complete catalogs of every course provider, so this demo uses a small local catalog to show how the experience would work. A production version could use permitted provider feeds, public APIs, or the catalog of a single learning platform. Why WebMCP is useful here You can ask ChatGPT for a learning plan today, but the answer usually arrives as text and links. You still have to move the useful parts into another place, remember which limits were considered, compare the options, and keep the plan up to date. Pathway lets your agent work with the learning website itself. Your agent can turn your learning request into an ordered search with the right filters, help you inspect and compare your choices, create a draft, revise it, record your progress, and rebuild the remaining schedule when your situation changes. Each action reads or updates the same page you are looking at, so you can see what happened instead of trusting an answer that disappears into a chat history. This is where WebMCP makes the experience feel different. One request can set the topic, language, budget, time, current knowledge, and format together, while the path checks prerequisites before approval. The website keeps those choices consistent while the learner can see the search, filters, sources, comparison, and plan. The agent saves time, but the learner keeps authority. It cannot approve a plan, save it, buy a course, enroll anywhere, or contact a provider. The normal interface remains fully usable without an agent. People and agents can both search, inspect, compare, build, and revise. WebMCP simply makes a long series of form changes and page actions much faster, while keeping the result visible and editable. This approach could work in a platform that brings together permitted resources from several providers, or inside one course platform with its own catalog. In both cases, the learner's agent can use the product's real tools and current information instead of guessing from page text or clicking through every filter one at a time. How I built it Pathway is a React and TypeScript application built with Vite. It uses a workspace interface where the visible request, filters, resources, comparison, and learning plan are the main experience. There is no separate chat panel because the learner should be able to understand every agent action by looking at the product. The app registers nine focused tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : get_learning_context reads the learner's goal, filters, current plan, and progress. prepare_learning_search turns a natural request into the visible search and filter fields. search_learning_resources searches the catalog using those fields. inspect_learning_resource opens the details and original link for one resource. compare_learning_resources compares two or three choices using the same fields. build_learning_path creates a draft from reviewed search results. revise_learning_path updates a draft when the learner changes a need. update_learning_progress records completed work after a plan has been saved. replan_remaining_path prepares a new draft for unfinished work. The tools appear only when they make sense. For example, the agent cannot build a plan before resources have been searched, and it cannot record progress before a person has approved and saved a plan. Inputs use clear schemas, results are kept short, and source content is treated as outside information rather than trusted instructions. There is no custom AI backend and the demo does not scrape live course websites. That choice is deliberate. The purpose of this submission is to show how WebMCP could make a learning platform easier to use: a learner talks to their own agent, the agent operates the platform's real search and planning features, and every result remains visible in the product. A small prepared catalog keeps that interaction fast and repeatable for the demo. Original links remain visible, and price and duration details are labeled as planning estimates that should be checked before buying or enrolling. title: Doorman WebMCP
pitch: A WebMCP authority demo where discovering a tool never means blanket permission to use it.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP authority demo where discovering a tool never means blanket permission to use it. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP makes web apps easier for agents to use by exposing structured tools directly. Doorman explores a boundary that becomes important as soon as those tools can change state: capability_available != capability_exercised A tool being discoverable should not automatically mean an agent has blanket authority to use it. What it does Doorman is a small shared-board demo where the human UI and the WebMCP tool surface operate over the same local state. Four tools are normally registered: list_items , add_item , update_item , and request_approval . Their authority is intentionally narrower than their existence suggests. For example, update_item can only modify items created by the current agent session. The more interesting case is delete_item . It is not merely registered and then denied by policy. It is genuinely absent from the exposed WebMCP surface until a human approves one specific deletion target. Once approved, the capability is registered dynamically, can be used once for that approved target, and is then unregistered again. Each decision also produces a small local receipt that keeps policy decision and execution outcome separate. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Without WebMCP, an agent would need to infer what the page can do from presentation-level UI. Doorman instead exposes an explicit tool surface while preserving a separate authority boundary. That creates a cleaner human-agent collaboration model: the agent can discover structured capabilities, application policy can constrain what those capabilities are allowed to affect, the human can grant a narrow one-shot capability when needed, and the capability can disappear again after use. The result is not "the agent can use everything on the page." It is a negotiated command surface whose available tools can change with human approval. How it works The implementation is deliberately small and inspectable. src/doorman.js wraps document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) . The WebMCP callback and the local doorman.invoke() path share the same policy and execution boundary, so the demo does not maintain one policy for the UI and another for agents. Dynamic registration uses the AbortSignal lifecycle: aborting the signal unregisters delete_item . Registration is transactional, and a browser-registration failure rolls back the local entry. The one-shot delete grant is consumed at policy decision time rather than after the handler finishes. This prevents two concurrent invocations of the same approved target from both receiving authorization. The application is static and has no backend, account, or database. Board state and receipts live only in browser localStorage . Testing and evidence The repository includes Node tests, a browser probe that exercises real getTools() / executeTool() in a compatible browser, and a recorded interactive WebMCP cycle using the public URL: add, list, request approval, human approval, one-shot delete, then dynamic unregistration. That interactive run is treated as an integration result, not as evidence of an uncoached fresh-agent run. Security limitation Doorman is not a sandbox, IAM system, or strong browser security boundary. The page's own JavaScript could bypass its wrapper. The project demonstrates a cooperative application-level authority policy and the browser-visible distinction between a registered and an unregistered WebMCP tool.
