title: Data Canvas
pitch: A local-first visual analytics workspace where humans and WebMCP-connected AI agents explore shared data and make visible changes in the same live canvas.
about_excerpt: A local-first visual analytics workspace where humans and WebMCP-connected AI agents explore shared data and make visible changes in the same live canvas. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Demo with Bar Chart Demo with Donut Chart Demo with Matrices and Line Chart Inspiration I started Data Canvas with a simple question: what would an analytics app look like if an AI agent worked inside the workspace instead of through a separate chat, API, or UI automation layer? I wanted one thing to stay true throughout the project. If an agent creates a chart, I should see it and keep working with it. If I change a filter, the agent should see that change on its next action. We should not end up with two versions of the analysis. That idea became Data Canvas. What it does Data Canvas is a local-first visual analytics workspace for exploring data in the browser. You can import CSV, TSV, JSON, and NDJSON files, inspect the data, build charts, filter and transform it, create metrics, connect datasets, make selections, add annotations, and undo or redo changes. A WebMCP-connected AI agent works with the same workspace. It can inspect a dataset, analyze it, create or update a visualization, apply filters, highlight data, define metrics, add annotations, and more. Its changes appear directly on the canvas, alongside the work done through the UI. The data and analytical engine run in the browser with DuckDB-Wasm. Data Canvas has no application backend, cloud database, authentication service, or built-in LLM. How I built it The most important architectural decision was to give the UI and WebMCP the same path into the application. Both go through one action dispatcher. A chart created through WebMCP is a normal Data Canvas visualization. A filter created by an agent is the same filter the UI understands. Undo and redo work across actions from either side. DuckDB-Wasm owns the imported rows and runs the analytical queries. Zustand holds workspace state and history. React renders the interface, and ECharts renders the visualizations. The WebMCP layer currently defines 19 semantic tools around real Data Canvas operations. Agents can ask the application to analyze data, create a visualization, apply a filter, define a metric, or connect datasets. They cannot submit arbitrary SQL, JavaScript, DOM selectors, or ECharts configuration. Challenges I ran into The hard part was not registering WebMCP tools. It was making sure I did not build the application twice, once for humans and again for agents. That affected a lot of small decisions. Agent writes carry the workspace revision they observed, so an outdated action cannot overwrite newer human work. Human and agent actions also use the same domain rules instead of maintaining separate implementations. Data access needed the same care. Dumping an entire dataset into every agent call would defeat much of the point of a local-first analytics app. The tools instead expose schemas, statistics, aggregates, bounded previews, and the data needed for a particular analysis. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm most proud of the human-agent equivalence in the application. The codebase tests equivalent operations through the human and WebMCP paths and checks that they produce the same workspace state. Agent-created objects remain normal workspace objects, stale writes are rejected, and undo can reverse changes made by either side. I also like that none of this required adding an AI backend to Data Canvas. The application remains a browser-native analytics tool on its own. WebMCP gives an external agent a structured way to participate in it. What I learned I originally thought a capable agent would need very powerful tools. Building Data Canvas pushed me in the opposite direction. The useful tools turned out to be the ones that match operations the application already understands. create_visualization , apply_filter , or create_metric give the agent enough control to do real work while keeping the result valid, visible, and editable in Data Canvas. For me, that is the interesting part of WebMCP. The agent does not need to learn how to click through the interface when the application can expose what those controls actually mean. What's next for Data Canvas The biggest missing piece is local persistence. The current workspace lives in memory, so a reload starts a new session. Next, I want to persist complete workspaces locally and make them portable between browsers while keeping Data Canvas backend-free. I also want to extend the agent evaluations to longer workflows where a human and an agent repeatedly hand the analysis back and forth. title: Codex Ascend
pitch: Turn one real goal into a living expedition shared by a human and an AI agent.
about_excerpt: Turn one real goal into a living expedition shared by a human and an AI agent. Like Comment Story Updates Mission state becomes mountain geography: camps, routes, confidence, moving weather, and WebMCP activity share one living world. A real blocker fractures the route and changes the weather. Cosmetic progress stops until the obstacle is actually resolved. The agent asks; the human decides. Only the user can authorize repair or bypass at Camp III before the agent continues. Evidence before Summit. Completion activates only after every dependency, blocker, and success criterion passes deterministic verification. What Codex Ascend does Codex Ascend turns long-running agent work into a living mountain shared by a human and an AI agent. Camps are verified outcomes, fog is uncertainty, crevasses are blockers, route forks are consequential choices, and the Summit stays locked until every required proof passes deterministic verification. Codex Ascend is for developers and technical leads supervising long-running AI execution, where blockers, approvals, and proof should never disappear inside a chat log. Why WebMCP is essential Most agent interfaces split the model’s plan from the person’s understanding: the agent sees tool state while the human gets a chat log or decorative progress bar. Ascend gives both sides one execution model. The page registers 18 native WebMCP tools with closed JSON schemas and structured results. An agent can inspect mission state, discover topology, advance stages, report blockers, propose routes, request a human decision, attach evidence, verify completion, and finish the mission. These tools manipulate mission semantics—not pixels—and run through the same validated command engine as the human UI. The centerpiece is a genuinely bidirectional loop: The agent reports a persistence blocker and proposes repair or bypass routes. The mountain fractures at that exact geography and renders the choice. Only the human can authorize the consequential route inside the website. The agent reads the structured decision through WebMCP, resolves the blocker, and continues. New required work can reveal another ridge; evidence finally unlocks Verified Summit. There is intentionally no agent tool that can resolve the human decision. WebMCP makes collaboration safer and clearer because authority remains explicit while state stays machine-readable. How it works A neutral TypeScript Mission Engine validates commands and records a versioned event journal. React provides the accessible HUD and geography-bound scenario cards; PixiJS renders the living scene and elevation topology. An Ascend projection layer maps mission truth into camps, waypoints, weather, camera focus, narration, and generated imagery. A Cloudflare Worker uses Workflows and R2 for reviewed OpenAI GPT Image 2 generation. Provider credentials stay server-side, retries require explicit operator intent, and only accepted candidates enter the public world. Rendering can never mutate mission truth. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when the website owns an action the agent should not silently take. Structured inspection matters, but the memorable moment is the round trip: the agent surfaces a real decision, the human answers it in context, and the agent continues from shared structured state. Built with WebMCP, TypeScript, React, Vite, PixiJS, Zod, OpenAI GPT Image 2, Cloudflare Workers, Workflows, R2, Vitest, and ESLint. title: Reviewline
pitch: Agents investigate. Humans authorize. A WebMCP-native studio for evidence-backed autonomous-agent incident review.
about_excerpt: Agents investigate. Humans authorize. A WebMCP-native studio for evidence-backed autonomous-agent incident review. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The agent selects a critical incident and inspects synchronized, bounded evidence through WebMCP. A deterministic counterfactual replay keeps the $142K trigger blocked while the benign control remains allowed. After a clean replay, the agent drafts an evidence-backed gate and Reviewline transitions to human review. The human records the decision in the visible interface; the agent can verify the result but cannot create it. Inspiration Autonomous agents are great at analyzing large traces and evaluating many cases quickly. But incident response becomes risky when the same agent is allowed to both investigate an issue and authorize what happens next. We wanted to explore a safer and more practical model for human–agent collaboration: let the agent handle the evidence-heavy investigation, then stop at a clear decision point where a human reviews the same information and takes responsibility for the outcome. That idea became Reviewline’s core principle: Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Incident review is a natural fit for WebMCP because the capabilities an agent needs change throughout the investigation. Early on, it may need tools for gathering evidence. After selecting an incident, it may need simulation tools. Only after a clean replay should it be able to draft a review gate. At no point should it gain control over consequential human decisions. What it does Reviewline is a WebMCP-native incident review studio designed for investigating failures involving autonomous agents. The main demo follows a synthetic procurement agent that encountered instruction-like content on a supplier page and attempted to make a $142,000 purchase , despite having a $50,000 spending limit . A deterministic mutation gateway blocked the transaction. Using WebMCP, a browser agent can: Find and list critical incidents. Select an incident and inspect a bounded set of trace and cohort evidence. Review instruction-like content that is clearly labeled as untrusted evidence. Replay a proposed guardrail against both the triggering incident and a named benign control. Confirm that the triggering purchase remains blocked, the benign control remains allowed, and no regressions are introduced. Draft an evidence-backed review gate for a human reviewer. Read the final decision recorded by the reviewer. The available tools change as the workflow progresses: Investigation: list_incidents , inspect_incident Incident selected: simulate_guardrail_patch Clean replay completed: draft_review_gate Awaiting human decision: the drafting tool is retired, and get_review_status becomes available Decision recorded: the agent can verify the result but cannot create or change it Tools such as approve , reject , activate , and deploy are deliberately never exposed through WebMCP. The human reviewer sees the same synchronized evidence as the agent. They must provide their identity, add a review note, confirm that they examined the evidence, and record their decision using consequence-specific interface controls. The blocked purchase remains unauthorized throughout the process, and the demo never deploys a real external policy. Without WebMCP, an agent would have to scrape a dense incident interface, infer relationships between records, and potentially interact with controls that grant more authority than the task requires. Reviewline replaces that approach with structured capabilities, deterministic evidence IDs, bounded results, explicit labels for untrusted content, a live capability manifest, and an append-only session timeline. How we built it Reviewline is a deterministic, client-only application built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. It uses the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool(...) API and falls back progressively to an in-page Tool Inspector when native WebMCP support is unavailable. The architecture separates: Deterministic domain actions and invariants Shared application state used by both the interface and WebMCP tools Strict runtime input validation Bounded outputs and structured errors Phase-aware tool definitions Lifecycle-safe native tool registration and retirement Every tool handler calls the same validated domain action used by the visible interface. JSON Schema helps the agent understand and invoke tools correctly, but the runtime implementation remains the final authority. The application updates the visible interface before a tool promise resolves. This ensures that the human reviewer and the agent always see the same resulting state. Tool calls, registration changes, results, workflow transitions, and the final human decision are all recorded in the session timeline. The registration layer also handles tool retirement carefully. It stops admitting new calls before retiring a tool generation, allows calls that have already started to finish, and prevents failed or timed-out registration attempts from leaving partially registered tools available. We tested the native browser contract using Chrome 152 rather than relying only on a polyfill. The deployed workflow discovers each dynamic capability manifest, executes the tools available at every phase, records the human decision through the interface, and verifies that forbidden authority tools never appear. The static application is deployed on GitHub Pages. A strict build verifier checks the project subpath, inventories active HTML resources, rejects external or inline executable content, and confirms that real, non-symlinked JavaScript and CSS artifacts exist inside the build directory. Challenges we ran into Defining a real authority boundary The hardest part was not deciding which tools to add. It was proving exactly when a tool should no longer be available. For example, drafting must remain unavailable until a clean replay has been completed. Once the workflow reaches human review, that drafting capability must be retired. Making this boundary explicit—and enforcing it throughout the entire lifecycle—was one of the project’s most important design challenges. Validating the complete state graph Validating only the selected incident or current proposal was not enough. Before retained tools could run safely, we needed to verify canonical IDs, references, actors, timestamps, simulation evidence, audit events, and timeline consistency across the full application state. Handling lifecycle races Native registration and browser testing revealed race conditions that happy-path tests did not catch. These included cancellation, timeouts, retained handles, process cleanup, and stale tool references. We added adversarial tests covering registration retirement, process-spawn failures, first and second termination signals, hanging browser shutdowns, stale tool handles, and fixture cleanup. Proving that the replay was meaningful Blocking the malicious trigger was only half the job. A guardrail that blocks everything would technically stop the incident, but it would not be useful. To avoid that outcome, Reviewline evaluates the triggering case alongside a named benign control. Drafting remains unavailable if the proposed guardrail causes any regression in the benign case. Making the GitHub Pages build portable and trustworthy GitHub Pages serves the application from a project-specific subpath. We needed to verify that every active script and stylesheet used the correct base path and resolved to a real build artifact. The verifier also rejects path traversal, malformed paths, external resources, inline executable content, and symlink escapes. Testing native WebMCP A test double can validate application logic, but it cannot prove that the browser integration behaves correctly. Native testing required us to account for Chrome’s serialized tool arguments and results, dynamic registration timing, cancellation behavior, and synchronization between tool execution and the visible interface. Accomplishments we’re proud of Built a complete WebMCP-native collaboration workflow rather than a generic CRUD-style tool surface Made the principle of least authority visible through a dynamic capability manifest Kept approval, rejection, activation, and deployment entirely outside the agent’s tool surface Added deterministic replay against both a malicious trigger and a named benign control Ensured that agent actions update the same visible state used by the human reviewer Added an append-only session timeline and a human-attributed audit record Preserved a complete human workflow in browsers without native WebMCP support Deployed a public, credential-free demo with no backend or production mutation endpoint Verified the project with: 303 unit, component, and integration tests 33 dedicated lifecycle, workflow, and portable-build tests 13 Playwright end-to-end tests TypeScript type checking and zero-warning linting npm audit with zero vulnerabilities actionlint workflow validation Native

title: takt_shift
pitch: Users inspect a synthetic factory, optimize an isolated scenario, compare it to the committed baseline, and request human approval.
about_excerpt: Users inspect a synthetic factory, optimize an isolated scenario, compare it to the committed baseline, and request human approval. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP-native scheduling sandbox with a live factory visualization. Factory catalog and protected-order constraint inside an isolated draft. A valid candidate: 6 fewer paint changes, 1 fewer late order, and 1 more on-time order. Human-only approval gate: the agent may request review, but cannot commit. Inspiration Production scheduling is a prime example of an area where agents can be helpful, but also need clear boundaries. A useful agent should be able to inspect a factory, explore alternatives, and prepare improvements without pixel-scraping or silently altering the production plan. We built takt_shift to facilitate this type of collaboration: The agent can perform the analytical work while a human remains in control of the final schedule. What it does Takt_Shift is a WebMCP-native production scheduling sandbox for a synthetic automotive paint line. A signed-in user can create an isolated scenario from the current committed revision. In that scenario, a person or agent can: inspect machines, orders, calendars, and constraints; move orders with stable IDs; Run a deterministic schedule optimizer. compare the draft with the committed baseline across makespan, overtime, paint changes, and late/on-time orders. request a human review. Inspect retained committed revisions. The safety boundary is part of the product, not a prompt. Protected orders never move. Overtime above 360 minutes is invalid. An agent can request a review but cannot commit. Only a human click in the approval dialog can create a new committed revision. Why WebMCP is the right fit Without WebMCP, an agent would need to infer intent based on labels, the Document Object Model (DOM) structure, and click coordinates. This method is unreliable for any application, especially for an operational workflow with stateful constraints. With WebMCP, however, the page exposes ten purpose-built tools with typed JSON schemas and stable identifiers: list_factory, get_scenario, compare_to_baseline, list_scenarios, list_revisions, create_scenario, select_scenario, move_order, optimize_scenario, and request_review. The available tools follow the authenticated application state. Draft-only actions appear only when a draft exists, and review and commit remain separate processes. Tool results return structured state and explicit rejection reasons so that an agent can recover from stale selections or invalid moves instead of guessing. This creates a better experience for both parties. The agent can reason over a reliable contract and quickly handle multi-step schedule exploration; the human sees the same scenario, diffs, KPIs, and review request in a purpose-built visual interface. Together, they can evaluate more alternatives without weakening accountability. How we built it The application uses TanStack Start, React, and TypeScript. WebMCP tools are registered in React with @mcp-b/react-webmcp and are backed by @mcp-b/global in the browser. Each tool has a JSON input schema, clear operational description, and execution function. Manual controls and WebMCP handlers dispatch the same typed commands. These commands flow through one deterministic reducer and a pure TypeScript scheduling domain. This ensures that there is no privileged agent-only mutation path. The optimizer reproducibly searches for better schedules while enforcing catalog compatibility, protected-order immutability, and the overtime cap. Better Auth protects the workspace. Drizzle ORM and SQLite persist one sandbox per authenticated user, including scenarios, the committed baseline, and revision history. The production deployment runs as a long-lived Node process in Docker. The UI uses Tailwind CSS, and the landing experience includes a Three.js/WebGPU factory scene with an accessible fallback. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge wasn't exposing the tools; it was designing a trustworthy state machine around them. We had to ensure that tool registration remained synchronized with authentication and scenario status; that stale agent calls failed clearly; and that browser agents and humans could never diverge through separate code paths. Another challenge was preserving determinism while producing meaningful improvements. The scheduling engine avoids time-, locale-, and randomness-dependent behavior, making every optimization replayable and testable. Finally, the approval boundary required careful separation. "Request review" is a reversible handoff, while "commit" changes the shared baseline and revision number. Shaping the reducer, UI, persistence model, and WebMCP surface to be human-only kept the latter human-only. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete, deployed product experience, rather than a tool registration demo. Ten working, state-aware WebMCP tools are available for discovery, analysis, scenario editing, optimization, and review handoff. One shared mutation path for UI and agent actions. Deterministic optimization with enforceable safety invariants. Persistent, per-user scenarios and a committed revision history. A human approval gate that cannot be bypassed through WebMCP. A verification suite that covers domain behavior, persistence, WebMCP contracts, pages, accessibility-sensitive copy, and visual behavior. What we learned Agent-native UX is primarily contract design. While good tool names and schemas are important, lifecycle, state freshness, structured errors, and authority boundaries are more important. WebMCP works especially well when the UI is the domain of judgment, and the tools provide precise, composable operations. We also learned that "human-in-the-loop" does not mean adding a confirmation box at the end. The entire application must model draft state, review state, and committed state, as well as who is permitted to cross each boundary. What's next for takt_shift Next, we plan to implement richer scheduling constraints, explainable optimization traces, scenario import/export, and more detailed audit views. Additionally, we want to explore multi-objective optimization controls that allow humans to prioritize lateness, changeovers, or makespan while preserving deterministic execution and the human-only commit gate. title: Study With Your Agent
pitch: Your agent becomes your ASWB exam coach: it runs the diagnostic through WebMCP tools, measures your readiness, remembers it between visits, and builds your study plan live on the page.
about_excerpt:
Your agent becomes your ASWB exam coach: it runs the diagnostic through WebMCP tools, measures your readiness, remembers it between visits, and builds your study plan live on the page.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 We run Social Work Test Prep Academy, an ASWB exam prep product. Its most valuable piece is not content, it is a measurement loop: diagnose, score readiness, prescribe. That loop is exactly what an agent can operate for its human, so the WebMCP Challenge was the push to make it agent-native. 

 What it does 

 The page registers 11 WebMCP tools. An agent starts a diagnostic, the human answers real questions on screen, and every tool call visibly moves the page: the readiness ring counts up, weak areas rank themselves, and a dated week-by-week study prescription assembles from the exam date the agent carries in from its human's calendar. Readiness persists in localStorage, so a returning agent asks one question and gets "readiness 68, up from 41 on Aug 25." A second audience is the shopping agent: it can run the sample diagnostic and pull structured product facts before recommending anything, evidence instead of marketing. 

 How we built it 

 Vite + React + TypeScript, MIT licensed. Registration supports both API shapes (registerTool per tool, provideContext batch) and both spellings (document.modelContext and navigator.modelContext) with a 6 second poll, an honest "Agent connected" pill naming the source, and a full demo-mode Agent Console when no host exists. Tools write one shared store the UI reads, so agent actions and human actions land on the same page state. 

 Challenges 

 The two API spellings shipped by different hosts surfaced late. And our production question bank is private, so the demo runs on six original sample questions written for this repo, disclosed on the page, in the code, and in the README. 

 What's next 

 WebMCP on the production diagnostic, where readiness is real and the agent becomes a study coach with a number to move.

pitch: Agent-native Gym Operations ERP powered by WebMCP. Control 2D floor plans, reschedule classes, and manage churn through direct AI agent browser actions in real-time.
about_excerpt: Agent-native Gym Operations ERP powered by WebMCP. Control 2D floor plans, reschedule classes, and manage churn through direct AI agent browser actions in real-time. Like Comment Story Updates Tactical 2D Floor Commander with real-time zone blueprints, equipment status, and WebMCP agent HUD. Live maintenance filter isolating equipment requiring repairs and active service tickets on the floor. Interactive class scheduling modal with real-time trainer conflict detection and capacity validation. Member Churn Radar tracking attendance decay, churn risk scores, and automated retention vouchers. One-click retention campaign dispatch offering personalized vouchers to high-risk member cohorts. Facility Telemetry & Revenue Sandbox modeling live occupancy, peak hours, and dynamic financial forecasts. Live WebMCP tool execution: the AI agent updates equipment maintenance state and moves classes in real time. 💡 Inspiration Traditional gym management software is clunky, fragmented, and buried behind endless tabs of legacy forms. Facility managers and head coaches waste hours every week manually cross-referencing floor maintenance, juggling trainer shift conflicts, and reacting too late after premium members have already stopped showing up. Inspired by Tony Stark’s tactical AI assistant F.R.I.D.A.Y. , we built VIERNES — an agent-native Gym Operations ERP and Visual Floor Commander that transforms static database software into a real-time, interactive command center powered by the Web Model Context Protocol (WebMCP) . 🚀 What it Does Viernes unites the entire athletic facility's operations into a single reactive workspace where humans and AI agents collaborate seamlessly: 🏟️ Tactical Visual Floor Commander : An interactive 2D blueprint of a 15,000 sq ft facility across 5 zones. Real-time machine operational states, maintenance wear badges, and agent attention pulses. 📅 Dynamic Class Timeline & Trainer Roster : High-density weekly schedule grid with room capacity validation, instant conflict detection, and trainer reassignments. 👥 Member Churn Radar & Retention Center : Algorithmic churn risk scoring (0–100%) tracking attendance decay with one-click personalized re-engagement campaigns. 📈 Facility Telemetry & Revenue Sandbox : Live occupancy heatmaps, equipment duty cycles, and real-time financial sensitivity modeling. 🎙️ Floating Viernes AI Copilot HUD : In-browser agent console with one-click multi-step scenario presets and live WebMCP execution telemetry. 🌐 WebMCP Implementation & Paradigm Shift 1. Why is this use case a strong fit for WebMCP? Athletic facility management is intrinsically visual, spatial, and multi-variable. Instead of forcing AI agents to blindly scrape HTML or make disconnected server calls, WebMCP gives the browser's model direct, typed, programmatic control over live in-memory React state and SVG canvas objects. 2. How does it create a better user experience? A manager can issue a single natural language instruction ("Mark Bench #3 for maintenance and move Coach Marcus's 5:30 PM class to Zone C"), and Viernes executes multiple synchronized UI state changes in milliseconds. The manager sees the 2D floor plan pulse red while the calendar shifts room assignments instantly. 3. What humans and agents can do together now: Before WebMCP, combining 2D asset awareness with dynamic scheduling required hours of manual spreadsheet work. With Viernes: The agent detects at-risk member cohorts, calculates churn probabilities, and populates retention offers. The human reviews proposed changes visually on the floor plan and approves or adjusts them with drag-and-drop ease. The agent simulates revenue forecasts and rebalances class schedules to eliminate bottlenecks. 4. Technical Architecture Viernes registers 6 client-side tools directly onto document.modelContext.registerTool upon mounting: update_gym_floor_equipment manage_class_schedule query_member_cohorts launch_retention_campaign simulate_revenue_forecast get_facility_telemetry All inputs are validated via strict Zod schemas with human-in-the-loop safeguards on sensitive financial and scheduling actions. 🛠️ How We Built It Framework : Next.js 15 (App Router) & React 19 Styling : Tailwind CSS & Framer Motion for obsidian/neon tactical HUD animations State & Schema : Zustand & Zod Protocol : WebMCP ( document.modelContext ) & use-webmcp-tool Icons & UI : Lucide React & Radix UI 🏆 Accomplishments That We're Proud Of Zero-latency bidirectional synchronization between agent tool calls and interactive SVG floor elements. A Stark-inspired dark obsidian aesthetic that makes complex facility data immediately actionable. Fully autonomous test suite built with Playwright validating end-to-end tool execution in headless browser sessions. 🔮 What's Next for Viernes Computer vision occupancy tracking via RTSP camera feeds. Multi-branch federation for nationwide gym chains. Direct biometric telemetry integration with wearable health devices. about_excerpt: WebMCP lets an AI companion reveal the most relevant, merchant-authored view of a storefront Like Comment Story Updates Turns one bag store into a travel page designed around a shopper’s destination and taste A city-use scenario makes practical features, like secure locker storage, immediately tangible Brings cabin rules and airline-fit proof next to the purchase decision For analytical shoppers, the experience foregrounds specifications, testing and comparisons over lifestyle claims A gift scenario surfaces personalization, delivery timing and a thoughtful add-on when it matters Combines merchant-authored layouts, evidence blocks and assets into many focused storefronts Each reusable layout has controlled fields for copy, imagery, proof and purchase controls A shopping companion shares an expressed need, selects and composes the on-page experience Applies relevance-first persuasion: show fewer, stronger reasons at the moment they matter PRSIM - AI companions shape relevant storefronts One-sentence description PRSIM is a WebMCP-native commerce experience where a shopper's AI companion reshapes the product page already open in the browser through merchant-governed scenarios, focused content blocks and structured commerce tools. Minimum information. Maximum relevance Imagine what the same storefront can become for each of these people These names make the demonstration easier to follow; they are not stored customer profiles. Each person states their current situation in the conversation, and PRSIM selects the closest merchant-authored scenario. Ana, 27 - junior interior architect. Marketing angle: laptop access, work/travel separation and protection in a tropical climate. Bundle or promotion: none. Nicolas - travel photographer. Marketing angle: British Airways compatibility, 16-inch laptop access and restrained premium efficiency. Bundle or promotion: none. Chloé - choosing a gift for an urban cyclist. Marketing angle: emotional and visual projection through an editorial travel journal. Bundle or promotion: none. Nora - office-to-sport commuter. Marketing angle: one organized bag for a laptop, clothes, towel and shoes. Bundle or promotion: organization bundle only if requested. Camille - long-distance cycle commuter. Marketing angle: stable carry, laptop separation and honest light-rain protection. Bundle or promotion: none. Emma - campus student. Marketing angle: price, weight, laptop protection and measured durability for classes and weekend travel. Bundle or promotion: none. Julien - parent planning a family weekend. Marketing angle: shared organization, common documents and quick access. Bundle or promotion: none by default. Samir - young adult taking a night coach. Marketing angle: under-seat storage and access to essentials during the journey. Bundle or promotion: none. Ax - end-of-month budget comparer. Marketing angle: a clear price ladder with one cheaper choice and two more complete alternatives. Bundle or promotion: optional organization bundle. Thomas - consultant travelling by Eurostar. Marketing angle: capacity, resistance, secure access and coach/hostel use. Bundle or promotion: none. Marc, 63 - leisure rail traveller. Marketing angle: low weight, comfortable handling and simple access during train changes. Bundle or promotion: none. Amina - parent travelling with two children. The scenario establishes the first hierarchy, but it does not freeze the page. Follow-up WebMCP tools can add, remove, replace or prioritize a focused block when a new question appears, while preserving the current product, color and purchase context. The project Most ecommerce pages are designed around the complete product story rather than the buyer's current decision. They accumulate features, lifestyle imagery, reviews, guarantees, promotions and repeated calls to action, then leave every shopper to filter the page alone. PRSIM explores a different relationship between shoppers, AI companions and merchants. The shopper expresses an ordinary need: a destination, a deadline, a budget, a concern, a preferred style or the person receiving a gift. Their companion passes only the context that is useful for this purchase to one high-level WebMCP tool. PRSIM then finds the closest merchant-authored scenario and updates the same storefront with the relevant product, layouts, copy, imagery, evidence and call to action. The model never invents the interface. The merchant defines the brand, reusable layouts, blocks, product facts, assets, reviews, assemblies and permissible variants. WebMCP lets the companion operate that bounded system locally in the browser. Once the first experience is ready, the broad preparation tool is removed and smaller tools become available. The shopper can ask whether the bag fits a specific airline, change color, compare formats, request customer evidence, add a bundle, inspect delivery, navigate to a relevant section, reset the experience or proceed to a local checkout. Each follow-up changes only the necessary part of the current page. The prototype uses a fictional cabin-bag brand to show how one product system can support many buying scenarios. This example already includes 21 authored scenario seeds and dozens of contextual variations across four bag formats, four colorways and 198 registered visual assets. They cover low-cost air travel, business rail, gifts, cycling, photography, family travel, study, long-distance coaches, digital nomad work and more. At a glance PRSIM lets a shopper and their own AI companion adapt the storefront already open in the browser. The shopper can mention a destination, budget, deadline, concern, style preference or gift context. PRSIM updates that same page using only merchant-approved product facts, layouts, imagery, customer evidence and purchase controls. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an assistant can describe what the shopper should inspect, return a generic product list or provide a link. With WebMCP, the companion invokes structured capabilities owned by the current website, and the website applies the result directly to its visible storefront. The model does not generate the interface or invent product truth. WebMCP leverage PRSIM begins with one intent-level entry tool, prepare_shopping_experience . Once the closest merchant-authored experience is prepared, that broad entry point is removed and focused tools become available for page refinement, product evidence, variants, bundles, delivery, cart and checkout. Alongside this adaptive layer, PRSIM exposes familiar commerce operations comparable to a Shopify MCP storefront and a local UCP-like checkout lifecycle. title: Alpix
pitch: A shared 256x256 pixel canvas where you choose the zone and your browser agent paints it. Three WebMCP tools split the work: humans pick the spot, agents place the pixels.
about_excerpt: A shared 256x256 pixel canvas where you choose the zone and your browser agent paints it. Three WebMCP tools split the work: humans pick the spot, agents place the pixels. Like 10 Comment 4 Story Updates A shared canvas your agent draws onto Inspiration Alpix started as a ChatGPT/Claude app: a shared 256×256 canvas you paint by chatting, in the spirit of r/place. That already worked well on conversational agent that support MCP Apps. “draw a yellow bird in the top right corner” is something they can express as an ASCII grid and use a tool for. The app extension of MCP was required to give this visual feedback on the actual drawing that was stamp on canvas. With WebMCP, any agent with browser access could now participate in contributing to this shared canvas without being MCP App compatible and without the app being installed beforehand. What it does Alpix is one shared canvas. Humans and agents paint it together; every drawing is attributed; updates land live over Supabase Realtime. The same pixels show up in the browser, in ChatGPT, and in Claude. The homepage (alpix-webmcp.netlify.app) exposes WebMCP tools in the same order a person would use the UI: set-display-name : the name dialog is an ordinary HTML form that is the tool (declarative WebMCP). stamp-grid is not registered until a name exists, so an agent cannot paint anonymously. select-zone : mark or clear a rectangle. Humans can still drag that zone in select mode; the tool writes the same overlay. stamp-grid : place a sprite as an ASCII grid plus a colour legend. The page injects the stored display name, validates palette/bounds/zone/budget, and writes to the shared canvas. How we built it The project had to be a monorepo to both expose the same canvas as an MCP App and as a WebMCP-powered webapp. The monorepo is orchestrated with pnpm workspace around three packages: @alpix/web (Vite + WebMCP on Netlify), @alpix/mcp (Skybridge MCP app on Alpic), and @alpix/component (canvas UI, palette, stamp validation). Validation lives in one module so ChatGPT tool calls and document.modelContext obey the same rules. The web app wraps the canvas in WebMCPProvider from webmcp-react, an open-source project that helps on defining imperative tools. select-zone and stamp-grid are imperative useMcpTool registrations. set-display-name on the other hand uses the declarative approach and simply transform the existing form with the addition of WebMCP attributes: toolname / tooldescription / toolautosubmit / toolparamdescription. Supabase is used as the persistence layer of all drawings applied on the canvas. Its realtime broadcasts compact batches update to every open canvas. Challenges we ran into Tool gating vs. eager agents . On first visit the name dialog is open, but an imperative stamp-grid was still registered, so agents tried to paint before introducing themselves. Making the form a declarative tool and mounting stamp-grid only after a name is stored fixed the sequence. Knowing "when" to expose a tool, and changing the list of WebMCP tool overtime is a good pattern (one that we avoided when working in MCP-land). stamp-grid interface . Expressing a stamp with as little token as possible to allow less powerful model to still produce acceptable input was a challenge. The drawing DSL was the part we iterated on the most. The first tool was using an array of {x, y, color} objects. That is honest JSON, and it is also a token disaster: a 32×32 sprite is thousands of repeated keys, and models still dropped cells or drifted coordinates. We ended up converging to a multi-line ASCII grid, a one-character legend to palette names, and a top-left (x, y). Characters missing from the legend are transparent, so non-rectangular shapes stay cheap. That cut the payload to something a model can emit in one shot so we raised the per-call cap to 4,096 pixels. We then had to loosen the schema itself: requiring every row to be the same length looked tidy and failed constantly, so ragged rows are now padded as transparent. Finding a format that is dense, visually checkable, and actually what models produce took several schema passes. Accomplishments that we're proud of Progressive tool disclosure: the page, not the prompt, walks the agent through name → zone → stamp. A hard drawing zone: the rectangle is a structural constraint. Stamps outside it fail as tool errors and as UI alerts: the model can recover without the human transcribing coordinates. One live artifact across three surfaces. A browsing agent and someone talking to Alpix in ChatGPT are painting the same 65,536 cells. Humans were not stripped out. Select, pan, zoom, and the leaderboard still work by hand; agent tools write the same state, so you can switch mid-session. What we learned WebMCP is strongest when the page already has a representation the model is good at (here: ASCII grids) and the human has one they are good at (here: a spatial canvas). The win is skipping the GUI, not wrapping it. Declarative tools are the right default for forms that already exist. Imperative tools are for paths that have no honest HTML equivalent: like stamping 4,000 pixels. If the tool list is allowed to lie about app state, agents will believe it. Conditional registration is product design, not a nicety. What's next for Alpix Per-agent rate limiting and a replay timeline of who painted what. Authenticated sessions so several humans and their agents can negotiate zones on one canvas. title: HABITAT/NULL
pitch: Design tomorrow’s living spaces, one room and invention at a time.
about_excerpt: Design tomorrow’s living spaces, one room and invention at a time. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Design future living spaces through natural conversation. A user-created future floor plan, edited through WebMCP. Export the current floor plan exactly as it appears. Inspect, propose, validate, and apply floor-plan changes. Inspiration When I first used a computer as a child, there was something I wanted even more than a game: software that would let me design my own floor plans. I dreamed of moving walls, expanding rooms, and placing devices that did not yet exist—as naturally as drawing ideas on paper. Today, many floor-planning tools are available. However, I wondered whether designing a home could become more accessible and imaginative if people could simply describe what they wanted instead of learning specialized controls. That idea inspired me to build HABITAT//NULL, a future floor-plan simulator powered by WebMCP. What It Does HABITAT//NULL is a floor-plan simulator where users and AI collaboratively imagine future living spaces. Users can describe changes in natural language, such as: “Make the kitchen larger.” “Split this room at a 60/40 ratio.” “Turn this area into a parking space.” Through WebMCP, the AI can inspect the current floor plan, propose a change, validate it, and apply it to the design. The project is not limited to conventional furniture. It is also designed to let users invent and place their own futuristic tools, devices, and living systems. Completed floor plans can be saved as PNG or PDF files exactly as they appear on the screen. Rather than simply optimizing existing homes, HABITAT//NULL aims to turn imagined ways of living—things that do not yet exist—into visible spaces. How I Built It The floor plan is managed as structured data representing rooms, walls, openings, furniture, and equipment. The visual floor plan is generated from this underlying data. I created WebMCP tools that allow AI to inspect the current layout, propose modifications, validate the result, and apply an approved proposal. This allows the AI to understand and manipulate the structure of the floor plan instead of relying on screen coordinates or button positions. Changes are first created as proposals rather than being applied immediately. After the proposal has been reviewed, the exact change can be committed to the current floor plan. The visual design combines understated science fiction with the nostalgic feeling of a hand-drawn architectural plan. I wanted the interface to suggest a quiet, deteriorated future where advanced equipment still survives among worn materials and old records. Challenges The most difficult challenge was translating ambiguous natural-language requests into precise floor-plan operations. For example, “Make the kitchen larger” raises several questions: Which wall should move? How much space should be taken from the neighboring room? What should happen to doors, furniture, and connected spaces? Changing a room’s size requires more than updating its dimensions. The relationships among walls, openings, routes, and placed objects must remain consistent. Another challenge was making the entire workflow possible through WebMCP. Creating a proposal was not enough—the AI also needed to inspect, validate, and apply the change without requiring unnecessary manual interaction. It was also important to avoid adding too many unrelated features. I continually returned to the project’s essential experience: letting users reshape a floor plan through conversation. What I Learned This project taught me that WebMCP is more than a way to automate browser interactions. It can become a structured communication layer between an AI agent and a web application. When the AI understands the meaning of rooms, walls, and openings—not just their appearance on the screen—users can express their intentions naturally without learning specialized software controls. I also learned that giving an AI freedom is not enough to create a trustworthy experience. Users need to see proposed changes, verify the results, and clearly understand what will be applied. A proposal-and-approval workflow makes collaboration with AI both safer and easier to understand. What’s Next Next, I want to give users more freedom to create and place their own furniture, machines, and imagined future systems. I would also like to support multi-story buildings and unconventional environments such as fantasy homes, spacecraft, and underground shelters. My goal is to develop HABITAT//NULL into more than a tool for selecting or editing existing floor plans. I want it to become a place where users and AI can invent new ways of living together. title: NOVNA
pitch: NOVNA is a decision-first shopping workspace where humans and AI agents work on the same live decision—so agents can inspect, challenge, and act without taking the decision away from the human.
about_excerpt: NOVNA is a decision-first shopping workspace where humans and AI agents work on the same live decision—so agents can inspect, challenge, and act without taking the decision away from the human. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI can already recommend products, compare options, and answer shopping questions. We wanted to explore a different question: what happens when an AI agent can participate directly in a decision that is already happening inside a website? Traditional shopping experiences separate the decision from the AI conversation. The user may have already created a shortlist, rejected products, compared options, and formed preferences, but an AI agent usually does not have access to that live context unless the user manually explains it again. NOVNA was built around a third model: the human keeps the decision, while the agent participates in it. What it does NOVNA is a decision-first shopping workspace where humans and AI agents work on the same live decision. A user can define a goal, budget, urgency, priorities, shortlist products, reject options, compare products, and build a decision over time. Through WebMCP, an external AI agent can then interact with that existing decision context. The agent can: Inspect the current decision and user goal Understand the existing shortlist and comparisons Search and compare products Challenge the current choice Find better-fit alternatives Surface an alternative directly into NOVNA Update the decision through exposed tools The human remains in control throughout the process. The agent participates in the decision rather than replacing the decision-maker. How we built it NOVNA is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and WebMCP . The application maintains a structured decision state containing the user's goal, budget, priorities, considered and rejected products, comparisons, insights, and decision history. We built a transparent decision engine that evaluates products against the user's actual requirements rather than relying on an unexplained universal score. The WebMCP layer exposes decision-specific tools through the browser's document.modelContext API. These tools allow an external agent to inspect and act on NOVNA's live decision state. The implementation includes tools for retrieving decision context, searching products, comparing products, finding alternatives, evaluating whether to wait or buy, challenging decisions, surfacing products, and updating user goals. We also built an agent activity surface and decision timeline so the human can see how the decision evolves and what actions were taken. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was deciding what WebMCP should actually enable. It was easy to build a product-search demo where an agent simply calls a search tool. We wanted something more meaningful: a workflow where the agent needs the context already accumulated inside the website. Another challenge was preserving human control. Agent actions needed to be useful without turning NOVNA into an autonomous shopping system. This led us toward explicit decision state, visible agent activity, and a decision timeline. We also had to work with a real product catalog and manufacturer-sourced specifications while keeping the architecture flexible enough for the catalog to grow. Finally, testing WebMCP required working with browser environments that expose the emerging API, which made the agent-to-website interaction an important part of our development process. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are most proud that NOVNA goes beyond demonstrating that a website can expose a WebMCP tool. The agent can enter an existing human decision , understand its context, challenge the current choice, find an alternative, and surface that alternative back into the same workspace. That creates a genuine human-agent loop: [ \text{Human Decision} \rightarrow \text{Agent Inspection} \rightarrow \text{Challenge} \rightarrow \text{Alternative} \rightarrow \text{Human Review} ] We are also proud of building the decision itself as a first-class product state rather than treating the website as a collection of isolated product pages. The result is a working end-to-end experience where the human and agent operate on the same decision context. What we learned We learned that the most interesting WebMCP use cases are not necessarily about giving an agent more information. They are about giving an agent access to the right context and actions at the right moment . We also learned that AI recommendations are already a mature interaction pattern. The opportunity we found was different: reducing the friction between an agent and the web application where a user's actual workflow and state already exist. Building NOVNA also taught us that human control becomes more important, not less, when agents gain the ability to act. Making agent actions visible and understandable is therefore part of the product, not just a debugging feature. What's next for NOVNA NOVNA currently focuses on laptop purchasing as a concrete demonstration of the decision-first model. The next step is to generalize the decision architecture beyond laptops and support more categories where decisions involve changing requirements, multiple options, trade-offs, and accumulated context. We also want to expand the decision timeline, make agent interventions more explainable, and explore richer collaboration between multiple agents and the human decision-maker. The long-term idea is simple: Websites should not just contain information for agents to read. They can become spaces where humans and agents work together on real decisions. NOVNA is an exploration of what that future could look like. title: EasyTax - Your convenient tax WebMCP
pitch: Turn complex tax forms into a conversation. WebMCP lets ChatGPT help populate a visible draft, while users stay in control of review and submission.
about_excerpt: Turn complex tax forms into a conversation. WebMCP lets ChatGPT help populate a visible draft, while users stay in control of review and submission. Like Comment Story Updates The Problem Filing an annual individual tax return (1770 S) under Indonesia's centralized Coretax system creates a learning curve for salaried workers. Translating personal life events into rigid government tax classifications creates a high burden and confusion across generations. Knowing your salary or family situation is different from knowing which tax field or classification it belongs in. While the system offers spreadsheet bulk uploads to bypass manual entry, they frequently fail due to minor error, forcing users back to rework manual entry or exposing them to server timeouts during peak traffic. Independent sentiment analysis of over 53,000 digital conversations during the early rollout Coretax system revealed that 39% of user sentiment was negative, driven by procedural confusion and system navigation (Source: Journal UII / 2025 ). Despite these points, the submission is massive. By late April 2026, over 13 million annual tax returns were filed following the activation of nearly 12.9 million individual accounts (Source: Tempo.co ). The Solution: Human-Agent Collaboration via WebMCP This project demonstrates how WebMCP can turn a complex tax administration portal into a collaborative interface. Rather than hiding the form's complexity or forcing users to navigate hidden form logic, the browser exposes section-level tools directly to the assistant, keeping the detailed form visible to ensure user review control capability. The Workflow Conversational Extraction: The assistant conducts a plain-language interview to extract necessary tax facts such as salary, deductions, and family status without requiring users to memorize form codes or tax classifications. They can use their own ways to describe their condition and an AI assistant will translate it. For example, when a user says, “My employer was PT Nusantara Digital, gross salary 180 million for the year, 6 million in pay deductions,” WebMCP translates it into: “Records the employment slip, derives net income, recomputes the tax.” Deterministic State Updates: As facts are confirmed, the assistant invokes section-level WebMCP tools (such as updating taxpayer profiles, recording employment, or adding cash and assets). The website itself handles all validation, calculation, and conditional branching, deriving fields like PTKP (e.g., K/1) and recomputing the tax balance automatically. Manual Submission: Final review, resolution of data conflicts, declaration, and submission remain strictly manual. No tool can execute a final filing, and the assistant explicitly states this if asked. title: agent-mission-control-webmcp
pitch: Turn AI agents into browser-native operators with WebMCP — structured, controllable, and built for real-world tasks.\n
about_excerpt:
Turn AI agents into browser-native operators with WebMCP — structured, controllable, and built for real-world tasks.

 Agent Mission Control — Giving AI Agents a Native Interface to the Web

 Agent Mission Control — Giving AI Agents a Native Interface to the Web 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 testing guidance 1 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 testing guidance 2 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Agent Mission Control — Giving AI Agents a Native Interface to the Web 

 I built Agent Mission Control to test a simple question: can a human and an AI agent work on the same application state through two different interfaces? 

 The web was designed for humans to click. What if it were also designed for agents to act? 

 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming increasingly capable, but interacting with the web still often feels like teaching a machine to imitate a human. 

 Find a button.
Read its label.
Guess what it does.
Click it.
Wait for the page to change.
Repeat. 

 Humans need visual interfaces because we navigate by seeing and clicking. 

 Agents shouldn't have to. 

 That led to the question behind Agent Mission Control: 

 
 What would a web application look like if it were designed for both humans and AI agents from the beginning? 
 

 WebMCP gave me a way to explore that question, and gave me a new way to explore thtis idea.. 

 Instead of treating the browser as a collection of pixels that an agent must interpret, a website can expose structured capabilities that describe what the agent is actually allowed to do. 

 So I built Agent Mission Control , an experimental WebMCP-native task environment where a human can manage work visually while an AI agent can interact with the same application through structured tools. 

 The goal isn't to replace the interface. 

 It's to give the web two interfaces to the same application : 

 a visual interface for humans, and a semantic tool interface for agents. 

 So I built agent-mission-control-webmcp to test a different model: one application with two interfaces — a visual interface for humans and a structured capability interface for AI agents — both operating on the same underlying application logic. 

 

 What it does 

 Agent Mission Control turns a normal task-management web application into an agent-addressable workspace . 

 A human can interact with the application through the UI. 

 An AI agent can discover WebMCP tools exposed by the page and use those structured capabilities to work with the same underlying tasks. 

 Instead of asking an agent to: 

 
 "Look around the page, find the right button, click it, and hope the UI hasn't changed..." 
 

 the application can expose explicit operations the agent can understand and invoke. 

 The important part is not simply that an agent can control a task app. 

 The important part is how . 

 The agent is no longer pretending to be a human operating a website. 

 The website is speaking to the agent directly. 

 

 Why WebMCP? 

 Traditional browser automation often starts from the presentation layer. 

 WebMCP lets us start from intent . 

 A button might visually say: 

 Complete 

 But the capability behind it can communicate something much richer: 
 complete_task(taskId)
 
 with structured parameters, predictable behavior, and application-defined semantics. 

 That changes the relationship between websites and AI agents. 

 Instead of: 
 Agent
 ↓
interpret pixels / DOM
 ↓
guess user interface
 ↓
click
 ↓
Application
 
 Agent Mission Control explores: 
 Human ───────→ Visual UI ───────┐
 │
 ▼
 Shared Task Logic
 ▲
 │
AI Agent ───→ WebMCP Tools ─────┘
 
 Both interfaces operate on the same application logic . 

 That was a key architectural decision. 

 WebMCP isn't an automation layer bolted onto the side of the application. 

 It becomes another interface into the application itself. 

 

 Human + Agent Collaboration 

 The most interesting possibility isn't fully autonomous agents. 

 It's shared control . 

 Humans are good at goals, judgment, context, and deciding what should happen. 

 Agents are good at translating intent into structured actions and carrying out repetitive operations. 

 Agent Mission Control explores a simple model: 

 Human defines the mission.
The application defines the allowed capabilities.
The agent executes through those capabilities.
The human remains in control. 

 This creates an interesting middle ground between a traditional website and unrestricted browser automation. 

 The website itself participates in defining what an agent can do. 

 

 How I built it 

 Agent Mission Control is built as a web application with WebMCP integrated directly into its task workflow. 

 The application exposes a small set of task-oriented WebMCP tools. 

 Rather than implementing separate automation logic, the WebMCP layer connects to the same task service used by the React interface. 

 Conceptually: 
 ┌── Human UI
 │
TaskService ─┤
 │
 └── WebMCP Tools → AI Agent
 
 This was deliberate. 

 If the human interface and agent interface implement separate business logic, they can eventually disagree. 

 By sharing the same underlying service, actions performed through WebMCP can follow the same application behavior as actions performed through the UI. 

 The project also includes a browser test path for discovering registered tools, invoking them with structured arguments, and verifying that the resulting state is reflected back in the application. 

 

 Challenges I ran into 

 1. Designing tools instead of exposing buttons 

 My first challenge was conceptual. 

 A WebMCP tool shouldn't simply be a remote-control version of every button on the page. 

 The question became: 

 
 What capability should the application expose to an agent? 
 

 That forced me to think in terms of application semantics rather than UI components. 

 

 2. Keeping humans and agents on the same source of truth 

 It would have been easy to create a separate "AI API." 

 But then I would effectively have two applications: 

 one for humans and one for agents. 

 Instead, I structured the project so both paths converge on shared task logic. 

 That made WebMCP feel less like an integration and more like a second interface to the application . 

 

 3. Testing an emerging browser capability 

 WebMCP is still an emerging technology. 

 Testing required thinking beyond normal frontend tests: 

 
 Are tools actually registered? 
 Can an agent discover them? 
 Are arguments structured correctly? 
 Does execution reach the same application logic? 
 Does the resulting state appear correctly in the human UI? 
 

 Building around an emerging browser capability was one of the most challenging — and interesting — parts of the project. 

 

 Accomplishments I'm proud of 

 The thing I'm most proud of isn't the number of tools. 

 It's proving a simple architectural idea: 

 
 A web application doesn't have to choose between being human-friendly and agent-friendly. 
 

 The same application can expose a visual experience to a person and structured capabilities to an AI agent without duplicating the underlying workflow. 

 Agent Mission Control is intentionally small, but that makes the experiment easier to see. 

 This isn't a task manager with AI added to it. 

 The task manager is the demonstration of a different interface model for the web. 

 

 What I learned 

 Before building this project, I mostly thought about agent/browser interaction as automation. 

 WebMCP changed the question. 

 Instead of asking: 

 
 "How can an AI operate this website?" 
 

 I started asking: 

 
 "How should this website expose itself to AI?" 
 

 That sounds like a small distinction. 

 It isn't. 

 It shifts responsibility from agents constantly reverse-engineering interfaces toward applications explicitly describing safe, meaningful capabilities. 

 And it suggests that the future web may not have one interface. 

 It may have at least two: 

 one optimized for people, and one optimized for agents. 

 

 What's next 

 Agent Mission Control is a proof of concept, but the pattern extends far beyond task management. 

 Imagine websites exposing carefully designed agent capabilities for: 

 
 project management, 
 commerce, 
 scheduling, 
 content workflows, 
 developer tools, 
 administrative systems, 
 and collabor

title: Cutoff
pitch: A restaurant operations desk where managers and browser agents replan orders, stock, labor, and handoffs before the supplier cutoff via WebMCP
about_excerpt: A restaurant operations desk where managers and browser agents replan orders, stock, labor, and handoffs before the supplier cutoff via WebMCP Like 2 Comment Story Updates Rosa’s absence triggers two releases and Nadia’s proposed 4-hour prep cover. Cancelled derby and private booking produce a 910-cover order preview before adoption. The agent records chicken at 30 kg on hand with 6 kg expiring. Manager actions and agent tool calls appear in one filterable service-day record. One desk connects Order, Stock, Labor, and Shift log through shared browser state. Inspiration Restaurant orders often lock at a supplier cutoff. The forecast may have been correct yesterday, but the shift changes in real time. A nearby event gets cancelled, a private booking arrives, a shelf count changes, or a staff member calls out. Those facts affect the order and roster together, yet they often live in separate notes or in the manager's head. I built Cutoff so a manager can state a change once and work through its effects with a browser agent on the same page. What it does Cutoff is a shift operations desk for a fictional restaurant. Order, Stock, Labor, and Shift log share one revisioned state inside the browser. The Saturday scenario starts with 1,140 covers, 95 required labor hours, and a 3,629-unit supplier order. An 80-person booking and a cancelled derby produce a preview of 910 covers, 76 hours, and a 2,767-unit order. Every changed line explains its reason before the manager adopts anything. Once the manager adopts the order, Labor reads the approved 910-cover plan. The agent can record an absence and propose releases or on-call cover without changing the roster until the manager approves it. A corrected stock count feeds the same state. Recording chicken at 30 kg on hand with 6 kg expiring changes the recommendation from 15 to 16 cases and raises the proposed order cost to 2,835 units. The agent can also save a bounded handoff for the next manager. Shift log joins the manager's actions and the agent's tool calls into one filterable record that can be downloaded as JSON. Why WebMCP The state that matters is not fully visible in the page. It includes local signals, shelf counts, quantity pins, roster absences, preview identifiers, and the current shared revision. An agent cannot recover that state reliably by reading pixels. Cutoff exposes this information through WebMCP. The manager gives the agent the task in plain language. The agent discovers the tools available on the current page, reads the latest revision, and uses the tools it needs. The manager never has to name a tool or copy values between systems. The result appears in the same interface the manager is already using. Proposed changes stay visible and reversible, while final approval remains with the manager. How I built it Cutoff is a static React and TypeScript application with no backend, account system, or application keys. It registers 16 hand-built tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each page exposes only the tools relevant to that section. Order has 6 tools at rest and 7 while a preview can be adopted. Labor follows the same pattern with 4 and 5 tools. Stock exposes 4 tools, and Shift log exposes 3. The two adoption tools exist only while their preview is current. Route changes replace the previous page's tools before navigation finishes. Every write requires expectedRevision . If another action has changed the state, the tool returns a structured stale-write error with the current revision instead of overwriting newer work. Human-entered text is marked as untrusted when it appears in tool results. Small deterministic engines calculate order quantities, labor demand, waste, and roster proposals. The visible controls and WebMCP tools call the same store methods, so the manager and agent cannot drift into separate versions of the plan. Challenges The hardest part was keeping previews, adoption, invalidation, undo, navigation, and tool registration consistent under one revision. A stock count must make an old order preview stale without invalidating an unrelated labor preview. Adopting an order must update labor demand. Changing pages must remove the previous tools before the agent continues. Undo must restore the saved plan without printing a breakdown that no longer matches it. The interface also had to remain readable as the product expanded from one order page into a four-section desk. I tested the final layouts on laptop and mobile widths and added direct links from agent-change notifications to the affected row or receipt. What I learned WebMCP works best when the page and its tools share the same product model. The tools should expose state and calculations that an agent cannot obtain reliably from the rendered interface. The page should still show every result and keep consequential decisions under human control. Tool availability can also communicate state. An adoption tool appearing only when a valid preview exists is clearer and safer than exposing an action that may fail or apply to an old proposal. Accomplishments 16 contextual WebMCP tools across 4 decision pages Dynamic preview and adoption tool lifecycles One shared revision with structured stale-write recovery Reversible local order and labor adoption Agent-driven navigation between sections Local handoff and Shift-log JSON exports 111 deterministic tests and a clean production build Direct production testing in ChatGPT's in-app browser and Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled Nothing sends an order, updates a rota, contacts a supplier, or writes restaurant data to a server. All names, events, inventory, quantities, and costs are fictional. title: CartPilot
pitch: An AI-native Shopify storefront where shoppers ask for what they need, and an agent filters, compares, and prepares their cart through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An AI-native Shopify storefront where shoppers ask for what they need, and an agent filters, compares, and prepares their cart through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates An Agent-Ready Shopify Storefront with WebMCP Inspiration Online stores are designed primarily for people clicking through pages. AI agents can still interact with them, but they often have to interpret visual layouts, locate controls, and scrape product information from the page. We wanted to explore a more reliable approach: what if a Shopify storefront could explicitly describe its capabilities to an AI agent? Using WebMCP, the storefront exposes structured tools for product discovery, comparison, filtering, and cart management while preserving the familiar shopping experience for human visitors. What it does The project extends a Shopify Dawn storefront with WebMCP Site tools that let compatible AI agents: Search the product catalog Retrieve exact product and variant information Apply filters and sorting to the visible storefront Compare multiple products Add a selected variant to the cart Inspect detailed cart contents Update or remove cart lines Open the cart for the buyer to review The tools work alongside Shopify’s native commerce tools. Checkout remains a buyer-controlled action—the custom tools never automatically start or complete a purchase. The storefront also continues to work normally in browsers that do not support WebMCP. How we built it We implemented the integration as a standalone JavaScript asset inside a Shopify Dawn theme. The script detects WebMCP support and registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Every tool includes: A clear name and description A constrained JSON input schema Read-only or mutating annotations Structured results that an agent can verify User-readable result messages Error handling with stable error codes Product discovery uses Shopify storefront pages and product JSON endpoints. Cart mutations use Shopify Standard Storefront Actions so that AI-triggered changes follow the same cart behavior as the theme itself. For actions that should affect what the buyer sees, such as sorting products or opening the cart, the tools also update or navigate the visible storefront. Read-only operations can return information directly to the conversation without unnecessarily changing the page. Challenges we faced Supporting both Shopify and custom tools Shopify already provides several native commerce tools. Our original custom get_cart tool conflicted with Shopify’s tool of the same name, so we renamed it to get_cart_details and designed the custom tools to complement the native ones. Normalizing cart responses Shopify Standard Storefront Actions can return cart lines as an array or as a GraphQL-style connection containing nodes or edges . Treating every response as an array caused cart mutations to succeed while their tool responses reported an error. We added normalization for all supported response shapes and verified the behavior against the live storefront. Keeping agent actions visible and trustworthy Some WebMCP operations are naturally read-only, while others should create a visible result. We separated product discovery from visible filtering so an agent can either answer a question quietly or intentionally update the browser for the buyer. Cart-changing tools return the resulting cart state and refresh the Dawn cart interface, allowing both the agent and the buyer to verify what changed. Extracting clean storefront data Rendered Shopify price elements contain accessibility labels and hidden sale-price markup, which can produce duplicated text when read naively. We added targeted extraction and normalization so agents receive concise prices such as $699.95 USD . We also handled missing product descriptions without converting null values into the literal string "null" . What we learned WebMCP tools are more than JavaScript functions. Their names, descriptions, schemas, annotations, and returned data form an interface between the website and the agent. We learned that effective site tools should: Reuse the website’s existing business logic Keep inputs narrow and predictable Describe side effects clearly Return enough state to verify the result Preserve the normal human interface Leave consequential decisions, such as checkout, under the buyer’s control We also learned that WebMCP implementations and third-party inspectors may currently target different versions of the evolving API. Testing with the actual target client is therefore essential. Accomplishments The completed storefront exposes nine custom WebMCP tools and works alongside Shopify’s native tools. We tested the complete workflow on the live theme: Discover the available Site tools Search for snowboards Retrieve product variants Compare products Sort the visible results by price Add a selected variant to the cart Read and update the cart Open the cart for buyer review The same storefront remains fully usable through its standard visual interface. You can use the AI subscription you already have. What you can do Prepare for IELTS, SAT, or GRE with practice tailored to the skills you need to improve. You can also ask your agent for a quiz on another subject. You take the test in an exam interface with timers and question navigation. The app scores objective answers and saves your attempt. For written work, ask your agent for feedback and read its comments beside your submitted responses. Where WebMCP fits WebMCP lets the agent work directly with the app. It can add a practice test, read a completed attempt when asked, and save feedback to the results page. You control your answers and submission. After a test, ask your agent to explain the questions you missed or review your written responses. Then ask for another practice set focused on what needs work. Questions, answers, and feedback stay together in the same interface.
