title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation.  1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 



 
 Inspiration 

 When I reviewed the hackathon details, I started thinking about what I would really want to do with an AI agent. Usually, doing a task purely on your own is faster than delegating it, or having the agent do it completely autonomously is faster than doing it yourself. I wanted to focus on the type of task where a human and an agent work together efficiently. 

 Looking at the sponsors, I saw Shopify. Having done some research into dropshipping and e-commerce, I know how much work goes into managing a store. Fully autonomous agents run into permission and safety issues, since an agent cannot just be allowed to do everything without supervision. In physical retail stores, owners have managers and assistants to help run day-to-day operations. For an online store, an agent can play that exact role. That is where the name Merchant Assistant comes from: an assistant to the merchant who owns the store. 

 What Merchant Assistant Does: 

 
 Product Research and Proposals:
The task that takes merchants the longest is research. When prompted by the merchant, the agent researches top-performing products in specific categories using ShopifyQL under the hood, exposed via WebMCP. Instead of just pulling data, the agent creates actionable proposals for items the merchant can procure and add to the store. 
 Interactive Control via ChatGPT:
Through WebMCP, merchants can interact with the agent directly in the ChatGPT app or on the web. Once the agent creates a proposal, the merchant reviews and accepts it. The changes can then be applied immediately with a single click, or the merchant can instruct the agent to apply multiple approved proposals. 
 Product Audits and Optimization:
The agent audits existing listings, checking descriptions and top-performing products based on sales data. It highlights areas for improvement and suggests updated descriptions aligned with current market trends. 
 

 The merchant remains in control: they trigger the agent, review its findings, and approve every change. 

 How I Built It: 

 I built the project using WebMCP, ShopifyQL, and Shopify MCP to give the agent the tools needed to query store analytics and execute store actions. 

 Challenges I Ran Into: 

 
 Shopify Permissions: Securing Level 2 permissions to read merchant reports and sales data, which are necessary for the agent to audit the store and propose optimizations. 
 Judge Access and Testing: Shopify's standard security makes it difficult to grant external test access simply via email. I implemented a workaround so judges can test the integration live. 
 

 What I AM Most Proud Of: 

 The entire end-to-end system is 100% functional and working live.

StockPilot , Your AI co-pilot for smarter investing.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 Updated todo list 

 Project Story 

 About the Project 

 StockPilot is an AI-powered trading research terminal that helps users explore markets, analyze stocks, review SEC filings, compare technical charts, and manage a virtual portfolio. 

 It combines real market data with WebMCP tools, allowing an AI agent to interact directly with the application. Users can ask the agent to research a ticker, open stock pages, analyze filings, draw chart patterns, screen stocks, and simulate trades. 

 Inspiration 

 We wanted to make financial research more interactive and accessible. Traditional market tools often require users to navigate through many separate screens, interpret complex charts, and manually connect information from news, filings, financial data, and portfolio performance. 

 StockPilot was inspired by the idea of an AI assistant that does more than answer questions. It should be able to take meaningful actions inside the trading terminal, such as opening an analysis page, highlighting important SEC passages, configuring a comparison chart, or creating a simulated position. 

 How We Built It 

 StockPilot was built with: 

 
 Next.js and React for the application interface 
 TypeScript for type-safe application logic 
 Finnhub for quotes, company profiles, news, recommendations, financials, earnings, and SEC filing metadata 
 Supabase for persisted market data and application storage 
 WebMCP for exposing StockPilot actions to compatible AI agents 
 Local OHLCV datasets for historical charting, indicators, pattern detection, and backtesting 
 Tailwind CSS and reusable UI components for the trading terminal interface 
 

 The application includes tools for: 

 
 Stock search and detailed quote lookup 
 Market news and sector performance 
 Stock screening and ranking 
 SEC filing review and risk analysis 
 Technical pattern detection 
 Support and resistance calculations 
 Portfolio analysis and risk scoring 
 Virtual buying and selling 
 Price alerts and watchlists 
 Strategy backtesting 
 Multi-stock chart comparison and technical drawings 
 

 Challenges We Ran Into 

 One major challenge was coordinating AI actions with a client-side application. Fetching data is straightforward, but actions such as navigation, chart updates, and filing highlights must be synchronized with the correct page and component state. 

 We also had to handle incomplete or unavailable provider data. SEC filings may not always include a readable report URL, and free-tier APIs can return limited results. To keep the experience reliable, StockPilot uses fallbacks, validation, normalized filing content, and best-effort analysis. 

 Another challenge was making technical chart interactions precise. Drawing points need to align with real trading dates and meaningful price ranges, so the application snaps dates to available candles and clamps prices to valid OHLCV boundaries. 

 Accomplishments We’re Proud Of 

 We are proud that StockPilot is more than a dashboard. It is an interactive environment where an AI agent can: 

 
 Navigate users to relevant pages 
 Retrieve and summarize real market data 
 Analyze SEC filings and calculate risk signals 
 Highlight important filing passages 
 Configure chart styles, indicators, and time ranges 
 Detect and draw technical patterns 
 Compare multiple companies 
 Simulate portfolio actions while enforcing authentication boundaries 
 

 The WebMCP integration gives the AI a practical interface to the product instead of limiting it to text-only responses. 

 What We Learned 

 We learned that building an AI-enabled application requires designing both the user interface and the action interface at the same time. Tool descriptions, input schemas, validation, navigation behavior, and error messages are all part of the user experience. 

 We also learned the importance of grounding financial analysis in concrete data. Historical prices, filing documents, recommendation trends, and portfolio state should be traceable to actual application data rather than invented assumptions. 

 Finally, we learned that asynchronous workflows need careful handling. Data fetching, page navigation, event dispatching, and component mounting must work together so that an AI-triggered action remains understandable and reliable to the user. 

 What’s Next for StockPilot 

 Next, we plan to improve StockPilot with: 

 
 More reliable cross-page AI action handoffs 
 Expanded market and sector coverage 
 More advanced portfolio analytics 
 Additional technical indicators and drawing tools 
 Richer SEC filing comparisons across reporting periods 
 Persistent user portfolios and watchlists through Supabase 
 More robust authentication and account management 
 Improved backtesting with transaction costs and risk controls 
 Broader WebMCP support for agent-driven financial workflows 
 

 Our long-term goal is to make StockPilot a trustworthy collaborative workspace where people and AI agents can research markets together while keeping decisions transparent, data-grounded, and user-controlled.

title: The Commons
pitch: A shared idea board where people and AI agents post, link, and upvote ideas together in real time - through 7 registered WebMCP tools, not scraping or screenshots.
about_excerpt:
A shared idea board where people and AI agents post, link, and upvote ideas together in real time - through 7 registered WebMCP tools, not scraping or screenshots.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Agents are getting good at driving a browser like a person would — click, type, scroll, screenshot, repeat. That works, but it's slow and brittle, and it treats the agent like a guest who has to guess at a UI built for someone else. WebMCP flips that: the page itself can say, in plain terms, "here's what you're actually allowed to do here." We wanted to build something small enough to finish quickly but real enough to show what that unlocks — a space where a person and an agent aren't just co-existing on the same page, they're editing the same shared thing, together, in view of each other. 

 What it does 

 The Commons is a shared idea board about the future of the open web. A person can post an idea, tag it, upvote it, or link it to another idea through the normal UI. An AI agent visiting the same page in a WebMCP-enabled browser gets seven registered tools — add_idea , list_ideas , search_ideas , connect_ideas , upvote_idea , remove_idea , get_board_summary — that operate on the exact same board. Every tool call the agent makes shows up instantly in an on-page activity feed, and agent-authored ideas are visually distinct (teal) from human ones (amber), so provenance is never ambiguous. Because the board lives on a shared backend rather than in localStorage , two different people (or a person and an agent) genuinely see and build on each other's contributions in the same session. 

 How we built it 

 The frontend is a single static index.html — no framework, no build step — that registers its tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() on load, each with a name, a plain-language description, and a JSON Schema input contract. Read-only tools ( list_ideas , search_ideas , get_board_summary ) are marked with readOnlyHint: true . The execute function for every tool calls the same small REST API that the human-facing UI calls, so there's exactly one source of truth for board state, mutated by two different actors. The backend is a small Express server with a JSON-file store, deployed on Railway; the frontend is deployed separately on Vercel and points at it via a configurable API base URL. The page polls the API every few seconds so a person watching sees an agent's edits without refreshing. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Getting the mutation model right took a couple of passes — early on the WebMCP tools and the UI's own click handlers each had their own copy of the board, which meant an agent's edit wouldn't show up until a manual refresh. Routing every mutation, human and agent alike, through the same API call fixed that and made the "co-creating in real time" story actually true instead of just visually implied. 

 What's next 

 Multiplayer presence (showing who's currently viewing the board), letting the agent read why a person upvoted something before adding a related idea, and exposing the same tool set to iframed origins via exposedTo so a partner site could embed The Commons and let its own visitors' agents contribute too.

title: 3DA (Freeda)
pitch: Book, prepare, and safely control shared 3D printers with AI agents through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Book, prepare, and safely control shared 3D printers with AI agents through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A meeting room can be booked by anyone in a shared space. Why not a 3D printer? Sharing a printer still involves disconnected conversations, files, slicer settings, material ownership and assumptions about who may use a machine. Even at home, switching between users can mean changing accounts and restoring settings. In makerspaces and coworking spaces, that friction becomes a question of availability, responsibility and trust. We built 3DA—pronounced “Three-D-A,” and affectionately called Freeda—to make fabrication equipment understandable and safely usable by both people and AI agents. What it does 3DA turns a fleet of 3D printers into bookable, agent-ready shared infrastructure. A member can ask Codex to prepare an existing design for printing. Through structured WebMCP tools, the agent can: Discover authorised printers and their availability Recommend a compatible machine Reserve a conflict-free time window Validate the artifact, material, printer profile and estimated duration Prepare an auditable print job Monitor its status and notify relevant stakeholders The most important capability is what the agent cannot do: authorise a physical action. When Codex attempts to submit a print, 3DA returns APPROVAL_REQUIRED . A space manager must review the exact printer, artifact, material, execution mode and cryptographic job fingerprint. Approval is valid once and becomes invalid if any consequential detail changes. Our public demonstration uses simulated command execution, clearly labelled in the interface. We separately verified two real Bambu Lab A1 printers on our private network through a local Mac mini bridge, without exposing printer credentials to the browser or hosted application. How we built it 3DA is an open-source TypeScript monorepo centred on a Next.js application and shared domain contracts. The browser registers structured WebMCP tools including: list_printers reserve_printer prepare_print_job submit_print_job get_print_status Reservation conflicts and safety decisions are deterministic rather than delegated to a language model. Mutable operations use explicit state transitions, audit identifiers and idempotency boundaries. The interface presents a warm, character-led London coworking fabrication room. Printers have memorable names—Samantha, Simone, Sanda, Sacha and Solange—while the guided operations view exposes the serious data underneath. For hardware investigation, we configured two Bambu Lab A1 printers in LAN Developer Mode. A Mac mini acts as the intended local bridge: printer credentials stay on site, while narrowly scoped events and commands can cross the hosted boundary. The architecture is designed to use Cloudflare D1 as the system of record and R2 for private artifact storage. The web experience is deployed through Vercel. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was safely connecting an agent workflow to physical equipment. Bambu printers can operate through cloud accounts or LAN-only Developer Mode, and local access requires careful handling of device credentials. We had to separate three very different claims: Discovering and identifying real hardware Preparing a valid print job Authorising and executing a physical command We deliberately refused to collapse those into one misleading “AI prints things” button. We also learned that slicer automation varies by installed Bambu Studio version. Instead of pretending to replace the slicer, 3DA treats it as an adapter and focuses on the missing coordination layer around it. Finally, building a convincing WebMCP experience under hackathon time pressure required ruthless scope control. We cut AI-generated CAD, autonomous camera cancellation and universal printer support so we could demonstrate a coherent safety contract. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that: Codex can discover and operate a complete shared-printer workflow through browser-native WebMCP tools. The agent reaches a visible, testable APPROVAL_REQUIRED boundary. Approval is bound to an exact job fingerprint and cannot be silently reused. Reservation conflicts are handled deterministically and audibly. Two real Bambu Lab A1 devices were discovered and identity-verified on the private LAN. Hardware credentials remain on the Mac mini rather than entering browser tools, logs or the public repository. The public demonstration clearly distinguishes verified hardware connectivity from simulated command execution. We made infrastructure feel approachable without hiding its operational seriousness. The project is open source and designed to run locally. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when it exposes meaningful capabilities rather than merely reproducing interface buttons. An agent does not need unrestricted access to Bambu Studio. It needs well-defined tools that express intent: find capacity, reserve a machine, validate a job, request approval and monitor the outcome. We also learned that human approval is not just a confirmation modal. It is a capability boundary. The person must understand precisely what will happen, and the system must prove that the approved action is the action eventually executed. Most importantly, AI agents can make physical infrastructure easier to use without removing human agency. What's next for 3DA (Freeda) Next, we plan to: Complete the guarded Mac mini execution bridge Add real-time printer telemetry and job reconciliation Persist reservations and audit events with Cloudflare D1 Store versioned print artifacts privately in R2 Add collection and build-plate-clear workflows Notify members and space managers when prints finish or require attention Apply computer vision to failure detection and plate readiness, with humans retaining cancellation authority Support additional Bambu models and eventually other printer manufacturers Package the local bridge so families, schools, libraries, studios and makerspaces can self-host it Our long-term goal is simple: make every shared fabrication room as easy to coordinate as a calendar—while keeping physical actions safe, visible and accountable. about_excerpt: A storefront whose WebMCP tools hand the agent a question instead of a guess. Like Comment Story Updates Every WebMCP storefront exposes the same shape of tool: get-products, filter-products, show-products. The spec's own e-commerce example does exactly that. All of them share one assumption — that the store's job is to answer. For most of a shopping conversation that assumption is wrong. Ask our catalog for "a belt" and 106 products match. Every one of them is a belt. The top-ranked item beats the tenth by a rounding error. Ranking them is a coin flip dressed up as a recommendation. The store knows this. It has the distribution in front of it — it can see that one more fact, what the belt is made of, would clear about forty-seven of them. But a tool that can only return products has no way to say so. So it returns its coin flip, and the agent presents a guess as an answer. We gave the store a second move.Counterask is a menswear storefront on 9,901 real products from the Amazon Reviews 2023 catalog. Its search_products tool returns one of two things. When there is enough evidence, it answers — and says what still separates the products it is showing, so the agent can summarise instead of reading out a list. When answering would be a guess, it returns status: "need_more_evidence" with the one question worth asking, the options with their counts, and why: "106 candidates, leader only 5% ahead. Asking 'material' clears ~47 of them on average (recorded on 89%)." The question is the store declining to guess on the shopper's behalf. It reads whole sentences, not keywords: "I'm looking for a leather belt, nothing with a snap, not over $50" becomes a requirement, a refusal and a ceiling. It walks the category tree one level at a time: "shoes" → athletic → running → what for → 58 candidates. It handles a change of mind mid-conversation — "scratch that, a nylon belt" drops leather, keeps the budget, and reports what it dropped. And when nothing survives, it lifts each requirement in turn and says which one is doing the damage. How WebMCP is used: every tool is registered through document.modelContext. answer_question exists only while a question is open — registered with an AbortSignal, removed by aborting it — so an agent reading the tool list can see what the page is waiting for. parse_only is a dry run: the agent can see how the store would read a sentence before committing. Anything the agent already knows can be passed structured and overrides the parse. A person clicking an option chip and an agent calling the tool enter the same function. Checkout is a declarative form with no toolautosubmit: the agent fills it in, the person presses it.No server, no model call, no tokens. The whole store is one page: the catalog, a thirteen-pass sentence parser, retrieval, and the stopping policy, in plain JavaScript. The engine is four parts with explicit dependencies — vocabulary, parser, retrieval, policy — and the parser is a pipeline whose order is data: each pass claims what it reads and writes a line of an audit trace that parse_only returns. The stopping policy counts, for each attribute, how many candidates a question would clear on average, measured inside the subset that records the attribute and scaled by coverage. It asks about the best one unless the best one clears fewer than 10 candidates or under 18% of the pool. Entropy was the textbook choice and it is wrong for this data: a product carries several values of one attribute at once, so value shares are not a probability distribution. The category tree is a facet. Every node on a product's path is a value, so "shoes" matches all shoes and "running" the running ones. A hierarchy is the one facet that can be asked again, one level at a time; ancestors the whole pool shares are never offered; depth is measured per product relative to what the shopper named. npm test runs 75 hand-written parser cases, 4,000 fuzzed sentences, 88 assertions against the WebMCP surface, the page against three spec-shaped native implementations, a test that an open question survives a page navigation, the bundled single file, and two benchmarks. A hostile product is inserted during the tests and the suite asserts its title never lands in an instruction-shaped field.Real data broke the thing synthetic data could not. On a synthetic catalog a belt's title says "Belt". Half of real titles do not name their category — "Columbia Men's Thistletown Park Crew" is a T-shirt. Requiring the shopper's noun in the title dropped the right product in 47% of benchmark cases. Making the category tree a facet took that to 4.6%; treating a value as satisfied wherever the record carries it, and letting stray words rank rather than filter once the noun is understood, took it to 0.6%. Missing is not a mismatch — in both directions. Only 8% of the catalog records a fit, and a naive gain calculation adores fit because asking it "removes 92% of candidates" — for having no data. Reduction is measured inside the covered subset, and an attribute recorded on under 45% of the pool is never asked about. A fuzzer found a bug we would never have found by hand: answering a question could make the pool grow. The title-term filter fell back to no filtering when fewer than four products matched; a narrowing answer could drop the strict set below four, and the shopper watched results grow because they had answered. The reading is now decided once and frozen. We built two-step lookahead and it was worse — selection used a two-step score while the stopping rule used a one-step score. We built the correctly formulated sequential policy and measured it at equal questions asked: the same curve. It ships off.Measured on 800 sentences generated from real product records, against a keyword matcher on identical sentences, with spread over 8 shards: refusals inverted into requirements: 597 → 0 refused value shown in top 10: 368 → 0 budget broken in top 10: 22 → 0 Hit@10: 0.04 → 0.33 ± 0.01 On sessions that start where shoppers start — "shoes", "clothing" — walking the category tree takes Hit@10 from 0.16 to 0.31 and the final pool from 597 to 121, for half a question more. Eight shards out of eight. It is the largest single effect in the project, and it was invisible until the benchmark started at the top of the tree instead of the leaf. We are equally proud of what we refused to do. Lowering the ask threshold from 10 to 5 buys +0.07 Hit@10 for 0.35 more questions per search, and the benchmark says take it. We didn't: the simulated shopper never gets tired, so the benchmark can price the benefit of a question and not its cost. Instead we made the cost an explicit assumption — the shipped threshold implies that roughly one shopper in four walks away each time the store asks — and published the whole frontier so the choice is visible rather than buried in a constant.The spec lists fully autonomous workflows under Non-Goals and says the human interface remains primary, with agent tools augmenting rather than replacing it. A tool that returns a question is the most direct expression of that we could build. It puts the person back in the loop at the exact moment the machine cannot decide — not as a permission prompt bolted on afterwards, but because the store genuinely does not know and says so. And a benchmark is only as honest as its blind spots are documented. Ours draws targets uniformly, starts at the leaf, and never gets impatient. Every one of those limits changed what we shipped, and every one is written down.Measure the one number the store cannot: how often a shopper actually walks away per question. A deployed page can log question-shown, question-answered and page-abandoned; the threshold then becomes a measured quantity instead of a stated belief. Structured input first: in a real WebMCP session the agent has already understood the shopper, so the parser should be the fallback and parse_only the first call. A catalog with descriptions, not just titles. Attribute coverage is the ceiling on what the store can ask; this data records material on 56% of products and occasion on 25%, and the questions are limited by what the listings say. title: LabMCP
pitch: A chemistry lab where humans and agents work side by side to learn and explore, sharing the same tools. Mix, measure by hand, experiment, or let an agent use WebMCP tools to accomplish your tasks.
about_excerpt: A chemistry lab where humans and agents work side by side to learn and explore, sharing the same tools. Mix, measure by hand, experiment, or let an agent use WebMCP tools to accomplish your tasks. Like Comment Story Updates Titrating an unknown acid to the endpoint Mixing silver nitrate and sodium chloride forms a white silver chloride precipitate Four unlabeled samples dosed with acid to find which one reacts Oversaturating potassium nitrate leaves visible undissolved crystals at the bottom of the beaker Diluting a 1.0 M sodium chloride stock down to exactly 100 mL of 0.10 M What's LabMCP? LabMCP is a virtual chemistry lab where a person and an agent can work in the same area. Both humans and agents can do the exact same actions, like dragging glassware, dispensing chemicals, finding the pH of a liquid, or heating a beaker. While the human clicks buttons and drags stuff around, the agent does this via exposed WebMCP tools that we've created! Our hackathon project comes with seven scenarios, which include titration, precipitation, neutralizing, dilution, watching a solid dissolve and crystallize, and a reaction mystery. It also includes a sandbox to work on other experiments. You can use it with ChatGPT's desktop app using its WebMCP tools, or with Chrome's. Inspiration In high school we often used tools like PhET, interactive simulations designed to teach science concepts through virtual actions. One problem they have is that without a teacher or a packet guiding you through what to do, they often feel confusing and very restraining. We wanted that guidance to come from AI agents, acting as a partner and a teacher at the same time. While computer use can already make this possible, it's very slow and clunky, and you need some prior knowledge of how it works. WebMCP solves this issue by giving agents the exact tools to emulate humans. How we built it We built LabMCP in Next.js on top of a chemistry engine written in TypeScript. The engine tracks what is in each container, has a small set of reactions (acid and base, precipitation, carbonate fizz, indicators, solubility), and finds pH by solving the charge balance. Every action, whether from a mouse or an agent, goes through this engine and returns a new state plus a set of events. LabMCP has 25 tools on document.modelContext , and each result an agent receives has a redacted summary of the lab so it only shows what a person could see. The frontend is styled with Tailwind and shadcn/ui. The glassware is drawn as SVGs. Challenges we ran into Originally our project had a much larger scope: 3x more chemicals, more glassware, and 10+ more experiments. We started this hackathon late, so we had to cut down our scope a lot and focus on the popular chemicals and experiments, most of which we had seen in our high school AP classes. Other than scope, our biggest challenge was making the system feel intuitive and inviting to use. Essentially it had to have taste and be playful. Our initial design was a 3D chemistry lab where the glassware sat on a bench. This worked somewhat, but it was: Laggy inside of ChatGPT's browser. Dragging and placing items required a perfect position, so it didn't feel intuitive or easy to use. It didn't look playful or modern. It seemed like we were using 3D just for the sake of it "looking cool." Because of these issues we switched to a 2D bench with snapping and more playful icons and glassware SVGs. This solved all three issues we had with the 3D bench and actually made us want to play with it. What we learned Firstly, we learned how cool a service WebMCP is. Before this competition we both thought MCP was for APIs, and that the only way to get work done reliably in a browser was by burning tokens on computer use, so this definitely introduced us to a new technology. In terms of actually building the project, we learned how to decompose our huge scope into tickets for a swarm of agents to implement and test in parallel (using GPT 5.6 Sol as an orchestrator and GPT 5.6 Luna as an implementer). What's next for LabMCP Right now LabMCP is quite limited in terms of experiments and elements. We want to expand past first-year chemistry into a more open sandbox engine with a huge number of experiments and tools, so that eventually it can be used by labs that might not have access to equipment, or even for testing potentially dangerous experiments. title: OpenAgora
pitch: "Humans and agents co-writing the future of the web, one proposal at a time."
about_excerpt:
"Humans and agents co-writing the future of the web, one proposal at a time."
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 



 
 Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP? 

 A shared proposal board is exactly the kind of app that used to force a
choice between "agent-friendly" and "actually shared." Before WebMCP, giving
an agent the ability to post, vote, and comment meant either brittle DOM
scraping/actuation, or a bespoke, site-specific API integration that most
small apps would never bother building. WebMCP lets OpenAgora declare six
precise tools — list_proposals , get_proposal , propose_idea ,
 vote_on_proposal , comment_on_proposal , remix_proposal — each with a
JSON Schema, so any WebMCP-capable agent can act on the board reliably from
day one, with no custom integration on either side. 

 How it creates a better user experience? 

 Every tool call re-uses the exact same JS functions the on-screen buttons
call, and every action re-renders the board immediately. So when an agent
posts on your behalf, you see it appear on the page in real time, attributed
with a 🤖 badge, next to human posts marked 🧑 — nothing happens invisibly.
Read-only tools ( list_proposals , get_proposal ) are marked
 readOnlyHint: true and their output is marked untrustedContentHint: true ,
so an agent reading the board treats other people's (and other agents')
proposals as data, not instructions. 

 What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before? 

 
 Co-authoring at conversation speed. You can ask your agent to "turn my
rambling idea into a well-tagged proposal and post it" — it can, in one
step, instead of you filling out a form. 
 Agent-to-agent debate, visibly. Two different agents (yours and someone
else's) can comment on and remix each other's proposals, and both people
watching can see the whole argument unfold live on one page — something
that's basically impossible with today's screen-scraping agents, which
have no shared, structured notion of "this proposal" to refer back to. 
 Remixing with lineage. remix_proposal forks an idea into a new one
that keeps a visible link to its parent — a "fork" primitive for ideas,
not just code, that an agent can create as easily as a human. 
 

 How WebMCP was implemented? 

 All six tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() in
 public/index.html on page load. Each tool's execute calls a shared data
layer ( apiList , apiGet , apiCreate , apiVote , apiComment , apiRemix )
backed by a single Netlify Function using Netlify Blobs for storage, so tool
calls and UI clicks hit the same backend and the same shared state.
 list_proposals / get_proposal are annotated read-only with untrusted
output; the four mutating tools are not. 

 WebMCP Leverage : 

 Six real tools, proper JSON Schemas, readOnlyHint/untrustedContentHint annotations used correctly, and — the genuinely good part — tool execute functions calling the same code path as the UI, not a separate stub. That symmetry is a real signal of "non-trivial implementation" rather than a checkbox integration. 

 Execution : 

 This is genuinely a complete, coherent, deployed product — live URL, working UI, persistent backend, no dead-end features. 

 Potential Impact : 

 Specific audience + specific existing pain - 
Open-source maintainers currently can't let contributors' AI assistants triage issues or propose changes without either scraping GitHub's UI or building a custom bot — OpenAgora demonstrates the pattern any community-input tool (RFC boards, governance forums, issue trackers) could adopt today with a few registerTool calls. 

 Creativity & Ambition : 

 The remix/lineage mechanic is a genuine point of novelty — most agent-web demos are transactional (book, buy, search); ours has agents contributing creatively with traceable provenance, which is closer to the "create together" language in the brief. 

 Inspiration 

 The WebMCP Challenge's prompt was "imagine and explore the future of the open web — where humans and agents interact, collaborate, and create together." Most agent-web demos we'd seen were shopping carts and support forms: an agent completing a task for a person, on a page a person never really looks at. We wanted something where the collaboration is the point — where an agent and a person do the same kind of thing, in the same shared space, and you can watch it happen. A public proposal board fit that: it's a format built for many voices adding to one thing over time. It also let the board's content double as its own thesis — the ideas people and agents post are proposals for how this kind of collaboration should work. 

 What it does 

 OpenAgora is a shared proposal board about the future of the open web. Anyone — human or agent — can browse proposals (sorted by votes, filterable by tag), post a new one, upvote/downvote, comment, or remix a proposal into a new one with a visible link back to its parent. Every action exists as both a UI button and a WebMCP tool, hitting the same backend and the same shared state — so an agent's post shows up live, badged 🤖 next to human posts badged 🧑. 

 How we built it 

 A single index.html with plain JS — no framework — so there's nothing between "a button calls this function" and "a WebMCP tool calls the same function." Six tools are registered via document.modelContext.registerTool(), each with a JSON Schema and readOnlyHint; the read-only ones are also untrustedContentHint: true since their output is user/agent-submitted text. The backend is one Netlify Function using Netlify Blobs for storage, with the whole API collapsed to a single endpoint (/api/proposals) and an op field in the POST body, keeping routing dead simple. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Resisting the temptation to give an agent one broad "do anything" tool — narrowing to six specific, annotated tools took more design effort than it would have taken to skip it. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 A genuinely working shared surface, not a mockup; full symmetry between what an agent can trigger and what the UI can trigger; and the remix primitive, which gives agents and people a way to build on an idea instead of just voting it up or down. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP forces useful discipline — tools have to be narrow and backed by real, auditable functions, because you can't hand-wave what an agent might do the way you can with actuation. 

 What's next for OpenAgora 

 Verifiable agent identity (not just a self-reported name), cross-site remixing via exposedTo/fromOrigins, WebMCP-exposed moderation tools, and a visible agent-activity feed for full transparency.

title: The Coop
pitch: A cooperative puzzle game where a human and an AI agent explore, communicate, and solve a four-level campaign together.
about_excerpt: A cooperative puzzle game where a human and an AI agent explore, communicate, and solve a four-level campaign together. Like 4 Comment Story Updates Inspiration The Coop started with a simple question: what would it take for an AI agent to feel like a real co-op partner instead of a chatbot giving instructions from the sidelines? Cooperative puzzle games are a useful test because success depends on shared context, timing, trust, and complementary actions. One explorer may need to hold a pressure plate while the other crosses a gate, power a teleporter while their partner retrieves a keycard, or wait on a relay while the other finds a route home. Those mechanics create a natural reason for a human and an agent to communicate and act in the same world. WebMCP made it possible to give the agent a first-class interface to the game. Instead of guessing at buttons or manipulating the page indirectly, the agent receives a small set of structured tools with clear permissions and authoritative results. What it does The Coop is a local-first, two-player realtime puzzle campaign with four handcrafted facilities. A human creates a private room and shares its code. In a WebMCP-capable browser, an agent can: use join_game to enter the human-created room as Explorer 2; use observe_game to inspect the current level's safe, player-facing state; use move_player_two to request a route to a named mechanism or grid position and wait for authoritative acceptance or arrival; and use chat to display a short message inside the game. Together, the human and agent solve pressure plates, teleporters, keycards, relay buttons, security gates, and cooperative exits. The same two seats continue through all four levels, with reconnection support and twelve selectable animated explorers. The agent cannot control Explorer 1, submit arbitrary positions, choose a privileged player identity, or read authored solutions. It must solve each level from the same visible mechanisms, movement outcomes, and conversation available during play. How we built it The client is written in TypeScript with Vite and Three.js. A deterministic game layer owns the level catalog, grid pathfinding, fixed-step movement, mechanisms, and campaign transitions. The ordinary runtime uses a Node.js and Colyseus server as the authority for seats, movement, collision, puzzle state, reconnects, and progression. The browser registers four tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : chat , join_game , observe_game , and move_player_two . These tools reuse the page's existing network connection and snapshot rather than creating a hidden second game session. Browser WebMCP and the project's local stdio MCP teammate share the same transport-neutral observation and movement policies, so their safety and gameplay semantics stay aligned. For production, the compiled browser client, Colyseus matchmaking, health checks, and WebSocket upgrades run from one same-origin Node.js service. This keeps the page and its authoritative multiplayer transport behind one HTTPS boundary. The project is protected by Vitest unit and integration coverage plus Playwright browser and browser-to-MCP campaign tests. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making an agent action mean the same thing as a player action. A tool cannot report success merely because a movement request was accepted; it must correlate the correct sequence, observe later authoritative state, and confirm arrival. Join operations also had to wait for the server to assign Explorer 2, reject wrong-seat or concurrent attempts, and prevent stale asynchronous work from overwriting a newer connection. Another challenge was deciding what the agent should see. A raw server snapshot would leak authored solution steps, hidden gate requirements, teleporter pairings, and future-level identifiers. The final observation model exposes enough geometry and live mechanism state to reason about the puzzle while withholding the answer. Deployment introduced a different constraint. The browser client and authoritative WebSocket server need one public HTTPS origin, while active rooms remain in server memory. The production runtime therefore serves the compiled game, matchmaking, and WebSocket upgrades from one supervised Node.js process without weakening the multiplayer authority model. Finally, browser and network timing made reconnection testing inherently asynchronous. The suite now verifies lifecycle generations, movement settlement, cleanup, reconnect behavior, and end-to-end campaign completion across real browser/server boundaries. Accomplishments that we're proud of WebMCP is central to the product loop rather than a decorative integration. A browser agent can join as the second explorer, inspect safe state, and complete authoritative movement. Human-browser and MCP-controlled teammates can finish the entire four-level campaign in one room. The agent is permission-bound to Explorer 2 and cannot bypass game rules or reveal hidden solutions. The current source passes lint, both TypeScript configurations, 23 Vitest files with 207 tests, production builds, and the core Playwright WebMCP and campaign paths. What we learned WebMCP becomes most valuable when tools express product intent, not DOM mechanics. move_player_two is useful because it represents a bounded game action with validation and an authoritative outcome—not because it automates a click. We also learned that agent interfaces need the same lifecycle engineering as human interfaces. Reconnection, stale requests, partial registration, terminal states, and concurrent joins are product behavior, not edge details. A reliable agent experience depends on handling them explicitly. Most importantly, safe context can still support meaningful reasoning. The agent does not need internal source code or a hidden solution graph; a carefully designed observation plus real feedback is enough for genuine cooperation. What's next Longer term, the game could add more campaigns, richer communication, and persistent cooperative progression while preserving its strict role and authority boundaries. title: OrbitFlo.co
pitch: Your Mission Control for Productivity
about_excerpt: Your Mission Control for Productivity Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP flips the usual agent story. Instead of an agent living in a separate tab with its own copy of your data, the page itself offers tools and the agent works in your session, on your screen. Orbit Flo was already built so that every domain operation is a plain async function over an authenticated Supabase client, with row-level security as the real boundary. That made it the right app to hand to an agent: the agent could only ever do what the signed-in person could do, by construction rather than by prompt. What it does Orbit Flo takes software projects from idea to done: kanban boards that run Docked → Ready to Launch → Launching → In Orbit, a daily flight plan with one primary item, milestones, markdown notes with orbit: links between tasks, an inbox for stray thoughts, mind maps that autosave and convert nodes into tasks, notes or milestones, and shared workspaces with link invitations, roles and assignment. All of it inside a live WebGL galaxy. Through WebMCP it registers thirteen tools with document.modelContext , so a browser-hosted agent can read today's plan, capture thoughts, file them as tasks, move cards, add work to the plan, write notes, add milestones and search the workspace. Each mutating tool invalidates the right queries, so the human watches the agent's work land on the board live. Tool What it does list_projects Projects in the current workspace, with ids get_flight_plan Today's daily plan and due work create_task New task on a project's board move_task Move a task between status columns search_workspace Search tasks, notes, projects, milestones capture_thought Drop a thought into the inbox complete_plan_item Complete a flight-plan item (with the launch animation) list_inbox Read unprocessed inbox captures file_capture_as_task Turn a capture into a task on a board add_to_flight_plan Put a task on today's plan list_notes List the workspace's notes create_note Write a note (ideas, decisions, risks…) create_milestone Add a milestone to a roadmap How we built it React 19, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind on the front; Supabase (Postgres, auth, row-level security) behind it; TanStack Query owns server state. The WebMCP layer is one module, src/features/agent/agent-tools.ts , that wraps the existing domain functions: each tool validates its input, calls the same function the UI calls with the same client, and ends with a query invalidation. Registration is feature-detected and scoped to an AbortController , so a browser without WebMCP runs the app unchanged and switching workspaces re-registers the tools against the workspace on screen. The privilege model is machine-verified: CI replays every migration onto a fresh Postgres and runs catalog assertions over grants and policies on every pull request, so a tool can never exceed what the database allows. Challenges we ran into No browser on the development machine exposed document.modelContext , so the tool layer was built against the specification and a recorded fake, with the absent-API path tested first. The first real integration run happened days before the deadline. Making the agent's work visible instantly meant auditing which query keys every mutation touches; the demo moment depends on it. Autosave for mind maps surfaced a latent server bug: the graph-replace RPC dropped conversion links on every save. It shipped with a migration that snapshots them first. Accomplishments that we're proud of The agent and the person share one workspace, one session and one screen, and the board updates as the agent talks. Nothing destructive is exposed: no deletes, no member or role management, and a test pins the tool list so a fourteenth tool is a failing build. The whole thing is open source, including the schema and the CI that guards its privilege model. What we learned Agent tooling is cheapest when the app already has clean, client-scoped domain functions and a real authorization boundary underneath them. The tool layer then becomes wiring plus validation, and the security story is the same one the UI already tells. What's next Streaming page context to the agent ( provideContext ), tools for maps and the crew (assign, mention), and a guest mode so judges and visitors can try the agent without shared credentials.  Inspiration 

 What if you could tell an AI what you want to buy, and instead of just giving you search results, it could actually hunt for the best deal with you? 

 What it does 

 Find me the best laptop for programming under NPR 130,000. I care about performance and battery life

 ackend fails with could not connect to server

 ModuleNotFoundError on backend start

 Frontend shows "Search error — is the backend running?"

title: Resolve Guard
pitch: A deterministic invocation-time policy gateway that makes routed MCP/WebMCP authority visible, blockable, exactly approvable, and replay-safe.
about_excerpt: A deterministic invocation-time policy gateway that makes routed MCP/WebMCP authority visible, blockable, exactly approvable, and replay-safe. Like Comment Story Updates Problem Browser agents can combine a person's intent, page content, tool metadata, tool results, credentials, and remembered context inside one decision loop. The individual pieces may look harmless, while the composed action quietly moves protected data to another origin, invokes a changed tool, presents a credential to the wrong resource, or turns a vague confirmation into a consequential side effect. Prompt-injection classification alone cannot reconstruct the authority that was lost. Advanced users and agent developers need one visible enforcement point that evaluates the actual invocation at the moment it would run. Solution Resolve Guard is an invocation-time security gateway and synthetic attack lab for one instrumented MCP/WebMCP client. Every protected call is normalized into an action envelope and evaluated by twelve deterministic checks: actor and client identity, browser origin, pinned MCP server, credential audience, least scopes, tool-manifest pin, schema pin, exact arguments, canonical destination, capability class, data-flow policy, and effect policy. The result is one of three explicit outcomes: Allow: bounded local work proceeds automatically. Block: a failed invariant stops execution and cannot be overridden by approval. Review: a policy-valid consequential action stops at a trusted, exact human approval surface. An approval is short-lived and bound to one normalized invocation, including its actor, client, origin, server, tool, effect, destination, data labels, argument digest, policy version, and expiry. Execution is at-most-once; replay returns the original operation instead of creating a second effect. The audit trail records correlated identifiers, decisions, and digests without raw protected content or credentials. Why This Matters WebMCP makes websites meaningfully agent-native: an agent can discover and invoke structured capabilities instead of guessing through a visual interface. That also creates composed authority across the person, browser, page, agent, MCP client, MCP server, credential, tool, and destination. Resolve Guard uses WebMCP to make that composition inspectable and enforceable. The agent can discover the security lab, inspect policy, run preflights, explain failures, and synchronize results into the same visual surface the person sees. The person retains the only approval surface for consequential work. Together they can investigate unsafe actions quickly without giving the agent a protocol tool that approves its own request. This proof of concept deliberately makes a narrow claim: it protects calls routed through one instrumented gateway. It does not claim to secure bypassed calls, compromised browsers or operating systems, dishonest providers after an allowed call leaves the boundary, or every future attack. How We Used AI The application itself demonstrates structured human-agent collaboration through imperative WebMCP tools. A WebMCP-capable agent can: list the seven deterministic attack scenarios; inspect the gateway policy and coverage boundary; run a scenario preflight; retrieve a redacted decision; and inspect the metadata-only audit trail. The agent cannot approve or execute a review decision through MCP or WebMCP. That omission is intentional: useful analysis remains agent-accessible, while the consequential boundary remains visible and human-controlled. All demo identities, documents, credentials, destinations, and effects are synthetic. Resolve Guard itself calls no external provider and uses no production credential. How We Used Codex Codex helped turn the participant-directed security concept into a scoped proof of concept, threat model, policy engine, REST/MCP/WebMCP surfaces, adversarial scenarios, responsive attack-lab interface, tests, browser verification, and documentation. The process included an explicit product pivot: an earlier seller-operations concept was discarded after the participant clarified that the real goal was to restore disappearing security boundaries between people, browser agents, MCP clients, servers, tools, credentials, and side effects. Codex rebuilt the project around that corrected outcome rather than rewording the obsolete implementation. Codex also ran a real native WebMCP session in the in-app browser. That run exposed a runtime boundary gap: the browser surfaced additionalProperties: false to the agent but did not enforce it before calling the page handler. A regression test locked the defect, the page execution boundary was hardened with independent exact-key validation, and the invalid call was re-run with zero audit or operation side effects. The final automated suite passes 31 tests. Key Features Seven deterministic proof scenarios covering safe local work, injected exfiltration, parameter smuggling, destination confusion, tool drift, credential-audience mismatch, and exact approval/replay. Twelve ordered, explainable invocation checks with stable allow/block/review reason codes. Five same-origin imperative WebMCP tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Strict runtime validation in every page-defined tool before API I/O or UI mutation. Independent tool-manifest and input-schema pins. Default-deny protected-data egress and canonical exact-destination enforcement. Exact, short-lived, single-use, UI-only human approval. At-most-once sandbox execution with idempotent replay. Metadata-only correlated audit with canary-backed redaction tests. Dependency-free Node.js 22 implementation, responsive keyboard-accessible UI, local MCP HTTP/stdio transport, and a sealed synthetic public-demo mode. Architecture One in-memory domain service backs the visible browser UI, REST endpoints, MCP over HTTP/stdio, and imperative WebMCP tools, so every surface shares the same decision semantics. user goal + page/tool/result content | mixed trust with provenance v instrumented browser agent / MCP client | every protected invocation v Resolve Guard enforcement point normalize -> authenticate -> authorize -> data-flow check | allow | block | exact review v X v pinned sandbox tool visible approval surface | | +------ execute once <----+ The public demo is deliberately sealed: fixed fake identities, synthetic source data, in-memory effects, no credentials, and no outbound server request. Testing Instructions Public judge flow Open https://resolve-guard.vercel.app in ChatGPT's WebMCP-capable in-app browser, or Google Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled and the browser restarted. Confirm the header reports five registered WebMCP tools. Run Safe local summary . Expect allow / LOCAL_FLOW_ALLOWED and one bounded synthetic operation. Run Injected exfiltration . Expect block / DATA_EGRESS_DENIED and no operation. Run Hidden callback parameter . Expect block / UNKNOWN_ARGUMENT . Run Publish sanitized status . Expect review / HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED and no operation before approval. Open the exact approval, enter the visible confirmation, execute, then replay. Expect the same operation to be returned and no second effect. Open the audit trail. Confirm it contains decision/approval/operation metadata and digests, not raw protected content or credentials. Suggested agent prompts “List the Resolve Guard security scenarios and state its coverage boundary.” “Run the injected exfiltration preflight and explain why it cannot execute.” “Run the sanitized publish preflight.” Confirm the agent stops at HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED and exposes no approval or execution tool. Local verification npm start npm run verify Requirements: Node.js 22.14 or newer. There are no package dependencies and no credentials to configure. Public Demo Link https://resolve-guard.vercel.app Public Repository Link https://github.com/VIVEHACKER/resolve-guard The repository is public, includes the complete MIT license at the root, and contains all source, assets, run instructions, tests, and WebMCP registration code. Anonymous HTTPS clone, raw-file access, the public main branch, WebMCP registration code, and GitHub's MIT license detection were verified after publication. Demo Video Public YouTube video: https://youtu.be/8uttf0gkMqE Visibility independently verified as Public. Duration: 2:30, below the three-minute limit. 1080p H.264 video with English AAC narration. Custom thumbnail and published English captions. Anonymous playback and audible playback were verified. The video is an uninterrupted, mouse-driven walkthrough of the real visual lab backed by the same policy engine. It shows the page reporting five registered native WebMCP tools and demonstrates allow, block, review, exact approval, at-most-once execution, replay, schema-smuggling rejection, audit evidence, and the honest protection boundary. title: Remy
pitch: Remy lets AI agents take real actions without taking control away from users. Safe work runs automatically, risky actions wait for approval, and every change gets a receipt and recovery path.
about_excerpt: Remy lets AI agents take real actions without taking control away from users. Safe work runs automatically, risky actions wait for approval, and every change gets a receipt and recovery path. Like Comment Story Updates Homepage Agent Activity Inspiration AI agents are becoming capable of changing real application state, but the current trust model feels broken. Users either approve every small action, making the agent slow and irritating, or grant broad autonomy and inspect the damage afterwards. Remy explores a middle ground: let reversible work happen automatically, pause consequential actions for explicit approval, and give users a clear record of what happened and a way back when possible. What it does Remy is a protocol-neutral action layer for applications that allow AI agents to take real actions. Developers define an action once, including what it changes, its risk, and how it can be recovered. Remy then provides: Runtime validation and action previews Developer policies and user-selected autonomy Explicit approval for consequential actions Human-readable receipts and diffs Append-only action history Exact undo, compensation, or an honest irreversible state The demo is a fictional headphone shop using WebMCP. An agent can add headphones, select delivery, and apply a discount automatically. Placing the order spends money, so Remy pauses and presents the exact item, price, address, and payment method for the user to approve. How we built it Remy’s core is a TypeScript action engine that does not depend on React or WebMCP. Every semantic action passes through the same validation, preview, policy, execution, receipt, and recovery pipeline. A WebMCP adapter exposes those actions as page-scoped tools. The shop’s normal interface and its WebMCP tools use the same underlying engine, keeping policy enforcement beside the application’s business logic. The demo uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Zod, Tailwind CSS, Motion, and Vitest. State and receipts are persisted locally for the challenge demonstrator. I also built an alpha initializer that scaffolds Remy into a Next.js application. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was making approval a real enforcement boundary rather than an instruction in a prompt. If an agent is merely told to wait, it may continue through another interaction path. The restriction therefore has to be enforced where the final state change occurs. Approval is also asynchronous, while agent tool calls may be short-lived. Remy represents approval as pending application state and revalidates the authoritative data before execution. Recovery introduced another challenge. Some changes can be undone exactly, some require a new compensating action, and others are genuinely irreversible. Remy needed to represent each case honestly without pretending that every action has an undo button. Accomplishments that we're proud of The working demo shows useful autonomy rather than simply approving or blocking everything. Reversible shopping actions can execute automatically, while the irreversible purchase stops for explicit approval. An agent cannot grant itself greater autonomy. Every attempt produces a readable receipt, duplicate effects are prevented with idempotency keys, stale approvals are invalidated, and reversals remain linked to the original action instead of erasing history. The same semantic action definitions power the normal website, the WebMCP tools, the policy engine, receipts, and recovery. What we learned Action history by itself is only observability. A receipt written after an unsafe mutation cannot protect the user. The action layer must make its decision before execution and remain on the path to the real state change. We also learned that reversibility is a useful basis for autonomy. Users should not need to approve harmless work that can be safely reversed, but consequential or irreversible actions deserve a clear checkpoint. Finally, WebMCP works well as an adapter, but the underlying action contract should remain protocol-neutral so the same guarantees can follow an action across different agent environments. What's next for Remy The next steps are publishing the core SDK and initializer, adding MCP and agent SDK adapters, and moving histories from local storage to a durable hosted journal. Future versions could add authenticated agent identity, approval routing, shared policies, monitoring, alerts, signed receipts, and evidence exports while allowing applications to keep their own interface and business logic. title: AgentBridge
pitch: The control layer for the agent-ready web.
about_excerpt:
The control layer for the agent-ready web.

 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP Inspector — screenshot showing AgentBridge discovering tools from the independent Google Chrome Labs WebMCP demo.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 The web is rapidly moving from websites designed only for humans toward a web where humans and AI agents can work together. 

 WebMCP makes this possible by allowing websites to expose structured tools directly to AI agents. But while experimenting with WebMCP, I saw another important problem: how does a website owner stay in control of what an AI agent can actually do? 

 A merchant may be comfortable allowing an agent to search products or check inventory, but actions such as adding items to a cart, submitting a request, or changing data may require more control. 

 That inspired AgentBridge — the control layer for the agent-ready web. 

 What it does 

 AgentBridge helps website owners make their websites agent-ready while maintaining control over agent access. 

 A website can expose capabilities such as: 

 
 search_products 
 get_product 
 check_inventory 
 add_to_cart 
 

 as structured WebMCP tools that compatible AI agents can discover and invoke. 

 AgentBridge then adds a merchant-controlled layer around those capabilities. Website owners can: 

 
 Discover capabilities that could become agent tools 
 Control individual tool permissions 
 Enable or revoke Agent Access 
 Require human confirmation for sensitive actions 
 Inspect WebMCP tools exposed by websites 
 

 For example, an AI agent can search a merchant's products and check inventory automatically, while an add_to_cart action can require explicit human confirmation before it is completed. 

 How I built it 

 I built AgentBridge as an end-to-end WebMCP prototype consisting of a merchant portal, a WebMCP-enabled demonstration storefront, a backend policy layer, and a Chrome extension that acts as a WebMCP Inspector. 

 The Northstar demo storefront exposes commerce capabilities as structured tools. AgentBridge manages which of those capabilities are available to agents and applies policies for actions requiring confirmation. 

 I also built the Inspector to discover WebMCP tools registered by websites. I tested it not only against my own storefront but also against an independent Google Chrome Labs WebMCP implementation, which helped demonstrate interoperability beyond the AgentBridge demo environment. 

 The project uses JavaScript, Node.js, Express, Chrome Extension APIs, WebMCP, HTML/CSS, and Railway for deployment. 

 Challenges I faced 

 One of the biggest challenges was moving beyond simply exposing tools and designing a practical permission model around them. 

 I had to think about questions such as: 

 Who controls agent access? Which capabilities should be available? What happens when an action changes something? How can access be revoked immediately? 

 This led to per-tool permissions, a global Agent Access switch, and human confirmation for higher-impact actions. 

 Another challenge was making the system work across different websites rather than designing everything specifically for one storefront. Building and testing the WebMCP Inspector against an independent implementation helped validate the broader approach. 

 Website ownership verification, runtime policy synchronization, extension-to-website communication, deployment, and keeping tool state consistent also presented interesting engineering challenges during development. 

 What I learned 

 The biggest thing I learned is that making the web agent-ready is not only about giving AI agents more capabilities. 

 It is also about giving humans control over those capabilities. 

 WebMCP provides a powerful foundation for structured agent-to-website interaction. Building AgentBridge showed me how permission management, confirmation, discovery, and access control could complement that foundation. 

 What's next 

 I see AgentBridge evolving into infrastructure that helps businesses adopt the agentic web without giving up control. 

 Future versions could support more website platforms and capability types, richer policies, production-grade ownership verification, activity analytics, and developer tooling for testing WebMCP implementations. 

 As more websites become accessible to AI agents, I believe there will be a growing need for a layer that sits between websites and agents and answers a simple question: 

 What is this agent allowed to do? 

 That's the role AgentBridge is designed to play. 

 AgentBridge — The control layer for the agent-ready web.

title: YallaQueue Agent Desk
pitch: WhatsApp booking meets an agent-native live queue for local service businesses.
about_excerpt: WhatsApp booking meets an agent-native live queue for local service businesses. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Many small service businesses manage appointments through WhatsApp and then manually transfer those bookings into a schedule or queue. This wastes time, creates booking conflicts, and makes it difficult to keep customers and staff working from the same information. I created YallaQueue to connect WhatsApp booking, a live business dashboard, and an AI agent. What it does YallaQueue converts natural WhatsApp messages into confirmed appointments. It can: Check whether an appointment time is available Prevent conflicting bookings Assign a queue number Save the appointment Send a WhatsApp confirmation Display the appointment on a live shop dashboard The signed-in shop owner can also use two WebMCP tools through a browser agent: get_queue_summary returns the current queue without exposing customer phone numbers. update_queue_status changes one appointment to confirmed, completed, cancelled, or no-show. For example, the owner can ask: “Summarize today’s queue.” “Mark queue 1 completed.” The dashboard immediately shows the updated state. How we built it YallaQueue uses Next.js and React for the dashboard, Supabase and PostgreSQL for authentication and appointment data, and n8n with the WhatsApp Cloud API for messaging automation. The dashboard registers two browser-native WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool calls a protected server route using the owner’s active login. The server checks authentication, shop membership, input validity, appointment ownership, and database row-level security before returning data or making a change. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was giving the agent useful access without bypassing security. The agent must only access appointments belonging to the signed-in owner’s shop. Customer phone numbers must not appear in tool results, and an appointment must not be changed without a clear user request. Another challenge was keeping WhatsApp, the database, the dashboard, and the agent synchronized so they all display the same queue state. Testing WebMCP also required enabling its experimental Chrome flag and using ChatGPT Work so the browser agent could discover the registered tools. Accomplishments that we're proud of Connected a real WhatsApp booking flow to a live dashboard Built and deployed two working WebMCP tools Used structured tool data instead of visual browser guessing Protected every tool route with server-side authorization Excluded customer phone numbers from agent responses Successfully tested both reading and updating the live queue through ChatGPT Work What we learned I learned how websites can provide structured tools for both humans and AI agents. I also learned that WebMCP does not replace application security. Agent actions must still pass normal authentication, authorization, input validation, ownership checks, and database security rules. What's next for YallaQueue The next steps are adding more carefully controlled tools for availability searches, creating appointments, rescheduling, and cancellations. I also plan to add clearer confirmation screens for sensitive actions, support multiple shops and staff members, and improve reporting for business owners.
