title: Nirnay
pitch: Agents can't read a canvas. Nirnay gives them the exact overshoot, settling time and stability margins behind its plots, so human and agent tune the same controller together, live.
about_excerpt: Agents can't read a canvas. Nirnay gives them the exact overshoot, settling time and stability margins behind its plots, so human and agent tune the same controller together, live. Like 1 Comment Story Updates These are the Parameters 1 a These are the Parameters 2 a These are the test results got by setting the parameters as in the Image Nirnay-Parameters 1 b and 1 a These are the Parameters 1 b These are the test results got by setting the parameters as in the Image Nirnay-Parameters 2 b and 2 a These are the Parameters 2 b This is image that depicts how Nirnay works. These are the Graphs got by setting the parameters as in the Image Nirnay-Parameters 1 b and 1 a These are the Graphs got by setting the parameters as in the Image Nirnay-Parameters 2 b and 2 a Home page After changing some parameters (Random parameters part B) Home page After changing some parameters (Random parameters part A) These are the test results that shows all passed 46/46 Inspiration We spend a lot of time in control systems coursework, and tuning a controller is a strange kind of work: it is entirely about numbers, but you do all of it by staring at pictures. You drag a gain, you squint at a step response, you decide the wobble looks a bit better, you drag again. When we started reading the WebMCP spec, the first thing we wanted to know was what an agent could actually do on a page like that. The answer turned out to be almost nothing, and the reason was specific enough to be interesting. A step response, a Bode plot and a root locus are drawn on an HTML <canvas> . A canvas is coloured pixels. There is no text under it, no DOM, nothing to scrape. Hand a vision model a screenshot of a step response and ask for the overshoot and you get "roughly 25%" — a guess read off pixel positions. You cannot tune a controller on "roughly". The entire task is hitting a number like "under 10%", and 12% and 18% call for opposite corrections. So this was not a case of an agent being clumsy with a UI. The information the agent needed did not exist anywhere it could reach. It only existed as floating point numbers inside the running program. That felt like the sharpest possible answer to "why WebMCP?", so we built the page around it. What it does Nirnay is a control-system design bench. You pick a plant, drag sliders for the three PID gains, and three plots redraw instantly — step response, Bode, and a root locus / pole-zero map. On the right there is a scoreboard: every performance metric with a green PASS or red FAIL chip against design targets you set yourself. The page exposes eight WebMCP tools, so an AI agent in the same page can read the exact simulation numbers and tune alongside you. The important part is that there is one shared state behind everything. The sliders and the agent's tools write to the same place. When the agent changes a gain, the sliders physically move, the plots redraw and the scoreboard updates while you watch. You can grab a slider back mid-conversation and the agent's next reading reflects it. Neither side is driving a copy of the other's world. There is also an agent activity log on the page that prints a line every time a tool is called, so a human watching the screen can see exactly what just happened and why. The page opens in a deliberately failing state — 50.6% overshoot against a 10% target, three of four specs red. That is on purpose. It gives the agent something real to fix instead of a victory lap. The eight tools Five read, three write. Read: get_system (full current setup), run_step_response (exact overshoot, rise time, settling time, steady-state error), get_frequency_response (gain and phase margins, crossover frequencies), get_pole_zero_map (closed-loop poles, damping, and how far the gain can be pushed before instability), evaluate_design (score against targets, and what is still failing and by how much). Write: set_controller_gains , set_plant , set_design_spec . Three design decisions shaped how well this actually works: Every write tool returns the full measured result. set_controller_gains does not reply "done". It replies with the new overshoot, settling time, margins, pole positions and a pass/fail verdict. The obvious design is write-then-read, two calls per attempt. Returning the measurement with the write halves the round trips, but the real reason is that it keeps the agent anchored to a measurement instead of to its own prediction of what those gains would do. Agents are good at confidently predicting the wrong outcome. No tool ever returns a bare OK. Every response carries numbers the agent can check itself against. That is what lets it notice a change made things worse and back it out, rather than marching in the wrong direction. Bad input gets a sentence, not a stack trace. Pass a string where a number belongs and you get Error: Kp must be a finite number, got a string. A crashed tool call teaches an agent nothing. A sentence naming the mistake lets it retry. Read tools are marked with readOnlyHint so the browser does not interrupt with a confirmation prompt on every measurement, which matters a lot once the agent starts iterating. How we built it Everything runs in the browser. No server, no backend, no libraries, no build step — plain JavaScript files the browser loads directly. That was a deliberate choice: one deployable artifact, one failure point, and nothing between the plot and the tool that could make them disagree. The numerics, roughly in layers: Polynomial arithmetic as the base, since transfer functions are ratios of polynomials. Durand–Kerner for root finding, which chases all roots simultaneously. Roots sitting exactly at zero stall it, so those get peeled off first. RK4 integration for the step response, running twenty times finer than it records so the stored curve is smooth and trustworthy. Bisection to locate the gain and phase crossover frequencies exactly, rather than reporting the closest point on a sampled grid. Root locus by sweeping gain and matching each root to its nearest previous position, so drawn branches follow one root smoothly instead of jumping where two roots pass close together. Tool registration sits behind a feature check, so in a browser without WebMCP the page is simply a complete engineering tool with no agent. Nothing breaks and nothing looks broken. Who built what Nirnay was built by two of us. Challenges we ran into The bug that the cross-check caught. The gain at which a system goes unstable can be computed two entirely different ways: from the root locus, tracking roots in one mathematical space, and from the frequency response, tracking phase in a completely different one. They share no code. We wrote a test asserting they agree. They did not. The root locus said 6, the frequency path said 6.0577. The root locus was right. The bug was a rare edge case in the frequency path: the search grid happened to land exactly on the answer, which broke an assumption the refinement step depended on. We would never have found that by looking at a graph. Both curves looked fine. It is exactly the kind of quiet wrongness that makes a tool useless to an agent, because the agent has no way to sanity-check what it is handed — it will act on 6.0577 with total confidence. Testing before implementing. The test suites were written independently of the implementation and check against answers known from theory, not from our own code: closed-form textbook formulas for second-order overshoot and peak time, matched to within 0.5%, and classic worked examples whose margins can be derived by hand. 46/46 numerics tests and 111/111 browser tests pass from a fresh clone. Testing the browser half. Node cannot test browser behaviour, so there is a second suite that loads the real page markup, fakes the WebMCP connection, and checks the things that only exist in a browser: that all eight tools register, that each describes its inputs properly, that read tools are correctly marked read-only, that bad input produces a readable error, and that when a tool changes a gain, the sliders on the page actually move. That last assertion is the entire human-and-agent premise in one line. Learning the platform. A few things cost us time and are not obvious from the spec alone: it is document.modelContext , not navigator.modelContext , which many older examples still use. Tools registered inside iframes are not discovered, even same-origin, so everything has to live on the top-level page. The declarative HTML form API is not supported yet, so registration is JavaScript only. And WebMCP is a secure-context feature, so opening the file over file:// silently gives you no tools at all. Writing descriptions the agent actually reads. Our first pass had terse tool descriptions and the agent kept reaching for generic browser control before listing site tools. Tightening the input schemas — real descriptions on every property, additionalProperties: false — was what made it go straight to the right tool. What we learned Th

title: OVERTURN
pitch: Health insurers deny 1 in 5 claims and almost no one fights back. Overturn pairs you with an agent that builds the appeal through WebMCP tools — and waits for your OK to file.
about_excerpt: Health insurers deny 1 in 5 claims and almost no one fights back. Overturn pairs you with an agent that builds the appeal through WebMCP tools — and waits for your OK to file. Like Comment Story Updates landing page with the problem stats parsed case file, 160-day deadline, evidence checklist after approval, confirmation and payer timeline in the console use this one first: the agent paused mid-tool with the drafted letter, strength score 78/Strong, and the "Approve & file / Decline" card Inspiration Health insurers deny about 1 in 5 in-network claims, and fewer than 1% of patients ever appeal — even though a large share of appeals that get filed succeed. The fight isn't hard because it's complicated; it's hard because it's tedious : decode the denial codes, find the payer's medical policy, match your facts to its criteria, cite guidelines, compute the deadline, draft the letter, file on time. That tedium is exactly what an agent should do. The judgment, the consent, and the signature are exactly what a human must do. The WebMCP Challenge asked for an app that gets meaningfully better when people and agents use it together — an appeals office is that, almost literally: two workers, one case file, a clear division of labor. What it does Paste a denial letter into Overturn (it stays in your browser — nothing is uploaded). The agent then works through 13 WebMCP tools: it parses the letter into a structured case, decodes the claim-adjustment codes, finds the payer medical policy that justified the denial, checks each coverage criterion against the record, attaches citable guideline evidence, computes the filing deadline by plan type, drafts a full appeal letter, and scores its strength with a factor-by-factor breakdown. Then the part the product exists for: when the agent calls submit_appeal , the tool pauses and an approval card appears. Nothing is filed until the human clicks Approve & file . After filing, human and agent watch the payer timeline together. No WebMCP available? A built-in "Run demo agent" walks the identical tool implementations — including the approval pause — so anyone can see the loop. How we built it A zero-dependency, zero-build static page (GitHub Pages), with a strict separation between pure logic and the WebMCP layer: js/tools.js registers 13 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) , each returning MCP-style { content: [{ type: "text" }] } envelopes with isError on failure. Following Chrome's WebMCP security guidance: annotations.readOnlyHint on every state-preserving tool, annotations.untrustedContentHint on every tool whose output embeds the (untrusted) denial letter, and Chrome's design budgets — ≤500-char tool descriptions, ≤150-char parameter descriptions, ~1.4K-char outputs. Tool descriptions teach workflow ("Call draft_appeal_letter first — the human must be able to read what will be filed"). The human's UI and the agent's tools are two surfaces over one shared pipeline : the app's own buttons call the same tool implementations with actor: "human" , so the console shows exactly who did what. The approval gate is a tool promise that only resolves when the human clicks — defense in depth on top of whatever the agent's host requires — with a 3-minute timeout that declines by default. Pure pipeline logic (parsing, criteria matching, deadline math, drafting, scoring) is unit-tested in Node: 25 assertions, all passing. Challenges we ran into Consent inside a tool call. submit_appeal has to stop mid-execution and wait for a human. We resolved it by parking the tool's promise on an approval card in the UI — which raised real questions (what if nobody answers? default-deny after a timeout) that most apps never have to think about. Parsing adversarial prose without a server. Extracting payer, claim, codes, and plan type from a letter using only regex and keyword rules — including a negation guard so "no red flags" doesn't count as evidence for red flags. The 1.5K output budget forced us to design tool results as agent-oriented summaries with pointers ("the full letter is in the human's editor") instead of dumping state. A delightful DST off-by-one: computing "days left to file" across a time-change boundary needs calendar arithmetic, not millisecond diffs. A unit test caught it. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full loop works end-to-end: paste → agent legwork → human edit → approval → confirmation and payer timeline — verified in a real browser against the deployed site. The approval moment is genuinely good product design, not a checkbox: the agent can do everything except the one step that matters, alone. Graceful degradation: feature-detecting document.modelContext means the app is fully usable everywhere, and the demo agent gives judges without WebMCP the exact same story. What we learned Tool descriptions are prompts. Writing them as workflow guidance (what to call next, what to do when data is missing) mattered more than any schema detail. Annotations are a design language. Marking untrusted content and read-only tools forced us to think about trust boundaries the way a security reviewer would. Output budgets are a feature. Constraining tool results made the agent interface better — small, pointed results with pointers beat dumps. Building for two users at once (human + agent) makes the product simpler, not more complex, when the state is genuinely shared. What's next for OVERTURN Real-world ingestion: PDF/photo import of denial letters and EOBs (still on-device). A payer-connector layer so submit_appeal can target real portals behind explicit per-payer consent, plus certified-mail and fax fallbacks. Multi-appeal dashboard with deadline tracking across a household's claims, and an exportable audit log of every agent action for regulators and advocates. Delegated review: let a family member or patient advocate be the approval authority. Keep contributing to the WebMCP conversation: this project is a strong argument for app-level consent gates as a standard annotation. title: oa::Network - WebMCP for native Vulkan applications
pitch: Safe, typed WebMCP tools for native C++ Vulkan, ML, and 3D applications.
about_excerpt: Safe, typed WebMCP tools for native C++ Vulkan, ML, and 3D applications. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents can operate websites, while serious compute, ML, media, and 3D applications still live behind native C++ runtimes and GPU APIs. Existing browser automation often forces agents to guess through pixels and UI controls, while conventional MCP servers operate separately from the live page the user is viewing. OA already provides a native Vulkan compute and ML runtime, a bounded MCP implementation, training sessions, rendering, video, and experimental prompt-to-motion generation. We wanted to connect those capabilities directly to WebMCP so a person and an agent can safely operate the same live native application—with OA remaining the execution engine rather than moving the workload into JavaScript or a hosted service. What it does oa::Network - WebMCP exposes validated OA application actions as page-local WebMCP tools. A native C++ OA process owns the Vulkan device, compute graphs, models, rendering resources, synchronization, and application state. A small TypeScript adapter discovers its registered tools, exposes them through WebMCP, and forwards calls to the same typed commands used by the human interface. The project is designed around two demonstrations: A tiny-language-model workspace for selecting a model and tokenizer, starting or pausing training, inspecting bounded metrics, evaluating, checkpointing, and generating text on a local Vulkan GPU. A prompt-to-motion workspace using OA’s experimental ALM stack, native rendering, timeline state, and deterministic motion-editing tools. Large tensors, model weights, video frames, and GPU handles never travel through WebMCP. The browser carries only bounded commands, status, metrics, identifiers, and verifiable results. How we built it The native implementation is built in C++20 as part of OA Network. oa::McpServer owns the immutable tool registry, JSON schemas, validation, bounded parsing, and application handlers. The WebMCP bridge composes that server through an explicitly owned network gateway rather than creating a second tool implementation. The browser integration is a small TypeScript layer that: discovers compatible OA tools; registers them with document.modelContext.registerTool ; maps WebMCP annotations and JSON schemas; forwards validated calls to the native process; preserves cancellation, revisions, and ordered results; updates the same React interface used by the human operator. OA’s Vulkan engine performs the actual ML, rendering, and media work. The browser remains a control and presentation surface. Generic interface components come from our existing Realm UI package, while application state and WebMCP registrations remain owned by the OA SDK demonstration. Challenges we ran into MCP and WebMCP are related but have different ownership and lifecycle models. An MCP server can operate independently, while WebMCP tools belong to an open browser page and disappear when that page closes or navigates away. Sharing tool semantics without accidentally creating two canonical execution paths required a careful composition boundary. Native GPU work is asynchronous and stateful. A WebMCP call being accepted does not mean a training mutation, checkpoint, render, or generation request has already completed. We needed explicit accepted, applied, completed, rejected, cancelled, and failed states. Security was another central challenge. The bridge must reject oversized or malformed input, arbitrary filesystem access, URLs, shader source, Vulkan handles, and unbounded allocation requests. Local execution also requires strict loopback binding, origin validation, per-launch credentials, bounded connections, and predictable shutdown. Finally, we needed to keep the browser responsive while the native Vulkan application continued running independently of page refreshes, reconnects, or agent availability. Accomplishments that we're proud of OA already provides a transport-independent MCP server with strict JSON parsing, bounded messages, deterministic tool registration, typed arguments, structured results, and adversarial tests. Its training adapter uses the existing oa::TrainingSession safe-point command system rather than mutating model or GPU state directly. The same session can therefore be controlled by native UI actions, MCP, and WebMCP without changing the underlying training semantics. We are particularly proud that OA remains the product: compute and rendering execute through our native Vulkan runtime; one oa::Engine owns GPU resources and scheduling; JavaScript does not emulate or replace the native workload; tool calls expose semantic actions rather than raw implementation handles; the human and agent work with the same live state; WebMCP becomes a reusable OA Network capability rather than challenge-specific glue. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when it exposes meaningful application operations instead of reproducing every button in the interface. The strongest human-agent experiences share visible state, history, selection, and results. The agent should be able to act precisely, while the user can immediately inspect what changed and undo or refine it. We also learned that control traffic and bulk data need separate paths. JSON and WebMCP are appropriate for commands, metrics, provenance, and resource identifiers—not tensors, model files, video frames, or GPU memory. Most importantly, a generic bridge between a validated native tool registry and WebMCP is more valuable than writing isolated JavaScript handlers for every demonstration. What's next for oa::Network - WebMCP for native Vulkan applications Our first milestone is the complete tiny-language-model demonstration: live Vulkan training, metrics, pause and resume, evaluation, checkpoint reload, generation, and WebMCP control through one shared browser workspace. If time permits, the second demonstration will add prompt-to-motion generation, native 3D preview, timeline inspection, deterministic edits, and export through OA’s ALM and rendering stack. After the challenge, we plan to: qualify the bridge under sanitizers and adversarial protocol tests; add installed-package and fresh-browser testing; expand reusable TypeScript bindings without moving compute into the browser; support additional OA vision, audio, video, and 3D applications; benchmark the complete native-to-browser control path; add authenticated remote deployment while preserving the secure local default. title: Cadence Workout Studio
pitch: Cadence gives self-coached cyclists and agents a shared workout canvas where WebMCP agents turn athlete intent into transparent, constraint-aware workouts, while athletes retain final approval.
about_excerpt: Cadence gives self-coached cyclists and agents a shared workout canvas where WebMCP agents turn athlete intent into transparent, constraint-aware workouts, while athletes retain final approval. Like Comment Story Updates Workout Studio Inspiration For the past couple of months, I have been building an AI Cycling Coaching application that provides recommended daily workouts based on readiness and past activity data. When analyzing this challenge, I realized that the WebMCP capabilities can be used to develop a standalone workout creation canvas as well as have it plugged into an AI Cycling Coaching app. Amateur cyclist have limited time, changing readiness, specific goals, and important sessions they need to protect. AI can offer recommendations, but they often arrive as opaque text with no shared editing surface, visible calculations, or reliable approval boundaries. Cadence Workout Studio explores a different model: the athlete and agent collaborate on the same visible workout, while Cadence owns the calculations, constraints, revision history, and safety boundaries. What it does Cadence is a shared workout-composition studio powered by seven focused WebMCP tools. An agent can inspect the rider’s planning context, select an approved workout structure, construct interval blocks, evaluate the athlete’s exact revision, request a bounded repair, and validate the result. Every agent action appears immediately in the same interface the athlete uses. The Studio shows interval changes, workout duration, intensity, training load, time in zone, constraint violations, repair tradeoffs, provenance, and exact-revision status. The athlete can edit the proposed workout at any time. Approval and export remain human-only actions, so an agent cannot silently finalize a workout. The complete workflow also works manually in browsers without WebMCP. How I built it I built Cadence as a public, synthetic-data challenge edition using Next.js, React, and TypeScript. The WebMCP integration registers seven narrow page tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool delegates to the same domain services used by the human interface, rather than maintaining a separate agent workflow. Workout calculations and validation are independent of the WebMCP transport. Cadence calculates duration, intensity factor, training load, power targets, and time in zone. Every edit creates a new revision, invalidates previous validation or approval, and rejects stale agent requests. The application uses browser-local persistence and a resettable fictional rider, so judges need no account, credentials, wearable, private database, or personal health data. Approved indoor workouts can be exported as .zwo or JSON files. The repository includes automated domain, schema, persistence, stale-revision, export-gate, and browser workflow tests, along with the complete challenge-period implementation history. Challenges I ran into The hardest challenge was making the agent and athlete true collaborators, not building a chat interface that generated a finished workout. I needed one revisioned artifact that both sides could inspect and change without losing authorship or allowing stale operations. That required exact-revision validation, approval fingerprints, visible provenance, and automatic invalidation after every edit. Designing repair behavior was another challenge. The agent should not directly invent arbitrary changes, so Cadence accepts a bounded objective and priorities, chooses the concrete repair itself, and records the resulting tradeoffs. I also had to keep the seven tools narrow enough for reliable agent use while returning enough structured state for both the agent and athlete to verify every result. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am proud that Cadence feels like a complete product that can integrate with its parent product, ThresholdLabs, to improve the recommendation engine or act as a standalone workout configurator. The athlete can deliberately change a workout, create a constraint violation, ask an agent to evaluate the exact revision, let Cadence repair it, validate the repaired workout, and then personally approve and export it. The same calculations, constraints, and state transitions power both the WebMCP tools and the manual interface. The app preserves human authority while making agent collaboration visible, structured, and useful. I am also proud that the public challenge edition requires no credentials or private infrastructure and contains only isolated synthetic data. What I learned I learned that the strongest WebMCP tools expose domain capabilities rather than mirroring buttons or asking an agent to scrape the interface. WebMCP becomes especially powerful when the webpage remains the source of truth. The agent contributes intent and priorities, the application enforces its domain rules, and the human can see and verify the result. I also learned that human approval is more meaningful when it is tied to an exact, validated revision rather than a general conversation or recommendation. What's next for Cadence Workout Studio Next, I would expand the approved workout library, add richer outdoor execution guidance, improve comparison between alternative repairs, integrate into ThresholdLabs intelligence engine, and support reusable athlete-created templates. A future production version could connect to athlete-owned training data with explicit consent, while preserving the same visible provenance, bounded agent actions, exact-revision validation, and human approval model demonstrated here. title: CargoPilot
pitch: Share a current Cargo page with your agent through WebMCP, with visible freshness and human-controlled editing boundaries.
about_excerpt:
Share a current Cargo page with your agent through WebMCP, with visible freshness and human-controlled editing boundaries.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Portfolio builders are visual, but collaborating with an AI in one often means describing a layout from memory or exchanging disconnected screenshots. CargoPilot explores a more explicit shared reference: the creator chooses a signed-in Cargo page, the agent receives its current visible context, and both know when that context is too old to trust. 

 What it does 

 CargoPilot connects a public WebMCP companion to a private local bridge. It exposes a screenshot, bounded semantic context, route and page information, capture time, and freshness state for a selected Cargo screen. The same context is available through a standard stdio MCP server. 

 There are two distinct connection paths. A Chrome extension lets the user click Share with Codex on an already signed-in Cargo tab. In Codex/ChatGPT's in-app browser, a browser-capable host agent can instead make an explicitly authorized capture and relay it using request_cargo_context and attach_cargo_context . Extensions cannot be installed inside that in-app browser; the hosted companion cannot independently inspect another tab or borrow its authentication. 

 The shared canvas is a read-only snapshot, not a second Cargo editor. Captures expire after 15 seconds. The UI marks stale and unavailable states, and context tools do not silently switch to another browser. The creator scrolls or edits in Cargo and asks the agent for a new capture when needed. 

 The Chrome extension also implements a separate time-limited approval path for two fixed recipes: exact text replacement and native Backdrop selection, with route and postcondition checks. Read-only sharing does not authorize these actions. The final live demonstration deliberately exercises only read-only context; it does not claim to demonstrate those editing recipes, asset uploads, arbitrary template editing, or publishing. 

 Why WebMCP 

 WebMCP turns the companion's collaboration boundary into named, typed tools. An agent can ask for workspace, screen, or editor context through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) instead of guessing what a screenshot or inactive canvas means. Inputs are validated, freshness is explicit, and inspection is separated from mutation authority. 

 The creator can discuss a specific page while the agent receives the relevant visual evidence and knows which site, page and capture it belongs to. The Chrome pointing interaction additionally shares viewport coordinates and a bounded accessible label. This reduces repeated manual explanation without treating unrestricted browser control as the default. 

 How we built it 

 
 Vite and TypeScript companion, hosted on Vercel, registering browser-native WebMCP tools. 
 Local Express service bound to 127.0.0.1 , with Zod input validation, short-lived context, audit state, and a standard MCP server. 
 Manifest V3 Chrome extension with explicit selected-tab sharing and a separate approved fixed-action path. 
 Browser-host attachment for the in-app browser, using actual screenshot capture and bounded visible context without moving cookies or passwords between browsers. 
 

 Codex assisted with implementation, debugging and testing. Remotion assembles real browser captures and measured capture sequences into the demo. The narration is AI-generated; the conversation section is explicitly labelled as a replay of our actual exchange, not a recording of the Codex interface. 

 Validation 

 The 4 September 2026 live pass retrieved a real authenticated Cargo dashboard and an editor page through the deployed WebMCP companion and an actual stdio MCP client. Both returned the relevant current screen and screenshot. Asking for editor context on the dashboard correctly failed. Expiry produced an explicit stale response and visible UI label. Losing the attachment removed the old canvas image and left unsupported typing controls disabled. 

 There are 64 passing automated tests, TypeScript checks pass, the hosted build passes, and extension 0.4.1 packaging and response-parsing checks pass. The installed Chrome extension's attach and mutation flow was not re-tested in this final live pass. No live Cargo mutation or publishing tool was called during validation or filming. 

 Challenges and lessons 

 Browser-session isolation was the central challenge: a hosted page cannot safely reuse an unrelated tab's login. The viable design is explicit sharing through a permitted Chrome extension or a browser-capable host, not a hidden second browser profile. Freshness also matters: an old screenshot must not be presented as live editor truth. 

 The lesson is that useful agent collaboration needs a trustworthy reference and a clear scope, not just many tools. CargoPilot is a local-assisted prototype, not a cloud-only mobile service or an autonomous general-purpose Cargo editor. 

 What's next 

 Package the local bridge as a signed installer, improve guided reconnection, and expand supported editing recipes only when each has deterministic verification. A first-party continuous host attachment API could reduce repeated captures without weakening consent.

title: Sealed Case
pitch: A one-player murder mystery where an AI agent runs the table through WebMCP - and never learns who did it.
about_excerpt: A one-player murder mystery where an AI agent runs the table through WebMCP - and never learns who did it. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We publish murder mystery scenarios — nine of them, sold on BOOTH, itch.io, The Game Crafter and Etsy. The single biggest thing standing between a customer and a game they have already paid for is not price or quality. It is that they need to find three to seven people who are free on the same evening, plus one more person willing to run the table and never get to play. The obvious fix is to have an LLM be the game master. We tried it. It does not work, and it fails for a reason that is structural rather than a matter of prompting: If you put the scenario in the model's context, the model knows who did it — and it then plays every suspect, judges every deduction, and narrates the whole evening while knowing. You watch a suspect's denial come out a shade too soft. You watch it steer. You watch a character answer something the character had no way of knowing. You cannot instruct your way out of it, because the information is in there. WebMCP was the first thing we had seen that could actually fix this, so we built the game we had been unable to build. What it does Sealed Case is a complete, playable one-player mystery. A man is dead in a bolted room above a second-hand bookshop in Jimbocho at 02:40. Three people are still in the building. The police arrive at 06:00. An agent connected to the page can read the case file, search the room, question the suspects, keep track of what has been found, reason out loud with you, and put an accusation on the table. What it cannot do — at any point, by any route — is learn the answer, or make the accusation. The idea: invert where the knowledge lives WebMCP lets the page hold the case and the agent hold the conversation, meeting at a boundary the page controls. In engine.js , the solution is captured in a module closure. It is never assigned to window , never written into the DOM, and never included in a value returned to a caller. Every tool reaches the game only through the object createEngine() returns, and that object has no path to the answer. So the agent can call every tool, in every order, as many times as it likes, and remain in exactly the position the player is in: holding evidence, and guessing. This is not a prompt instruction a model may or may not respect. It is an absence. The information is not in the agent's context, so there is nothing to leak, soften or let slip. We did not want to just assert that, so three tests walk every tool-reachable path, collect the combined output of every call, and assert the solution does not appear in it. npm test runs them — 30 tests, no dependencies. Measured against the real API in Chrome 151: 30 tool calls, 13,857 characters returned to the agent, and not one occurrence of the culprit, the method or the motive. The tool that does not exist propose_accusation puts a name, a method and a motive on the table and raises a confirmation card in the page. It resolves nothing. There is no confirm_accusation tool, in any phase, and a test sweeps every phase to prove it. Confirming is a click, by the person sitting there. This is the Chrome guidance on sensitive actions taken literally, but it is also the design of the game: a mystery you did not solve yourself is not entertainment. The agent is a very good game master. The accusation has to be yours. Tools change with the phase Each phase gets its own AbortController . When the phase moves, the previous controller is aborted and the next set is registered, so the agent's vocabulary is the game's turn structure rather than prose in a prompt that it has to be trusted to follow. Phase Tools always read_case_file · list_suspects · get_progress briefing begin_investigation investigation search_room · examine · interview · review_notebook · get_accusation_options · propose_accusation · withdraw_accusation verdict read_epilogue · reopen_case · restart_case never confirm_accusation read_epilogue exists in the verdict phase but refuses unless the player confirmed a correct accusation. The gate is the page's, not the caller's word for it. Two more details that matter at the table: interview returns lines the page wrote. The tool description tells the agent to quote, not invent. Some of those lines are lies — the page knows which; the agent does not. Questions are finite. Eight, across all three suspects. An agent cannot brute-force the testimony space, which is what makes choosing the questions the actual game. How we built it Four ES modules and a stylesheet. No framework, no build step, no dependencies, hosted on GitHub Pages. case/lantern-room.js — the scenario; the only place solution exists engine.js — game state, holding the solution in a closure webmcp.js — the WebMCP surface: per-phase registerTool with AbortController , no confirmation tool ui.js — the human interface; the only path to confirmAccusation() test/ — 30 tests, including the containment proofs and a headless playthrough of the whole UI Every tool has a button, so the page is fully playable with no agent at all and WebMCP is a true progressive enhancement. An agent joining mid-game inherits exactly the state the player built, because both drive the same engine. Challenges we ran into Proving a negative. "The agent cannot learn the answer" is easy to claim and worthless unless it is checked. We ended up writing a harvester that calls every tool with every argument in every phase, concatenates the results, and greps for the solution — including for the two words that appear only in the epilogue. That test is the one we would want a judge to read. Making the containment a feature rather than a limitation. The first version simply refused things, which is annoying rather than interesting. The fix was to show the boundary: the right-hand rail lists the tools the agent can call right now, logs each call as it happens, and displays confirm_accusation struck through, permanently. The restriction becomes the most legible thing on the screen. Writing a mystery that is fair to a player and opaque to an agent at the same time. Every fact the ending turns on has to be reachable from a tool result, or the game is a cheat — but no tool result may assemble them. There is a test for that too, asserting that the three load-bearing clues are each visible. Two rough edges in the current implementation. executeTool intermittently rejects with a transient UnknownError, and speechSynthesis stops after about fifteen seconds firing neither end nor error . The walkthrough retries once and then drives the engine directly, and splits narration on sentence boundaries with a keep-alive and a word-count ceiling. Accomplishments that we're proud of A game master that is structurally incapable of spoiling the game, demonstrated rather than promised — and a product that is finished rather than a proof of concept: a complete scenario, a real ending, a wrong-answer path with a hint, and a page that stands on its own without an agent. What we learned WebMCP is usually described as a way to give an agent more access to a page. The interesting property turned out to be the opposite one. Because the page decides what a tool returns, WebMCP is the first web API that lets a site collaborate with an agent while keeping something from it — and keeping it in a way that does not depend on the model's cooperation. That generalises well past games: a tutoring site that will not hand over the answer key, an interview tool that will not reveal the rubric, an escape room, a clinical vignette. Any product where the agent should be a capable participant rather than an oracle. What's next for Sealed Case Multiple cases behind one shell, and — for our actual catalogue — a mode where the agent runs a scenario for a table of real people, holding the parts of the script that belong to each player and to no one else. That is the same containment property, one step out: today the page keeps a secret from the agent; next it keeps a different secret for each person at the table. Newly built for this hackathon All of it. Every file in the repository was written during the submission period; the commit history is the record. Nothing existed beforehand. The scenario is original and written for this project — our commercial scenarios are not included and their solutions do not appear anywhere in the repository, since publishing them would destroy the thing we sell. Every person, publisher and establishment in the scenario is fictional. title: OpenAct
pitch: A confirmation-first WebMCP agent for screen reader users. The screen reader stays the interface; WebMCP is the actuator.
about_excerpt: A confirmation-first WebMCP agent for screen reader users. The screen reader stays the interface; WebMCP is the actuator. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP can expose higher-level page actions, but putting agent-oriented tools into the accessibility tree would make them appear as page content to screen readers. OpenAct explores the indirect model instead: an agent can reason about available actions while the screen reader remains the user's interface. What it does An NVDA user describes an action in natural language. OpenAct discovers native WebMCP tools, or conservatively infers tools when native tools are unavailable. It proposes exactly one call, presents an accessible and editable confirmation dialog, executes only after explicit confirmation, and speaks the result. The demo is a fictional Northstar City permit workflow with two equivalent routes: /baseline : a keyboard and screen-reader-operable form without WebMCP. /instrumented : the same form with four native tools registered through document.modelContext . The tools are save_property_details , save_project_details , review_application , and submit_application . Why WebMCP OpenAct uses WebMCP as an action layer rather than another interface a screen reader must navigate. Native tools give an agent structured actions and schemas while the user keeps the familiar NVDA interaction model. This makes higher-level assistance possible without placing agent-only content or metadata in the accessibility tree. How it works One shared action definition generates both the accessible HTML form and each WebMCP tool. A parity test fails the build if their labels, required fields, enums, or schemas drift. The Chrome MV3 extension discovers page tools and enforces authorization. The NVDA add-on owns the reasoning layer, confirmation dialog, settings, speech, and a standard-library localhost relay. The relay binds to 127.0.0.1 and pairs through a one-time code. At runtime, the NVDA add-on uses the OpenAI Responses API with a configurable model that defaults to gpt-5.4-mini . It sends bounded context with store: false and requires a strict call , clarify , or refuse decision. The model can propose an action, but it cannot authorize or execute one. Safety and accessibility Every call requires confirmation. Unknown reversibility is treated as irreversible. HMAC covers the call ID, tool name, timestamp, and canonical arguments. Expired, replayed, invalid, or retargeted confirmations are rejected. A kill switch blocks new requests and clears queued work. The autobridge fails closed on ambiguous, stale, unnamed, or unsupported controls. Telemetry is metadata-only and excludes utterances, arguments, form values, API keys, and unrestricted URLs. No agent-oriented text or metadata is added to the accessibility tree. The visible form remains fully usable without OpenAct. Verification The repository includes unit, property, cross-language, browser, accessibility, native Chrome, coverage, and mutation checks. Native verification drives all four tools in installed Chrome 151 with WebMCP enabled and no injected modelContext . Axe reports zero automated violations on the tested routes and states. Honest limits WebMCP does not make an inaccessible website accessible. It exposes actions, not missing labels, keyboard support, structure, or comprehension. This prototype has not been validated with disabled participants and makes no measured task-completion claim. Northstar City and all demo data are fictional. The native page round trip is verified in Chrome. ChatGPT's in-app browser and the complete packed extension, relay, and installed NVDA path remain pending manual verification. title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP
video_title: Zingposts — Human + Agent Commerce on One WebMCP Canvas
video_transcript_excerpt: What if a marketplace did not contain its own AI? What if it simply gave people and any outside agent a beautiful shared place to work? This is Zing Posts, peer-to-peer commerce designed for Web MCP. The first visit is deliberately small. While signed out, the browser exposes only five setup tools. An agent can inspect the bootstrap guide, prepare a handoff for the person, or accept a one-use credential. After sign-in, it re-discovers the real workspace. Now, human and agent share the same durable canvas. The person can browse visually, flip through finds, drag items onto colored boards, and set preferences. The agent can search the same listings, compare candidates, rank a board, tag discoveries, and leave its reasoning beside the work. Web MCP is not hidden behind one giant prompt. Zing Posts keeps a persistent core, then activates the focus capability for the page. Here, the marketplace pack includes search, view control, comparison, board organization, and the option to open exactly the item a person should review. On a listing, the collaboration gets deeper. An outside agent can build a cited research notebook, record comparable sales, calculate a price range, and draft an offer plan with repair, transport, tax, contingency, and budget assumptions. The evidence stays visible. The private target stays private. The workbench is the shared memory: agent findings, human notes, decisions, undo history, alerts, conversations, offers, and even multi-party trade rooms persist as structured marketplace state. The agent does not own the experience. It helps move evidence toward a decision, while the person stays in control. That control becomes explicit at the verification boundary. Browsing, organizing, research, and drafting stay fluid. Publishing a listing, enabling an alert, contacting a seller, sending an offer, or advancing a trade creates a pending approval. Only the human can cross that line, and every outcome is recorded. The result is a web MCP native marketplace with no built-in model and no agent lock-in. Five tools for setup, 34 focused tools on this marketplace canvas, and 121 across the complete signed-in catalog. zingpost.com Bring your agent and find something worth saving.

title: MUTUA
pitch: MUTUA is a WebMCP-native decision workspace where humans and AI agents share the same application state, explore changes together, simulate consequences, and commit only after explicit human approval.
about_excerpt: MUTUA is a WebMCP-native decision workspace where humans and AI agents share the same application state, explore changes together, simulate consequences, and commit only after explicit human approval. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agents are getting good at acting on the web, but almost every agentic product still asks you to pick one of two shapes. An agent that advises : it talks about your work from a chat panel, and you translate its advice into the application by hand. An agent that operates : it acts through tools or APIs, and you find out afterwards what changed. Both give something up. The first leaves the agent outside the work. The second takes the human out of the loop at exactly the moment the stakes are highest. We wanted to know what a third shape looks like: what if the application itself were the shared surface, where a human and an agent reason about the same problem, and the human keeps authority over what becomes real? That question is what made WebMCP interesting to us. Not as a way to make an existing app agent-compatible, but as a way to let a page say these are the actions that make sense right now — and to have that answer change as the human works. What it does MUTUA demonstrates the model through one focused scenario: software launch recovery . A team is four weeks from a September 30 launch. Five engineers, a $420,000 budget, a stated tolerance of 15 % workload overload. Everything is on track. Then one QA engineer becomes unavailable. You mark it in the interface. The workspace recomputes: peak load 134 %, overload 34 %, launch slipping two working days. You ask the agent to keep the September launch without increasing burnout . It reads the same state you are looking at, and creates Proposal A — on time, +$12,000 , overload down to 4 % , but the Analytics dashboard deferred out of launch scope. Your plan has not changed. This is a proposal, sitting beside reality, with every operation spelled out in a readable diff. Analytics is a commitment you made, so you lock it. Proposal A immediately shows a conflict — it is never rewritten behind your back, just re-measured against your new constraint and frozen for comparison. You ask for another option. Proposal B — on time, +$4,000 , 9 % overload, no scope loss , every lock respected. It gets there differently: instead of dropping a feature, it defers work that was never a launch commitment, splits QA effort across whoever has the skill and the room, and books the smallest useful block of contractor capacity. You compare them side by side, on numbers the application computed. Then the moment the whole project is built around. Look at the Agent Capabilities panel: commit_proposal is not there. The agent does not have the capability to make this real. You click Approve Proposal B , and it appears. You say use B . The agent commits. The plan becomes September 30, 9 % overload, $424,000, full scope — and every step, human and agent, is in the timeline with its author. The four primitives Shared state. One store backs the interface and every WebMCP tool. There is no agent-side copy of reality that can drift out of date. Proposal state. Agent changes are explicit reversible operations applied to a cloned plan. Exactly one tool can touch canonical state, and it is gated. Human locks. A locked item cannot be rescoped, delayed, reassigned or resized. The lock is enforced when an operation is attempted and re-evaluated against proposals that already exist. Dynamic capability surface. The set of registered WebMCP tools is a function of workflow phase. Comparison does not exist before simulation. Commit does not exist before approval. How we used WebMCP Twelve semantic capabilities, grouped by what they are for: Observe — get_workspace_state , get_active_scenario , inspect_constraint , list_conflicts Propose — create_proposal , modify_proposal , add_constraint , lock_entity Evaluate — simulate_proposal , compare_scenarios Finalize — discard_proposal , commit_proposal They are never all registered at once. A capability map turns the current phase into a tool set, and the registry synchronises against the WebMCP host on every material state change — registering what became meaningful, unregistering what did not. The Capability Inspector in the interface renders the live registry , not the map, so what a judge reads is exactly what an agent can call. There is deliberately no tool for approval . That transition belongs to the interface, and to the person using it. How we built it Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS. No backend, no database, no ML, no external API on the golden path. Every material mutation — from a click or from a tool — follows the same path: validate, apply, bump the state version, re-score every scenario, recompute the phase, refresh the WebMCP registry, append an audit event, persist. The consequence engines are pure functions. The agent chooses operations ; the application computes consequences : deadline slip, per-person load, recovery spend, scope loss, constraint results. No model calculates anything, which is why the demo replays identically and the tests can assert exact figures. The recovery planner is deterministic and is not a lookup table. It implements two policies with genuinely different trade-offs — one that will spend more and sacrifice scope to keep tasks whole, one that preserves scope by fragmenting work and buying the minimum outside capacity. Which policy applies is read from the state of the workspace: once every non-critical launch commitment is locked, the first has nothing left to give. The lock does not filter operations; it changes which recovery is possible at all. Challenges we ran into Designing for collaboration instead of automation. The easy build is a bag of tools that edit application state directly. We rejected it, and then had to design an actual lifecycle — propose, review, simulate, constrain, adapt, approve, commit — where each transition is legible. Making a lock mean something. It is trivial to reject an operation that targets a locked entity. It is harder to decide what happens to a proposal that was already valid when the lock arrives. Rewriting it silently would have destroyed the story we were telling, so proposals are re-scored after every change and surface as conflicts instead. Calibrating the dataset. The demo numbers had to fall out of the engine, not be typed into a component. Getting a dataset where the baseline is healthy, one absence produces 34 % overload, and the two policies land on 4 % / +$12k and 9 % / +$4k took real iteration — and it is guarded by tests that assert the exact values. Making capability changes visible. Dynamic registration is invisible by nature. The Capability Inspector exists so that the contract between the application and the agent is something you can watch change. Accomplishments we're proud of MUTUA reaches what we think of as the third level of WebMCP use. Level one, the agent can understand the application — it reads structured state. Level two, the agent can participate — it creates and modifies visible, reversible proposals. Level three, the application governs the agent — its current state determines which capabilities exist at all. The third level is the submission. And it is not decorative: commit_proposal is unregistered before approval and independently re-validates approval, simulation freshness, state version and hard constraints in its handler. A test calls it directly, bypassing the registry, and asserts the refusal. What we learned Agent capabilities can be part of the user experience. We stopped asking which tools should this agent have and started asking which actions make sense in this exact application state . That turns tool design from an API problem into an interaction design problem — and WebMCP is what makes the question answerable, because the page's own state is right there to answer it with. What's next for MUTUA Extract the shared-state and capability lifecycle into reusable primitives, and prove them in a second domain — incident response is the obvious one, because it has the same shape: observe, investigate, propose mitigation, human authorisation, execution capability unlocked. The same model fits procurement, staffing, infrastructure operations, financial planning and compliance. We deliberately did not build any of them. One workflow implemented deeply demonstrates WebMCP better than five implemented shallowly.
